and "the Muslim" in the language is the one who abases himself to the command of God and complies with Him. **[Saʿdī]** As for the Jews, the Christians and the idolaters, Abraham is quit of them and of their allegiance, because his religion is the tolerant *ḥanīfiyyah*, in which is belief in all the messengers and all the books — and this is the distinguishing mark of the Muslims. **[Maʿārif]** The way of Abraham, which is referred to at the end of the previous verse as known to God alone, has been described in verse 67. **[Study Quran]** Related to this verse is 2:135, "And they say, 'Be Jews or Christians and you shall be rightly guided.' Say: 'Rather, ours is the creed of Abraham, the ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters.'"

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** *Ḥanīf* is one who follows God's command, upright upon the clear road of guidance; and "submitter" is one humble in heart and limb, compliant with what God has ordained. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ḥanīf* is the one who declares God one, performs the ḥajj, sacrifices, circumcises and faces the qiblah; and *al-muslim* in the language is the one who abases himself to the command of God. **[Jalālayn]** *Ḥanīf* is one who inclined away from every other religion towards the upright one. **[Ibn Kathīr]** *Ḥanīf* here is paired with *muslim* and glossed as shunning *shirk* and living in faith.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7211 — al-Shaʿbī said: the Jews said, "Abraham is upon our religion", and the Christians said, "He is upon our religion" — so God sent down "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian", the verse; and God belied them and refuted their argument — meaning the Jews who claimed that Abraham died a Jew. **[Ṭabarī]** 7212 — al-Rabīʿ said the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7213 — from Mūsā b. ʿUqbah, from Sālim b. ʿAbdullāh, from his father: Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl went out to Syria, asking about the religion and following it, and he met a learned man of the Jews and asked him about his religion, saying: "Perhaps I shall profess your religion, so tell me about it." **[Ṭabarī]** The Jew said to him: "You will not be upon our religion until you take your share of the wrath of God." **[Ṭabarī]** Zayd said: "I flee only from the wrath of God, and I will never bear anything of the wrath of God while I am able. Can you direct me to a religion in which there is none of this?" **[Ṭabarī]** He said: "I know of none except that it be *ḥanīf*." He said: "And what is the *ḥanīf*?" He said: "The religion of Abraham — he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he worshipped none but God." **[Ṭabarī]** Then Zayd went out from him and met a learned man of the Christians, and asked him about his religion. *(the report continues with the Christian's answer)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse does three things at once: it belies the claimants, declares Abraham quit of them, and assigns his religion to the community of Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Ibn Kathīr]** He was a *ḥanīf*, shunning idolatry, and a *muslim*, and explicitly not of the idolaters. **[Saʿdī]** The mark of Abraham's religion is belief in all the messengers and all the books, and that is the distinguishing characteristic of the Muslims. **[Qurṭubī]** *Ḥanīfiyyah* is a creed with visible practices attached — unity, pilgrimage, sacrifice, circumcision and facing the qiblah.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:135 for the parallel; 2:140, which adds Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes among those who were neither Jews nor Christians; 2:111–13 and 5:18 for the related claims of special status; 2:135c for the concept of *ḥanīf*; 3:19c for "submitter". **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:135, "And they say, 'Be Jews or Christians and you shall be rightly guided'". **[Qurṭubī]** His treatment of *islām* in Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:104–108 for his discussion of the meaning of *ḥanīf*.

**Reflection.** Al-Ṭabarī's opening sentence is unusually dense and worth unpacking: the verse belies a claim, declares Abraham quit of the claimants, and *awards* his religion to someone **[Ṭabarī]**. It is that third function that turns a piece of chronology into a verdict, and the next verse will name the winners **[Ṭabarī]**. The two words used for Abraham are both defined by the commentators in the same direction — *ḥanīf* as upright on a road rather than merely negative, and *muslim* as humility of heart and limb before what God has ordained **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Qurṭubī's definition of *ḥanīf* is the one that surprises: a creed with practice attached — unity, pilgrimage, sacrifice, circumcision, qiblah **[Qurṭubī]**. And the report Ṭabarī places here is the loveliest thing in the passage: Zayd b. ʿAmr asking a Jewish scholar for a religion, being told it comes with a share of God's wrath, and answering that he flees *from* the wrath of God — then being told the only alternative is *ḥanīf*, which is "the religion of Abraham: he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he worshipped none but God" **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:68 — إِنَّ أَوْلَى ٱلنَّاسِ بِإِبْرَٰهِيمَ لَلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ وَهَٰذَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ وَلِىُّ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ

*"Indeed, the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him, and this prophet, and those who believe. And God is the Protector of the believers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by "the people most entitled to Abraham": the people most deserving of Abraham, and of his support and his allegiance. **[Ṭabarī]** "Are those who followed him" — those who travelled his road and his way, declaring God to be one, sincere to Him in the religion, establishing his *sunnah* and legislating his laws, and being *ḥanīfs* submitting to God, not associating anything with Him. **[Ṭabarī]** "And this prophet" — meaning Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Ṭabarī]** "And those who believe" — those who believed Muḥammad and what he brought them from God. **[Ṭabarī]** "And God is the Protector of the believers" — God is the helper of those who believe in Muḥammad, affirming him in his prophethood and in what he brought them from Him, against those who oppose them among the people of the religions. **[Jalālayn]** "Surely the people with the best claim" — most worthy — "of Abraham are those who followed him during his time, and this Prophet", Muḥammad ﷺ, "on account of his according with him as regards most of the rulings of his law, and those who believe" from among his community; "they are the ones that ought to say 'We follow his religion', and not you; and God is the Protector of the believers", their Helper and Preserver. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This verse means: "The people who have the most right to be followers of Ibrāhīm are those who followed his religion, and this Prophet, Muḥammad ﷺ, and his Companions from the Muhājirīn, the Anṣār and those who followed their lead." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And Allāh is the *Walī* (Protector and Helper) of the believers" — Allāh is the Protector of all those who believe in His Messengers. **[Qurṭubī]** *Awlā* means "more entitled"; it is said: to help and support; and it is said: to the proof. **[Qurṭubī]** "Those who followed him" — upon his religion and his *sunnah*. **[Saʿdī]** God informed that the people most entitled to Abraham are Muḥammad ﷺ and his followers, and the followers of the Friend before Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Saʿdī]** "And God is the Protector of the believers": the stronger the servant's faith, the more God takes charge of him with His kindness, and eases him to the easier way and keeps him from the harder. **[Maʿārif]** Verse 68 declares that the closest of people to Abraham were those who followed him during his time, and now the closest to him is the Prophet of Islam, Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, and so are the believers in him and in the past prophets. **[Maʿārif]** These believers are the community of Muḥammad ﷺ, and their guardian is God, and He will reward them for their belief. **[Study Quran]** "Worthiest of Abraham" means having the most claim on him, the most right to be associated with him. **[Study Quran]** "Worthiest" translates *awlā*, a term related to *walī*, "protector" or "friend", which appears later in this verse in the description of God as the Protector of the believers; in this sense, to say that they are *awlā* means they have the strongest bond of *walāyah* — inheritance, protection, friendship, alliance — with Abraham.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** "And this prophet" — He singled out his mention to magnify him, just as He said, "In both of them are fruits, and date-palms and pomegranates" (55:68). **[Qurṭubī]** *Hādhā* is in the nominative, conjoined to *alladhīna*; *al-nabiyyu* is an adjective of *hādhā* or an explicative apposition; and were it put in the accusative, that too would be admissible in speech, conjoined to the *hāʾ* in *ittabaʿūhu*. **[Study Quran]** *Awlā* is related to *walī*, so the claim to Abraham and the protection of the believers are expressed through the same root. **[Ṭabarī]** "Followed him" is glossed as travelling his road, singling out God, establishing his *sunnah* and legislating his laws.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7214 — Qatādah, on "the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him": those who followed him upon his religion, his *sunnah*, his way and his natural constitution; "and this prophet" — the prophet of God, Muḥammad; "and those who believed" with him, meaning the believers who believed the prophet of God and followed him; the Messenger of God ﷺ and those with him among the believers were the people most entitled to Abraham. **[Ṭabarī]** 7215 — al-Rabīʿ said the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7216 — from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā, from Masrūq, from ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every prophet has protectors (*wulāh*) from among the prophets, and my protector among them is my father, the Friend (*khalīl*) of my Lord" — then he recited "the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him, and this prophet, and those who believe; and God is the Protector of the believers". *(the editor of the printed Tabarī grades this isnād ṣaḥīḥ muttaṣil)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Saʿīd b. Manṣūr recorded that Ibn Masʿūd said that the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ said: "Every Prophet had a *Walī* from among the Prophets. My *Walī* among them is my father Ibrāhīm, the *Khalīl* of my Lord, the Exalted and Most Honoured" — and the Prophet ﷺ then recited this verse. **[Study Quran]** A ḥadīth of the Prophet states: "Every prophet has protection (*walāyah*) from among the prophets, and my protector among them is my father, the Friend of God (*Khalīl Allāh*), Abraham"; the *walāyah* mentioned in this ḥadīth can also evoke the sense of succession and inheritance in the spiritual sense. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: the chiefs of the Jews said, "By God, O Muḥammad, you know well that we have more right than you and anyone else to the religion of Abraham, for he was a Jew, and you are motivated by nothing but envy" — so God sent down this verse. **[Qurṭubī]** And from Ibn Masʿūd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every prophet has protectors from among the prophets, and my protector among them is my father and the Friend of my Lord" — then he recited "the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him, and this prophet".

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** Entitlement to Abraham is measured by following his road — singling out God, sincerity, his *sunnah* and his laws — not by descent or by claim. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Those with the most right to be his followers are those who followed his religion, and this prophet, and his Companions and those who followed their lead. **[Saʿdī]** God's taking charge of a believer increases with his faith, easing him to the easier way. **[Qurṭubī]** *Awlā* has been taken both as "more entitled to his help and support" and as "more entitled by the proof".

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:67 for the dissociation that precedes. **[Qurṭubī]** 55:68 for the device of singling out one item to magnify it; 2:139 for his treatment of the same idea in Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Ṭabarī]** 1:489, 564 and 5:424 for his treatment of *walī*; 3:65–67 for the dispute that leads here. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:69, which follows.

**Reflection.** Having cleared Abraham of both claimants in 3:67, the sūrah now says who gets him — and the answer is not a lineage but a description: the people who walked his road **[Ṭabarī]**. The Prophet is named separately from "those who believe", and Qurṭubī explains why: singling him out after a general group is a device of magnification, the way dates and pomegranates are named after "fruits" **[Qurṭubī]**. There is a deliberate word-play in the verse that the Study Quran draws out — *awlā*, "most entitled", sharing a root with *walī*, "protector", so that the claim to Abraham and God's protection of the believers are bound into one another **[Study Quran]**. And the ḥadīth placed here closes the circle: every prophet has a protector among the prophets, and this one's is Abraham — his father and the Friend of God — after which he recited the verse itself **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The occasion report Qurṭubī records gives the verse its edge: the Jewish chiefs had accused the Prophet of envy, and the answer is that entitlement is a matter of following, not of blood **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:69 — وَدَّت طَّآئِفَةٌۭ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَوْ يُضِلُّونَكُمْ وَمَا يُضِلُّونَ إِلَّآ أَنفُسَهُمْ وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ

*"A party of the People of the Scripture wish they could lead you astray; but they lead none astray except themselves, and they do not perceive it."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by "wished": hoped for and desired. **[Ṭabarī]** "A party" — a group. **[Ṭabarī]** "Of the People of the Scripture" — the people of the Torah among the Jews and the people of the Gospel among the Christians. **[Ṭabarī]** "They could lead you astray" — they say: would that they could turn you, O believers, away from Islām and bring you back from it to the unbelief they are upon, destroying you by that. **[Ṭabarī]** And "leading astray" (*iḍlāl*) in this place means destruction, as in the saying of God, "And they say: when we are lost (*ḍalalnā*) in the earth, shall we then be in a new creation?" (32:10) — meaning, when we perish; and as in the saying of al-Akhṭal satirising Jarīr: "You were the speck in a dark, foaming wave — the torrent cast it and it perished (*ḍalla*) utterly", meaning it perished completely. *(digression: al-Ṭabarī goes on to discuss a variant reading of al-Nābighah's line and rejects al-Aṣmaʿī's explanation of it)* **[Jalālayn]** When the Jews called Muʿādh b. Jabal, Ḥudhayfah b. al-Yamān and ʿAmmār b. Yāsir to join their religion, the following was revealed: "There is a party of the People of the Scripture who yearn to make you go astray; yet they cause none to stray except themselves, because the sin for their leading others astray falls upon them, while the believers do not heed them in this; but they are not aware of this." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh states that the Jews envy the faithful and wish they could misguide them; and Allāh states that the punishment of this behaviour will fall back upon them, while they are unaware. **[Qurṭubī]** It was revealed concerning Muʿādh b. Jabal, Ḥudhayfah b. al-Yamān and ʿAmmār b. Yāsir, when the Jews of Banū al-Naḍīr, Qurayẓah and Qaynuqāʿ called them to their religion. **[Qurṭubī]** On this reading, *min* is partitive; and it is said: all the People of the Scripture, in which case *min* specifies the genus. **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning of "they could lead you astray" is: they make you acquire sin by turning back from the religion of Islām and opposing it. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Jurayj said: "they lead you astray" means they destroy you, and from it is the saying of al-Akhṭal: "You were the speck in a dark, foaming wave — the torrent cast it and it perished utterly", meaning it perished completely. **[Qurṭubī]** "And they do not perceive" — they are not aware that they will not reach the believers to mislead them; and it is said: "they do not perceive" means they do not know the soundness of Islām, while it is obligatory upon them to know, because the proofs are manifest and the arguments are dazzling. **[Saʿdī]** This is among God's favour upon this community, that He informed them of the plotting of their enemies among the People of the Scripture, and that out of their eagerness to mislead the believers they vary their evil plots. **[Maʿārif]** Verse 69 exposes the cherished desire of the People of the Book to mislead Muslims away from the true faith they are on; the text then firmly declares that the victim of their effort to misguide is no one other than themselves, something they do not realise. **[Study Quran]** Some People of the Book go astray themselves insofar as they reject the truth that exists before them in the person of the Prophet Muhammad and the revelation of the Qurʾān; or they go astray because they wish to turn you back into disbelievers after your having believed, out of envy in their souls.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** *Waddat* is glossed as hoping and desiring; *ṭāʾifah* as a group; and *iḍlāl* in this place as destruction, supported by 32:10 and by a line of al-Akhṭal. **[Qurṭubī]** The *min* of "a party of the People of the Scripture" is either partitive or specifies the genus, depending on whether the whole or a part is meant. **[Qurṭubī]** "And they lead none astray except themselves" is a negation followed by an affirmation. **[Jalālayn]** "They cause none to stray except themselves" — because the sin for their leading others astray falls upon them, while the believers do not heed them in it.

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse was revealed concerning three named Companions whom the Jewish tribes of Madinah invited to their religion. **[Jalālayn]** The same occasion: the Jews called Muʿādh b. Jabal, Ḥudhayfah b. al-Yamān and ʿAmmār b. Yāsir to join their religion. **[Saʿdī]** The plotting described here is varied and persistent, and God's informing the believers of it is counted as a favour to the community. **[Ibn Kathīr]** What is described is envy of the faithful and the wish to misguide them.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The harm they intend is destruction, and it rebounds on the plotters. **[Jalālayn]** The sin of the attempt falls on those who make it, since the believers do not heed them. **[Qurṭubī]** Their unawareness is twofold in the reports: unaware that their plotting will not reach the believers, or unaware of the soundness of Islām, which it was incumbent on them to know because the proofs are manifest. **[Saʿdī]** The plotters did not know that the religion of God is the truth: when its reality reaches hearts, its possessor only increases in faith and certainty the longer time goes on, and doubts only increase him in holding fast to his religion and in praise and thanks to God for His favour upon him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 2:109, "Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy", as the counterpart verse; 3:72 for the specific plot described later. **[Study Quran]** 2:9, "They would deceive God and the believers, yet they deceive none but themselves, though they are unaware"; 2:57, "They wronged Us not, but themselves did they wrong"; 3:118, "They wish you to suffer"; 4:89; 60:2; 68:9. **[Ṭabarī]** 32:10 for *ḍalalnā* in the sense of perishing; 2:495–496 for his earlier treatment of the root. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:70, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is built on a rebound: the harm intended lands on the one who intended it **[Jalālayn]**, **[Maʿārif]**. Al-Ṭabarī takes the verb in its strongest sense — *iḍlāl* here is destruction, not merely confusion — and supports it from the Qurʾān itself and from a line of satire poetry **[Ṭabarī]**. The occasion reports make it concrete: three named Companions, invited by three named Jewish tribes to leave Islām **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Jalālayn]**. Qurṭubī adds a small grammatical fork with a large consequence — whether "a party of" means some of them or is simply identifying the kind, that is, whether this is a faction or the whole community of the People of the Scripture **[Qurṭubī]**. And the clause that stings most is the last: they do not perceive. Ibn Kathīr and Qurṭubī both turn that into the failure it really is — not a failure of cleverness but a failure to see what the proofs in front of them plainly show **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Saʿdī reads the whole thing from the believers' side: being told is a favour, and the plot that was meant to unsettle them only settles them further **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:70 — يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لِمَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَأَنتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ

*"O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you bear witness?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: "O People of the Scripture" — of the Jews and the Christians — "why do you disbelieve", meaning: why do you deny — "in the signs of God", meaning: in what is in the Book of God which He sent down to you upon the tongues of your prophets, of His signs and His proofs — "while you bear witness" that it is the truth from your Lord. **[Ṭabarī]** This is a rebuke from God to the people of the two scriptures for their disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ and their denial of his prophethood, while they find him in their books, together with their testifying that what is in their books is the truth and is from God. **[Jalālayn]** "O People of the Scripture! Why do you disbelieve in God's verses" — the Qurʾān, that includes all the descriptions of Muḥammad ﷺ — "when you yourselves bear witness?", when you know that it is the truth. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh criticises them: "O People of the Scripture! Why do you disbelieve in the Āyāt of Allāh, while you bear witness?" — you know for certain that Allāh's Āyāt are true and authentic. **[Ibn Kathīr]** And: "Why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth, while you know?" — by hiding what is in your Books about the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, while you know what you do. **[Qurṭubī]** "While you bear witness" — that is, to the soundness of the signs you have in your books, according to Qatādah and al-Suddī; and it is said the meaning is: while you bear witness to the like of them among the signs of the prophets, which you affirm. **[Maʿārif]** Verse 70, addressing the People of the Book, asks them why they disbelieve in the signs of God, such as the verses in the Torah and the Gospel which prove the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ — because the denial of his prophethood amounts to declaring these verses to be false, which is infidelity, although they themselves confirm these as true. **[Maʿārif]** This is an admonition on their error in belief. **[Study Quran]** These verses are usually understood to refer to the rejection of the mission of the Prophet by Jews and Christians, even though he is foretold, according to Islamic belief, in their sacred books; and some say that their being witnesses means that they bear witness to the truth of the prophets in their own tradition, who themselves manifest the same truths. **[Saʿdī]** They reject while knowing, and God has informed this community of the plotting of its enemies among the People of the Scripture, and that in their eagerness to mislead the believers they vary their evil plots.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Signs of God" is glossed as what is in the Book God sent down upon the tongues of the prophets, of His signs and proofs; and "bear witness" as testifying that it is the truth from their Lord. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The bearing of witness is explained as knowing for certain that God's signs are true and authentic. **[Jalālayn]** "God's verses" is taken as the Qurʾān, which contains all the descriptions of Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Maʿārif]** The words "you are yourselves a witness" (3:70) and "you know" (3:71) should not be taken to mean that disbelief would become permissible for them if they did not attest to the truth or had no knowledge of it — this is because *kufr* is intrinsically an abominable thing to practise and is prohibited under all conditions; however, the mention of disbelief after knowledge and attestation is to increase the impact of the reproachment. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7219 — Qatādah, on "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you bear witness": you bear witness that the description of Muḥammad, the prophet of God ﷺ, is in your book, and then you disbelieve in him and deny him and do not believe in him, while you find him written with you in the Torah and the Gospel: "the unlettered prophet who believes in God and His words". **[Ṭabarī]** 7220 — al-Rabīʿ said: you bear witness that the description of Muḥammad is in your book, then you disbelieve in him and do not believe in him, while you find him with you in the Torah and the Gospel: "the unlettered prophet". **[Ṭabarī]** 7221 — al-Suddī: "the signs of God" is Muḥammad; and as for "you bear witness" — they bear witness that it is the truth, finding it written with them. **[Ṭabarī]** 7222 — Ibn Jurayj: that the religion with God is Islām; God has no religion other than it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh's reply to their concealment was to guide the hearts of the faithful to perfect faith through the clear signs, plain proofs and unequivocal evidence that He sent down to His servant and Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ — and this occurs, O you Jews, even though you hide the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, the unlettered Prophet whom you find in your Books that you received from the earlier Prophets. **[Jalālayn]** The report that the Jews called Muʿādh b. Jabal, Ḥudhayfah b. al-Yamān and ʿAmmār b. Yāsir to their religion stands as the setting for this and the preceding verse.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The charge is not ignorance but contradiction: they testify that their books are true and then deny the one their books describe. **[Ibn Kathīr]** They know for certain that the signs are true and authentic, and the concealment is of the description of Muḥammad ﷺ found in their own Books. **[Qurṭubī]** The testimony is either to the soundness of the signs in their books or to the like of them among the signs of the prophets they already affirm. **[Maʿārif]** Denying his prophethood amounts to declaring those verses false, which is itself unbelief — and this is an admonition on an error in belief, not merely in conduct.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:99, "O People of the Book! Why do you turn those who believe from the way of God, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses?"; 3:71 and 2:42 for "confound not truth with falsehood, nor knowingly conceal the truth"; 7:157 for the foretelling of the Prophet. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:71 for what they conceal; 3:72–74 for the plots that follow. **[Qurṭubī]** 2:109 for the envy. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:69 for the preceding verse.

**Reflection.** The question is rhetorical and the sting is in its last two words — "while you bear witness" **[Ṭabarī]**. What they bear witness to is spelled out in the reports: the description of the unlettered prophet, written in the Torah and the Gospel, which they themselves attest is true, and then deny **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Al-Suddī goes so far as to say that "the signs of God" here *is* Muḥammad **[Ṭabarī]**. Maʿārif adds the careful point that mentioning knowledge and testimony is not to make unbelief conditional upon them — unbelief is abominable in any case — but to deepen the rebuke **[Maʿārif]**. And Ibn Jurayj's terse gloss closes the matter from the other side: the religion with God is Islām, and He has no religion besides it **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:71 — يَا أَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لِمَ تَلْبِسُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ وَأَنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ

*"O People of the Scripture, why do you confound the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: O people of the Torah and the Gospel — "why do you confound", meaning: why do you mix — "the truth with falsehood". **[Ṭabarī]** Their mixing of the truth with falsehood was their showing with their tongues affirmation of Muḥammad ﷺ and of what he brought from God, while what was in their hearts was Judaism and Christianity. **[Ṭabarī]** "And why do you conceal the truth?" — O People of the Scripture. **[Ṭabarī]** And the "truth" which they concealed is what is in their books of the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, of his sending and of his prophethood. **[Ṭabarī]** "While you know" — while you know that what you are concealing of the truth is the truth, and that it is from God; and this saying of God is a report of the People of the Scripture's deliberately disbelieving in him and concealing what they already knew of the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, which they found in their books and which their prophets brought them. **[Jalālayn]** "O People of the Scripture! Why do you confound" — why do you mix — "truth with falsehood", by distorting and falsifying scripture, "and conceal the truth" — the descriptions of the Prophet — "while you know?" that it is the truth? **[Ibn Kathīr]** "O People of the Scripture: Why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?" — by hiding what is in your Books about the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, while you know what you do. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-labs* is mixing, as has already been set out in Sūrat al-Baqarah; and the meaning of this verse and of the one before it is that meaning. **[Qurṭubī]** "And you conceal the truth" — *taktumūna* is admissible [in the jussive] as the apodosis of the interrogation; and "while you know" is a clause in the position of the circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). **[Maʿārif]** The words "you are yourselves a witness" (3:70) and "you know" (3:71) should not be taken to mean that disbelief would become permissible for them if they did not attest to the truth or had no knowledge about it — this is because *kufr* is intrinsically an abominable thing to practise, and is prohibited under all conditions; however, the mention of disbelief after knowledge and attestation is to increase the impact of the reproachment.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Labs* is mixing; and "while you know" is a clause standing in the position of the *ḥāl*. **[Qurṭubī]** The jussive *taktumū* is admissible as the apodosis of the interrogative. **[Ṭabarī]** The "truth" is identified by the commentators in two ways — as the religion of God, Islam, and as what is in their own books; the concealment is of the description of Muḥammad ﷺ.

**Readings.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Wa-taktumūna* is also read *wa-taktumū*, in the jussive, as the apodosis of the interrogation.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7223 — from Ibn Isḥāq, through Muḥammad b. Abī Muḥammad, from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd b. Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās: ʿAbdullāh b. al-Ṣayyif, ʿAdī b. Zayd and al-Ḥārith b. ʿAwf said to one another, "Come, let us believe in what was sent down to Muḥammad and his companions in the morning and disbelieve in it in the evening, so that we may confound their religion for them — perhaps they will do as we do and turn back from their religion!" — so God sent down concerning them, "O People of the Scripture, why do you confound the truth with falsehood?" up to His saying "and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing". **[Ṭabarī]** 7224 — Qatādah: "why do you confound the truth with falsehood" — why do you mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, when you know that the religion of God, which accepts no other than it, is Islam, and He does not recompense except by it? **[Ṭabarī]** 7225 — al-Rabīʿ said the like of it, except that he said "which He does not accept from anyone other than it: Islam", and did not say "and He does not recompense except by it". **[Ṭabarī]** 7226 — Ibn Jurayj: "why do you confound the truth with falsehood" — Islam with Judaism and Christianity. **[Ṭabarī]** 7227 — Ibn Zayd: "the truth" is the Torah which God sent down to Moses, and "the falsehood" is what they wrote with their own hands. **[Ṭabarī]** 7228 — Qatādah, on "and you conceal the truth while you know": they concealed the affair of Muḥammad, while they found him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, commanding them to what is right and forbidding them what is wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** 7229 — al-Rabīʿ said the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7230 — Ibn Jurayj: "you conceal the truth" — Islam and the affair of Muḥammad ﷺ — "while you know" that Muḥammad is the messenger of God and that the religion is Islam.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The charge has two halves, and they compound each other: an outward profession that contradicts what is in the heart, and the concealment of what is certainly known to be from God. **[Ṭabarī]** What is being concealed is a description found in their own books and brought by their own prophets. **[Maʿārif]** The mention of knowledge and attestation is not a condition that, if absent, would excuse disbelief — it is there to deepen the rebuke. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The concealment is specific: the description of Muḥammad ﷺ in their Books.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 1:566–572 for the parallel verse and its reports; 1:567–568 for the meaning of *labs*. **[Qurṭubī]** Volume 1, p. 340, for his treatment of *labs* in Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:69–70 for the preceding rebukes. **[Study Quran]** 3:70, with which this verse is paired in the printed text. **[Maʿārif]** 3:70 for the parallel phrase "while you bear witness".

**Reflection.** The two halves of the charge are not the same act, and the commentators keep them apart **[Ṭabarī]**. Confounding is doing it — showing with the tongue an assent the heart does not hold; concealing is not doing it — hiding a description they know to be true **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The reports disagree about what "the truth" and "the falsehood" are, and the disagreement is instructive: Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj say truth is Islam and falsehood is Judaism and Christianity, while Ibn Zayd says truth is the Torah as revealed and falsehood is what they wrote with their own hands **[Ṭabarī]**. The second reading is the harsher one, since it makes the corruption a matter of authorship rather than of preference. And Maʿārif's warning at the end is worth keeping in view whenever this verse is quoted: naming knowledge and witness as aggravating factors does not make ignorance an excuse **[Maʿārif]**.

*Source note:* Saʿdī treats 3:69–74 as a single block; its material on the plotting of the People of the Scripture, the morning-and-evening stratagem, the envy behind it and the singling-out of this community is assigned to 3:72–3:74 by content, and there is nothing in it that bears specifically on 3:71. The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:71; its combined note for 3:70–71 is cited at 3:70.

## 3:72 — وَقَالَت طَّآئِفَةٌۭ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ ءَامِنُوا۟ بِٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَجْهَ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَٱكْفُرُوٓا۟ ءَاخِرَهُۥ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ

*"And a party of the People of the Scripture said: 'Believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that they may return.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over the description of the meaning which this party commanded those it commanded — of believing at the beginning of the day and disbelieving at its end. **[Ṭabarī]** Some of them said: it was a command from them to affirm the Prophet ﷺ in his prophethood and in what he brought from God, and that it is the truth — outwardly, without affirming it by resolve and conviction of the heart — and to disbelieve in it and deny all of that at the end of it. **[Jalālayn]** "A party of the People of the Scripture" — the Jews — "say to some among them: 'Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe', that is, the Qurʾān, 'at the beginning of the day and disbelieve in it at the end of it, so that they' — the believers — 'might then turn back' from Muḥammad's religion, and that they will then say: these Jews are knowledgeable, and they could only have turned away from it after accepting it because they know it to be false". **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is a wicked plan from the People of the Book to deceive Muslims who are weak in the religion: they decided that they would pretend to be believers at the beginning of the day by attending the dawn prayer with the Muslims; however, when the day ended they would revert to their old religion, so that the ignorant people would say, "They reverted to their old religion because they uncovered some shortcomings in the Islamic religion". **[Qurṭubī]** It was revealed concerning Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf, Mālik b. al-Ṣayf and others besides them, who said to the lowly ones of their people: "Believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning (*wajh*) of the day" — meaning its first part. **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning of the verse is that the Jews said to one another: "Show faith in Muḥammad at the beginning of the day, then disbelieve in him at its end; for if you do that, doubt in his religion will appear to whoever follows him, and they will turn back from their religion to your religion, saying, 'the People of the Scripture know better about it than we do'". **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: the meaning is "believe in his prayer at the beginning of the day towards Jerusalem, for it is the truth, and disbelieve in his prayer at the end of the day towards the Kaʿbah, that they may return to your qiblah" — from Ibn ʿAbbās and others. **[Saʿdī]** A party of them said: "Believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day" — that is, its start — "and turn back from their religion at the end of the day; for if they see you turning back, while they hold you to be people of knowledge, they will doubt their religion and say: had they not seen in it what displeased them and did not agree with the previous scriptures, they would not have turned back." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Some from among the People of the Book chose a strategy of deception in order to mislead Muslims: according to their agreed plan they would declare their belief in the Qurʾān in the morning and then reject it in the evening. **[Maʿārif]** They thought that this quick about-turn would create doubts in the minds of Muslims about the Qurʾān and Islam, and that they might turn away from their faith, thinking that there must be something wrong with Islam visible to such learned people who were open-minded enough to accept it first. **[Maʿārif]** They also made it a point to reserve their feigned declaration of belief in Islam to hoodwink Muslims only; their true belief, they planned, would be affirmed before none but those who follow their own creed — the rule being: sincerity with the latter, expediency with the former. **[Study Quran]** It is thought that this verse refers to a stratagem on the part of some Jews to pray with the Muslims at the start of the day, affirming their belief in Islam, but then at the end of the day to revert back to their own religion with the intention of creating doubt and uncertainty in the minds of the Muslims about Islam. **[Study Quran]** That is, their about-face would be a more powerful cause of doubt in the minds of the Prophet's followers, that haply they may return to their pre-Muslim ways.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Wajh al-nahār* is the first part of the day; it is called "the face" because it is the finest of it and the first part of it that one is faced with. **[Qurṭubī]** And the poet said: "And it shines in the face of the day, luminous, like a pearl of the sea whose string has been slipped" — the verse is Labīd's; and another said: "Whoever is pleased by the killing of Mālik, let him come to our women at the face of the day". **[Qurṭubī]** *Wajh* is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and likewise *ākhirahu*. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ṭāʾifah* is a group, from *ṭāfa yaṭūfu*, "he went around"; and it is sometimes used of a single person in the sense of "a soul, a party".

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7231 — Qatādah, on "believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day and disbelieve at its end": some of them said to others, "Give them acceptance of their religion at the beginning of the day and disbelieve at its end; for that is more likely to make them believe you, and to make them know that you have seen in them what you dislike — and it is more likely to make them turn back from their religion". **[Ṭabarī]** 7232 — Abū Mālik: the Jews said, "Believe with them at the beginning of the day and disbelieve at its end, that they may return with you". **[Ṭabarī]** 7233 — al-Suddī: there were twelve rabbis of the villages of ʿArabiyyah, and they said to one another: "Enter the religion of Muḥammad at the beginning of the day and say, 'We bear witness that Muḥammad is true and truthful'; then, when the end of the day comes, disbelieve and say, 'We went back to our scholars and our rabbis and asked them, and they told us that Muḥammad is a liar and that you are not upon anything; and we have returned to our religion, for it is more pleasing to us than your religion' — perhaps they will doubt and say: these were with us at the beginning of the day, so what is the matter with them?" So God informed His messenger ﷺ of that. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Abī Najīḥ said that Mujāhid commented about this verse, which refers to the Jews: "They attended the dawn prayer with the Prophet ﷺ and disbelieved at the end of the day in order to misguide the people; this way, people would think that they have uncovered shortcomings in the religion that they briefly followed." **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil said: the meaning is that they came to Muḥammad ﷺ at the beginning of the day and left him and said to the lowly ones, "He is the truth, so follow him"; then they said, "Wait until we look into the Torah" — and they came back at the end of the day and said, "We have looked into the Torah, and he is not the one" — saying that he is not the truth, and intending only to confound the lowly ones and to cast doubt in them. **[Qurṭubī]** Qatādah's view is that they did this in order to cast doubt in the Muslims.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The stratagem is aimed at the convictions of the weak rather than at the arguments of the strong. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is described as a wicked plan from the People of the Book to deceive Muslims who are weak in the religion. **[Maʿārif]** The calculation was that an apostasy by people reputed to be learned would count as evidence against Islam. **[Study Quran]** The about-face was intended to be a stronger cause of doubt than any argument could have been.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:69 for the wish that precedes; 3:71 for the confounding of truth with falsehood, which the same report of Ibn ʿAbbās names as the purpose. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:73 for the continuation of their speech. **[Study Quran]** 3:69–70 for the passage. **[Qurṭubī]** 2:109 for the envy behind it.

**Reflection.** What is described here is not an argument but a piece of theatre, and every commentator reports it with the same mixture of grudging clarity: believe audibly in the morning, recant audibly in the evening, and let the recantation do the work **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**. The mechanism is worth naming — the apostasy of a reputed scholar counts as *evidence* in a way that the unbelief of a stranger never would, and that is what the plot was buying **[Maʿārif]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. Al-Suddī's version has the whole script written out, including the line they were to deliver about consulting their rabbis **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī adds a second reading, from Ibn ʿAbbās and others, on which the belief and disbelief concern the prayer towards Jerusalem and then the Kaʿbah — a different plot with the same shape **[Qurṭubī]**. And the verse is quoted by the Qurʾān without comment, which is itself the comment: it is reported so that the believers can see the machinery **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:73 — وَلَا تُؤْمِنُوٓا۟ إِلَّا لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ ۗ قُلْ إِنَّ ٱلْهُدَىٰ هُدَى ٱللَّهِ أَن يُؤْتَىٰٓ أَحَدٌۭ مِّثْلَ مَآ أُوتِيتُمْ أَوْ يُحَآجُّوكُمْ عِندَ رَبِّكُمْ ۚ قُلْ إِنَّ ٱلْفَضْلَ بِيَدِ ٱللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشَآءُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمٌۭ

*"And do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion." Say: "Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of God — that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue against you before your Lord." Say: "Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills. And God is All-Encompassing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: and do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion and is a Jew. **[Ṭabarī]** And this is a report from God of the saying of the party who said to their brothers among the Jews, "believe in what was sent down to those who believe at the beginning of the day". **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over the interpretation of "Say: the guidance is the guidance of God — that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue against you before your Lord". **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: "Say: the guidance is the guidance of God" is a parenthetical insertion in the middle of the speech, a report from God that the clarification is His clarification and the guidance is His guidance; and the rest of the speech after it is connected to the first speech, reporting what the Jews said to one another — so the meaning is: "and do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you have been given, or that they will argue against you before your Lord". **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: its interpretation is "Say, O Muḥammad: the guidance is the guidance of God", the clarification is God's clarification; "that anyone should be given" — meaning, no one of the communities will be given the like of what you were given, as He said "God makes clear to you, lest you go astray" (4:176), meaning "lest you should go astray", and as in "Thus We have inserted it into the hearts of the criminals; they do not believe in it" (26:200–201), meaning "so that they do not believe"; "the like of what you were given" — meaning the like of what you, O Muḥammad, and your community were given of Islam and guidance; "or that they should argue against you before your Lord" — and the meaning of "or" here is "except" — that is, except that they should argue with you before your Lord when your Lord has dealt with them as He did. **[Jalālayn]** "And they also said: 'And do not believe except in one who'" — the *lām* of *li-man* is extra — "'follows' — accords with — 'your religion'". **[Jalālayn]** God says: "Say to them, O Muḥammad: 'True guidance is God's guidance', that is, Islam, everything else being error" — this statement is parenthetical — "that anyone should be given the like of what you have been given" of the Book, wisdom and the virtues; "or that they" — the believers — "should dispute with you", that they should prevail over you, "before your Lord" on the Day of Resurrection, for you have the sounder religion. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And believe no one except the one who follows your religion" — they said: do not trust anyone with your secret knowledge except those who follow your religion; therefore they say, do not expose your knowledge to the Muslims, in order to prevent them from believing in it and thus using it as proof against you. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Say: 'Verily, right guidance is the guidance of Allāh'" — Allāh guides the hearts of the faithful to the perfect faith through the clear signs, plain proofs and unequivocal evidence that He sent down to His servant and Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ; this occurs, O you Jews, even though you hide the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, the unlettered Prophet whom you find in your Books that you received from the earlier Prophets. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Say: 'All the bounty is in the Hand of Allāh; He grants it to whom He wills'" — all affairs are under His control, and He gives and takes; verily Allāh gives faith, knowledge and sound comprehension to whomever He wills, and He misguides whomever He wills by blinding his sight and mind, sealing his heart and hearing, and stamping his eyes closed; Allāh has the perfect wisdom and the unequivocal proofs. **[Qurṭubī]** This is a prohibition, and it is part of the speech of the Jews, some of them to others — that is, the chiefs said it to the lowly ones; and al-Suddī said: it is from the saying of the Jews of Khaybar to the Jews of Madinah. **[Qurṭubī]** And this verse is the most difficult verse in the sūrah. **[Qurṭubī]** "That anyone should be given the like of what you were given" — of the Torah, the manna and the quails, the dividing of the sea and other signs and merits. **[Saʿdī]** And their saying "that anyone should be given the like of what you have been given, or that they should argue against you before your Lord" means: what drove them to these reprehensible deeds was envy and transgression and the fear of being argued against — as God said, "Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy from themselves, after the truth had become clear to them". *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** That these tricks are low is proved later in this very verse, when the Holy Prophet ﷺ has been asked to declare that their clever moves are not going to work for them, since the guidance given to the servants of God is certainly from God — so it is He Who, with guidance in His control, can make whomever He will steadfast upon that guidance, and no one can succeed in weaning such a person away from it with any trick, plan or enticement whatsoever. **[Study Quran]** The subtle grammatical structure of this verse lends itself to several interpretations: as translated, the first clause is a continuation of what was said by a group of the People of the Book in the previous verse; their words are then interrupted by a command that the Prophet say to them "Truly guidance is God's Guidance", after which the words of the People of the Book resume; then the Prophet is commanded to say "Truly bounty is in God's Hand". **[Study Quran]** Alternately, the Prophet may have been given two successive commands to speak to the People of the Book, in which case it would be translated: "Say, 'Truly guidance is God's Guidance, [this guidance being] that someone be granted the like of what you were granted or dispute with you before your Lord.' Say, 'Truly bounty is in God's Hand…'" **[Study Quran]** Another reading would make the intervening clause a partial question: "Say, 'Truly guidance is God's Guidance. Is it that someone be granted the like of what you were granted or dispute with you before your Lord [that leads you to object]?'"

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The *lām* in "li-man tabiʿa dīnakum" is like the *lām* in "ʿasā an yakūna radifa lakum" (27:72), meaning *radifakum*. **[Jalālayn]** The *lām* of *li-man* is extra. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Akhfash held that the meaning is "and do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given, and do not believe that they will argue against you" — taking it as conjoined. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that *an* is in the nominative, on the view of those who put the noun in the nominative in "a-Zaydun ḍarabtahu?", with the predicate suppressed — the estimate being "that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, [and] you believe it or acknowledge it", meaning "an giving exists, believed or acknowledged" — that is, you do not believe that. **[Study Quran]** As in other instances, *al-Wāsiʿ* means also "Generous" and "Munificent".

**Readings.** **[Jalālayn]** A variant reading has *a-an*, "such that", with the extra *hamzah* denoting rebuke — in other words, the Jews say: do not believe that another has been given the like of it, such that you might affirm it.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7246 — Qatādah: "and do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion" — this is some of them saying to others. **[Ṭabarī]** 7247 — al-Rabīʿ said the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7247m — al-Suddī: "and do not believe anyone except one who follows your religion" — do not believe anyone except one who follows Judaism. **[Ṭabarī]** 7248 — Ibn Zayd: do not believe anyone except one who believes your religion; and whoever opposes it, do not believe him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7249 — Mujāhid, on "that anyone should be given the like of what you were given": out of envy on the part of the Jews that prophethood should be in other than them, and out of the desire that they be followed upon their religion. **[Ṭabarī]** 7250 — the like of it, through another chain. **[Ṭabarī]** 7251 — al-Suddī: God said to Muḥammad ﷺ: "Say: the guidance is the guidance of God — that anyone should be given the like of what you were given...", then God said to His prophet ﷺ: "Say, O Muḥammad: 'bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills', and 'the guidance is the guidance of God'". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh's reply was: "Say: 'All the bounty is in the Hand of Allāh; He grants it to whom He wills'" — and He has endowed you, O believers, with tremendous virtue, in that He honoured your Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ over all other prophets, and by directing you to the best Sharīʿah there is.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The sentence rests on who gives: guidance is God's, and bounty is in His hand to give to whom He wills — which is precisely what the Jews' advice denies. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Concealment does not work, because God guides the hearts of the faithful through the clear signs He sent down, even while the description of the Prophet is hidden. **[Saʿdī]** The motive named for the whole stratagem is envy and the fear of being out-argued before God. **[Maʿārif]** The reply declares the tricks futile in advance: the one whom God makes steadfast cannot be weaned away by any trick.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:14 for similar words spoken by the People of the Book; 2:76, "Do you speak to them of what God has unveiled to you, that they may thereby dispute with you before your Lord? Do you not understand?" **[Ṭabarī]** 4:176 and 26:200–201 for the elliptical negation; 27:72 for the extra *lām*. **[Qurṭubī]** 2:109 for the envy. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:74, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:72 for the saying resumed here.

**Reflection.** Qurṭubī calls this the most difficult verse in the sūrah, and the difficulty is visible in every line: a reported saying, interrupted by a command to the Prophet, resumed, then interrupted again **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The commentators sort it into a small number of readings — the interruption as a parenthetical, or two separate commands to the Prophet, or a rebuke-shaped question — and al-Ṭabarī sets out two of them at length **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. Underneath all of them the substance is the same: the advice was to keep their knowledge to themselves so that no one else could be given what they had been given, or use it against them **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Mujāhid's gloss names the feeling behind it in one word — envy that prophethood should be in other than them **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**. And the reply that God dictates is a statement about ownership rather than about argument: guidance is His, and bounty is in His hand **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**, which is why the stratagem is not merely wrong but beside the point **[Maʿārif]**.

## 3:74 — يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِۦ مَن يَشَآءُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ ذُو ٱلْفَضْلِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ

*"He singles out for His mercy whom He wills; and God is the possessor of great bounty."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills": *yakhtaṣṣu* is of the pattern *iftaʿala*, from one's saying "I singled out so-and-so for such-and-such" (*khaṣaṣtu fulānan bi-kadhā akhuṣṣuhu bihi*). **[Ṭabarī]** And as for "His mercy" in this place, it is Islam and the Qurʾān, together with prophethood. **[Ṭabarī]** "And God is the possessor of great bounty" — possessor of bounty with which He favours whom He loves and wills of His creation; then He described His bounty as great, saying "His bounty is great", because nothing of the bounty with which creatures favour one another resembles it in the greatness of its effect upon the one favoured, nor comes near it in the gravity of its momentousness. **[Jalālayn]** "He singles out for His mercy whom He will; God is of bounty abounding." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "He selects for His mercy whom He wills, and Allāh is the Owner of great bounty" — meaning: He has endowed you, O believers, with tremendous virtue, in that He honoured your Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ over all other prophets, and by directing you to the best Sharīʿah there is. **[Qurṭubī]** That is, by His prophethood and His guidance — from al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others besides them; Ibn Jurayj said: by Islam and the Qurʾān, "whom He wills". **[Qurṭubī]** Abū ʿUthmān said: He made the saying general, so that the hope of the hopeful and the fear of the fearful might remain with it; "and God is the possessor of great bounty". **[Saʿdī]** And God is the One who guides whom He wills, and in His hand is the bounty which He singles out for whom He wills — so He singled you out, O this community, with what He did not single out others for. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** That this envy is based on not knowing the nature, timing and wisdom of God's grace and mercy is explained in the later part of verse 73 and in verse 74. **[Study Quran]** "Selects for His Mercy" could also mean "singles out for His Mercy"; the language used to describe God's Mercy reflects that describing His Bounty in the previous verse, both of which He bestows upon whomsoever He will, underscoring the vastness and generosity of God and the limitless ways in which He provides and shows kindness. **[Study Quran]** More specifically, the one He selects for His Mercy here refers to the Prophet (al-Muṣṭafā, "the Chosen One"), who has been selected for prophethood even if others object; it may also refer to the Qurʾān or to Islam itself.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** *Yakhtaṣṣu* is of the pattern *iftaʿala*, from *khaṣṣa*; and "His mercy" is here identified with Islam, the Qurʾān and prophethood. **[Ṭabarī]** The greatness of the bounty is explained comparatively: no creature's favour resembles His in the greatness of its effect. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū ʿUthmān notes the rhetorical effect of leaving the object unspecified — hope and fear are both kept in play.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7256 — Mujāhid: "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills" — prophethood; He singles out for it whom He wills. **[Ṭabarī]** 7257 — the like of it through another chain. **[Ṭabarī]** 7258 — al-Rabīʿ: He singles out for prophethood whom He wills. **[Ṭabarī]** 7259 — Ibn Jurayj: the Qurʾān and Islam. **[Ṭabarī]** 7260 — the like of it, from Ibn Jurayj through another chain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The bounty with which the believers have been endowed is the honouring of their Prophet above all other prophets and the direction to the best Sharīʿah. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid: by His prophethood and His guidance; Ibn Jurayj: by Islam and the Qurʾān.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Mercy" here is concrete: Islam, the Qurʾān and prophethood, given to whom He wills. **[Qurṭubī]** Leaving the recipient unnamed is deliberate, so that both hope and fear remain. **[Study Quran]** The reference has been taken as the Prophet himself — the Chosen One — and also as the Qurʾān or Islam. **[Saʿdī]** The community of Muḥammad ﷺ was singled out with what no other community was given. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The singling out is a favour to be acknowledged, not a claim to be made.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:26 for the giving and withholding of authority, and for the title al-Muṣṭafā; 3:73 for the bounty in the preceding verse. **[Ṭabarī]** 2:471 for his earlier treatment of *yakhtaṣṣu*; 3:72–73 for the stratagem this verse answers. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:73 for the bounty to which this is the counterpart. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:75, which follows.

**Reflection.** A short verse, and the commentators make it do a surprising amount of work. The first question is what "mercy" names, and the answers are not vague — prophethood, or Islam and the Qurʾān **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. The Study Quran adds the reading that the one singled out is the Prophet himself, *al-Muṣṭafā*, which is the same word as the verb in this verse **[Study Quran]**. Then there is Abū ʿUthmān's small, shrewd observation, which Qurṭubī alone records: the object is left general so that the hopeful keep hoping and the fearful keep fearing **[Qurṭubī]**. And al-Ṭabarī's closing gloss is the one that gives the verse its weight — God's bounty is called "great" not as praise but as comparison, because no favour among creatures resembles it in what it does to the one who receives it **[Ṭabarī]**. Placed where it is, the verse is also simply the answer to the envy named in 3:73: what they grudged was never theirs to withhold **[Maʿārif]**, **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:75 — وَمِنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مَنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ بِقِنطَارٍۢ يُؤَدِّهِۦٓ إِلَيْكَ وَمِنْهُم مَّنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ بِدِينَارٍۢ لَّا يُؤَدِّهِۦٓ إِلَيْكَ إِلَّا مَا دُمْتَ عَلَيْهِ قَآئِمًۭا ۗ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَالُوا۟ لَيْسَ عَلَيْنَا فِى ٱلْأُمِّيِّۦنَ سَبِيلٌۭ وَيَقُولُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلْكَذِبَ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ

*"And among the People of the Scripture is he who, if you entrust him with a hundredweight, will render it to you; and among them is he who, if you entrust him with a single dinar, will not render it to you unless you keep standing over him. That is because they say, 'There is no way against us in respect of the unlettered.' And they speak falsehood against God while they know."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** This is a report from God that among the People of the Scripture — the Jews of the Children of Israel — are people of trust who render it and do not betray it, and among them is the one who betrays his trust, the libertine in his oath, who treats [the property of the unlettered] as lawful. **[Ṭabarī]** And were someone to ask: what is the point of God informing His prophet ﷺ of this, when you know that people have never ceased to be like that — some rendering their trust and some betraying it? — the answer is: God intended, by informing the believers of their report, as He has set it out in His book in these verses, to warn them against entrusting them with their wealth and to frighten them away from being deceived by them, because many of them treat the wealth of the believers as lawful. **[Ṭabarī]** So the interpretation of the speech is: and among the People of the Scripture is he who, if you, O Muḥammad, entrust him with a great and abundant amount of wealth, will render it to you and not betray you in it; and among them is he who, if you entrust him with a dīnār, will betray you in it and not render it to you, unless you press him with demanding and claiming. **[Jalālayn]** "And of the People of the Scripture is he who, if you trust him with a hundredweight" — that is, with much money — "he will return it to you" on account of his trustworthiness, the like of ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, to whom a man entrusted twelve hundred plates of gold and who then returned them to him; "and of them is he who, if you trust him with one dinar, will not return it to you" on account of his treachery, "unless you keep standing over him", not leaving him for one minute, for as soon as you leave him he will deny it — as was the case with Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf, to whom a man of Quraysh entrusted a dīnār and who later denied it. **[Jalālayn]** That refusal to return things is because they say "We have no duty towards" — namely, no possibility of acquiring sin because of — "the Gentiles", the Arabs; for they considered it lawful to be unjust towards any person of a different religion, and they attributed the source of this conviction to God. **[Jalālayn]** God says: "They speak falsehood against God" by attributing such things to Him, "while they are aware" that they are liars. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh states that there are deceitful people among the Jews, and He warns the faithful against being deceived by them, because some of them, if entrusted with a *qinṭār* of money, will readily pay it back — and this verse indicates that this type would likewise give what is less than a *qinṭār*, as is obvious — however, "and among them there is he who, if entrusted with a single silver coin, will not repay it unless you constantly stand demanding" and insisting on acquiring your rightful property; and if this is what he would do with one dīnār, then what about more than a dīnār? **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Because they say: 'There is no blame on us to betray and take the properties of the illiterates (Arabs)'" — what made them reject the truth, or what they owed, is that they said: there is no harm in our religion if we eat up the property of the unlettered ones, the Arabs, for Allāh has allowed it for us. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh replied, "But they tell a lie against Allāh while they know it" — for they invented this lie and word of misguidance; rather, Allāh would not allow this money for them unless they had a right to it. **[Qurṭubī]** "Among the People of the Scripture is he who, if entrusted with a qinṭār, will readily pay it back" — the like of ʿAbdullāh b. Salām. **[Qurṭubī]** "And among them there is he who, if entrusted with a single silver coin, will not repay it" — and he is Finḥāṣ b. ʿĀzūrāʾ the Jew, with whom a man deposited a dīnār and who betrayed him; and it is said: Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and his companions. **[Saʿdī]** God informs about the People of the Scripture that among them is a party who are trustworthy, such that if you entrusted him with *qinṭārs* of money — that is, much wealth — he would render it to you; and among them is a party of treacherous ones who would betray you in the least of the little. **[Saʿdī]** And along with this hideous treachery they interpret matters with false excuses and say "There is no way against us in respect of the unlettered" — meaning: there is no blame upon us if we betray them and treat their wealth as permissible, because they have no sanctity. **[Saʿdī]** God said, "and they speak falsehood against God while they know" — that upon them is the severest blame; so they combined treachery with contempt for the Arabs and with lying against God, and they know it — they are not like one who does it out of ignorance and error. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In the previous verses (70–72), breach of faith committed by the People of the Book was mentioned — disbelieving in the verses of God, confusing the truth with what is false, concealing the truth, and conspiring to mislead Muslim believers; in this verse their breach of trust in matters of property has been mentioned, and since some of them happened to be trustworthy, both types were identified. **[Study Quran]** Distinguishing between the good and bad among the People of the Book is revisited in 3:113: "They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite God's signs in the watches of the night, while they prostrate." **[Study Quran]** A quintal (*qinṭār*) is an amount many times larger than a dīnār, though not necessarily a precise measure; and what is entrusted can refer to a loan, a purchase, or simply something given for safekeeping.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The *bāʾ* in "with a dīnār" and *ʿalā* alternate in this position, just as one says "I passed by him" (*marartu bihi*) and "I passed over him" (*marartu ʿalayhi*). **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over "unless you keep standing over him": some said "unless you keep demanding it from him". **[Study Quran]** *Ummiyyūn*, "the non-Jews", is elsewhere rendered "illiterate" (2:78) or "unlettered" (3:20; 7:157–58; 62:2); here it is understood to mean that, from the point of view of the Jews speaking, the contractual obligations with non-Jews were different and did not have to be observed with the same care, if at all, even with those Jews who had become Muslims. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Waththāb and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī read "man in tīmanhu", on the dialect of those who read "nistaʿīnu" — the dialect of Bakr and Tamīm.

**Readings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Waththāb and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī read *man in tīmanhu*, on the dialect of those who read *nistaʿīnu*, which is the dialect of Bakr and Tamīm; and in the codex of ʿAbdullāh, "mā laka lā taymannā ʿalā Yūsuf", while the rest read it with the alif. **[Qurṭubī]** Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī read *yuʾaddihī* with a *yāʾ* in connected speech; Abū ʿUbayd said that Abū ʿAmr, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah in the transmission of Abū Bakr all agreed on pausing on the *hāʾ*, reading *yuʾaddih ilayka*. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Naḥḥās said: quiescing the *hāʾ* is not admissible except in poetry, according to some grammarians, while others do not allow it at all and consider it an error on the part of those who read it, supposing that the jussive falls on the *hāʾ* — but Abū ʿAmr is greater than that such a thing should be admissible against him; what is sound from him is that he vowelled the *hāʾ* with *kasrah*, and that is the reading of Yazīd b. al-Qaʿqāʿ. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū al-Mundhir Sallām and al-Zuhrī read *yuʾaddihu* with *ḍammah* on the *hāʾ* without a *wāw*.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7261 — Qatādah, on "unless you keep standing over him": except what you sought and pursued. **[Ṭabarī]** 7262 — Qatādah, through another chain: you demand it from him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7263 — Mujāhid: assiduously. **[Ṭabarī]** 7264 — the like of it, through another chain. **[Ṭabarī]** And others said the meaning is "unless you keep standing at his head". **[Ibn Kathīr]** ʿAbd al-Razzāq recorded that Ṣaʿṣaʿah b. Yazīd said that a man asked Ibn ʿAbbās: "During battle we capture some property belonging to *ahl al-dhimmah*, such as chickens and sheep." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "What do you do in this case?" The man said: "We say that there is no sin in this case." He said: "That is what the People of the Book said: 'There is no blame on us to betray and take the properties of the illiterates.' Verily, if they pay the *jizyah*, then you are not allowed their property, except when they willingly give it up." **[Ṭabarī]** 7275 — al-Suddī: "and he speaks falsehood against God while he knows" — meaning the one among them who, when it is said to him "why do you not render your trust?", says "there is no blame upon us in the property of the Arabs; God has made it lawful for us!" **[Ṭabarī]** 7276 — Ibn Jurayj: "and they speak falsehood against God while they know" — meaning their claim that they found in their book their saying, "there is no way against us in respect of the unlettered". **[Study Quran]** It is said that some Muslims came to Ibn ʿAbbās and made a similar claim against members of a non-Muslim treaty-holding community, saying "There is nothing to stop us when it comes to them"; they were corrected by Ibn ʿAbbās, who told them that it was not permissible to take any wealth from the treaty peoples beyond what they paid in indemnity, or *jizyah*. **[Study Quran]** Al-Qurṭubī quotes a long ḥadīth stating that, regarding the weighty matter of returning trusts to their owners, resentment leads to perfidy, and perfidy leads to a lack of compassion, which in turn leads to being cursed and outcast, which ultimately leads to Islam leaving one's heart.

**Rulings.** **[Ṭabarī]** The point of the report is practical: warn the believers against entrusting their wealth to those who consider it lawful. **[Ibn Kathīr]** If they pay the *jizyah*, their property is not permitted to the Muslims except by their own willing consent. **[Study Quran]** Many commentators use this verse as an occasion to speak of the importance of protecting trusts and repaying what one owes. **[Maʿārif]** It is from the phrase "unless you keep standing over him" that Imām Abū Ḥanīfah deduced the ruling that the lender has the right to keep the borrower under demand.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is not a general remark about human nature but a warning about a specific community's doctrine. **[Jalālayn]** They considered it lawful to be unjust towards anyone of a different religion, and attributed the source of that conviction to God. **[Maʿārif]** Praising a good quality in a non-Muslim is correct: for an action to be acceptable with God is one thing, and having a word of praise for it is another — from praising something it does not follow that it is acceptable with God; the purpose is to point out that something good, even if it be that of a disbeliever, is good to a certain degree, the benefit of which he receives as a good reputation in this world, and in the Hereafter as a reduction in the punishment for his disbelief. **[Maʿārif]** This also makes it clear that Islam does not resort to prejudice and short-sightedness; on the contrary, it shows open-hearted appreciation of the excellence of even its adversary in respect of his achievements.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:113 for "they are not all alike"; 3:14 for the plural of *qinṭār*, translated "heaps"; 4:20, where it means a great sum; 2:78, 3:20 and 7:157–58 for *ummī*; 9:29 for the *jizyah*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The beginning of this sūrah for the meaning of *qinṭār*. **[Ṭabarī]** 1:313 for the alternation of *bāʾ* and *ʿalā*; 3:70–72 for the preceding breaches of faith. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:76, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:70–72 for the sequence.

**Reflection.** Two things are being said at once, and the commentators refuse to flatten either: some of them are scrupulous, and some of them are not **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**. Maʿārif draws out why that matters — the verse praises a good quality in people who are not Muslims, and it is right to do so, because praising something is not the same as declaring it acceptable with God, and the benefit of it reaches its possessor as a good name here and as lightening there **[Maʿārif]**. The second half of the verse is the alarming part: the treachery is not weakness but doctrine — "there is no way against us in respect of the unlettered" — and the Qurʾān adds that they attributed the doctrine to God **[Jalālayn]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. The story Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī both record shows how easily the doctrine migrates: Muslims on campaign took property from treaty-holding people and said there was no sin in it, and Ibn ʿAbbās answered them with this very verse **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**. And al-Ṭabarī's preliminary question — why tell us at all, when everyone knows some people are honest and some are not? — has a blunt answer: the point is not information but protection **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:76 — بَلَىٰ مَنْ أَوْفَىٰ بِعَهْدِهِۦ وَٱتَّقَىٰ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ

*"Nay — whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God, God loves the God-fearing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** This is a report from God about what belongs to the one who renders his trust to the one who entrusted him with it, out of fear of God and watchfulness of Him. **[Ṭabarī]** So He said: the matter is not as these who lie against God among the Jews say — that there is no blame and no sin upon them in the property of the unlettered — then He said: "Nay, but whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God", meaning: but the one who fulfils his covenant, which is His charge to them that He charged them in the Torah, of belief in Muḥammad ﷺ and in what he brought them. **[Jalālayn]** "Nay" — there is a duty incumbent over them in this regard; "but whoever fulfils his covenant", the one he has made or the covenant of God, by restoring a trust and other such things, "and has fear of God", by refraining from disobedience and performing deeds of obedience — "for truly God loves the God-fearing"; "He loves them" means that He will reward them; the overt noun *al-muttaqīn*, "the God-fearing", has replaced the third-person pronominalisation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Yes, whoever fulfills his pledge and fears Allāh much" — fulfils his promise and fears Allāh among you, O People of the Book, regarding the covenant Allāh took from you to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ when he is sent, just as He took the same covenant from all Prophets and their nations; whoever avoids Allāh's prohibitions, obeys Him and adheres to the Sharīʿah that He sent with His Final Messenger ﷺ and the master of all mankind — "verily, then Allāh loves the *Muttaqīn*". **[Qurṭubī]** *Man* is in the nominative as the subject, and it is a conditional; *awfā* is in the position of the jussive; and *ittaqā* is conjoined to it — meaning: and he feared God, and did not lie, and did not treat as lawful what was made unlawful for him. **[Qurṭubī]** "For truly God loves the *muttaqīn*" — that is, He loves those; and the meaning of God's love for His friends has already been set out. **[Qurṭubī]** The pronoun in "his covenant" goes back to God; His mention having occurred in "and they speak falsehood against God while they know" — and it is admissible that it goes back to the one who fulfils, and who fears unbelief, treachery and the breaking of covenants; and *ʿahd* is a verbal noun that is annexed to both the agent and the object. **[Saʿdī]** Then God said, exalted is He: "Nay" — meaning: the matter is not as they said. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** "Whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God" — meaning: upholds the rights of God and the rights of His creation, for this is the God-fearing one, and God loves him; and whoever is otherwise, and does not fulfil his covenant and the contracts between him and creation, and does not uphold the fear of God — then God hates him, and will recompense him for that with the gravest punishment. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Earlier, in "they say" (3:75), there was a refutation of the claim made by the People of the Book; onwards from there, in verses 76–77, the same refutation has been re-asserted, and the merit of fulfilling a commitment as well as the condemnation for its breach have been clarified. **[Maʿārif]** *ʿAhd* (pledge or covenant) is what gets settled between the parties concerned after mutual discussions and by which both of them have to abide; contrary to this is *waʿdah*, or promise, which issues from a single side — that is, *ʿahd* is bilateral while *waʿdah* is unilateral. **[Study Quran]** The blessing pronounced on those who fulfill their pact stands against the claim in the previous verse that no obligation is owed to non-Jews.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Man* is nominative as the subject and functions as a conditional; *awfā* is in the jussive position and *ittaqā* is conjoined to it; *ʿahd* is a verbal noun annexed to either the agent or the object. **[Jalālayn]** The overt noun *al-muttaqīn* replaces the expected pronoun, and "He loves them" means He will reward them. **[Maʿārif]** *ʿAhd* is bilateral; *waʿdah* is unilateral. **[Ṭabarī]** *Balā*, "nay", directly negates the claim recorded at the end of 3:75.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The covenant in view is the one taken in the Torah: to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ and what he brings. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The same covenant was taken from every prophet and their nations, and the fulfilment of it is adherence to the Sharīʿah sent with the Final Messenger. **[Saʿdī]** Fulfilment has two directions — the rights of God and the rights of His creation — and both are included in "fearing God". **[Maʿārif]** Fulfilment of commitments is stressed in the Qurʾān and Sunnah time and again.
