**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:77 for the condemnation of the breach. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:75 for the claim refuted. **[Maʿārif]** 3:77 for the five warnings. **[Saʿdī]** 3:75, "and they speak falsehood against God while they know", as the statement being overturned. **[Study Quran]** 3:75 for the claim that no obligation is owed. **[Jalālayn]** 3:77 for what follows.

**Reflection.** One word opens the verse — *balā*, "nay" — and it does the whole work of overturning the claim that closed the previous one **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**. What replaces that claim is not a rule about property but a description of a person: one who fulfils his covenant and fears God **[Jalālayn]**. The commentators differ instructively about which covenant is meant — al-Ṭabarī says the charge given in the Torah to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ, Ibn Kathīr says the covenant taken from every prophet and their nations, and Qurṭubī notes that the grammar permits either the covenant with God or the covenant a person makes **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Saʿdī's gloss keeps both directions in view at once: the rights of God and the rights of people, which is why "fears God" covers returning a trust as much as it covers prayer **[Saʿdī]**. And Maʿārif's small lexical distinction is worth keeping — a covenant is made by two parties and binds both, which is precisely what the People of the Scripture were denying **[Maʿārif]**.

*Source note:* The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:76; its combined note for 3:75–76 is cited at 3:75.

## 3:77 — إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَشْتَرُونَ بِعَهْدِ ٱللَّهِ وَأَيْمَٰنِهِمْ ثَمَنًۭا قَلِيلًا أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ لَا خَلَٰقَ لَهُمْ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَلَا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَلَا يَنظُرُ إِلَيْهِمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ وَلَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌۭ

*"Those who purchase with the covenant of God and their oaths a small price — those have no share in the Hereafter; God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them; and theirs is a painful punishment."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: those who substitute — in exchange for abandoning the covenant of God which He covenanted to them, and the charge He charged them in the Books which God sent down to His prophets, of following Muḥammad ﷺ, affirming him, and acknowledging him and what he brought from God — and in exchange for their false oaths, by which they treat as lawful what God made unlawful for them of the wealth of the people who entrusted them — a "price", meaning a vile substitute and exchange from the goods and debris of this world. **[Ṭabarī]** "Those have no share (*khalāq*) in the Hereafter" — those who do that have no portion of the good things of the Hereafter, and no share of the bliss of Paradise and what God has prepared for its people therein, to the exclusion of others. **[Ṭabarī]** And as for "nor will God speak to them", it means: God will not speak to them with what pleases them; "nor look at them" means: He will not incline to them with good, out of detestation from God for them — like one saying to another, "look at me, may God look at you", meaning "incline to me, may God incline to you with good and mercy"; and as one says to a man, "may God not hear your supplication", meaning "may God not answer you" — and nothing hidden is hidden from God; and as the poet said: "I called upon God until I feared that God would not hear what I say" — meaning, would not answer, as in "God hears the one who praises Him". **[Jalālayn]** The following was revealed with regard to the Jews when they distorted the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ and God's covenant with them in the Torah, and God's covenant with them regarding one that swears an oath to a falsehood when bearing witness or when selling merchandise: "Those that sell" — exchange — "God's covenant with them" that they believe in the Prophet and return faithfully what has been entrusted to them, "and their own oaths", their invoking God's name mendaciously, "for a small price" of this world — "there shall be no share", no lot, "for them in the Hereafter; and God shall not speak to them" out of wrath against them, "nor look upon them", nor have mercy upon them, "on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them", cleanse them, "and theirs will be a painful chastisement". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh states that whoever prefers the small things of this short, soon-to-end life instead of fulfilling what they promised Allāh — of following Muḥammad ﷺ, announcing his description to people and affirming his truth — then "they shall have no portion in the Hereafter": they will not have a share or part in the Hereafter's rewards. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Neither will Allāh speak to them nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection" with His mercy — this verse indicates that Allāh will not speak words of kindness to them, nor look at them with any mercy; "nor will He purify them" from sins and impurities; rather, He will order them to the Fire; "and they shall have a painful torment". **[Qurṭubī]** Two matters. First — the imāms narrated from al-Ashʿath b. Qays: "There was land between me and a Jewish man, and he denied me; so I brought him before the Prophet ﷺ, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to me, 'Do you have evidence?' I said, 'No.' He said to the Jew, 'Then swear.' I said, 'Then he will swear and take my property away' — and God sent down 'Those who purchase with the covenant of God and their oaths a small price', to the end of the verse." **[Qurṭubī]** The imāms also narrated from Abū Umāmah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever seizes the right of a Muslim man by his oath, God has made the Fire necessary for him and forbidden Paradise to him." A man said to him: "Even if it be something small, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Even if it be a twig of *arāk*." **[Qurṭubī]** Second — this verse and the ḥadīths indicate that the judgement of a judge does not make property lawful inwardly, by an outward ruling, when the one judged in whose favour knows it to be false. **[Saʿdī]** Meaning: those who buy the world with the religion, choosing the paltry debris of this world and resorting to false oaths and broken covenants to reach it — for those, "God will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and theirs is a painful punishment": the wrath of God has become due against them, His punishment has become incumbent upon them, and they are denied His reward and prevented from *tazkiyah*, which is purification; rather, they will come to the Resurrection stained with crimes, defiled with enormous sins. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** That commitments should be fulfilled has been stressed in the Qurʾān and Sunnah time and again — for instance, right here in this verse, five warnings have been given to those who break their solemn pledge. **[Study Quran]** "No share in the Hereafter" means no share of its goodness and blessings, not that one will have no experience of the events after death. **[Study Quran]** Although some commentators understand from this verse that God will not speak to or look at such people at all, others understand this to be an expression of displeasure and punishment, since other verses describe God speaking even to disbelievers on the Day of Judgment; to not wish to speak with or look upon a person is an expression of anger or wrath and, when coming from God, is a severe form of punishment, just as God's looking upon or speaking with a person is a great form of blessing.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "They purchase" (*yashtarūna*) is glossed as substituting and exchanging, and "a small price" as a vile substitute from the goods and debris of this world; and the divine "speaking", "looking" and "hearing" are all read idiomatically — speaking with what pleases, inclining with good, and answering — with a pre-Islamic verse as witness. **[Jalālayn]** "Sell" is glossed as "exchange". **[Study Quran]** The phrase *lā khalāq* is also used to describe someone who lacks virtues; and the verb *zakkā* can mean both to purify and to deem purified, as in 53:32, "So do not deem yourselves purified".

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Dharr said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There are three persons whom Allāh will not speak to, look at on the Day of Resurrection, or purify, and they shall taste a painful torment." He said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allāh! Who are they, may they gain failure and loss?' He said" — repeating this statement three times — "'The *musbil* (the man whose clothes reach below the ankles), he who swears while lying so as to sell his merchandise, and the one who gives charity and reminds people of it.'" This was also recorded by Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAdī b. ʿAmīrah al-Kindī said: Imruʾ al-Qays b. ʿĀbis, a man of Kindah, disputed with a man of Ḥaḍramawt before the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning a piece of land; the Prophet ﷺ required the man of Ḥaḍramawt to produce his evidence, but he had none; so the Prophet ﷺ required Imruʾ al-Qays to swear — and the man of Ḥaḍramawt said, "O Messenger of Allāh! If you only require him to swear, then by the Lord of the Kaʿbah, my land is lost." **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever swears while lying to acquire the property of others will meet Allāh while He is angry with him" — and Rajāʾ, one of the narrators, said that the Messenger of God ﷺ then recited "Verily, those who purchase a small gain at the cost of Allāh's covenant and their oaths...". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imruʾ al-Qays said, "What if one forfeits this dispute — what will he gain, O Messenger of Allāh?" The Prophet ﷺ answered, "Paradise." Imruʾ al-Qays said, "Bear witness that I forfeit all the land for him." Al-Nasāʾī also recorded this. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAbdullāh said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever takes a false oath to deprive a Muslim of his property will meet Allāh while He is angry with him" — and al-Ashʿath said: "By Allāh! This verse was revealed concerning me. I owned some land with a Jewish man who denied my right, and I complained against him to the Messenger of Allāh; the Prophet ﷺ asked me, 'Do you have evidence?' I said, 'I don't have evidence.' He said to the Jew, 'Take an oath then.' I said, 'O Allāh's Messenger! He will take a false oath immediately and I will lose my property' — and Allāh revealed 'Verily, those who purchase a small gain at the cost of Allāh's covenant and their oaths...'". The Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Three persons whom Allāh shall not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, or look at, or purify, and they shall taste a painful torment: a man who does not give the wayfarer some of the water that he has; a man who swears, while lying, in order to complete a sales transaction after the ʿAṣr prayer; and a man who gives his pledge of allegiance to an Imām, and if the Imām gives him something he fulfils the pledge, but if the Imām does not give him he does not fulfil it." Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī also recorded it, and al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. **[Qurṭubī]** Umm Salamah said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "You bring your disputes to me, and I am only a human being; perhaps some of you are more eloquent in his argument than others, and I only judge between you on the basis of what I hear from you — so whoever I judge in favour of, of the right of his brother, let him not take it; for I have only cut for him a piece of the Fire, which he will bring on the Day of Resurrection." **[Maʿārif]** In a ḥadīth, the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that one who usurps the right of a Muslim under a false oath makes the Fire of Hell compulsory for himself; the narrator asked whether the Fire becomes compulsory even if the matter is very insignificant, and he replied: "Even if it be the green bough of a tree."

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse and the ḥadīths together establish that a judge's ruling does not make property lawful inwardly when the beneficiary knows the ruling to be false, since the judge only rules on the outward evidence — and there is no disagreement among the imāms on this. **[Maʿārif]** The five warnings listed against the breaker of a solemn pledge are: no share in the blessings of the Hereafter; God will not speak to them with glad tidings; God will not look at them mercifully on the Day of Doom; God will not forgive them their sins, since they wasted the rights of a servant of God through breach of trust, and God does not forgive what one human being owes another — this is known in Islamic terminology as *ḥaqq al-ʿabd*, the right of the servant; and a grievous punishment awaits them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah extends the warning to withholding water from a traveller, to false oaths in trade after ʿAṣr, and to conditional allegiance to a ruler.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** What is sold is not a thing but a set of obligations: the covenant to follow and affirm the Messenger, and the truthfulness of one's oaths. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The four negations are read by him as the withdrawal of mercy, kindness, purification and, finally, the ordering to the Fire. **[Study Quran]** Others read the negations as an expression of displeasure rather than a literal description, since other verses have God speaking even to disbelievers on the Day of Judgement. **[Saʿdī]** The consequence is described as coming to the Resurrection stained with crimes and defiled with enormous sins.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:174 as the parallel; 2:41, 3:199, 5:44 and 9:9 for selling God's signs; 2:79 and 3:187 for selling God's Book; 16:95 for an oath with God; 7:6, 15:92–93 and 23:108 for God speaking to the disbelievers; 53:32 for *zakkā* as "deem purified". **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:75–76 for the trust and covenant. **[Qurṭubī]** Volume 2, p. 234, for the parallel phrase in Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Maʿārif]** 3:76 for the merit of fulfilling a commitment.

**Reflection.** The verse names a price before it names the thing bought, and the price is small **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**. What is given for it is twofold — the covenant to follow and affirm the Messenger, and the honesty of one's own oaths — and both are spent to acquire the debris of this world **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Jalālayn]**. The occasion reports make the abstraction concrete: a land dispute, a man with no evidence, a Jew about to swear, and a revelation that arrives while the case is still before the Prophet ﷺ **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Then the four negations, and the commentators divide over how to take them — Ibn Kathīr reads them as the withdrawal of mercy and the order to the Fire, while the Study Quran notes that other verses have God speaking to disbelievers, so some take the whole set as an expression of wrath rather than a literal account **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī's treatment is the most careful: he reads each verb idiomatically, with Arabic usage and a line of poetry as evidence, so that "not speaking" means not speaking what pleases and "not looking" means not inclining with good **[Ṭabarī]**. And the jurist's point that Qurṭubī draws is the one that still bites: a court ruling in your favour does not make the thing yours if you know the oath was false **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:78 — وَإِنَّ مِنْهُمْ لَفَرِيقًۭا يَلْوُۥنَ أَلْسِنَتَهُم بِٱلْكِتَٰبِ لِتَحْسَبُوهُ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَمَا هُوَ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَيَقُولُونَ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ وَيَقُولُونَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلْكَذِبَ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ

*"And indeed among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Book, that you may reckon it to be from the Book — though it is not from the Book. And they say, 'It is from God', though it is not from God; and they speak falsehood against God while they know."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: and among the People of the Scripture — that is, the Jews who were around the city of the Messenger of God ﷺ in his time, of the Children of Israel. **[Ṭabarī]** The pronoun in "among them" goes back to the "People of the Scripture" whom He mentioned in "and among the People of the Scripture is he who, if you entrust him with a qinṭār, will render it to you". **[Ṭabarī]** "A party" — a group. **[Ṭabarī]** "They twist" — they distort. **[Ṭabarī]** "Their tongues with the Book, that you may reckon it to be from the Book" — that you may think that what they distort with their speech is from the Book of God and His revelation; and God says: and that which they twisted their tongues with, distorted, and introduced is not from the Book of God — and they claim that what they twisted their tongues with, of distortion, lying and falsehood, and attached to the Book of God, is "from God", meaning from what God sent down to His prophets. **[Ṭabarī]** "And it is not from God" — that which they twisted their tongues with and introduced is not from what God sent down to any of His prophets, but is what they invented of themselves, a fabrication against God. **[Ṭabarī]** "And they speak falsehood against God while they know" — meaning: they deliberately speak falsehood about God, bear witness against Him falsely, and attach to the Book of God what is not of it, seeking leadership and the vile debris of this world. **[Jalālayn]** "And there is a group" — a party — "of them", the People of the Scripture, like Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf, "who twist their tongues with the Book", altering it by reciting it not according to the way in which it was revealed but according to the way in which they have distorted it, as in the case of the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ and other similar matters, "so that you may suppose" such distortion to be "part of the Book" that God revealed, "yet it is not part of the Book; and they say 'It is from God', yet it is not from God, and they speak falsehood against God while they know" that they are liars. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh states that some Jews distort Allāh's Words with their tongues, change them from their appropriate places, and alter their intended meanings; they do this to deceive the ignorant by making it appear that their words are in the Book of Allāh, and they attribute their own lies to Allāh even though they know that they have lied and invented falsehood. **[Qurṭubī]** Meaning: a party of the Jews. **[Qurṭubī]** "They twist their tongues with the Book" — and Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah read *yalūwūna*, for abundance; the word is used of inclining a thing, and the meaning is that they distort the speech and turn it away from the intended aim. **[Saʿdī]** And among the People of the Scripture is a faction who distort the Book of God: "they twist their tongues with the Book so that you may reckon it to be from the Book" — and this includes distortion of wording and distortion of meaning. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Then, along with this hideous distortion, they give the impression that it is from the Book — and they are liars in that — and they state falsehood against God openly, while they know their state and the evil of their consequence. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** It was during the presence of the deputation from Najrān that some Jews and Christians had said: "O Muḥammad, do you want us to worship you the way Christians worship Jesus, son of Mary?" He said: "I seek refuge with God that we worship someone other than God, or call on others to do so; God Almighty has not sent us to do that" — and thereupon this verse was revealed. **[Study Quran]** Much like 2:79 — "So woe unto those who write the book with their hands, then say, 'This is from God'" — this verse has been interpreted to mean outright forgery; obfuscation, by means of misinterpretation, of the prophecies foretelling the coming of the Prophet Muhammad; or the deception for worldly purposes of ignorant people who were told that the Torah says so-and-so when they did not have the ability to read the Torah for themselves. **[Study Quran]** "Twist their tongues with the Book" means their tongues are twisted for the purposes of distorting or misrepresenting the Book of God; that is, they bend or contort their words while reciting the Book so as to change or misrepresent it.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** The root of *al-layy* is inclining: *lawā bi-yadihi*, he motioned with his hand, and *lawā bi-raʾsihi*, he turned his head; and "with a twist of their tongues" (4:46) means obstinacy against the truth and inclining away from it to something else. **[Qurṭubī]** And the meaning of "do not turn aside for anyone" (3:153) is: you do not stop for him — one says *lawā ʿalayhi* when he stops and stays. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-layy* is also the delaying of a debt: *lawāhu bi-daynihi yalwīhi layyan wa-liyānan*, he put him off in his debt; and the poet said: "I had lent to Ḥassān, for fear of bankruptcy and delay — selling the capital and the goods is good"; and Dhu al-Rummah said: "You want my delay, though you are wealthy — and the better thing, O wearer of the sash, is to settle". **[Qurṭubī]** And in the ḥadīth: "The delay of the rich man makes his honour and his punishment lawful". **[Qurṭubī]** *Alsinah* is the plural of *lisān* in the dialect of those who make it masculine; those who make it feminine say *alsun*. **[Ṭabarī]** "A party" is a group, and "they twist" is "they distort".

**Readings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah read *yalūwūna*, on the pattern denoting abundance.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7290 — Mujāhid: "and among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Book" — they distort it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7291 — the like of it, through another chain. **[Ṭabarī]** 7292 — Qatādah: "and among them is a party who twist their tongues with the Book", up to "while they know" — they are the enemies of God, the Jews. *(the report continues)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas all said that "they distort the Book with their tongues" means "they alter them". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Bukhārī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said that the verse means they alter and add — although none among Allāh's creation can remove the Words of Allāh from His Books; they alter and distort their apparent meanings. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Wahb b. Munabbih said: "The Tawrāh and the Injīl remain as Allāh revealed them, and no letter in them was removed; however, the people misguide others by addition and false interpretation, relying on books that they wrote themselves" — then, "they say: 'This is from Allāh', but it is not from Allāh"; as for Allāh's Books, they are still preserved and cannot be changed. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this statement. **[Ibn Kathīr]** If Wahb meant the books currently in the hands of the People of the Book, then we should state that there is no doubt that they altered, distorted, added to and deleted from them — for instance, the Arabic versions of these books contain tremendous error, many additions and deletions and enormous misinterpretation, and those who made these translations have incorrect comprehension in most, rather all, of these translations; and if Wahb meant the Books of Allāh that He has with Him, then indeed these Books are preserved and were never changed. *(digression: Ibn Kathīr's long qualification of Wahb's report)* **[Jalālayn]** The party is exemplified by Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf, and the matter distorted is given as the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The offence has a motive named at the end of it: leadership, and the vile debris of this world. **[Ibn Kathīr]** What cannot be done is removing God's words from His Books; what is done is altering their apparent meanings, or adding and falsely interpreting. **[Saʿdī]** The distortion is of two kinds, of wording and of meaning, and in both cases the claim made for it — that it is from the Book — is a lie told knowingly. **[Study Quran]** The interpretations range from outright forgery to obfuscation of the prophecies to the deception of those unable to read the scripture themselves.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:79 for the parallel; 2:75, 4:46, 5:13 and 5:41 for the "distortion" of scriptures. **[Qurṭubī]** 4:46, "with a twist of their tongues"; 3:153, "do not turn aside for anyone". **[Ṭabarī]** 2:244–245 and 3:549 for *farīq*; 3:75 for the People of the Scripture referred to. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:79 for what follows.

**Reflection.** The image is physical before it is doctrinal — tongues being twisted, bent around the text until the reader hears something that is not there **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. What is at stake is a recitation: the words are read aloud in a way that makes a gloss sound like scripture **[Jalālayn]**. Ibn Kathīr is careful about the limits of the claim, and the distinction he draws is worth keeping — no one can remove God's words from His Books, so what happens is alteration of apparent meaning, or reliance on books they wrote themselves **[Ibn Kathīr]**. His long qualification of Wahb b. Munabbih's statement is the most candid passage in the whole discussion: if Wahb means the scriptures in people's hands today, they have certainly been altered; if he means the Books as they are with God, they are preserved **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And al-Ṭabarī's closing sentence names the motive, which is not theology: leadership, and the debris of this world **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:79 — مَا كَانَ لِبَشَرٍ أَن يُؤْتِيَهُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحُكْمَ وَٱلنُّبُوَّةَ ثُمَّ يَقُولَ لِلنَّاسِ كُونُوا۟ عِبَادًۭا لِّى مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَٰكِن كُونُوا۟ رَبَّٰنِيِّۦنَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تُعَلِّمُونَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَبِمَا كُنتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ

*"It is not for any human being that God should give him the Book, the judgement and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, 'Be servants to me apart from God' — but rather: 'Be masters, by virtue of what you teach of the Book and by virtue of what you study.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: and it is not fitting for any human being. **[Ṭabarī]** *Al-bashar* is the plural of the children of Adam, having no singular of its own form, like *al-qawm* and *al-khalq*; and it may be a name for one. **[Ṭabarī]** "That God should give him the Book" — that God should send down His book to him; "and the judgement" — and teach him the separation of wisdom; "and prophethood" — and give him prophethood; "then he should say to the people, 'be servants to me apart from God'" — then call the people to the worship of himself rather than God, after God has given him what He has given him of the Book, the judgement and prophethood. **[Ṭabarī]** But when God gives him that, he only calls them to knowledge of God, and urges them to the knowledge of the laws of His religion, and to be leaders in knowledge of God's command and His prohibition, and exemplars in obeying and worshipping Him, by their being teachers of the Book to the people and by their studying it. **[Jalālayn]** When the Christians of Najrān claimed that Jesus had commanded them to take him as a divinity, and some Muslims asked that they should be permitted to prostrate themselves before the Prophet ﷺ, the following was revealed: "It belongs not to any mortal that God should give him the Book", the Judgement — the understanding of the Divine Law — "prophethood, then that he should say to men, 'Be servants to me instead of God.' Rather he should say, 'Be masters'" — scholars, labouring; *rabbāniyyūn*, "those of the Lord", is derived from *rabb*, "lord", with the extra *alif* and *nūn*, as a superlative of *rabbiyyūn* — "by virtue of what you know" — *taʿlamūn*, also read as *tuʿallimūn*, "you teach" — "of the Book and in what you study", that is, on account of the fact that you used to do this; for its benefit is that you engage in action. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This verse means: it is not for a person whom Allāh has given the Book, knowledge in the Law and prophethood to proclaim to the people, "Worship me instead of Allāh", meaning, along with Allāh; and if this is not the right of a Prophet or a Messenger, then indeed it is not the right of anyone else to issue such a claim. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Be you *Rabbāniyyūn*, because you are teaching the Book, and you are studying it" — the Messenger recommends the people to be *Rabbāniyyūn*; Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Razīn and several others said that *Rabbāniyyūn* means "wise, learned, and forbearing". **[Qurṭubī]** *Mā kāna* means "it is not fitting", as in "it is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake" (4:92), "it is not for God to take a son" (19:35) and "it is not for us to speak about this" (24:16). **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-bashar* applies to one and to many, being of the status of a verbal noun; and the one meant by it here is Jesus, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī. **[Qurṭubī]** "The Book" is the Qurʾān; "the judgement" is knowledge and understanding — and it is also said: the rulings, meaning that God does not choose liars for His prophethood, and were any human being to do that, God would strip him of the signs and marks of prophethood. **[Qurṭubī]** *Thumma yaqūla* is in the accusative, sharing between *an yuʾtiyahu* and *yaqūla* — that is, the giving of prophethood and his saying "be servants to me apart from God" cannot be combined in a prophet. **[Saʿdī]** It is impossible and utterly precluded for a human being upon whom God has bestowed revelation, the Book and prophethood, and given the legal judgement, to command people to worship him — because that is unbelief, so how could he, when he was sent with Islam, which contradicts unbelief in every respect, command its opposite? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** This is impossible because his state, what he is upon, and the virtues and distinctions God has bestowed upon him require complete servitude and total submission to God, the One, the Subduer. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The verse implies that a person whom God invests with the Book, the Wisdom and the power of making decisions, and places on the great station of prophethood, is always faithful to his mission when he communicates the Divine message to people and calls on them to become His faithful servants. **[Maʿārif]** That he should start moving people away from the worship of the One God and start asking them to become his own worshippers, or the worshippers of some other creature, is something he can never do. **[Study Quran]** It is reported that the Prophet was asked by the Jews whether he wanted to be an object of worship, as Jesus was among the Christians; or that he was asked whether he thought people should prostrate themselves before him, an act associated with worship, rather than greet him normally. **[Study Quran]** *Judgment* (*ḥukm*) can also mean "rule"; to be servants (*ʿibād*) means to be worshippers of something; and although most commentators draw a connection between this verse and the Islamic rejection of the worship of Jesus, other types of worship directed at human beings are similarly deplored, as in 9:31, "They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords apart from God".

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Mā kāna* is "it is not fitting"; *al-bashar* applies to one and to many; and "the judgement" is knowledge and understanding, or the rulings. **[Qurṭubī]** The *rabbāniyyūn* are attributed to the *rabb*, "lord"; and the *rabbānī* is the one who nurtures people with the smaller matters of knowledge before the greater, and it is as though he follows the Lord in making matters easy — this meaning is related from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Qurṭubī]** Some said it was originally *rabbiyy*, and the *alif* and *nūn* were inserted for intensification, as one says of a man with a great beard *liḥyānī*, of one with a great forelock *jummanī*, and of one with a thick neck *raqabānī*. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mubarrid said: the *rabbāniyyūn* are the lords of knowledge, its singular being *rabbān*. **[Jalālayn]** *Rabbāniyyūn* is derived from *rabb* with an extra *alif* and *nūn*, as a superlative of *rabbiyyūn*. **[Ṭabarī]** *Bashar* is a collective with no singular of its own form, and may be used of one.

**Readings.** **[Jalālayn]** *Taʿlamūn*, "you know", is also read *tuʿallimūn*, "you teach". **[Study Quran]** An alternate reading of the verse's final phrase would give "from having known the Book and from having taught it".

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7296 — from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad b. Abī Muḥammad, from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd b. Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Abū Rāfiʿ al-Quraẓī — that is, Sallām b. Abī al-Ḥuqayq the Jew — said, when the rabbis of the Jews and the Christians of Najrān gathered before the Messenger of God ﷺ and he called them to Islam: "Do you want, O Muḥammad, that we should worship you, as the Christians worship Jesus son of Mary?" And a Christian man of Najrān called al-Ribbīs said: "Is that what you want from us, O Muḥammad, and to it you call us?" — or words to that effect. **[Ṭabarī]** The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God forbid that we worship other than God, or command the worship of other than Him! Not for that did He send me, and not with that did He command me" — or words to that effect; and God sent down concerning their saying [this verse]. *(the report continues)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḍaḥḥāk commented concerning "because you are teaching the Book, and you are studying it": "Whoever learns the Qurʾān deserves to become a *faqīh* (learned)"; and "you are studying it" — preserving its words. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Razīn and several others said that *Rabbāniyyūn* means "wise, learned, and forbearing". **[Jalālayn]** The occasion was the claim of the Christians of Najrān that Jesus had commanded them to take him as a divinity, together with the request of some Muslims to be permitted to prostrate themselves before the Prophet ﷺ. **[Maʿārif]** It was during the presence of the deputation from Najrān that some Jews and Christians said: "O Muḥammad, do you want us to worship you the way Christians worship Jesus, son of Mary?" and he said: "I seek refuge with God that we worship someone other than God, or call on others to do so; God Almighty has not sent us to do that". *(this report is placed by Maʿārif at 3:78)* **[Qurṭubī]** It is said that this verse was revealed concerning the Christians of Najrān; and it is likewise related that the whole sūrah up to "and when you left your family early" (3:121) had the Christians of Najrān as its occasion of revelation — though the Jews are mixed in with them, because they did the same kind of denial and obstinacy that the Christians did.

**Belief.** **[Maʿārif]** The verse grounds the infallibility (*ʿiṣmah*) of the prophets: any government appointing a representative considers both his competence and his loyalty, and no king or parliament would appoint one about whom there exists the least doubt of deviating from its policy; it is possible for a government to misjudge ability or loyalty, but with God even that element of doubt does not exist — if He knows that a man would not overstep the bounds of loyalty and obedience in the slightest degree, then it is impossible that he could later prove contrary to that assessment, for otherwise it would mean that divine knowledge is defective. **[Maʿārif]** Now that the blessed prophets are free of minor sins, how can the probability of committing *shirk* be entertained? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** This criticism refers to the ignorant rabbis, priests and teachers of misguidance, unlike the Messengers and their sincere knowledgeable followers who implement their knowledge — for they only command what Allāh commands them, and forbid what Allāh forbade for them. **[Qurṭubī]** God does not choose liars for His prophethood; were a human being to do that, God would strip him of the signs and marks of prophethood. **[Ṭabarī]** What a prophet calls people to is knowledge of God, knowledge of the laws of His religion, and leadership in His command and prohibition.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 9:31, "They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords apart from God"; 5:116, "Didst thou say unto mankind, 'Take me and my mother as gods apart from God?'"; 5:44 and 5:63 for *rabbāniyyūn*; 3:146 for *ribbiyyūn*, "devoted men". **[Ibn Kathīr]** 21:25, "None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me"; 16:36; 43:45; 21:29. **[Qurṭubī]** 4:92, 19:35 and 24:16 for *mā kāna*; 3:121 for the extent of the Najrān material. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:80, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:78 for the setting.

**Reflection.** The verse is usually read as a statement about Jesus, and al-Qurṭubī says plainly that the *bashar* meant is him, following al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Suddī **[Qurṭubī]**. But the occasion reports attached to it are about Muḥammad — the Najrān delegation asking whether he wanted them to worship him as the Christians worship Jesus, and his answering, "God forbid that we worship other than God, or command the worship of other than Him" **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Maʿārif]**. That double reference is the point: the principle is stated about a prophet generally and lands on this prophet specifically **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The positive half of the verse is easy to skip over and should not be: what a prophet does call people to is *rabbāniyyūn* — and the commentators define it as those who nurture people with the small matters of knowledge before the great, and who study the Book and preserve its words **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Maʿārif takes the verse as the scriptural basis for the infallibility of the prophets, by an argument from God's knowledge: He would not appoint one whom He knew would defect **[Maʿārif]**. And there is the small human detail Jalālayn preserves — some Muslims had asked to be allowed to prostrate to the Prophet, and this was the answer **[Jalālayn]**.

## 3:80 — وَلَا يَأْمُرَكُمْ أَن تَتَّخِذُوا۟ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةَ وَٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ أَرْبَابًا ۗ أَيَأْمُرُكُم بِٱلْكُفْرِ بَعْدَ إِذْ أَنتُم مُّسْلِمُونَ

*"Nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The readers differed concerning the reading of *wa-lā yaʾmurakum*. **[Ṭabarī]** The generality of the readers of the Hijaz and Madinah read *wa-lā yaʾmurukum* [with the indicative], as a fresh beginning from God, reporting about the Prophet ﷺ that he does not command you, O people, to take the angels and the prophets as lords; and they support this with a reading they report from Ibn Masʿūd, namely *wa-lan yaʾmurakum*, inferring from the entry of *lan* that the speech is cut off from what precedes it and begins a fresh report — they say: since *lā* was put in the place of *lan* in our reading, it must be read with the indicative. **[Ṭabarī]** And some of the Kufans and Basrans read *wa-lā yaʾmurakum* [with the subjunctive], conjoining it to "then he should say to the people", with the interpretation: it is not for a human being that God should give him the Book and then say to the people — nor that he should command you, meaning: nor was it for him to command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī: the reading I prefer is *wa-lā yaʾmurakum* with the subjunctive, connected to what precedes it, with the interpretation: it is not for a human being that God should give him the Book, the judgement and prophethood, and then say to the people, "be servants to me apart from God" — nor that He should command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords; because the verse was revealed on account of the people who said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Do you want us to worship you?" So God informed them that it is not for His prophet ﷺ to call people to the worship of himself, nor to the taking of the angels and the prophets as lords; rather, what is for him is to call them to be *rabbāniyyūn*. **[Jalālayn]** "He would never order you" — read *lā yaʾmurukum* to denote a new clause, meaning "God would not order you"; or, if read *lā yaʾmurakum*, it would be a supplement to *yaqūla*, "he should say", meaning "it belongs not that… a mortal should order you" — "to take the angels and the prophets as lords", in the way that the Sabaeans have taken the angels, the Jews Ezra and the Christians Jesus; "Would He order you to disbelieve after you have submitted?" — He would not do this. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Nor would he order you to take angels and Prophets for lords" — the Prophet does not command worshipping other than Allāh, whether a sent Messenger or an angel. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Would he order you to disbelieve after you have submitted to Allāh's will?" — meaning, he would not do that; for whoever calls to worshipping other than Allāh will have called to *kufr*, and the Prophets only call to *īmān*, which commands worshipping Allāh alone without partners. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read it in the accusative, conjoined to *an yuʾtiyahu*; and what strengthens this is that the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Do you want us to take you, O Muḥammad, as a lord?" — so God said, "It is not for a human being that God should give him the Book, the judgement and prophethood", up to "nor would he command you", in which there is a pronoun referring to the human being: that is, the human being — meaning Jesus and Ezra — would not command you. **[Qurṭubī]** The rest read it in the nominative, as a resumption and a severance from the first speech, with a pronoun referring to the name of God: that is, God would not command you to take them; and what strengthens this reading is that in the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is *wa-lan yaʾmurakum*, which indicates a resumption, and the pronoun too refers to God — this was mentioned by Makkī, and said by Sībawayh and al-Zajjāj. **[Qurṭubī]** And Ibn Jurayj and a group said: *wa-lā yaʾmurukum* [means] Muḥammad, peace be upon him — and this is the reading of Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī and the people of the two sanctuaries. **[Saʿdī]** It is utterly precluded for a human being upon whom God has bestowed the Book and prophethood and given the legal judgement to command the worship of the prophets and the angels, or the taking of them as lords. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And this is an answer to the delegation of Najrān when their delusion went too far and their pride carried them to the point that they said, "Do you command us, O Muḥammad, to worship you?" — when he had commanded them to worship God and obey Him; so the Maker made clear the negation of what they said, and that their speech and the speech of their like in this matter is manifestly false. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The impossibility extends to commanding the worship of the prophets and the angels and taking them as lords, since that is unbelief — and how could one sent with Islam, which contradicts unbelief in every respect, command its opposite? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān, on 3:79–80)* **[Study Quran]** This verse can also be read as resuming from the middle of the previous verse, meaning, "It is not for any human being… to command you to take the angels and prophets as lords"; and "he would not" means the Prophet would not do so, although others read this as "and He would not", meaning that God does not command the worship of angels and prophets.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The difference between the indicative and the subjunctive changes who the subject is — the Prophet, or the human being spoken of in 3:79, or God. **[Qurṭubī]** On the accusative reading the pronoun is that of the human being, meaning Jesus and Ezra; on the nominative reading it is that of God; and Ibn Jurayj and a group took the subject to be Muḥammad ﷺ himself. **[Jalālayn]** "To take the angels and the prophets as lords" is exemplified by the Sabaeans with the angels, the Jews with Ezra and the Christians with Jesus.

**Readings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read *wa-lā yaʾmurakum* in the accusative; the rest read it in the nominative; and this last is the reading of Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī and the people of the two sanctuaries. **[Qurṭubī]** In the codex of ʿAbdullāh it is *wa-lan yaʾmurakum*. **[Jalālayn]** *Lā yaʾmurukum* denotes a new clause; *lā yaʾmurakum* is a supplement to *yaqūla*. **[Study Quran]** Some read the subject as the Prophet and others as God.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Whoever calls to the worship of other than God has called to unbelief, and the prophets call only to faith, which is the worship of God alone without partners. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh said concerning the angels: "And if any of them should say, 'Verily, I am a god besides Him,' such a one We should recompense with Hell" (21:29). **[Qurṭubī]** God has forbidden the prophets to take people as worshippers who deify them; but He has made their inviolability binding on creation. **[Jalālayn]** Taking angels or prophets as lords is what the Sabaeans did with the angels, the Jews with Ezra and the Christians with Jesus. **[Saʿdī]** The claim that a prophet could command his own worship is manifestly false in itself.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** It is established that the Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you should say 'my slave' (*ʿabdī*) or 'my slave-woman' (*amatī*); rather let him say 'my lad' (*fatāya*) and 'my lass' (*fatātī*); and none of you should say 'my lord' (*rabbī*); rather let him say 'my master' (*sayyidī*)" — and in the revelation: "Mention me before your lord" (12:42). **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh said: "And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: 'None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me'" (21:25); "And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger: 'Worship Allāh and avoid ṭāghūt'" (16:36); "And ask those of Our Messengers whom We sent before you: 'Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious?'" (43:45). **[Ibn Kathīr]** And concerning the angels: "And if any of them should say, 'Verily, I am a god besides Him,' such a one We should recompense with Hell" (21:29). **[Jalālayn]** "Mention me before your lord" (12:42) is cited by Qurṭubī as the parallel for the ordinary use of the word "lord".

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:64 and 9:31 for the taking of other figures as lords. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 21:25, 16:36, 43:45 and 21:29. **[Qurṭubī]** 12:42 for the ordinary use of *rabb*; 3:79 for the verse continued. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:79 for the saying to which this is conjoined. **[Jalālayn]** 3:79 for the setting.

**Reflection.** The verse looks like a tail-piece to 3:79 and turns out to be a small masterpiece of ambiguity, because the one word that decides its meaning is a single vowel **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Read one way, it continues the sentence: it is not for a human being whom God has given the Book to say "worship me" — nor to command you to take angels and prophets as lords; read the other way, it begins a new sentence, and the subject becomes God, or the Prophet himself **[Jalālayn]**, **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī chooses the connected reading and gives a reason that is not grammatical at all but historical: the verse came down because of the people who asked the Prophet whether he wanted to be worshipped, and the connected reading answers them directly **[Ṭabarī]**. He also rejects the report from Ibn Masʿūd's codex that is used to support the other reading, on the grounds that its chain is unsound **[Ṭabarī]**. The substance is the same on every reading, though, and Ibn Kathīr states it in one line: whoever calls to the worship of other than God has called to unbelief, and the prophets call only to the worship of God alone **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And Qurṭubī adds the ḥadīth that keeps the principle from becoming remote — do not call another human being "my lord" **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:81 — وَإِذْ أَخَذَ ٱللَّهُ مِيثَٰقَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ لَمَآ ءَاتَيْتُكُم مِّن كِتَٰبٍۢ وَحِكْمَةٍۢ ثُمَّ جَآءَكُمْ رَسُولٌۭ مُّصَدِّقٌۭ لِّمَا مَعَكُمْ لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِۦ وَلَتَنصُرُنَّهُۥ ۚ قَالَ ءَأَقْرَرْتُمْ وَأَخَذْتُمْ عَلَىٰ ذَٰلِكُمْ إِصْرِى ۖ قَالُوٓا۟ أَقْرَرْنَا ۚ قَالَ فَٱشْهَدُوا۟ وَأَنَا۠ مَعَكُم مِّنَ ٱلشَّٰهِدِينَ

*"And when God took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom — then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall help him.' He said: 'Do you affirm, and do you take up My burden on that condition?' They said: 'We affirm.' He said: 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: and remember, O People of the Scripture, "when God took the covenant of the prophets" — meaning: when God took the covenant of the prophets, and "their covenant" is that by which they bound themselves to obedience of God in what He commanded them and forbade them. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over who is meant by "then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall help him". **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: those meant by it are the prophets themselves, whose covenants were taken that they should affirm one another and help him — and we have mentioned the report of those who said it. **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: they are the People of the Scripture, commanded to affirm Muḥammad ﷺ when God sends him and to help him, their covenant having been taken in their books for that. **[Ṭabarī]** And others — of those who hold that the ones whose covenant God took in this verse are the prophets — said: His saying "then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you" is directed at the People of the Scripture. **[Jalālayn]** "And mention when God made a covenant with the prophets: 'What if' — read *lamā*, it would be introducing a subject clause and emphasising the aspect of the oath in this 'making of the covenant'; if it is read *limā* it would then be connected to the verb *akhadha*, 'He took'; the *mā* is a relative particle in both cases, meaning *la'lladhī* or *li'lladhī* respectively — 'I have given you' — *ātaytukum*, or in a variant reading *ātaynākum*, 'We have given you' — 'of the Book and wisdom; then there shall come to you a messenger confirming what is with you' of the Book and wisdom, and that is Muḥammad ﷺ — 'you shall believe in him and you shall help him'" — this constitutes the response to the oath, if you reach his time and perceive him, and their communities of descendants follow them in what is incumbent upon them. **[Jalālayn]** He, God, said to them: "Do you affirm this? And do you take" — do you accept — "My load", My covenant, "on you on that condition?" They said: "We affirm." He said: "Then bear witness to this before your own souls and those of your followers, and I shall be with you among the witnesses" before you and them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh states that He took a pledge from every Prophet whom He sent, from Ādam until ʿĪsā, that when Allāh gives them the Book and the *Ḥikmah*, thus acquiring whatever high grades they deserve, then if a Messenger came afterwards they would believe in and support him; even though Allāh has given the Prophets the knowledge and the prophethood, this fact should not make them refrain from following and supporting the Prophet who comes after them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Do you agree (to it) and will you take up *Isrī*?" — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and al-Suddī said that *Isrī* means "My covenant"; and Muḥammad b. Isḥāq said that *Isrī* means "the responsibility of My covenant that you took", meaning the ratified pledge that you gave Me. **[Qurṭubī]** It is said: God took the covenant of the prophets that they should affirm one another and that some of them should command belief in others — and that is the meaning of "help" by affirmation; and this is the saying of Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Qatādah, Ṭāwūs, al-Suddī and al-Ḥasan, and it is the apparent sense of the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** Ṭāwūs said: God took the covenant of the first of the prophets that he would believe in what the last of them brought. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Kisāʾī said: it is admissible that "and when God took the covenant of the prophets" means "and when God took the covenant of those who were with the prophets"; and the Basrans said: when God takes the covenant of the prophets, He has taken the covenant of those with them, because they have followed them and affirmed them. **[Saʿdī]** This is a report from Him, exalted is He, that He took the covenant of the prophets and their compact, all of them, by reason of what He gave them and favoured them with of the Book and the Wisdom, which requires the complete upholding of the right of God and the rendering of it in full: that if a messenger comes to them confirming what is with them, sent with what they were sent with of *tawḥīd*, the truth, equity and the fundamentals upon which the revealed laws agree, they will believe in him and help him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** So they affirmed that, acknowledged it and bound themselves to it; and He took them as witnesses and witnessed against them, and threatened whoever opposes this covenant. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The particle *lamā*, rendered here as "by that which" and as "should", gives rise to different possible translations that are nonetheless substantively similar; it can be interpreted to mean that the Book and Wisdom are invoked in a covenant that binds a prophet, and by extension his followers, to follow a later true messenger, should he come confirming that which is with you. **[Study Quran]** Here "by that which I have given" is understood to be an oath. **[Study Quran]** Some commentators see this as a direct command to the various prophets to affirm Muhammad, should he appear during their own lifetime; the verse may actually be referring to the followers of the prophets, since prophets would never turn away or become iniquitous, though their followers might — that is, since belief in the Prophet Muhammad or any true prophet is incumbent upon prophets themselves, it is also incumbent upon their followers. **[Maʿārif]** In this there is the necessary refutation of the Christians, who claimed that it was the Messiah who asked them to have belief in his sonship and godhead; also chastised were the Muslims who had gone to the Holy Prophet ﷺ trying to find out if it was all right for them to prostrate before him rather than greet him with the usual *salām*; and also admonished were the People of the Book who had invested their rabbis and monks with the station of God. *(Tafsīr ʿUthmānī; Maʿārif's block covers 3:79–3:84 as a single unit)*

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** Read *lamā*, it introduces a subject clause and emphasises the oath; read *limā*, it connects to the verb "He took"; the *mā* is a relative in both cases. **[Qurṭubī]** The *mā* in *lamā* has the sense of *alladhī*; Sībawayh said: I asked al-Khalīl b. Aḥmad about "and when God took the covenant of the prophets, *lamā* I have given you of Book and wisdom", and he said: *lamā* means *alladhī*. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Naḥḥās said: the estimate, on al-Khalīl's view, is "la-lladhī ātaytukumūhu", the pronoun then being elided because of the length of the noun; *alladhī* is nominative as the subject and "of Book and wisdom" is its predicate, with *min* specifying the genus — like one's saying "la-Zaydun afḍalu minka"; and this is al-Akhfash's view, that it is the *lām* of inception. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mahdawī said: "then there comes to you" and what follows is a clause conjoined to the relative clause, the resumptive pronoun to the relative being elided, the estimate being "then there comes to you a messenger confirming *it*". **[Ṭabarī]** The readers of the Hijaz and Iraq generally read *lamā* with the *lām* vowelled *fatḥah*, though they differ over "ātaytukum": some read it in the singular and others read "ātaynākum" in the plural. **[Ṭabarī]** Some Basran grammarians said: the *lām* that is with *mā* at the beginning of the speech is the *lām* of inception, as in "la-Zaydun afḍalu minka", because *mā* is a noun and what follows it is its relative clause; and the *lām* in "you shall believe in him and you shall help him" is the *lām* of the oath — as though He said "by God, you shall believe in him" — so that the speech is emphasised at its beginning and at its end. **[Ṭabarī]** And some Kufan grammarians declared all of that erroneous, and said: the *lām* that enters at the beginnings of apodoses is answered by the answers of oaths — one says "la-man qāma la-ātiyannahu". **[Ibn Kathīr]** *Isrī* is "My covenant", according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ, Qatādah and al-Suddī; and Muḥammad b. Isḥāq glossed it as the ratified pledge given to God.

**Readings.** **[Ṭabarī]** The generality of the readers of the Hijaz and Iraq read *lamā* with *fatḥah* on the *lām*; and they differed over "I have given you" — some reading *ātaytukum* in the singular and others *ātaynākum*, "We have given you", in the plural. **[Jalālayn]** *Ātaytukum* is also read *ātaynākum*, "We have given you". **[Qurṭubī]** And Ibn Masʿūd read "and when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book" (3:187).

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7335 — from Ibn Ṭāwūs, from his father, on "and when God took the covenant of the prophets: whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom": God took the covenant of the prophets that they should affirm one another; then He said, "then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you — you shall believe in him and you shall help him" — and this verse, he said, is for the People of the Scripture: God took their covenant that they should believe in Muḥammad ﷺ and affirm him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7336 — Qatādah: God took from the prophets their covenant that they should affirm one another and that they should convey the Book of God and His message to His servants; so the prophets conveyed the Book of God and His messages to their peoples, and they took the covenants of the People of the Scripture — in their Book — [to believe in Muḥammad ﷺ]. *(the report continues)* **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī answers the argument of al-Rabīʿ b. Anas that the People of the Scripture must be meant, from the words "you shall believe in him and you shall help him": that is not evidence for the soundness of what he said, because the prophets were commanded to affirm one another, and their affirming one another is a helping of one another. **[Ṭabarī]** And against the same doubt he argues: it is the same whether a person says "their Lord did not take that covenant from them" or "He did not command them to convey what they were sent with" — for both are reports from God about them, one that He took from them and the other that He commanded them; so if doubt were admissible in one of them, it would be admissible in the other. **[Ibn Kathīr]** ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and his cousin ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAbbās said: "Allāh never sent a Prophet but after taking his pledge that if Muḥammad ﷺ were sent in his lifetime, he would believe in and support him; and Allāh commanded each Prophet to take a pledge from his nation that if Muhammad were sent in their time, they would believe in and support him." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ṭāwūs, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah said: "Allāh took the pledge from the Prophets that they would believe in each other" — and this statement does not contradict what ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās stated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Therefore Muḥammad is the Final Prophet ﷺ until the Day of Resurrection; he is the greatest Imām, who, if he existed in any time period, deserves to be obeyed rather than all other Prophets — and this is why Muḥammad ﷺ led the Prophets in prayer during the night of the Isrāʾ when they gathered in Bayt al-Maqdis, and why he is the intercessor on the Day of Gathering: that is the praised station (17:79) that only Muḥammad deserves, a responsibility which the mighty Prophets and Messengers will decline to assume. **[Qurṭubī]** The "messenger" here is Muḥammad ﷺ, in the saying of ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās; and though the word is indefinite, the reference is to a specific person — as in "and God strikes a similitude" *(the comparison continues)*.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The two reports about the prophets — that God took the covenant from them and that He commanded them to convey it — stand or fall together, so neither may be doubted in isolation. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The pledge covers both the prophet himself and, through him, his nation; and the universality of it is what makes Muḥammad ﷺ the imām of the prophets. **[Qurṭubī]** The covenant is that the prophets affirm one another — and that affirmation is itself the "help" named in the verse. **[Saʿdī]** This is a general matter among the prophets: their way is one, and the call of each of them is something they agreed upon and covenanted together; and generally, He took from all of them the covenant of belief in and help of Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Study Quran]** Commentators typically emphasise that it is the Prophet Muhammad to whom reference is made here, though al-Rāzī acknowledges that the covenant pertains to any prophet who fulfils the criteria in the verse.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 7:157 for the foretelling of the Prophet inscribed in the Torah and the Gospel; 17:79 for the praised station. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 17:79 for al-Maqām al-Maḥmūd. **[Ṭabarī]** 1:414 and 2:156–157, 288 for the root meaning of *mīthāq*; 3:79–80 for the preceding verses. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:187 for the variant reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd. **[Saʿdī]** 3:82 for the threat that follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:82 for the consequence.

**Reflection.** The verse is famous and harder than it looks, and the argument the commentators have about it is worth following **[Study Quran]**. It turns on one pronoun: who is the "you" in "then there comes to you a messenger"? Al-Ṭabarī sets out three positions patiently — the prophets themselves, pledged to one another; the People of the Scripture, pledged to Muḥammad ﷺ; and a mixed reading on which the covenant is taken from the prophets and the message clause is then addressed to their communities **[Ṭabarī]**. He also knocks down al-Rabīʿ b. Anas's proof, pointing out that "help" is not decisive, since the prophets affirming one another *is* a form of helping one another **[Ṭabarī]**. The report that carries the most weight in later tradition is the one Ibn Kathīr leads with: God never sent a prophet without taking his pledge that if Muḥammad ﷺ were sent in his lifetime he would believe in him and help him, and each prophet in turn took that pledge from his nation **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And there is a grammatical dispute underneath the theological one, about whether the opening *lām* is the *lām* of inception or the *lām* that introduces an apodosis answered like an oath **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]** — with al-Khalīl's reported answer to Sībawayh sitting at the centre of it.

## 3:82 — فَمَن تَوَلَّىٰ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْفَٰسِقُونَ

*"Then whoever turns away after that — those are the transgressors."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: so whoever turns away from belief in My messengers whom I sent to affirm what was with My prophets of the Books and the wisdom, and from helping them, and turns his back and does not believe in that and does not help, and breaks his covenant and his compact — "after that", meaning after the covenant and the compact which God took from him — "those are the transgressors", meaning: that those who turn away from belief in the messengers whose affair He has described, and from helping them, after the covenant and the compact which were taken from them for that, "are the transgressors" — meaning by that: those who go out of the religion of God and the obedience of their Lord. **[Jalālayn]** "Then whoever turns his back" in rejection "after that" covenant — "they are the wicked". **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Then whoever turns away after this" — from fulfilling this pledge and covenant — "they are the rebellious". **[Qurṭubī]** *Fa-man* is a conditional; so whoever turns away, of the communities of the prophets, from belief after the covenant was taken — "those are the transgressors", meaning: those who go out of belief; and *al-fāsiq* is the one who goes out. **[Saʿdī]** Whoever claims to be of the followers of the prophets — this is their religion which God took from them and which they affirmed and acknowledged; and whoever turns away from following Muḥammad ﷺ, from among those who claim to be of their followers, is a transgressor, outside the obedience of God, beliing the messenger he claims to follow, opposing his way. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And in this is the establishing of the proof and the demonstration against everyone who does not believe in Muḥammad ﷺ among the people of the books and the religions — and that they cannot believe in their messengers, whose followers they claim to be, until they believe in their leader and their seal ﷺ. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Fa-man* is a conditional particle, and *al-fāsiq* is the one who goes out. **[Ṭabarī]** "Turns away" is glossed as turning one's back and refusing to believe and to help, and "transgressors" as those who exit the religion of God and His obedience. **[Jalālayn]** The turning away is specified as rejection after the covenant.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7339 — from Sayf b. ʿUmar, from Abū Rawq, from Abū Ayyūb, from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib: "then whoever turns away from you, O Muḥammad, after this covenant, of all the communities — those are the transgressors", meaning: the disobedient in unbelief. *(weak: Sayf b. ʿUmar is generally held weak in transmission)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7340 — Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī, on "then whoever turns away after that": after the covenant and the compact which were taken from them — "those are the transgressors". **[Ṭabarī]** 7341 — al-Rabīʿ b. Anas said the like of it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAbbās said that Allāh never sent a Prophet but after taking his pledge that if Muḥammad ﷺ were sent in his lifetime he would believe in and support him, and that Allāh commanded each Prophet to take a pledge from his nation to the same effect. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:81–82)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** Transgression here is defined by exit — leaving the religion and the obedience of the Lord — not by any particular sin. **[Saʿdī]** The verse is the proof against anyone who claims to follow a prophet and refuses Muḥammad ﷺ: they cannot believe in the messenger they claim until they believe in their leader and seal. **[Qurṭubī]** The ones addressed are the communities of the prophets, and what they go out of is belief. **[Study Quran]** Since prophets would never turn away or become iniquitous, the verse is best understood as referring to their followers. *(the Study Quran's note for 3:81–82, cited at 3:81)*

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:81, with which this verse is paired; 7:157 for the foretelling. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:81 for the covenant referred to; 3:83 for what follows. **[Qurṭubī]** Volume 1, p. 244, for his treatment of *fāsiq*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:83, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:81 for the covenant.

**Reflection.** A single sentence, and its force comes almost entirely from the word "after" **[Ṭabarī]**. Turning away is not described in the abstract; it is turning away from a covenant that has just been sworn to, with God and the prophets both named as witnesses **[Jalālayn]**, **[Saʿdī]**. The commentators disagree about who can turn away, and the disagreement is not trivial: some take the address to be the prophets' communities, since a prophet would not do this, and the Study Quran notes that reading explicitly **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī's gloss of "transgressors" is the one worth keeping — those who *exit*, which is the literal sense of *fāsiq* and makes the word a description of departure rather than of vice **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. And al-Saʿdī draws the consequence that makes the verse uncomfortable for its original audience: no one can claim to follow Moses or Jesus while refusing the one their scriptures and their covenants point to **[Saʿdī]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:79–3:84 is a single unit on the infallibility of the prophets, cited at 3:79 and 3:81; it has nothing separate for 3:82. The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:82; its combined note for 3:81–82 is cited at 3:81.

## 3:83 — أَفَغَيْرَ دِينِ ٱللَّهِ يَبْغُونَ وَلَهُۥٓ أَسْلَمَ مَن فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ طَوْعًۭا وَكَرْهًۭا وَإِلَيْهِ يُرْجَعُونَ

*"Do they seek other than the religion of God, when to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they shall be returned?"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The interpretation of the speech is: O assembly of the People of the Scripture, "do you seek other than the religion of God?" — meaning: do you seek and desire other than the obedience of God? **[Ṭabarī]** "And to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth" — meaning: and to Him has become humble whoever is in the heavens and the earth, abasing himself to Him in servitude, acknowledging to Him the singling out of lordship, and yielding to Him in the sincerity of *tawḥīd* and divinity. **[Ṭabarī]** "Willingly or unwillingly" — meaning: there submitted to God willingly the one whose submission to Him was willing, and that is like the angels, the prophets and the messengers, for they submitted to God willingly; and "unwillingly" — the one among them who was unwilling. **[Jalālayn]** "What! Do they" — the ones who turn away — "desire" — *yabghūna* is also read *tabghūna*, "do you desire?" — "other than God's religion, when to Him has submitted", to Him has yielded, "whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly" without refusal, "or unwillingly", by the sword and by seeing what such refusal results in, "and to Him they shall be returned?" — *yurjaʿūna* may also be read *turjaʿūna*, "you shall be returned"; the *hamzah* at the beginning of the verse, *a-fa-ghayra*, denotes a disavowal. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh rebukes those who prefer a religion other than the religion that He sent His Books and Messengers with, which is the worship of Allāh alone without partners, to Whom "submitted all creatures in the heavens and the earth", willingly or not. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Therefore the faithful believer submits to Allāh in heart and body, while the disbeliever unwillingly submits to Him in body only, since he is under Allāh's power, irresistible control and mighty kingship that cannot be repelled or resisted. **[Qurṭubī]** "And to Him has submitted" — that is, He has surrendered, yielded, humbled himself and abased himself; and every creature is yielding and surrendering, because it is constituted upon what it cannot leave. **[Qurṭubī]** Qatādah said: the believer submits willingly, and the disbeliever at the time of his death submits unwillingly — and that does not benefit him, as in 40:85, "but their believing benefited them not when they saw Our Might". **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: the submission of the disbeliever unwillingly is by his prostrating to other than God, while his shadow prostrates to God — as in 16:48 and 13:15. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said the meaning is that God created creation as He willed from them, and among them are the good and the ugly **[and the obedient]**. *(the sentence continues in Qurṭubī)* **[Saʿdī]** It has already been set out in Sūrat al-Baqarah that these foundations, which are the foundations of faith which God commanded this community, are agreed upon by the Books and the messengers; that they are the aim directed at everyone, and that they are the religion and the true Islam. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** So whoever turns away from it and desires other than it — where will he go? To the worship of trees, stones and fires; or to the taking of rabbis, monks and crosses; or to the denial of the Lord of the worlds; or to the false religions which are from the whispering of devils? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** For some, "whosoever is in the heavens" refers to the angels, while those on the earth refer to human beings. **[Study Quran]** "Submits" (*aslama*) is the verbal form of *islām*, or "submission"; "willingly" (*ṭawʿan*) can also be rendered "obediently", while "unwillingly" (*karhan*) can mean "grudgingly". **[Study Quran]** In an apparent paradox, this verse asserts that all beings submit to God, and some do so unwillingly; some explain this by saying that all beings must in some sense succumb to God's Will, implying a passive rather than active submission; others mention that believers submit in life willingly, while disbelievers submit in death unwillingly — but their submission at the moment of death does them no good.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Religion" is glossed as obedience, and "submitted" as becoming humble, abasing oneself in servitude, acknowledging the singling out of lordship and yielding in the sincerity of *tawḥīd*. **[Jalālayn]** The opening *hamzah* of *a-fa-ghayra* denotes disavowal, and *ghayra* is in the accusative as the object of *yabghūna*. **[Qurṭubī]** *Aslama* is surrender, yielding, humility and abasement; and every creature is so constituted. **[Study Quran]** *Ṭawʿan* can be "obediently" and *karhan* can be "grudgingly".

**Readings.** **[Ṭabarī]** The readers differed: the generality of the readers of the Hijaz, Makkah and Madinah, and the readers of Kufa read *a-fa-ghayra dīni Allāhi tabghūna* and *wa-ilayhi turjaʿūna*, in the second person; some of the people of the Hijaz read both with the *yāʾ*, *yabghūna* and *yurjaʿūna*, as a report about the absent; and some of the people of Basrah read *yabghūna* as a report about the absent and *turjaʿūna* in the second person. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Ṭabarī: the reading I prefer is *tabghūna* in the second person with *turjaʿūna*, because the verse before it is an address to them, and following an address with its like is preferable to diverting the speech to what is not its like — though the other reading is admissible, since reported speech sometimes comes out entirely as address, sometimes entirely as a report about the absent, and sometimes partly one and partly the other. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū ʿAmr alone read *yabghūna* with the *yāʾ* as a report, and *turjaʿūna* with the *tāʾ* as address — because the first is specific and the second general, so he differentiated them as they differ in meaning. **[Qurṭubī]** Ḥafṣ and others read *yabghūna* and *yurjaʿūna* with the *yāʾ* in both, because of "those are the transgressors" [3:82]; and the rest read both with the *tāʾ* as address, because of "whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom" [3:81]. **[Jalālayn]** *Yabghūna* is also read *tabghūna*, "do you desire?"; and *yurjaʿūna* may also be read *turjaʿūna*.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** Wakīʿ reported that Mujāhid said that "while to Him submitted all creatures in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly" is similar to "And verily, if you ask them: 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' Surely, they will say: 'Allāh'" (39:38). **[Ibn Kathīr]** And he reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said about it: "When He took the covenant from them." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Kalbī said: Kaʿb b. al-Ashraf and his companions disputed with the Christians before the Prophet ﷺ and said, "Which of us has more right to the religion of Abraham?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Neither of the two parties is upon his religion." They said: "We are not satisfied with your judgement and we will not take your religion" — so "do they seek other than the religion of God?" was revealed, meaning "they seek". **[Qurṭubī]** Qatādah said: the believer submits willingly and the disbeliever at his death unwillingly, and it does not benefit him. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: the disbeliever's unwilling submission is by his prostrating to other than God while his shadow prostrates to God.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** Submission is universal in fact, but divided in kind: the angels, the prophets and the messengers submit willingly, and others unwillingly. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The believer submits in heart and body; the disbeliever submits in body only, being under a power he cannot resist. **[Qurṭubī]** The unwilling submission of the disbeliever at death profits him nothing, as 40:85 states. **[Study Quran]** The paradox is usually resolved by distinguishing passive from active submission, or by placing the disbeliever's submission at the moment of death. **[Saʿdī]** Turning away from this leaves nothing but the worship of created things, or the elevation of religious figures, or denial, or false religions.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 13:15, "And unto Allāh falls in prostration whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly"; 16:48–50; 39:38. **[Qurṭubī]** 40:85, "but their believing benefited them not when they saw Our Might"; 16:48; 13:15. **[Study Quran]** 41:11 and 13:15 for the willingness and unwillingness of those in the heavens and the earth; 22:18 for all creatures prostrating; 17:44 for all things glorifying God. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:81–82 for the address that precedes; 1:115, 221 and 6:273–274 for *dīn*.

**Reflection.** The verse is a question and the question is rhetorical, but two things in it are genuinely difficult and the commentators take them on **[Jalālayn]**. The first is the claim that everything in the heavens and the earth has *submitted*, which cannot mean that everything is Muslim **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī's reading is the cleanest: submission is universal, but the willing and the unwilling are different classes of being, with the angels and the messengers on one side **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Kathīr and Qurṭubī both prefer the sharper version — the believer submits in heart and body, the disbeliever in body only, because he is under a power he cannot resist — and both are careful to add that the disbeliever's submission at death does him no good **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Mujāhid's image is stranger and more memorable: the disbeliever prostrates to something other than God while his own shadow prostrates to God **[Qurṭubī]**. The second difficulty is the pronoun, and there is a real disagreement about whether the verse addresses them or reports about them, with al-Ṭabarī preferring the address and giving a reason that is purely stylistic — the verse before it is an address, so the address should continue **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. And al-Saʿdī's question at the end is the one the verse really asks: if not this, then what — trees, stones, fires, monks, or nothing at all **[Saʿdī]**?

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:79–3:84 is a single unit on the infallibility of the prophets, cited at 3:79 and 3:81; it has nothing separate for 3:83.

## 3:84 — قُلْ ءَامَنَّا بِٱللَّهِ وَمَآ أُنزِلَ عَلَيْنَا وَمَآ أُنزِلَ عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ وَإِسْمَٰعِيلَ وَإِسْحَٰقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَٱلْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَآ أُوتِىَ مُوسَىٰ وَعِيسَىٰ وَٱلنَّبِيُّونَ مِن رَّبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍۢ مِّنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُۥ مُسْلِمُونَ

*Say: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what Moses, Jesus and the prophets were given from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: "Do you seek other than the religion of God, O assembly of the Jews, when to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him you shall be returned?" — so if they seek other than the religion of God, O Muḥammad, then say to them: "We believe in God";
