and the mention of "if they say: yes", or the mention of "if they seek other than the religion of God", is omitted because what appears of the speech indicates it. **[Ṭabarī]** "Say: we believe in God" — say to them, O Muḥammad: we have affirmed that God is our Lord and our God, there is no god other than Him, and we worship none besides Him. **[Ṭabarī]** "And in what has been sent down to us" — and say: and we have also affirmed what has been sent down to us of His revelation, and we acknowledge it. **[Ṭabarī]** "And in what was sent down to Abraham" — and we have also affirmed what was sent down to Abraham, the Friend of God, and to his two sons Ishmael and Isaac, and to his son's son Jacob; and what was sent down to "the Tribes", who are the twelve children of Jacob — and we have set out their names sufficiently already. **[Ṭabarī]** "And what Moses and Jesus were given" — and we have also affirmed, along with that, what God sent down to Moses and Jesus of the Books and the revelation, and what He sent down to the prophets from Himself; and what God gave Moses and Jesus, of what God commanded Muḥammad ﷺ to affirm them in and believe in, is the Torah which He gave Moses and the Gospel which Jesus was given. **[Ṭabarī]** "We make no distinction between any of them" — we do not affirm some of them and deny others, and we do not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and the Christians disbelieved in some of God's prophets and affirmed others; but we believe in all of them and affirm them. **[Ṭabarī]** "And to Him we submit" — meaning: and we profess the religion of Islam to God, and we profess no other; rather, we declare ourselves quit before Him of every religion besides it and of every community other than it. **[Ṭabarī]** And by "we submit to Him" He means: we yield to Him in obedience, abase ourselves in servitude, and acknowledge to Him divinity and lordship, and that there is no god [other than Him]. *(the sentence continues in Ṭabarī)* **[Jalālayn]** "Say to them, O Muhammad: 'We believe in God and that which has been revealed to us and that which has been revealed to Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the Tribes', the latter's sons; 'and in that which was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord; we make no division between any of them', by believing in some and disbelieving in others; 'and to Him we submit'", devoting worship sincerely to Him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Say: 'We believe in Allāh and in what has been sent down to us'" — the Qurʾān; "and what was sent down to Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb" — the scriptures and revelation; "and the Asbāṭ" — the twelve tribes who originated from the twelve children of Isrāʾīl (Yaʿqūb); "and what was given to Mūsā, ʿĪsā" — the Tawrāh and the Injīl; "and the Prophets from their Lord" — and this encompasses all of Allāh's Prophets. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "We make no distinction between one another among them" — we believe in all of them; therefore faithful Muslims believe in every Prophet whom Allāh has sent and in every Book He revealed, and never disbelieve in any of them. **[Qurṭubī]** "And to Him we have submitted" — devoting worship sincerely to Him. *(Qurṭubī's block for 3:83–84 is a single unit; its material on the readings and on *aslama* is cited at 3:83)* **[Saʿdī]** These foundations, which are the foundations of faith which God commanded this community, are agreed upon by the Books and the messengers, and they are the religion and the true Islam. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** See 2:136, which is nearly identical with this verse, and commentary.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "The Tribes" are the twelve children of Jacob, whose names al-Ṭabarī says he has already set out; and "we make no distinction" is defined precisely as not affirming some and denying others. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "What was sent down to" is the scriptures and revelation; "what was given to Moses and Jesus" is the Torah and the Gospel; and "the prophets from their Lord" encompasses all of them.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is a creed with two halves: universal affirmation of every prophet and every book, and an exclusive profession of Islam to the exclusion of every other religion. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Muslims believe in every prophet sent and every book revealed, and disbelieve in none of them. **[Jalālayn]** "We make no division" is glossed as not believing in some and disbelieving in others. **[Saʿdī]** The foundations named here are the ones upon which all the Books and all the messengers agree.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:136, which is nearly identical. **[Ṭabarī]** 2:120–121 and 3:111–113 for the names of the Tribes; 3:83 for the verse that occasions this. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:85, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:83 for the setting. **[Saʿdī]** Sūrat al-Baqarah for the foundations.

**Reflection.** This is one of the two nearly identical declarations of the Muslim creed in the Qurʾān, and al-Ṭabarī is careful about where it begins: it is not a free-standing statement but an answer, given when the People of the Scripture seek a religion other than God's **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The grammar he notes is small but telling — a condition is omitted because the sense supplies it, so that what is said is "say: we believe in God" where what is meant is "if they persist, say this" **[Ṭabarī]**. The list is deliberately long and deliberately uneven: patriarchs, then the Tribes, then Moses and Jesus specifically, then every prophet — which is what makes the closing clause bite **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And the closing clause is the one the commentators dwell on: "we make no distinction between any of them" is defined as refusing to do exactly what the Jews and Christians did, affirming some messengers and denying others **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Jalālayn]**. Saʿdī's framing is the useful one — these are the foundations on which all the Books and all the messengers agree, so affirming them is not a new religion but the old one stated whole **[Saʿdī]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:79–3:84 is a single unit on the infallibility of the prophets, cited at 3:79 and 3:81; it has nothing separate for 3:84. Qurṭubī likewise treats 3:83–84 as one block, whose readings material is cited at 3:83.

## 3:85 — وَمَن يَبْتَغِ غَيْرَ ٱلْإِسْلَٰمِ دِينًۭا فَلَن يُقْبَلَ مِنْهُ وَهُوَ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ مِنَ ٱلْخَٰسِرِينَ

*"And whoever seeks a religion other than submission, it shall not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by this: and whoever seeks a religion other than the religion of Islam to profess, God will not accept it from him. **[Ṭabarī]** "And in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers" — meaning: among those who defraud themselves of their portion of the mercy of God. **[Jalālayn]** The following was revealed regarding those who apostatized and became disbelievers: "Whoever desires a religion other than Islam, it shall not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he shall be among the losers", because he will end up in the Fire made everlasting for him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted of him" — whoever seeks other than what Allāh has legislated, it will not be accepted from him; "and in the Hereafter he will be one of the losers". **[Ibn Kathīr]** As the Prophet ﷺ said in an authentic ḥadīth: "Whoever commits an action that does not conform to our matter (religion), then it is rejected." **[Qurṭubī]** *Ghayra* is the object of *yabtaghi*, and *dīnan* is in the accusative as a specification; and it is admissible that *dīnan* is in the accusative by *yabtaghi*, with *ghayra* in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the religion. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid and al-Suddī said: this verse was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, the brother of al-Ḥullās b. Suwayd, who was of the Anṣār, and who apostatised from Islam together with twelve others and joined Makkah as disbelievers — so this verse was revealed, and then he sent to his brother seeking repentance; and that is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and others. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: and he embraced Islam after the verses were revealed. **[Saʿdī]** And whoever seeks other than these foundations, his work is rejected and he has no religion to rely upon — and all of these, in the Hereafter, are among the losers. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The literal meaning of "Islam" is submission and obedience; as a term, "Islam" stands for submission to that particular religion which God has sent through His prophets to guide human beings, because the fundamental principles are the same in the religious codes of all the prophets. **[Maʿārif]** Correspondingly, there are occasions when "Islam" is used in that general sense, while there are other occasions when it is used exclusively to identify the Last Sharīʿah which was revealed to the Last of the Prophets — and both kinds of application are present in the Qurʾān. **[Maʿārif]** That the past prophets called themselves "Muslim" and their communities the "Muslim" community stands proved under the authority of several wordings of the Qurʾānic text: "It was He who named you Muslims before, and in this (Qurʾān)" (22:78). **[Study Quran]** It is reported that this verse was revealed in connection with one of the Companions who left Islam along with twelve other people and went to Makkah. **[Study Quran]** Although some commentators record the opinion that considers 2:62 to have been abrogated by this verse, this type of abrogation is not recognized by mainstream Islamic Law and Quran interpretation, since only a ruling or legal command can be abrogated, not a truth or a report. **[Study Quran]** However, the idea that 3:85 abrogates 2:62 is connected to the interpretation expressed by some commentators that this verse denies the "acceptability" of any form of religion other than that brought by the Prophet Muhammad — an opinion not without its inconsistencies, since it does not take into account the more general and universal use of *islām* and *muslim* in the Quran to refer to all true, monotheistic religion.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Ghayra* is the object of *yabtaghi* and *dīnan* is a specification; alternately, *dīnan* is the object of *yabtaghi* and *ghayra* is a circumstantial qualifier. **[Qurṭubī]** Hishām said, on "and he in the Hereafter is among the losers": meaning he is a loser in the Hereafter, among the losers — and were it not for this I would have separated the relative clause from its antecedent; and al-Māzinī said: the *alif* and *lām* are as they are in "the man". **[Maʿārif]** "Islam" means submission and obedience literally, and as a term stands for submission to the religion sent through the prophets, since the fundamentals are the same in all their codes.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7356 — ʿIkrimah said, on "and whoever seeks a religion other than Islam": the religious communities said, "We are the Muslims!" — so God sent down "and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by all people who are able to make their way to it; and whoever disbelieves, God is in no need of the worlds" (3:97), and so the Muslims performed the pilgrimage and the disbelievers sat. **[Ṭabarī]** 7357 — ʿIkrimah, through another chain: "and whoever seeks a religion other than Islam as a religion, it shall not be accepted from him" — the Jews said, "Then we are the Muslims!" — so God sent down, that His prophet ﷺ might argue against them: "and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by all people who are able to make their way to it; and whoever disbelieves, God is in no need of the worlds". **[Ṭabarī]** 7358 — ʿIkrimah, through a third chain: when "and whoever seeks a religion other than Islam" was revealed to the end of the verse, the Jews said, "Then we are Muslims!" — so God said to His prophet ﷺ: "Say to them: 'and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by all people who are able to make their way to it; and whoever disbelieves'" — of the people of the religious communities — "'God is in no need of the worlds'". *(the report continues)* **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid and al-Suddī: the verse was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, who apostatised with twelve others and joined Makkah; and Ibn ʿAbbās said that he embraced Islam after the verses were revealed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Prophet ﷺ said in an authentic ḥadīth: "Whoever commits an action that does not conform to our matter, then it is rejected."

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The losers are those who defraud themselves of their share of God's mercy. **[Maʿārif]** Whichever of the two senses of "Islam" is taken here does not differ much in outcome, since the "Islam" of earlier prophets was for a limited group and a specified period; when a prophet departed and was replaced, the Islam of that time ceased to be operative — whereas the Islam given through the Last Prophet ﷺ will remain unabrogable and permanent up to the Day of Judgement, and all previous religions stand abrogated after he was sent. **[Maʿārif]** It appears in authentic aḥādīth that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said: "Had Moses been living this day, following me would have been incumbent upon him too"; and in another ḥadīth, that Jesus, when he appears close to the Day of Resurrection, will follow no code other than his. **[Study Quran]** In 2:62 the issue is whether *īmān* can be applied to Jews, Christians and Sabeans, while in this verse the question is whether *islām* can include others beyond the followers of the Prophet Muhammad — and opinions seem to leave the interpretation open. **[Study Quran]** Ibn Kathīr understands "a religion other than submission" here to mean "a path other than what God has laid down", which can include the People of the Book; al-Zamakhsharī says that in this verse *islām* means recognising Divine Unity and submitting one's face to God, attributes not limited to the followers of Muhammad. **[Study Quran]** Reading the verse in the context of those that precede and follow it, and taking the occasion of revelation into account, one could reasonably conclude that its scope is limited to those who, after having accepted Islam, then make a conscious decision to leave it.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:62 and 2:62c; 2:128c; 2:131–32c; 3:19c; 3:52c; 5:111c. **[Maʿārif]** 22:78, "It was He who named you Muslims before, and in this". **[Ṭabarī]** 3:97 for the pilgrimage verse; 3:83–84 for the verses that precede. **[Qurṭubī]** Volume 2, p. 133, for the parallel "and he in the Hereafter is among the righteous" (2:130). **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:86, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:86–89 for the apostates' case.

**Reflection.** Everything here turns on the scope of one word, and the commentators know it **[Study Quran]**. Maʿārif sets out the two senses of "Islam" — the general one, submission to whatever religion God sent through any prophet, and the specific one, the final Sharīʿah — and then argues that the difference does not ultimately matter, because the earlier codes were for their time and ceased when their prophet's successor came, while the last one does not **[Maʿārif]**. The Study Quran is more cautious and records the disagreement plainly, including the view that 3:85 abrogates 2:62 and the standard objection that a report cannot be abrogated, only a ruling **[Study Quran]**. The occasion of revelation narrows the field: al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd and twelve others left Islam for Makkah, and the Study Quran notes that reading the verse in its context would limit it to those who leave Islam after accepting it **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. And al-Ṭabarī preserves a report that is easy to miss and rather wonderful in its bluntness — when the verse came down, every community claimed to be the Muslims, so God sent down the pilgrimage verse, and the Muslims went and the others stayed home **[Ṭabarī]**. It is a test, in other words: the claim is settled by practice, not by argument.

## 3:86 — كَيْفَ يَهْدِى ٱللَّهُ قَوْمًۭا كَفَرُوا۟ بَعْدَ إِيمَٰنِهِمْ وَشَهِدُوٓا۟ أَنَّ ٱلرَّسُولَ حَقٌّۭ وَجَآءَهُمُ ٱلْبَيِّنَٰتُ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهْدِى ٱلْقَوْمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ

*"How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and bore witness that the Messenger is true, and the clear proofs came to them? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over who is meant by this verse and concerning whom it was revealed. **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: it was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd al-Anṣārī, who was a Muslim and then apostatised after his Islam. **[Jalālayn]** "How shall God guide" — that is to say, He shall not guide — "a people who have disbelieved after their belief and bore witness", that is, and after their bearing witness that the Messenger is true, "and after the clear signs" — the manifest proofs of the truth of the Prophet — "had come to them? God guides not the evildoing", that is, the disbelieving, folk. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "How shall Allāh guide a people who disbelieved after their belief and after they bore witness that the Messenger is true and after clear proofs came to them?" — means: the proofs and evidences were established, testifying to the truth of what the Messenger was sent with; the truth was thus explained to them, but they reverted to the darkness of polytheism; therefore, how can such people deserve guidance after they willingly leapt into utter blindness? **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is why Allāh said, "And Allāh guides not the people who are wrongdoers." **[Qurṭubī]** "How" is a word of interrogation whose meaning is negation — that is, God does not guide; and its parallel is "How can there be a covenant with God and with His Messenger for the idolaters?" (9:7), meaning: they have no covenant — and as the poet said: "How can I sleep on a bed when the raid has not yet engulfed the people?", meaning: there is no sleep for me. **[Saʿdī]** It is far, utterly far, that God should guide a people who knew faith, entered into it, and bore witness that the Messenger is true, then turned back on their heels, retreating and breaking. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Because they knew the truth and rejected it; and because whoever is described by this state, God punishes him with relapse and the overturning of the heart as a recompense for him, since he knew the truth and abandoned it, and preferred falsehood — so God gives him charge of what he took charge of for himself. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** On a superficial view of "How shall Allāh give guidance…", there emerges a doubt that whoever turns an apostate receives no guidance afterwards — although the fact is contrary to this, for there are many who, after having become apostates, re-embrace the faith and become recipients of guidance. **[Maʿārif]** The answer is that the withholding of guidance mentioned here is in accordance with common usage: for instance, some criminal, when punished by a certain ruler, may say, "I have been given special treatment by the ruler with his own hands" — and in answer to him it is said: "Why are we going to give special treatment to such a criminal?", that is, there is just no special treatment called for in this case, while it does not mean that such a person cannot in any way become deserving of special treatment even if he behaved well. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** "People" refers to either apostates or the People of the Book; those who uphold the former interpretation point to the case of a Companion who left Islam and went to Makkah, but later repented, returned to Islam and was accepted — his repentance is mentioned in 3:89, "except those who repent after that". **[Study Quran]** The clause beginning "having borne witness" could also be translated "and who bore witness that the Messenger is true; and that clear proofs came to them".

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** "How" is formally an interrogative but carries the sense of negation, with 9:7 and a line of poetry as parallels. **[Jalālayn]** "The clear signs" are the manifest proofs of the truth of the Prophet, and "the evildoing" folk are the disbelieving folk. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The proofs and evidences are those testifying to the truth of what the Messenger was sent with. **[Saʿdī]** The verb is glossed as something utterly remote rather than strictly impossible.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7360 — from Dāwūd b. Abī Hind, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās: a man of the Anṣār embraced Islam, then apostatised and joined the idolaters; then he regretted it and sent to his people: "Send to the Messenger of God ﷺ — is there any repentance for me?" — so "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" was revealed, up to "and God is Forgiving, Merciful" [3:89], and his people sent to him and he embraced Islam. **[Ṭabarī]** 7361 — the like of it through another chain, though not raised to Ibn ʿAbbās — except that he said: his people wrote to him, and he said, "My people have not lied to me!" and he returned. **[Ṭabarī]** 7362 — the like of it, through a third chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Ṭabarī]** 7363 — Mujāhid said: al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd came and embraced Islam with the Prophet ﷺ, then al-Ḥārith disbelieved and returned to his people; so God sent down the Qurʾān concerning him, "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" up to "except those who repent after that and make amends, for God is Forgiving, Merciful" — and a man of his people carried it to him and read it to him, and al-Ḥārith said: "By God, I have known you to be truthful; and the Messenger of God ﷺ is more truthful than you; and God is the most truthful of the three" — and he returned. *(the report continues)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Jarīr recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "A man from the Anṣār embraced Islam, but later reverted and joined the polytheists. He later became sorry and sent his people to ask the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ if he could repent" — and then 3:86 up to 3:89 was revealed, and his people sent word to him, and he re-embraced Islam. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is the wording recorded by al-Nasāʾī, al-Ḥākim and Ibn Ḥibbān; al-Ḥākim said: "Its chain is Ṣaḥīḥ, and they did not record it." **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: a man of the Anṣār embraced Islam, then apostatised and joined the idolaters, then regretted it and sent to his people — "ask the Messenger of God ﷺ for me, is there any repentance for me?" — and "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" was revealed up to "Forgiving, Merciful", so he sent to him and he embraced Islam; al-Nasāʾī recorded it. **[Qurṭubī]** And in one version: a man of the Anṣār apostatised and joined the idolaters, so God sent down "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved" up to "except those who repent" [3:89], and his people sent it to him; and when it was read to him he said: "By God, my people did not lie to me about the Messenger of God ﷺ, and I do not deny the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning God — and God is the most truthful of the three" — and he returned repentant, and the Messenger of God ﷺ accepted it from him and left him. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, because they used to give good tidings of the Prophet ﷺ and seek victory through him over those who disbelieved — but when he was sent they were obstinate and disbelieved, so God sent down "Those — their recompense is that upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind all together" [3:87].

**Belief.** **[Qurṭubī]** "How" is a negation: God does not guide such a people. **[Maʿārif]** The negation is to be taken in the ordinary way of speaking rather than as an absolute impossibility, since apostates do in fact return to guidance — the point is that there is nothing in this case that calls for it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The reasoning is that the proofs were established and the truth was explained, and they then chose blindness knowingly. **[Saʿdī]** The punishment fits the fault: having known the truth and abandoned it, they are left with what they chose. **[Study Quran]** The verse is read either of apostates or of the People of the Book.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 9:7, "How can there be a covenant with God and with His Messenger for the idolaters?" as the parallel for the negating "how". **[Study Quran]** 3:85 for the Companion who left; 3:89 for his repentance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:87 for the recompense. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:85 for the beginning of the story; 3:87–89 for what follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:87–88 for the curse.

**Reflection.** The verse opens with "how", and the first thing the commentators settle is that it is not a question **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Jalālayn]**. But the negation is sharper than a plain "God does not guide", because the verse supplies the reason: they believed, they bore witness that the Messenger is true, the clear proofs reached them — and then they turned back **[Ibn Kathīr]**. That is why the sentence reads as an argument rather than a verdict. The reports give it a face and a name — al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, who apostatised with twelve others, who sent to ask whether repentance was possible, and who, when the verses were read to him, reasoned his way back: his people would not lie to him, the Messenger would not lie about God, and God is the most truthful of the three **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Maʿārif raises the obvious objection — apostates do return — and answers it with an analogy about a criminal and "special treatment", concluding that the verse says there is nothing here that calls for guidance, not that guidance is impossible **[Maʿārif]**. And al-Ḥasan's alternative reading, recorded by Qurṭubī, sets the verse against the Jews who used to pray for victory through the Prophet and then rejected him when he came **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:87 — أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ جَزَآؤُهُمْ أَنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةَ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ

*"Those — their recompense is that upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind all together."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** "Those — their requital is that there shall rest on them the curse of God and of the angels and of men altogether." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "They are those whose recompense is that on them rests the curse of Allāh, of the angels and of all mankind" — Allāh curses them, and His creation also curses them. **[Qurṭubī]** That is, if they persist in their unbelief; and the meaning of the curse of God and of mankind has already been set out in Sūrat al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating it. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over who is meant by this verse and concerning whom it was revealed — some said al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, and others the Jews. *(Ṭabarī's block covers 3:86–89; the dispute is set out at 3:86)* **[Saʿdī]** Those — upon them is the curse of God and of the angels and of mankind all together. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** On being cursed — widely interpreted to mean being distanced from God and driven away from mercy — see 2:161c, where the joint curse of God, the angels and human beings is also discussed. **[Study Quran]** See also 7:38, "Every time a community enters [the Fire], it curses its sister", and 29:25, "Then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another, and you will curse one another". **(the Study Quran's note covers 3:87–88)**

**[Ṭabarī]** 7369 — al-Ḥasan, on "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" — the whole verse: the Jews and the Christians. **[Ṭabarī]** 7370 — Qatādah said: al-Ḥasan used to say, on this verse: they are the People of the Scripture among the Jews and the Christians; they saw the description of Muḥammad ﷺ in their Book and acknowledged it and bore witness that it was true; but when he was sent from other than them they envied the Arabs for that, and so they denied him and disbelieved after their acknowledgement — out of envy of the Arabs, because he was sent from other than them. **[Ṭabarī]** 7371 — from Maʿmar, from al-Ḥasan: they are the People of the Scripture; they used to find Muḥammad ﷺ in their Book and seek victory through him, then they disbelieved after their belief. **[Ṭabarī]** 7368 — from Ibn ʿAbbās, on "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief": they are the People of the Scripture, who knew Muḥammad ﷺ and then disbelieved in him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7364 — al-Suddī said: it was revealed concerning al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd al-Anṣārī, who disbelieved after his belief, and God sent down these verses concerning him, up to "those are the companions of the Fire; they abide therein" — then he repented and embraced Islam, and God abrogated it for him, saying "except those who repent after that and make amends, for God is Forgiving, Merciful".

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** "Requital" (*jazāʾ*) is the noun of recompense, and the curse rests *upon* them. **[Study Quran]** "Cursed" is widely interpreted to mean being distanced from God and driven away from mercy. **[Qurṭubī]** The curse is conditional on their persisting in unbelief.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, because they used to give good tidings of the Prophet ﷺ and seek victory through him over those who disbelieved — but when he was sent they were obstinate and disbelieved, so God sent down "Those — their recompense is that upon them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of mankind all together". *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:86–89; the report is placed at 3:86)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7360 — from Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿIkrimah: the man of the Anṣār who apostatised sent asking whether there was repentance for him, and these verses were revealed down to "and God is Forgiving, Merciful"; his people sent to him and he embraced Islam. *(the report is cited in full at 3:86)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh curses them and His creation also curses them.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The curse is God's, and the creation's as well. **[Study Quran]** To be cursed is to be distanced from God and driven away from mercy. **[Ṭabarī]** The reports divide the referent between the apostate — al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd and his companions — and the People of the Scripture who acknowledged the description of Muḥammad ﷺ and then denied him when he was sent. **[Qurṭubī]** The sentence is conditional on persisting — it is not pronounced over those who return. **[Saʿdī]** The curse is the recompense named for the state described in 3:86.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:161c for the joint curse of God, the angels and human beings; 7:38; 29:25. **[Qurṭubī]** Volume 2, p. 188, for his treatment of the curse of God and of mankind in Sūrat al-Baqarah; 3:88–89 for what follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:86 for the people described; 3:88, which continues. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:86 for the identification of those meant. **[Saʿdī]** 3:86 for the state and 3:88 for the duration.

**Reflection.** The verse is short and the commentators treat it as the second half of a sentence begun in 3:86 — "those" picks up the apostates and names what they get **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Jalālayn]**. What is striking is the breadth of it: the curse is not God's alone but the angels' and all mankind's, which is to say that the one who knowingly abandons the truth after seeing it is abandoned by everything **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**. Qurṭubī's one-word qualification matters a great deal — "that is, if they persist in their unbelief" — because it is what keeps the verse from contradicting 3:89, where the same people are offered repentance **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ḥasan's reading, which applies the verse to the Jews who had prayed for victory through the Prophet and then rejected him, gives the curse a particular edge: it is pronounced on people who had once wanted exactly what they later refused **[Qurṭubī]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:86–3:91 is a single unit; its discussion of the apparent difficulty in "How shall God guide…" belongs to 3:86, and it has nothing separate for 3:87.

## 3:88 — خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَا لَا يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ ٱلْعَذَابُ وَلَا هُمْ يُنظَرُونَ

*"Abiding therein — the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be reprieved."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** "Abiding therein" — that is, in the curse, or in the Fire implied by the curse — "the chastisement shall not be lightened for them, and they shall not be reprieved", they shall not be given any respite. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "They will abide therein" — in the curse — "neither will their torment be lightened nor will it be delayed or postponed"; for the torment will not be lessened, not even for an hour. **[Qurṭubī]** "Nor shall they be reprieved" — that is, they are not deferred and not given more time. **[Qurṭubī]** Then He excepted those who repent, saying "except those who repent" [3:89] — and that is al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, as has already been mentioned; and everyone who returns to Islam and is sincere enters into the verse by its meaning. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over who is meant by these verses and concerning whom they were revealed. *(Ṭabarī's block covers 3:86–89; the dispute is set out at 3:86)* **[Saʿdī]** Abiding in the curse and the punishment, "the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be given respite" — when the command of God comes to them, because God gave them a long life in which to remember what is to be remembered, and the warner came to them. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **(the Study Quran's block for 3:87–88 is cited at 3:87)**

**[Ṭabarī]** 7367 — Ibn Jurayj reported from Mujāhid that the man was one of the Banū ʿAmr b. ʿAwf who disbelieved after his belief; and ʿAbdullāh b. Kathīr reported from Mujāhid that he joined the land of the Byzantines and became a Christian, and then wrote to his people: "Send word — is there any repentance for me?" **[Ṭabarī]** And Ibn Jurayj reported from ʿIkrimah that it was revealed concerning Abū ʿĀmir al-Rāhib, al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd b. al-Ṣāmit and Waḥwaḥ b. al-Aslat — twelve men who turned back from Islam and joined Quraysh, then wrote to their families, "Is there any repentance for us?" — and "except those who repented after that", the verses, were revealed. **[Ṭabarī]** 7364 — al-Suddī said that these verses came down concerning al-Ḥārith down to "they abide therein", and that he then repented and it was lifted from him. *(digression: the reports differ over whether al-Ḥārith's Islam was good thereafter — one chain adds "and his Islam was good")*

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** The pronoun of "therein" is referred either to the curse or to the Fire that the curse implies. **[Qurṭubī]** "They are not reprieved" means they are not deferred and not granted more time. **[Saʿdī]** The reason given for the absence of respite is that they were given the time and the warner already.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7363 — Mujāhid said: al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd came and embraced Islam with the Prophet ﷺ, then disbelieved and returned to his people; so God sent down the Qurʾān concerning him, "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" up to "except those who repent after that and make amends, for God is Forgiving, Merciful" — and a man of his people carried it to him and read it to him, and al-Ḥārith said: "By God, I have known you to be truthful; and the Messenger of God ﷺ is more truthful than you; and God is the most truthful of the three" — and he returned. *(the report is cited in full at 3:86)* **[Qurṭubī]** It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd sent asking whether there was repentance for him, and that these verses were revealed down to "Forgiving, Merciful" — and the exception in 3:89 is him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Nasāʾī, al-Ḥākim and Ibn Ḥibbān recorded the report of the man of the Anṣār who apostatised, sent asking about repentance, and returned when the verses reached him; al-Ḥākim graded its chain ṣaḥīḥ. *(the report is cited in full at 3:86)*

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The abiding is in the curse, and neither lessening nor postponement applies — not even for an hour. **[Qurṭubī]** The exception that follows shows that theverse is not the last word on a person, and that anyone who returns to Islam and is sincere falls within it by meaning. **[Saʿdī]** The absence of respite is justified by the fact that the time and the warning were both already given. **[Jalālayn]** "Abiding" is referred to the curse or to the Fire implied by it.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 3:89 for the exception; 3:86–87 for the people described. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:87 for the curse in which they abide; 3:89, which follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:86–87 for the setting. **[Saʿdī]** 3:89 for the repentance that follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:87 for the referent of "therein".

**Reflection.** Two negations, and together they close every exit: the punishment is not lightened, and it is not postponed **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The first removes the hope that it might ease; the second removes the hope that it might wait **[Qurṭubī]**. There is a small grammatical hesitation recorded by Jalālayn about what "therein" refers to — the curse just named, or the Fire that the curse implies — and the hesitation is itself instructive, since on either reading the abiding is in a state rather than a place alone **[Jalālayn]**. Al-Saʿdī supplies the reason the verse's own logic requires: they had already been given a long life and a warner, so there is nothing left to defer **[Saʿdī]**. And the verse must be read with the one that follows, which Qurṭubī insists on: the exception is announced in the very next words, and it is the same man **[Qurṭubī]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:86–3:91 is a single unit, whose discussion belongs to 3:86; and the Study Quran has no separate block for 3:88 — its combined note for 3:87–88 is cited at 3:87.

## 3:89 — إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ تَابُوا۟ مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ وَأَصْلَحُوا۟ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌ

*"Except those who repent after that and make amends — for God is Forgiving, Merciful."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** "But those who repent thereafter and make amends" in their actions — "then truly God is Forgiving, Merciful" to them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Except for those who repent after that and do righteous deeds. Verily, Allāh is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" — this verse indicates Allāh's kindness, graciousness, compassion, mercy and favour on His creatures when they repent to Him, for He forgives them in this case. **[Qurṭubī]** Then He excepted those who repent, saying "except those who repent" — and that is al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, as has already been mentioned; and everyone who returns to Islam and is sincere enters into the verse by its meaning. **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over who is meant by these verses — some said al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, and others the Jews. *(Ṭabarī's block covers 3:86–89; the dispute is set out at 3:86)* **[Saʿdī]** Then He, exalted is He, excepted from this threat those who repent from their unbelief and their sins and mend their faults — for God forgives them what they have sent ahead and pardons them what they have done before. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The Companion who left Islam reportedly wrote a letter to his family asking if repentance was possible, and this verse was revealed.

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** "Make amends" is glossed as amending their actions. **[Qurṭubī]** The exception is particular in its occasion and general in its meaning. **[Saʿdī]** "Mend" is glossed as mending faults, and the forgiveness covers what has been sent ahead.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7360 — from Dāwūd b. Abī Hind, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās: a man of the Anṣār embraced Islam, then apostatised and joined the idolaters; then he regretted it and sent to his people, "Send to the Messenger of God ﷺ — is there any repentance for me?" — so "How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" was revealed, down to "and God is Forgiving, Merciful", and his people sent to him and he embraced Islam. **[Ṭabarī]** 7363 — Mujāhid said: a man of al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd's people carried the verses to him and read them to him, and al-Ḥārith said: "By God, I have known you to be truthful; and the Messenger of God ﷺ is more truthful than you; and God is the most truthful of the three" — and he returned. *(the report is cited in full at 3:86)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Jarīr recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that the man of the Anṣār who apostatised sent his people to ask the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ if he could repent, and then these verses were revealed, and his people sent word to him and he re-embraced Islam. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is the wording recorded by al-Nasāʾī, al-Ḥākim and Ibn Ḥibbān; al-Ḥākim said: "Its chain is Ṣaḥīḥ, and they did not record it." **[Qurṭubī]** In one version: when the verses were read to him he said, "By God, my people did not lie to me about the Messenger of God ﷺ, and I do not deny the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning God — and God is the most truthful of the three" — and he returned repentant, and the Messenger of God ﷺ accepted it from him and left him. *(the report is cited in full at 3:86)*

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Although the occasion is one man, everyone who returns to Islam and is sincere falls within the exception by its meaning.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse is evidence of God's kindness, graciousness, compassion and mercy to His creatures when they repent. **[Saʿdī]** What is forgiven is what they sent ahead, and the amendment is of their faults. **[Qurṭubī]** The exception is general in meaning even though particular in occasion. **[Jalālayn]** The condition is repentance and amendment.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:85–86 for the Companion's story. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:86–88 for the threat from which this is the exception; 3:90, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:86 for al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd; 3:90 for the contrasting case. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:86 for the setting. **[Saʿdī]** 3:90 for those who persist.

**Reflection.** Four words do an enormous amount of work: "except those who repent" **[Qurṭubī]**. The threat in 3:86–88 is absolute in its phrasing — curse, abiding, no lightening, no reprieve — and then it is qualified in a single clause **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The commentators are emphatic that the exception is not a loophole attached to one man: Qurṭubī says plainly that although it came down about al-Ḥārith b. Suwayd, everyone who returns to Islam and is sincere enters it by meaning **[Qurṭubī]**. The story that carries it is one of the best in the sūrah — a man who left, who wanted to come back, who was too ashamed to ask directly, and who reasoned his way to belief from the reliability of the people who brought him the verses **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And the two conditions are kept together, as Jalālayn and al-Saʿdī both note: repentance and amendment, turning back and mending what was broken **[Jalālayn]**, **[Saʿdī]**. Immediately after this, 3:90 describes the case where neither happens.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:86–3:91 is a single unit, whose discussion belongs to 3:86; it has nothing separate for 3:89.

## 3:90 — إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ بَعْدَ إِيمَٰنِهِمْ ثُمَّ ٱزْدَادُوا۟ كُفْرًۭا لَّن تُقْبَلَ تَوْبَتُهُمْ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلضَّآلُّونَ

*"Those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief — their repentance shall not be accepted, and those are the astray."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The commentators differed over the interpretation of this. **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: God means by "those who disbelieved", [their disbelieving] in some of His prophets who were sent before Muḥammad ﷺ; "after their belief, then they increased in disbelief" — by their disbelieving in Muḥammad ﷺ; "their repentance shall not be accepted" — at the presence of death and its rattle in the throat. **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: the meaning is — those who disbelieved in Muḥammad, of the People of the Scripture, after their belief in their own prophets; "then they increased in disbelief", meaning: in sins; "their repentance shall not be accepted" — from their sins, while they persist in unbelief. **[Jalālayn]** The following was revealed regarding the Jews: "Surely those who disbelieve in Jesus after they have believed in Moses, and then increase in unbelief" in Muḥammad ﷺ — "their repentance shall not be accepted" when they are drawing their last gasps of life, or when they have died as disbelievers; "those are the ones who go astray". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allāh threatens and warns those who revert to disbelief after they believed and who thereafter insist on disbelief until death; He states that in this case no repentance shall be accepted from them upon their death. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Never will their repentance be accepted. And they are those who went astray" — to those who abandon the path of truth for the path of wickedness. **[Qurṭubī]** Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and al-Ḥasan said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel and then increased in disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qurʾān. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians, who disbelieved in Muḥammad ﷺ after their belief in his description and his attributes — "then they increased in disbelief" by persisting in their unbelief. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: "they increased in disbelief" by the sins they acquired — and this is the choice of al-Ṭabarī, who holds it to concern the Jews. **[Qurṭubī]** "Their repentance shall not be accepted" is problematic, in view of "and He it is Who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons the evil deeds" (42:25) — so it is said the meaning is: their repentance shall not be accepted at the time of death; and al-Naḥḥās said: this is a good saying, as in "and of no effect is the repentance of those who continue to do evil deeds until death faces one of them, and he says, 'Now I repent'" (4:18) — and this is related from al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and ʿAṭāʾ. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: "their repentance shall not be accepted" refers to the repentance they were upon before they disbelieved, because the unbelief has nullified it. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: "their repentance shall not be accepted" if they repent from one unbelief to another unbelief; their repentance is accepted only when they repent to Islam. **[Saʿdī]** But whoever disbelieves and persists in his unbelief, and increases only in unbelief until he dies upon his unbelief — those are the astray ones from the path of guidance, the travellers of the path of wretchedness, and they have merited by this the painful punishment. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And they have no helper against the punishment of God; and even if they offered the earth full of gold to ransom themselves with, it would not avail them at all. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān, referring forward to 3:91)* **[Maʿārif]** The Companion who left Islam, and those like him, are excepted from the threat only if they repent; whoever persists has merited the punishment. *(Maʿārif's block covers 3:86–3:91 as a single unit; its discussion belongs to 3:86)* **[Study Quran]** "Their repentance shall not be accepted" can refer to those who repent only at the moment of death, as in 4:18; or it can mean that any repentance from such a person would not be sincere; or it can be saying that an initial repentance is nullified by the increase in disbelief — if a person disbelieves, repents, and disbelieves again, the first repentance is no longer valid. **[Study Quran]** "Then increase in disbelief" can also refer to the sins that ensue after one leaves belief or faith (*īmān*). **[Study Quran]** Although the context would seem to indicate that Muslim apostates are spoken of in this verse, commentators also mention that it could refer to People of the Book who believed in the coming of the Prophet Muhammad but then rejected him and went on to show enmity toward him and the believers; it could also refer to the Jews who believed in Moses but rejected Jesus.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The two interpretations turn on what "increased in disbelief" means — a further act of disbelief, or an accumulation of sins. **[Qurṭubī]** "Increased" has been read both as persistence in unbelief and as the piling up of sins; al-Ṭabarī chose the latter. **[Jalālayn]** The disbelief is specified as a sequence: disbelief in Jesus after belief in Moses, then increase by disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7372 — al-Ḥasan, on "those who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief, their repentance shall not be accepted, and those are the astray": the Jews and the Christians — their repentance shall not be accepted at death. **[Ṭabarī]** 7373 — Qatādah: "those who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief" — those are the enemies of God, the Jews; they disbelieved in the Gospel and in Jesus, then increased in disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Furqān. **[Ṭabarī]** 7374 — Qatādah, through another chain: "then they increased in disbelief" — they increased in disbelief until death came to them, and their repentance was not accepted when death came to them; and Maʿmar said: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī said the like. **[Ṭabarī]** 7375 — Qatādah, through a third chain: they are the Jews; they disbelieved in the Gospel, then increased in disbelief when God sent Muḥammad ﷺ, and they denied him and called him a liar. **[Ṭabarī]** 7376 — Abū al-ʿĀliyah: "then they increased in disbelief" — they increased in sins while they were unbelievers; "their repentance shall not be accepted" — from those sins, so long as they remain in their unbelief and their error. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Bazzār recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said that some people embraced Islam, reverted to disbelief, became Muslims again, then reverted from Islam; they sent their people inquiring about this matter and they asked the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ — and on that this verse was revealed: "Verily, those who disbelieved after their belief and then went on increasing in their disbelief, never will their repentance be accepted". Al-Bazzār said the chain of narration is satisfactory. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Prophet ﷺ was asked about ʿAbdullāh b. Judʿān, who used to be generous to guests, helpful to the indebted and who gave food to the poor — will all that benefit him? The Prophet ﷺ said: "No, for not even one day during his life did he pronounce, 'O my Lord! Forgive my sins on the Day of Judgment.'" *(the report is attached to 3:91, which Ibn Kathīr treats together with 3:90)* **[Qurṭubī]** Quturb said: this verse was revealed concerning some people of Makkah who said, "We will wait upon Muḥammad for the vicissitudes of fortune; and if a return seems good to us, we will return to our people" — so God sent down "those who disbelieved after their belief, then increased in disbelief, their repentance shall not be accepted", meaning their repentance will not be accepted while they persist in unbelief — and He called it a repentance that is not accepted. *(the passage continues)* **[Qurṭubī]** It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "God accepts the repentance of the servant so long as the rattle has not reached his throat."

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The choice between the two readings determines the subject: on the first, it is the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and then in Muḥammad ﷺ; on the second, the People of the Scripture who disbelieved in Muḥammad ﷺ after believing their own prophets, and whose further sins are not forgiven while they persist. **[Qurṭubī]** The apparent conflict with 42:25 is resolved three ways — the repentance meant is at death, or the earlier repentance nullified by later unbelief, or a repentance from one unbelief to another. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The threat is against insisting on disbelief until death; no repentance is then accepted at the point of death. **[Study Quran]** Although the context suggests Muslim apostates, the commentators also apply it to the People of the Book who rejected the Prophet after expecting him, and to the Jews who believed Moses and rejected Jesus. **[Saʿdī]** Persistence until death is what distinguishes this case from the one in 3:89.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 4:18, "And of no effect is the repentance of those who continue to do evil deeds until death faces one of them"; 2:123, "nor shall compensation be accepted from him, nor shall intercession be of use to him"; 14:31, "on which there will be neither mutual bargaining nor befriending"; 5:36; 3:91. **[Qurṭubī]** 42:25, "and He it is Who accepts repentance from His servants"; 4:18; 3:89 for the exception. **[Study Quran]** 4:18 for repentance at death. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:86–89 for the preceding case. **[Jalālayn]** 3:89 for the exception that has just been made.

**Reflection.** The verse is the mirror of 3:89 and must be read against it — same people, opposite outcome, and the difference is persistence **[Saʿdī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The commentators divide over what "increased in disbelief" adds: al-Ṭabarī's own preference is that it means piling up sins while remaining an unbeliever, while Qatādah and al-Ḥasan read it as a second act of unbelief — rejecting Jesus, then rejecting Muḥammad ﷺ **[Ṭabarī]**. Then there is the harder problem, which Qurṭubī states outright: how can any repentance not be accepted, when 42:25 says God accepts repentance from His servants? He records three answers — that it means repentance at the point of death, that the earlier repentance is nullified by later unbelief, or that a repentance from one unbelief to another is no repentance at all **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The reports give the verse two quite different faces: al-Bazzār's, about people who came in and out of Islam repeatedly, and Quturb's, about the Makkans who said they would wait to see how fortune turned **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. What both share is the thing the verse is actually about — a person who keeps the way back open and never takes it.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:86–3:91 is a single unit, whose discussion of the apparent difficulty in "How shall God guide…" belongs to 3:86; it has nothing separate for 3:90.

## 3:91 — إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَمَاتُوا۟ وَهُمْ كُفَّارٌۭ فَلَن يُقْبَلَ مِنْ أَحَدِهِم مِّلْءُ ٱلْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًۭا وَلَوِ ٱفْتَدَىٰ بِهِ ۗ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌۭ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن نَّٰصِرِينَ

*"Those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers — there shall not be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold, though he should ransom himself with it. Those — for them is a painful punishment, and they have no helpers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by "those who disbelieve": those who denied the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ and did not believe in him nor in what he brought from God, of the people of every community — its Jews, its Christians, its Magians and others; "and die while they are disbelievers", meaning: and die upon that denial of his prophethood and denial of what he brought. **[Ṭabarī]** "There shall not be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold, though he should ransom himself with it" — He says: there shall not be accepted from anyone who is of this description, in the Hereafter, any compensation, nor any bribe for leaving off his punishment for his unbelief, nor any wage for pardoning him — even if he had gold to the measure of what would fill the earth from its east to its west, and he bribed and paid with it to have his punishment for his unbelief left off and to be pardoned for it, in exchange for the punishment God is bringing down upon him. **[Ṭabarī]** For bribes are only accepted by one who has need of what he is bribed with; as for Him to whom belong this world and the Hereafter, how should He accept a ransom, when He is the creator of every ransom with which anyone ransoms himself or another? **[Jalālayn]** "Surely those who disbelieve and die disbelieving, the whole earth full" — the amount needed to fill it up — "of gold shall not be accepted from any one of them": the *fāʾ* of *fa-lan yuqbala* has been included in the predicate of the *inna* clause because the statement about "those who disbelieve" resembles a conditional statement. **[Jalālayn]** And it is a declaration of the reason for it: repentance is not acceptable in the case of one who dies in unbelief, if he would ransom himself thereby. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Those who die while disbelievers shall have no good deed ever accepted from them, even if they spent the earth's fill of gold in what was perceived to be an act of obedience. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-milʾu*, with *kasra*, is the measure with which a thing is filled; *al-malʾu*, with *fatḥa*, is the verbal noun of "I filled the thing". **[Saʿdī]** These are the astray ones from the path of guidance, the travellers of the path of wretchedness, and they have merited by this the painful punishment; so they have no helper against the punishment of God — and even if they offered the earth full of gold to ransom themselves with, it would not avail them at all. So we seek refuge with God from unbelief and its branches. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** Dying as disbelievers is also mentioned in 2:161, 217; 4:18; 9:125 and 47:34; the idea of trying to give ransom in the Hereafter is also discussed at 2:48, and the inadequacy of an earth full of goods as ransom is mentioned in 5:36; 10:54; 13:18; 39:47. **[Study Quran]** The opposite of dying in disbelief — dying as a believer — is mentioned in 3:102, where believers are commanded "Die not except in submission", the same command that Abraham and Jacob enjoined upon their children in 2:132.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Gold" is in the accusative as a specification drawn out of the measure that precedes it, like one's saying "I have the measure of a skin of clarified butter" or "the measure of a *ratl* of honey" — the honey specifies the measure, an indefinite in the accusative as the *tamyīz* of the measure. **[Ṭabarī]** The grammarians of Basra held that "the gold" is in the accusative because "the fill" is occupied by "the earth" and the gold comes after both, so its accusative is like the accusative of the ḥāl — as in "I have the like of you as a man", meaning "among men". **[Ṭabarī]** The *wāw* in "though he should ransom himself with it" is inserted because of something omitted after it, which the entry of the *wāw* indicates, as in "and that he might be of those who are certain" (6:75) — the estimate being "and that he might be of those who are certain, We showed him the kingdom of the heavens and the earth". Were there no *wāw*, the sentence would still be sound, with nothing omitted. **[Qurṭubī]** Some said the *wāw* is intrusive and superfluous, the meaning being simply "there shall not be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold, though he should ransom himself with it"; but the people of speculation among the grammarians said it cannot be superfluous, because it indicates a meaning — the meaning being "as a free gift, and even if he ransomed himself with it". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Farrāʾ said "gold" is in the accusative as specification (*tafsīr*); al-Mufaḍḍal said the condition of the specification is that the sentence be complete but ambiguous, as when you say "I have twenty" — the number is known and the thing numbered ambiguous, so when you say "dirhams" you have specified it; and it is in the accusative because there is nothing to govern it in the genitive or nominative, and the accusative is the lightest of the vowels. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Kisāʾī said it is in the accusative through an elided *min* — that is, "of gold" — like "or the equivalent of that in fasting" (5:95), meaning "of fasting". **[Jalālayn]** *Alīm* is the same as *muʾlim*, "painful", and "helpers" are those who would protect them from it.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7384 — from Saʿīd, from Qatāda: Anas b. Mālik said that the Prophet of God ﷺ used to say: "The disbeliever will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to him: Do you see — if you had the earth full of gold, would you ransom yourself with it? He will say: Yes! It will be said: You were asked for what is easier than that!" — and that is His saying "those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, there shall not be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold, though he should ransom himself with it". *(al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it from Qatāda from Anas)* **[Qurṭubī]** In al-Bukhārī and Muslim, from Qatāda, from Anas b. Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to him: Do you see — if you had the earth full of gold, would you ransom yourself with it? He will say: Yes. And it will be said to him: You were asked for what is easier than that" — this is al-Bukhārī's wording; and Muslim has in place of "you were asked", "you lied, you were asked". **[Ṭabarī]** 7385 — al-Ḥasan, on "those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, there shall not be accepted from any one of them the earth full of gold": it is every disbeliever. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Prophet ﷺ was asked about ʿAbdullāh b. Judʿān, who used to be generous to guests, helpful to the indebted and who gave food to the poor — will all that benefit him? He said: "No, for not even one day during his life did he pronounce, 'O my Lord! Forgive my sins on the Day of Judgment.'" *(Ibn Kathīr attaches this to 3:91, which he treats together with 3:90)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** And in the report of Anas: the man of the Fire will be brought and God will say to him, "O son of Ādam! How do you find your dwelling?" He will say, "It is the worst dwelling, O Lord." He will ask, "Would you ransom yourself from Me with the earth's fill of gold?" He will say, "Yes, O Lord." He will say, "You have lied. I asked you to do what is less and easier than that, but you did not do it," and he will be sent back to the Fire.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** Nothing is accepted in the Hereafter in place of the punishment — neither compensation, nor bribe, nor wage for pardon — for God has no need of what He created. **[Ibn Kathīr]** No good deed is ever accepted from one who dies a disbeliever, whatever he spent. **[Jalālayn]** The verse declares the reason: repentance is not accepted from one who dies in unbelief even if he would ransom himself with it. **[Study Quran]** The contrast is with expiation or ransom offered in this life, where such deeds are accepted if sincerely offered, as against striking a bargain after one's life has ended and the opportunity to choose between good and evil is gone. **[Saʿdī]** The punishment is merited, and no helper and no ransom avails against it.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 2:161, 2:217, 4:18, 9:125, 47:34 for dying as disbelievers; 2:48 for ransom in the Hereafter; 5:36, 10:54, 13:18, 39:47 for the earth full of goods being inadequate; 3:102 and 2:132 for dying in submission. **[Ṭabarī]** His earlier treatment of "ransom" as compensation given in place of the one ransomed. **[Jalālayn]** 3:90 for the deathbed repentance that is not accepted. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:90 for the threat that precedes; 3:92, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is the closing panel of a single argument that runs from 3:86: apostasy, curse, abiding, the exception for repentance, and now the case where there is no exception at all **[Ṭabarī]**. What it adds is the image of a man who owns the whole earth in gold and cannot buy his way out **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī's reason is theological and very brief: bribes are taken by people who need things, and God needs nothing — He made every ransom there is **[Ṭabarī]**. The ḥadīth turns the image into a courtroom scene, and it is the last line that stings: "you were asked for what is easier than that" **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]** — the earth-full of gold was never the price; the price was belief, and it was offered first. Al-Ḥasan's one-line gloss keeps the verse general rather than tying it to any group: it is every disbeliever **[Ṭabarī]**. And Ibn Kathīr's report of ʿAbdullāh b. Judʿān supplies the hardest version of the point — a man famous for feeding the poor and settling debts, who is told that none of it counts, because he never once asked God to forgive him **[Ibn Kathīr]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:86–3:91 is a single unit; its discussion of the apparent difficulty in "How shall God guide…" belongs to 3:86, and it has nothing separate for 3:91.

## 3:92 — لَن تَنَالُوا۟ ٱلْبِرَّ حَتَّىٰ تُنفِقُوا۟ مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ ۚ وَمَا تُنفِقُوا۟ مِن شَىْءٍۢ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِهِ عَلِيمٌ

*"You shall not attain piety until you spend of what you love; and whatever you spend of anything, God knows it."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: you shall not attain, O believers, *al-birr* — and that is "the *birr* of God" which they seek from Him by their obedience to Him and their worship of Him and which they hope for from Him, and that is His favour to them by admitting them to His Garden and turning His punishment away from them. **[Ṭabarī]** And it is for that reason that many of the people of interpretation said "al-birr is the Garden", because the *birr* of the Lord to His servant in the Hereafter is His honouring him by admitting him to the Garden. **[Ṭabarī]** The meaning of the sentence is then: you shall not attain, O believers, the Garden of your Lord "until you spend of what you love" — until you give in charity of what you love and desire to be yours, of the precious part of your wealth. **[Jalālayn]** "You will not attain piety" — that is the reward for it, which is Paradise — "until you expend", until you give voluntary alms, "of what you love" of your wealth; "and whatever thing you expend, God knows of it" and He will requite it accordingly. **[Ibn Kathīr]** *Al-Birr* is spending from the best of one's wealth. **[Qurṭubī]** In this verse there is evidence for acting upon the apparent and general sense of the address, for the Companions, God's pleasure be on them all, understood nothing else from the tenor of the address when the verse came down. **[Qurṭubī]** Do you not see that Abū Ṭalḥa, when he heard "you shall not attain piety until you spend", did not need to pause until a clarification should come from another verse or an explanatory sunna as to what God wants His servants to spend of, since they love many things? And Zayd b. Ḥāritha did the same: he made for what he loved, a horse of his called Sabal, and said: "O God, You know that I have no wealth more beloved to me than this horse of mine." **[Saʿdī]** You will not attain and reach *al-birr*, which is a comprehensive name for all goods and is the path that leads to the Garden, until you spend of the best of your wealth and its purest. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** For spending from the good that souls love is among the greatest proofs of the soul's generosity and its being described with noble character, mercy and tenderness, and among the clearest proofs of the love of God and of giving His love precedence over the love of wealth, to which souls are naturally strongly attached; so whoever prefers the love of God over the love of his own self has reached the highest summit of perfection. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** But however much the servant spends, small or great, of the good or other than it, "God knows it", and He will recompense every spender according to his deed — in this world with immediate replacement and in the Hereafter with deferred bliss. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The literal and real meaning of the word *birr* is the perfect fulfilment of someone's rights; it is also used in the sense of charity, the performance of good deeds and fine conduct, and *barr* is used of a person who fulfils, fully and totally, all rights due on him — as in "good to my mother" (19:32) and "good to his father and mother" (19:14), used there as a personal attribute of prophets who fulfilled the rights of their parents fully. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Also stated in this last sentence of the verse is that Allah is fully aware of the real quality of what a man spends and knows whether or not it is dear to him, and whether he is spending it for the good pleasure of Allah or for pretence and publicity; the mere verbal claim by somebody that he is spending what he cherishes in the way of Allah is not enough for this purpose. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** *Birr* can also mean the rewards of piety; depending on the context it carries a sense of goodness, kindness, loyalty, sincerity or obedience. **[Study Quran]** Many commentators connect this verse with the story of a Companion who had a tract of land in Madinah that was his most prized possession and that he desired to give in the way of God; but the Ḥadīth is so replete with examples of the Prophet and Companions giving charity that this verse could not be limited in its import to a single incident. **[Study Quran]** Spiritually speaking, one cannot advance until one gives away one's ego, which one loves above all things. *(Aj)*

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** *Al-birr* is God's *birr* to His servants — His admitting them to the Garden and turning His punishment away. **[Jalālayn]** "Until you expend" is glossed as giving voluntary alms. **[Maʿārif]** *Birr* is the perfect fulfilment of rights, from which come *barr* and *abrār*. **[Study Quran]** The word carries goodness, kindness, loyalty, sincerity or obedience according to context.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7386 and 7387 — from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿAmr b. Maymūn, on "you shall not attain piety": the Garden. **[Ṭabarī]** 7388 — al-Suddī: "*al-birr* — as for *al-birr*, it is the Garden". **[Ṭabarī]** 7389 — Qatāda: "you shall not attain the *birr* of your Lord until you spend of what pleases you and of what you desire of your wealth". **[Ṭabarī]** 7391 — Qatāda, on "whatever you spend of anything, God knows it": that is preserved for you; God knows it and is thankful for it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7392 — Mujāhid said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī to buy him a slave-girl from Jalūlāʾ, on the day the cities of Chosroes were opened in the campaign of Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ; and ʿUmar called for her and said: "God says 'you shall not attain piety until you spend of what you love'" — and ʿUmar freed her. *(Mujāhid added that it is like 76:8 and 59:9)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7394 — Ḥumayd, from Anas b. Mālik: when this verse came down — or the verse "who is it that will lend God a goodly loan" (2:245 / 57:11) — Abū Ṭalḥa said: "O Messenger of God, my walled garden in such-and-such a place is charity; and had I been able to make it secret I would not have made it public!" And the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Put it among the poor of your family." *(recorded by Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7398 — from Maʿmar, from Ayyūb and others: when "you shall not attain piety until you spend of what you love" came down, Zayd b. Ḥāritha brought a horse of his that he loved and said: "O Messenger of God, this is in the way of God" — and the Messenger of God ﷺ mounted Usāma b. Zayd on it; and Zayd seemed to feel something in himself, and when the Prophet ﷺ saw that in him he said: "God has accepted it." *(a mursal report)* **[Qurṭubī]** The imams recorded, with the wording of al-Nasāʾī, from Anas: when this verse came down, Abū Ṭalḥa said: "Our Lord is asking us for our wealth; I call you to witness, O Messenger of God, that I have given my land to God" — and the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Put it among your relatives, Ḥassān b. Thābit and Ubayy b. Kaʿb." **[Qurṭubī]** In al-Muwaṭṭaʾ: the most beloved of his wealth to him was the well of Ḥāʾ, which faced the mosque, and the Messenger of God ﷺ used to enter it and drink of the sweet water in it. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: by this verse He guided them to *futuwwa* — that is, "you shall not attain My *birr* to you except by your *birr* to your brothers and your spending upon them from your wealth and your standing; and if you do that, My *birr* and My affection will reach you." **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: it is like His saying "and they give food, for the love of it, to the poor, the orphan and the captive" (76:8). **[Ibn Kathīr]** In his Tafsīr, Wakīʿ reported that ʿAmr b. Maymūn said that "you shall not attain *al-birr*" refers to attaining Paradise. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad reported that Anas b. Mālik said: "Abū Ṭalḥa had more property than any other among the Anṣār in al-Madīnah, and the most beloved of his property to him was the Bayrūḥāʾ garden, which was in front of the (Messenger's) masjid; sometimes the Messenger of God ﷺ used to go to the garden and drink its fresh water." **[Ibn Kathīr]** When the verses were revealed Abū Ṭalḥa said: "O Messenger of God, God says 'you shall not attain *al-birr* until you spend of that which you love'; and no doubt the Bayrūḥāʾ garden is the most beloved of all my property to me. So I want to give it in charity in God's cause, and I expect its reward and compensation from God. Spend it where God makes you think is feasible." **[Ibn Kathīr]** He said: "Well done! It is profitable property, it is profitable property. I have heard what you have said, and I think it would be proper if you gave it to your kith and kin" — and Abū Ṭalḥa distributed it among his relatives and cousins. *(in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** They also recorded that ʿUmar said: "O Messenger of God, I never gained possession of a piece of property more precious to me than my share in Khaybar; what do you command me to do with it?" He said: "Retain the land and give its fruits in God's cause."

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** The verse is evidence for acting upon the apparent and general sense of the address without waiting for a further clarification. **[Ibn Kathīr]** ʿUmar's question about his share of Khaybar and the Prophet's answer — "retain the land and give its fruits in God's cause" — is the basis of the endowment (*waqf*).

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** *Al-birr* named as the goal is God's *birr* to the servant — admission to the Garden and deliverance from the punishment. **[Saʿdī]** Spending what one loves is the proof that the love of God has been preferred to the love of wealth, and whoever does that has reached the summit of perfection. **[Maʿārif]** The closing clause makes God's knowledge the test: whether the spending is really of what is dear, and whether it is for His pleasure or for show. **[Study Quran]** The spiritual reading is that one cannot advance until one gives away one's ego.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 76:8 and 59:9, cited by Mujāhid alongside ʿUmar's freeing of the slave-girl; 2:245 and 57:11, the "goodly loan" verse Anas linked with this one. **[Qurṭubī]** 76:8. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:91 for what precedes; 3:93, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:44, 2:177 and 2:189 for *birr*; 2:267 for spending of the good things one has earned; 76:5, 3:193 and 82:13 for the *abrār* and their rewards; the ḥadīth "None of you believes until he desires for his neighbour what he desires for himself". **[Maʿārif]** 19:32 and 19:14 for *barr*; 76:5 for the *abrār*.

**Reflection.** The verse sets the bar at the precise point where it hurts — not "spend", but "spend of what you love" **[Jalālayn]**. Al-Ṭabarī's framing is worth pausing on: he does not treat *birr* as a moral quality one acquires but as something God does — His *birr* to the servant, which is Paradise — and so most of the early authorities simply glossed the word as "the Garden" **[Ṭabarī]**. The reports that follow are the verse made flesh, and they are all about the same thing: people giving away the single item they were most attached to. Abū Ṭalḥa's garden, which the Prophet used to visit for its water; Zayd's horse Sabal, which he gave and then watched being given to someone else, and was told by the Prophet that God had accepted it; ʿUmar's slave-girl from Jalūlāʾ, bought and freed on the spot; ʿUmar again at Khaybar, and the ruling that produced the endowment **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Qurṭubī draws the legal point the Companions' behaviour proves — they did not wait for a second verse to tell them what to spend, because the apparent sense of the address was enough **[Qurṭubī]**. And both al-Saʿdī and Maʿārif close on the same caution: the last clause of the verse is there because a claim to be spending what one loves is easy to make, and God knows the difference **[Saʿdī]**, **[Maʿārif]**.

## 3:93 — كُلُّ ٱلطَّعَامِ كَانَ حِلًّۭا لِّبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ إِلَّا مَا حَرَّمَ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ مِن قَبْلِ أَن تُنَزَّلَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةُ ۚ قُلْ فَأْتُوا۟ بِٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ فَٱتْلُوهَآ إِن كُنتُمْ صَٰدِقِينَ

*"All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel forbade for himself before the Torah was sent down. Say: 'Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: He had not forbidden to the Children of Israel — and they are the children of Jacob the son of Isaac the son of Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful — anything of foods before the Torah was sent down; rather, all of it was lawful to them except what Jacob had forbidden himself, for his children forbade it following their father Jacob's example, without God's having forbidden it to them in any revelation or sending down, or upon the tongue of any messenger of His to them, before the Torah came down. **[Jalālayn]** When the Jews said to the Prophet, "You claim that you follow the creed of Abraham, but Abraham did not eat camel's meat nor drink its milk", the following was revealed: "All food was lawful to the Children of Israel save what Israel" — Jacob — "forbade for himself", namely camels, when he was afflicted with sciatica, *ʿirq al-nasā*: he made a vow that if he were cured he would not eat of it again, and so it was forbidden him — "before the Torah was revealed", which was after the time of Abraham, since it was not unlawful in his time as they claimed. **[Jalālayn]** "Say to them: 'Bring the Torah now and recite it, so that the truth of what you say may become clear, if you are truthful'" in what you say; and they were stupefied and did not bring it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Before the Tawrah was revealed" means Isra'il forbade that for himself before the Tawrah was revealed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** There are two objectives behind revealing this segment: first, he forbade himself the most delightful things for God's sake, and this practice was allowed during the period of his Law, and is thus suitably mentioned after "you shall not attain piety until you spend of what you love" [3:92]; what we are allowed in our Law is to spend in God's obedience from what we like and covet, but not to prohibit what God has allowed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The second reason is that, after God refuted the false Christian beliefs and allegations about ʿĪsā and his mother, He started refuting the Jews here. **[Qurṭubī]** *Ḥillan* means *ḥalālan*, "lawful"; then He excepted, saying "except what Israel forbade for himself" — and he is Jacob, upon him be peace. **[Saʿdī]** Among the matters by which the Jews attacked the prophethood of Jesus and Muḥammad ﷺ was their claim that abrogation is false and that no prophet can come differing from the prophet before him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** So God declared them liars by something they themselves know: they admit that all food before the sending down of the Torah was lawful for the Children of Israel except a few things which Israel — Jacob, upon him be peace — forbade himself, being prevented from them by an illness that afflicted him;
