and then the Torah contains many prohibitions that abrogated what had been lawful before that. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Say to them, if they deny that: "Then bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful" in your claim that there is no abrogation, no making lawful and no forbidding. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** This is among the most eloquent of arguments — that a man should be argued against from something he himself says and acknowledges and does not deny; if he submits to the truth, that is what is due; and if he refuses and does not submit after this clarification, his lying, his fabricating, his wrongdoing and the falsity of what he is upon become clear — and that is what actually happened with the Jews. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** One such argument, reported in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* on the authority of Wāḥidī and al-Kalbī, recounts the incident when the Holy Prophet ﷺ stated his adherence to the community of Abraham with reference to all the fundamentals of the religious code and most of the subsidiaries, and the Jews objected: "You eat camel meat and partake of its milk although these were unlawful for Abraham." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The Holy Prophet ﷺ said: "No, this was lawful for him." The Jews said: "All that we consider unlawful has continued to be unlawful since the days of Noah and Abraham until this unlawfulness reached us" — and thereupon God revealed this verse to refute the Jewish claim. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** Before the revelation of the Torah there were no prohibitions to abide by for the descendants of Jacob except those that Jacob had imposed on himself and that his children followed him in observing. **[Study Quran]** The verse is interpreted as a response to those Jews who claimed that the current prohibitions in the Torah were always in effect, as part of their argument against the possibility of one religion abrogating another. **[Study Quran]** Some commentators believe that the Torah then enshrined the prohibitions that were already being observed; and it is possible that the message of this verse is found in some form in Genesis 32:32, where it is said that Israelites do not eat the thigh muscle on the socket of the hip, where Jacob was injured — such a prohibition would have predated the Torah. **[Study Quran]** Even so, some commentators are reticent to attribute to the pre-Torah Jews the eating of carrion or pork, and understand this verse to refer to the misattribution to Abraham of the detailed prohibitions — for example those dealing with dietary restrictions — found in Jewish Law.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Ḥillan* is glossed as *ḥalālan*. **[Jalālayn]** "Israel" is Jacob, and *ʿirq al-nasā* is sciatica. **[Ṭabarī]** "What Israel forbade for himself" is something he forbade by his own oath, his children following him by way of example, not by any divine prohibition.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7399 — al-Suddī: the Jews said, "We only forbid what Israel forbade himself" — and Israel forbade the sinews (*al-ʿurūq*); he was seized by *ʿirq al-nasā*, which took him by night and left him by day, and he swore that if God healed him he would never eat a sinew, so God forbade it for them; then He said: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful" — none forbade this for you but Me, because of your insolence, and that is His saying "So, because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful to them" (4:160). **[Ṭabarī]** 7400 — al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "Israel" is Jacob; *ʿirq al-nasā* seized him and he could not rest at night for the pain of it, though it did not hurt him by day; so he swore that if God cured him he would never eat a sinew, and that was before the Torah came down to Moses; and the Prophet of God ﷺ asked the Jews what it was that Israel had forbidden himself. **[Qurṭubī]** In al-Tirmidhī, from Ibn ʿAbbās: the Jews said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Tell us — what did Israel forbid for himself?" He said: "He used to live in the desert, and he complained of *ʿirq al-nasā* and found nothing to agree with him except the flesh of camels and their milk, and so he forbade them." They said: "You have spoken the truth." **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that he vowed that if he were cured of it he would give up the food and drink most beloved to him — and the food and drink most beloved to him were the flesh of camels and their milk. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda and al-Suddī said: Jacob was coming from Ḥarrān, making for Jerusalem, when he fled from his brother Esau, who was a strong and powerful man; an angel met him and Jacob thought him a thief and wrestled with him to throw him, so the angel pressed Jacob's thigh, then ascended to heaven while Jacob watched; and *ʿirq al-nasā* flared up in him and he suffered greatly from it, and he could not sleep at night for the pain and would spend the night moaning. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "Talk to us about some things we will ask you, which only a prophet would know." He said: "Ask me about whatever you wish; however, give your pledge to God, similar to the pledge that Jacob took from his children, that if I tell you something and you recognize its truth you will follow me in Islam." They said: "Agreed." **[Ibn Kathīr]** They said: "Tell us about four matters — what kinds of food did Israel prohibit for himself? What about the sexual discharge of the woman and the man, and what role does each play in producing male or female offspring? Tell us about the condition of the unlettered Prophet during sleep. And who is his guardian among the angels?" — and he took their covenant that they would follow him if he answered. **[Ibn Kathīr]** On the fourth, he said: "My guardian is Jibrīl, and God never sent a prophet but Jibrīl is his guardian." They said: "We then shun you; had you a guardian other than Jibrīl, we would have followed you" — and on that God revealed "Say: whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl" (2:97). **[Ibn Kathīr]** On the second: "If the man's discharge is more than the woman's, the child will be male, by God's leave; if the woman's is more than the man's, the child will be female." On the third: "The eyes of this unlettered Prophet sleep, but his heart does not sleep." And he said each time: "O God, be Witness against them." **[Ibn Kathīr]** God then refuted them by stating that abrogation, which they denied, already occurred in their own Law: the Tawrah states that when Noah departed the ark, God allowed him the meat of all types of animals; Israel then forbade the meat and milk of camels for himself and his children imitated him, and the Tawrah later prohibited this and added several more prohibitions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God allowed Adam to marry his daughters to his sons, and this was later forbidden; the Law of Abraham allowed a man to take female servants alongside his wife, as Abraham did with Hagar while married to Sarah, and the Tawrah later prohibited it; it was previously allowed to take two sisters as wives at the same time, as Jacob married two sisters, and this was later prohibited in the Tawrah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** All these examples are in the Tawrah and constitute abrogation of the Law; therefore let the Jews consider what God legislated for Jesus, and whether it falls under abrogation or not, and why they do not then follow Jesus in this regard. **[Qurṭubī]** On the legal question of whether Jacob's prohibition was by revelation or by his own reasoning: the correct view is the first, because God attributed the prohibition to Himself by His saying "except what Israel forbade", and because when a prophet's reasoning leads him to something it becomes a religion that must be followed when God confirms him in it. **[Qurṭubī]** Our Prophet forbade honey — or his handmaid Māriya — and God did not confirm his prohibition, and "Why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?" (66:1) was revealed. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt: the remedy for ʿirq al-nasā reported at the end of Qurṭubī's discussion — the fat-tail of an Arab sheep neither young nor old, cut small and its grease removed and divided into three parts, taken fasting one third each day — which Anas said he prescribed for more than a hundred people and they were cured by God's leave)*

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Where a prophet's reasoning is confirmed by God it becomes binding religion; where it is not confirmed it is corrected, as happened with the Prophet's prohibition of honey and the revelation of 66:1. **[Maʿārif]** A vow that renders things unlawful is in reality an oath, and that is not permissible in our Sharīʿah — in such a case it is obligatory to break the oath and make *kaffārah*, in accordance with "Why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?" (66:1). *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** Nothing was forbidden to the Children of Israel before the Torah by revelation; what Jacob forbade himself, his children followed by example. **[Saʿdī]** The argument is designed to be unanswerable because it is taken from what the Jews themselves admit, and its purpose is to establish that abrogation is real. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Abrogation is attested within the Torah itself — in the case of Noah, of Adam's children, of Hagar and of Jacob's two wives — so the Jews cannot consistently deny it in the case of Jesus and Muḥammad. **[Maʿārif]** The prohibition that began with a vow came to be treated among the Children of Israel as a divine injunction, and the verse corrects that attribution. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Ṭabarī]** God's informing His Prophet of this — knowledge hidden even from most of the Jews themselves, and he an *ummī* from outside their community — is itself among the greatest proofs of his prophethood, since he could only have known it by revelation.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 4:160, "So, because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful to them", as the sequel of al-Suddī's account. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:97 for the revelation occasioned by the Jews' rejection of Jibrīl; 2:177 and 76:8 for spending of what one loves; 3:92, which precedes. **[Jalālayn]** 3:95 for "follow the creed of Abraham"; 3:94, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 4:160 and 6:146 for the prohibitions laid on the Jews; Genesis 32:32 for the thigh muscle. **[Qurṭubī]** 66:1 for the Prophet's own prohibition of honey; Sūrat al-Taḥrīm. **[Maʿārif]** 66:1 for the *kaffārah* of an oath. **[Saʿdī]** 3:94–95 for what follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is a courtroom move, and the commentators all say what the move is: the Jews are being refuted out of their own Book **[Saʿdī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**. The dispute began, on the account Maʿārif preserves, with a taunt about the dinner table — you claim Abraham's religion, but you eat camel meat, which Abraham never did — and the answer is that the camel was never forbidden by Abraham at all but by Jacob, for a reason that was purely personal **[Maʿārif]**, **[Jalālayn]**. What the story of Jacob's sciatica contributes is the exact opposite of what the Jews wanted: the prohibition entered Israel's law as a man's vow, not as a divine command, and was only later written into the Torah **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. That is abrogation from the inside, and Ibn Kathīr hammers it home with four more cases from their own Law — Noah's meat, Adam's children, Hagar, Jacob's two sisters — all permitted first and forbidden later **[Ibn Kathīr]**. So the challenge "bring the Torah and recite it" is not rhetorical bravado; it is a test they can in principle pass, and they fail it, and their silence is the proof **[Jalālayn]**. And al-Ṭabarī adds the point that closes the circle: that an unlettered man from outside their community knew the details of their own hidden history at all is itself evidence of where he got it **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:94 — فَمَنِ ٱفْتَرَىٰ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلْكَذِبَ مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ

*"Then whoever invents falsehood against God after that — those are the wrongdoers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: whoever lies about God, of us and of you, after your bringing the Torah and your reciting it and your not finding in it what you claimed of God's forbidding the sinews and the flesh and milk of camels — "those are the wrongdoers": those who do that are the disbelievers, the speakers of falsehood about God. **[Jalālayn]** "Whoever invents falsehood against God after that" — that is, after the proof has become manifest that the prohibition was made by Jacob and not during the time of Abraham — "those are the evildoers", those who transgress the truth into falsehood. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is in reference to those who lie about God and claim that He made the Sabbath and the Tawrah eternal, and who claim that God did not send another prophet calling to God with the proofs and evidences. **[Saʿdī]** If he submits to the truth, that is what is due; but if he refuses and does not submit after this clarification, his lying and his fabricating and his wrongdoing become clear, and the falsity of what he is upon — and that is what actually happened with the Jews. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:93–94 as a single unit)* **[Study Quran]** "That" refers to the challenge to recite from the Torah in 3:93, in which case "after that" would mean after it is shown that the body of prohibitions by which the Israelites lived did not exist before the revelation of the Torah; presumably the Torah would show that Abraham's life was lived before these prohibitions went into effect.

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** "After that" is specified as after the manifestation of the proof, and "the evildoers" as those who cross from truth into falsehood. **[Ṭabarī]** "Those are the wrongdoers" is glossed as "the disbelievers, the speakers of falsehood about God". **[Study Quran]** The referent of "that" is the challenge in the previous verse.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7421 — from Zakariyyā, from al-Shaʿbī: "Then those are the wrongdoers" — it was revealed concerning the Jews. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is in reference to those who claim that God made the Sabbath and the Tawrah eternal, and that He sent no further prophet. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:93–95)*

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The falsehood in question is the claim that the Torah and the Sabbath are eternal and that no further prophet would come — which is why the verse follows the argument about abrogation. **[Jalālayn]** The wrongdoing is precisely the transgression from truth into falsehood after the proof has appeared. **[Saʿdī]** Refusal after clarification is what makes the lying and the fabrication manifest. **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is addressed to anyone, "of us and of you", who fabricates against God after the evidence. **[Study Quran]** The "after" is what gives the verse its force — the wrong is committed once the Torah has been produced and shown not to contain what was claimed.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:93 for the challenge that "that" refers to. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:93 for the setting; 3:95 for what follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:93 for the abrogation argument; 3:95 for the creed of Abraham. **[Jalālayn]** 3:93 for the prohibition of Jacob; 3:95 for the creed. **[Saʿdī]** 3:95 for what follows.

**Reflection.** A single sentence, and almost every word of it is carried by the verse before. "After that" is the hinge: the wrong is not ignorance but persistence once the Torah has been produced and found not to contain the prohibition **[Study Quran]**, **[Jalālayn]**. Al-Shaʿbī's one-line report fixes the referent: it came down about the Jews **[Ṭabarī]**. The structure is worth noting too, because the verse does two things at once: it closes the argument begun at 3:93 — the Torah was demanded, it was not produced, and the claim it was supposed to support therefore stands exposed as something said about God rather than by Him — and it opens the one that follows, since immediately afterwards the Qurʾān names the creed of Abraham as the thing that all the parties already agree upon **[Jalālayn]**, **[Study Quran]**. That is why the falsehood Ibn Kathīr identifies is not a mistake about food but a claim about history: that the Torah and the Sabbath are eternal and that no further prophet would come **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The wording al-Ṭabarī preserves is unusually even-handed in its address — whoever lies about God, "of us and of you" — which keeps the principle general, attached to the act of fabricating against God rather than only to the Jews who happened to do it **[Ṭabarī]**. And Ibn Kathīr sharpens what the falsehood actually is — not merely a dietary claim but the claim that the Torah and the Sabbath are eternal and that God would send no further prophet, which is exactly what the argument about abrogation in 3:93 was designed to demolish **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Al-Saʿdī's reading supplies the psychological sequence that makes the verse cohere: a man is argued against from what he himself admits; if he yields, well; if he refuses after the clarification, then what is exposed is not an error but a lie — and he says that this is precisely what happened **[Saʿdī]**. The word chosen for the wrongdoers matters too, and al-Ṭabarī glosses it without softening: they are the disbelievers, the ones who speak falsehood about God **[Ṭabarī]**.

*Source note:* Qurṭubī treats 3:93–94 as a single block, whose material on the food prohibitions is cited at 3:93; and Maʿārif's block for 3:93–95 is likewise a single unit, cited at 3:93 — neither has anything separate for 3:94.

## 3:95 — قُلْ صَدَقَ ٱللَّهُ ۗ فَٱتَّبِعُوا۟ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ حَنِيفًۭا ۖ وَمَا كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ

*"Say: 'God has spoken the truth. So follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf — and he was not of the idolaters.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: "Say", O Muḥammad, "God has spoken the truth" in what He has told us in His saying "all food was lawful to the Children of Israel", and that God did not forbid to Israel or to his children the sinews, nor the flesh of camels nor their milk, and that it was only a thing that Israel forbade himself and his children without God's forbidding it to them in the Torah — and in every report He has given His servants, as opposed to you; and you, O assembly of Jews, are the liars in your attributing the prohibition of that to God upon you in the Torah, the fabricators of falsehood against God in your claiming against Him what is not true. **[Ṭabarī]** "So follow the creed of Abraham" — so if you are, O Jews, truthful in your claim that you are upon the religion God approved for His prophets and His messengers, then follow the creed of Abraham, the Friend of God; for you know that it is the truth that God approved for His creation as a religion and sent His prophets with — and that is the *ḥanīfiyya*, meaning uprightness upon Islam and its laws, as opposed to Judaism, Christianity and polytheism. **[Ṭabarī]** "And he was not of the idolaters" — he did not associate anyone of His creation in His worship; so you too, O Jews, do not take one another as lords besides God, obeying them as Abraham obeyed his Lord; and you, O assembly of idol-worshippers, do not take idols and images as lords and worship anything besides God. **[Ṭabarī]** All of you acknowledge that Abraham was upon the truth and a straight guidance, so follow what all of you have agreed to be sound of his ḥanīf creed, and leave what you differ about of the rest of the religions, O factions, for those are innovations you have introduced on top of what you have all agreed is the truth — for that which you have agreed is right and true of the creed of Abraham is the truth that I have approved and sent My prophets and messengers with, and all else is the falsehood that I will accept from none of My creation who brings it to Me on the Day of Resurrection. **[Jalālayn]** "Say: 'God has spoken the truth'" in this matter, just as He has in all that He has related; "therefore follow the creed of Abraham, the one which I follow, a ḥanīf" — inclining away from all religions towards submission, *islām* — "and he was not an idolater". **[Qurṭubī]** That is: say, O Muḥammad, "God has spoken the truth" — it was not forbidden in the Torah. **[Qurṭubī]** "So follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf" is a command to follow his religion; and "he was not of the idolaters" is a rebuttal of them in their false claim, as has already been stated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It is the perfect way, and no prophet has brought a more complete, clear, plain and perfect way than he did. **[Saʿdī]** Say: "God has spoken the truth" in everything He has said — and who is truer than God in speech and in word? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** He has set out in these verses the proofs of the truth of the message of Muḥammad ﷺ and the evidences of his call and the falsity of what the deviant among the People of the Book are upon, who denied His messenger and rejected his call; and God has spoken the truth in that and has convinced His servants of it with proofs and arguments before which mountains would split and men would submit. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** It is therefore incumbent upon all people to follow the creed of Abraham: the unification of God alone with no partner, and the affirmation of every messenger God sent and every book He revealed, and turning away from the false deviant religions — for Abraham turned away from everything that opposed *tawḥīd* and declared himself quit of polytheism and its people. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** God has spoken true here specifically regarding Jacob and what was made lawful and forbidden in the Torah. **[Study Quran]** *Ṣadaqa Allāh* is often uttered by Muslims after completing a passage of recitation from the Quran outside of the canonical prayers.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The *ḥanīfiyya* is defined as uprightness upon Islam and its laws, set against Judaism, Christianity and polytheism; and "he was not of the idolaters" is explained as not being of their number or of their partisans and friends, since idolaters are of one another in backing one another in their unbelief. **[Jalālayn]** *Ḥanīf* is glossed as inclining away from all religions towards submission. **[Study Quran]** The phrase "God has spoken true" is also the formula uttered after recitation outside the formal prayer.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse rests on a piece of common ground: all parties acknowledge that Abraham was upon the truth, so the argument is that they should follow what they already agree upon and abandon what they have innovated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The creed of Abraham is the perfect way, and none of the prophets brought a more complete one. **[Saʿdī]** Following that creed consists of *tawḥīd*, affirmation of every messenger and every book, and turning away from the false religions. **[Jalālayn]** The *ḥanīf* is the one who turns from every religion to submission. **[Qurṭubī]** The closing clause is a rebuttal of the claim that Abraham was upon their religion.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 6:161, "Say: truly my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters"; 16:123, "Then We revealed to you: follow the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolaters". **[Study Quran]** 2:135 for Abraham and the concept of *ḥanīf*. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:93–94 for the dispute this concludes. **[Jalālayn]** 3:93–94 for the setting; 2:135 for the creed. **[Saʿdī]** 3:96 for what follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:93 for the claim being rebutted.

**Reflection.** "Say: God has spoken the truth" is one of those short formulae that carries more than it seems, and al-Ṭabarī unpacks the whole of it: God is true in the specific factual claim about food, true in every report He has given, and you — the Jews — are the liars in attributing the prohibition to Him **[Ṭabarī]**. The second half of the verse is the more interesting move, because it is an argument from agreement rather than from difference: every party in the dispute already concedes that Abraham was upon the truth, so follow the thing you all concede and drop the things you invented on top of it **[Ṭabarī]**. That is a striking way to settle a religious quarrel, and Ibn Kathīr puts the same point as a claim about completeness — no prophet brought a more complete, clear, plain and perfect way than his **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Al-Saʿdī's summary of what the creed consists of is worth keeping: *tawḥīd*, affirming every messenger and every book, and turning away from the false religions, which is to say that the creed of Abraham is not a tribal claim but an inclusive one **[Saʿdī]**. And the closing clause does the work of exclusion that every creed must do — Abraham was not of the idolaters, and al-Ṭabarī is careful to say that this includes not being of their partisans **[Ṭabarī]**.

*Source note:* Maʿārif's block for 3:93–95 is a single unit, cited at 3:93; it has nothing separate for 3:95.

## 3:96 — إِنَّ أَوَّلَ بَيْتٍۢ وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ لَلَّذِى بِبَكَّةَ مُبَارَكًۭا وَهُدًۭى لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ

*"The first house established for mankind was that at Bakka — blessed, and a guidance for all the worlds."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The people of interpretation differed over the interpretation of this. **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: its interpretation is — the first house established for mankind, in which God is worshipped, blessed and a guidance for the worlds, is the one at Bakka; and they said it is not the first house established on the earth, for there were many houses before it. **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: rather, it *is* the first house established for mankind; then those who say that differed about the manner of its being established first, some saying that it was created before all the earths and the earths were then spread out beneath it. **[Jalālayn]** When they said "Our direction of prayer came before yours", the following was revealed: "The first house for worship established for the people on earth was that at Bakka", a variant of Makka, so called because it "crushes" — *tabukku* — the necks of tyrants. **[Jalālayn]** It was built by the angels before the creation of Adam, and after it the Aqṣā in Jerusalem was built, a period of forty years separating them, as reported in the ḥadīth of the two Ṣaḥīḥs; and in the ḥadīth, "the first thing to appear on the surface of the water at the creation of the heavens and the earth was a white foam, beneath which the earth was unrolled". **[Jalālayn]** "A blessed place" — a circumstantial qualifier referring to *la-lladhī*, meaning a place of blessings — "and a guidance to all worlds", because it is their qibla. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "The first House appointed for mankind" — for all people, for their acts of worship and religious rituals; they go around the House in *ṭawāf*, pray in its vicinity and remain in its area in *iʿtikāf*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Was that at Bakkah" — meaning the Kaʿbah that was built by Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl, whose religion the Jews and Christians claim they follow; however, they do not perform ḥajj to the house that Ibrāhīm built by God's command and to which he invited the people to perform ḥajj. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Full of blessing" — sanctified; "and a guidance for all the worlds". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan said: it is the first mosque in which God was worshipped on the earth. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid and Qatāda said: no house was placed before it. **[Qurṭubī]** ʿAlī, God be pleased with him, said: there were many houses before it, and the meaning is that it is the first house placed for worship. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: the Muslims and the Jews boasted against one another, and the Jews said: "Bayt al-Maqdis is better and greater than the Kaʿbah, for it is the place of migration of the prophets and is in the holy land"; and the Muslims said: "Rather the Kaʿbah is better" — so God revealed this verse. **[Saʿdī]** God, exalted is He, informs of the greatness of His Sacred House: that it is the first of the houses that God placed on the earth for His worship and the establishing of His remembrance; that in it are blessings, kinds of guidance, and varied benefits and advantages for the worlds — much and abundant bounty. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:96–97 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** And in it are clear signs that remind of the stations of Abraham the Friend and his movements in the ḥajj, and after him of the stations of the master of the messengers and their leader; and in it is the security — whoever enters it is secure by decree and commanded by law and religion. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The verse points to the distinction and superiority of the House of Allah over the houses, and even the mosques, of the whole world; there are several reasons for this status, which have been mentioned in this verse. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Among the true houses of worship in this world, the Kaʿbah enjoys the distinction of being the first; it is full of blessings; and it is a source of guidance for the entire world. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Adam was a prophet of Allah, and given his stature and his eminent position as Allah's vicegerent, it is likely that he, soon after his appearance on the earth, elected to build the House of Allah even before building his own residence; it is for this reason that ʿAbdullāh b. ʿUmar, Mujāhid, Qatādah and others among the Companions and their successors hold that the Kaʿbah is the first house in the world. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān — Isrāʾīliyyāt: the report that God created the site of the House two thousand years before He created anything of the earth)* **[Study Quran]** One interpretation is that the Kaʿbah was not the first house ever built, but that it was the first one established for all human beings — not only some — to come for worship. **[Study Quran]** Others say it is first in being full of blessing and a guidance for the worlds, in which case "first" could connote "foremost", as in "I am the first of those who submit" (6:163), referring to priority or status rather than temporal sequence. **[Study Quran]** Commentators also mention interpretations based on traditional accounts describing the Kaʿbah's foundations as dating back to the time of Adam, thus interpreting it as being literally the first house ever built, and referring not to the stones from which it was built but to the ground plan and the place where it stands. **[Study Quran]** If one understands "mankind" as "the people" — namely, the people of the region — it could mean that the Kaʿbah was the first temple established for the Arabs, which would reflect the story of Abraham and Ishmael in 2:125–27 as well as the idea that God assigned for Abraham the place of the House in 22:26, rather than helping him to discover it.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Blessed" is in the accusative; on the view that it is the first house established for mankind the estimate is "the first house established for mankind is the house that is at Bakka, blessed" — "blessed" being an indefinite, in the accusative as a *ḥāl* or by way of *qaṭʿ* — and "guidance" is in the accusative as a conjunction to it. **[Qurṭubī]** Mālik b. Anas said: Bakka is the site of the House and Makka is the rest of the town; Muḥammad b. Shihāb said: Bakka is the Mosque and Makka is the whole ḥaram, the houses included; and Mujāhid said: Bakka *is* Makka, the *mīm* being substituted for the *bāʾ*, as they say *lāzib* and *lāzim* — and al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Mu'arrij said the same. **[Qurṭubī]** Then it is said: Bakka is derived from *al-bakk*, which is crowding — *tabākka al-qawm*, "the people crowded" — and it was called Bakka because of the crowding of the people in the place of their *ṭawāf*; and *al-bakk* is also the crushing of the neck, so it is said it was called that because it crushes the necks of tyrants when they commit heresy in it with wrongdoing. **[Qurṭubī]** As for Makka, it is said it was so called for the scarcity of its water; and it is said because it draws out — *tamukku* — the marrow from the bone, from the hardship that befalls one who makes for it. **[Study Quran]** Bakkah is another name for Makkah, a different pronunciation of the same name resulting from an exchange of the *m* and *b* sounds, a common pronunciation alteration in Arabic. **[Study Quran]** Some opine that Bakkah meant the actual ground of the Kaʿbah itself and Makkah referred to the land around it; others derive the name from the verb *bakka*, meaning "to crowd", in reference to the crowding that takes place as a result of pilgrimage. **[Study Quran]** Later scholars have speculated as to whether the valley of Baca mentioned in Psalm 84:6 refers to Makkah, a question highly dependent upon various elements in that psalm, including the meaning of Baca, which could be "weeping" or "balsam trees". **[Study Quran]** To be full of blessing derives from *barakah*, which has the root meanings of growth and permanence. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Makkah's names include the City of Safety and al-Ma'mūn, Umm Raḥm, Umm al-Qurā and Ṣalāḥ, among others.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7422 — Khālid b. ʿUrʿura said: a man stood before ʿAlī and said, "Will you not tell me about the House — is it the first house established on the earth?" He said: "No; but it is the first house established in blessing, the station of Abraham, and whoever enters it is secure." **[Ṭabarī]** 7423 — Khālid b. ʿUrʿura said: I heard ʿAlī, when it was said to him "'the first house established for mankind is that at Bakka' — is it the first house that was on the earth?" He said: "No!" He was asked: "Then where were the people of Noah? And where were the people of Hūd?" He said: "But it is the first house established for mankind, blessed and a guidance." **[Ṭabarī]** 7424 — Ḥafṣ asked al-Ḥasan, and I was listening, about His saying "the first house established for mankind is that at Bakka, blessed" — and he said: "It is the first mosque in which God was worshipped on the earth." **[Ṭabarī]** 7425 — Maṭar: there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for worship. **[Ṭabarī]** 7426 — al-Ḥasan: "the first house established for mankind", in which God is worshipped. **[Ṭabarī]** 7427 — Saʿīd: it was established for worship. **[Ṭabarī]** 7428 — ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr said: God created the House two thousand years before the earth, and when His throne was upon the water it was a white foam, and the earth was spread out beneath it. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7429 — Mujāhid said: the first thing God created was the Kaʿbah, then He spread the earth beneath it. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7431 — al-Suddī: on the day when the earth was water, it was a foam upon the earth; and when God created the earth He created the House with it, so it is the first house established on the earth. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7432 — Qatāda: the first house God established; Adam circumambulated it, and those after him. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Qurṭubī]** It is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Dharr: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the first mosque established on the earth. He said: 'Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'Al-Masjid al-Aqṣā.' I said: 'How long between them?' He said: 'Forty years — then the earth is a mosque for you, so wherever the prayer overtakes you, pray.'" **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: God created the site of this House two thousand years before He created anything of the earth, and its foundations are in the lowest, seventh earth. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Qurṭubī]** As for al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, Sulaymān built it, as al-Nasāʾī transmitted with a sound chain from ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr. **[Qurṭubī]** ʿAbdullāh b. al-Zubayr said: no tyrant ever aimed at it with evil but God, exalted is He, crushed him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Dharr said: "I said, 'O Messenger of God, which masjid was the first to be built on the surface of the earth?' He said, 'Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām.' I said, 'Which was built next?' He said, 'Al-Masjid al-Aqṣā.' I said, 'How long between them?' He said, 'Forty years; then the earth is a mosque for you, so wherever the prayer finds you, pray.'"

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The safer reading is that the House is first in dignity and function — the first house established for the worship of God — not necessarily the first structure of any kind ever raised, since ʿAlī pointed to the peoples of Noah and Hūd. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse was revealed to settle a contest between the Muslims and the Jews over which sanctuary is greater, and it settles it for the Kaʿbah. **[Maʿārif]** Its superiority rests on three things named in the verse: it is first among the true houses of worship, it is full of blessings, and it is a guidance for the whole world. **[Study Quran]** To be "full of blessing" derives from *barakah*, whose root meanings are growth and permanence. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The House was built by Abraham, and the Jews and Christians claim to follow his religion yet do not perform the ḥajj to it.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** His earlier treatment of the building of the House and the first to build it, in Sūrat al-Baqarah; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim for the Abū Dharr ḥadīth; al-Nasāʾī for Sulaymān's building of al-Aqṣā. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:125 for the command to take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer; 3:97 for the signs and the ḥajj. **[Study Quran]** 2:127 for the foundations going back to Adam; 6:163 for "first" as "foremost"; 2:125–27 and 22:26 for the place of the House assigned to Abraham; Psalm 84:6 for the valley of Baca; the ḥadīth "One prayer at this Mosque is like a thousand prayers in all other mosques". **[Jalālayn]** 3:97 for the signs; the ḥadīth of the two Ṣaḥīḥs for the forty years. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:97 for what follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:97 for the obligation that follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is a claim about priority, and the commentators immediately ask what kind of priority it is — first in time, or first in rank **[Ṭabarī]**. ʿAlī's answer is the most disarming: of course it is not the first building on earth, he says — where were the peoples of Noah and Hūd? — it is the first house *established*, blessed and a guidance **[Ṭabarī]**. That distinction is what lets the tradition hold both the sober position and the reports that God created the site two thousand years before the earth and spread the land beneath it like a white foam on the water **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Jalālayn]**; the Study Quran's parallel suggestion, that "first" may mean "foremost" as in 6:163, arrives at the same place by a different route **[Study Quran]**. The occasion Qurṭubī records gives the verse its edge: it came down to settle a boasting match between the Muslims and the Jews about which sanctuary is greater, and it settles it for the Kaʿbah **[Qurṭubī]**. Ibn Kathīr's note is the uncomfortably practical one — this is the house Abraham built, the very house whose religion Jews and Christians claim to follow, and they do not come to it **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And the two names, Bakka and Makka, are explained two ways that are worth holding together: the philological, that the letters are simply exchanged, and the moral, that it is called Bakka because it crushes the necks of tyrants **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:97 — فِيهِ ءَايَٰتٌۢ بَيِّنَٰتٌۭ مَّقَامُ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ ۖ وَمَن دَخَلَهُۥ كَانَ ءَامِنًۭا ۗ وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ حِجُّ ٱلْبَيْتِ مَنِ ٱسْتَطَاعَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلًۭا ۚ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ عَنِ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ

*"In it are clear signs — the station of Abraham; and whoever enters it is secure. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by mankind, for those who can find a way to it. And whoever disbelieves — God is independent of all the worlds."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The readers differed over the reading of this: the readers of the cities read "in it are clear signs", *āyātun bayyinātun*, in the plural, meaning "in it are clear marks"; and Ibn ʿAbbās read it "in it is a clear sign", *āyatun bayyinatun*, meaning the station of Abraham — one sign being intended. **[Ṭabarī]** Then the people of interpretation differed over what those signs are: some said the station of Abraham and the Mashʿar al-Ḥarām and the like; others said the signs are the station of Abraham together with "whoever enters it is secure"; and others said the clear signs *are* the station of Abraham. **[Ṭabarī]** On "and pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by mankind": He means an obligation binding upon those who are able, of the people who are accountable, to find a way to the ḥajj of His Sacred House. **[Ṭabarī]** Then they differed over what "the way" is, the finding of which makes the ḥajj obligatory: some said it is provision and a mount; others said strength in expenditure, in the body and in the mount. **[Jalālayn]** "Therein are clear signs, among which is the station of Abraham" — that is the stone upon which he stood to build the House and on which his footprints remain; and the House has endured all this length of time and the constant passing of hands over it. **[Jalālayn]** Among these signs are the fact that the reward for good deeds is multiplied in it, and that birds never fly over it; "and whoever enters it is in security", not liable therein to be killed or oppressed or otherwise. **[Jalālayn]** "It is the duty of people towards God to make the pilgrimage to the House" — read either as *ḥijj al-bayt* or *ḥajj al-bayt*, two variants of the verbal noun from *ḥajj*, meaning the intention to journey there — "if he is able to make his way there", *man istatāʿa ilayhi sabīlan*, substituting for "people". **[Jalālayn]** As for the one who disbelieves in God or in what He has made obligatory with regard to the Pilgrimage, God is Independent of all worlds — the humans, the jinn and the angels — and Independent of their devotions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "In it are manifest signs" means clear signs that Ibrāhīm built the Kaʿbah and that God has honoured and blessed it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And Hajj to the House is a duty that mankind owes to God, for those who are able to undertake the journey" — this verse established the obligation of performing ḥajj; there are many ḥadīths that mention it as one of the pillars and fundamentals of Islam, and this is agreed upon by the Muslims; and according to the texts and the consensus of the scholars it is only obligatory for the adult Muslim to perform it once during his lifetime. **[Qurṭubī]** On "whoever enters it is secure": it was related from a group of the Salaf, among them Ibn ʿAbbās and others, that if a man incurs a *ḥadd* and then seeks refuge in the ḥaram, it protects him, because of His saying "whoever enters it is secure" — God having made security for whoever enters it. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn al-ʿArabī said: everyone who says this has erred from two directions — one, that he did not understand that the verse is a report about what has passed and was not intended to establish a ruling for the future; the other, that he did not know that this security has gone, and that killing and fighting occurred there after that, while God's report cannot be contrary to what it reports — which shows it was in the past. **[Qurṭubī]** Yaḥyā b. Jaʿdah said: the meaning of "whoever enters it is secure" is secure *from the Fire*; and Qurṭubī said: this is not in its generality, for in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, in the long ḥadīth of intercession from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, it is said to the believers interceding for their brothers in the Fire, "Bring out those whom you recognise" — and those brothers used to fast, pray and perform ḥajj with them. **[Qurṭubī]** Rather, one is secure from the Fire who enters it to perform its rites, magnifying it, knowing its right and drawing near to God thereby. **[Saʿdī]** Because it contains all this, God made its ḥajj obligatory upon those who are accountable and able to find a way to it — that is, whoever is able to reach it by any mount suited to him and provision he takes with him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And it is for this reason that He brought this wording, which can be applied to all mounts, existing and yet to come — and this is one of the signs of the Qurʾān, that its rulings are sound for every time and every condition, and there can be no complete soundness without them. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** So whoever submits to that and performs it is one of the guided believers; and whoever disbelieves and does not commit himself to the ḥajj of His House has left the religion — "and whoever disbelieves, God is independent of the worlds". *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Related in this verse are distinctions and merits of the House of Allah: firstly, it has many signs of Allah's power, one of them being the station of Abraham; secondly, one who enters there becomes a recipient of peace and remains protected, and cannot be killed by anybody; thirdly, it is obligatory on all Muslims around the world to make the ḥajj of the House of Allah, subject to the condition that one has the means and ability to reach it. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The clear signs refer to the station of Abraham; some say they refer to the footprints of Abraham that are believed to be preserved on the ground there. **[Study Quran]** "Whosoever enters it shall be secure" is read by some as referring to the past, in which case it would be rendered "Whosoever entered it was secure", since in pre-Islamic Arabia the *ḥaram* was a place where one could seek sanctuary and not be captured or arrested. **[Study Quran]** Many believe that under Islam the Kaʿbah and the *ḥaram* no longer serve this function — that one can no longer hide there from prosecution, and that any crimes committed there are equally liable to penalty, although the penalty is not carried out there. **[Study Quran]** Pilgrimage to the House is a duty is thought to be the passage that institutes the ḥajj as a requirement; others believe it is 2:196 that does so. **[Study Quran]** "Who can find a way" refers to those who are physically and financially able to undertake the ḥajj; and "whosoever disbelieves" can refer to denial of the obligatory nature of the ḥajj or to a general rejection of God and the Day of Judgment.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The *hāʾ* and *alif* in "you seek for it crookedness" style constructions go back to the feminine noun — here, "the way", *al-sabīl*, is treated as feminine. *(Ṭabarī's grammatical note on the preceding verse's construction)* **[Qurṭubī]** "In it are clear signs" is in the nominative as the subject or as the adjective; and the people of Makkah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd b. Jubayr read "a clear sign" in the singular. **[Jalālayn]** The verbal noun is read either *ḥijj* or *ḥajj*, both from *ḥajj* meaning the intention to journey there. **[Study Quran]** There is a minority opinion that reads "signs" in the singular, in which case it would refer to the station of Abraham.

**Readings.** **[Ṭabarī]** "In it are clear signs" — *āyātun bayyinātun*, the reading of the readers of the cities, in the plural; and Ibn ʿAbbās read *āyatun bayyinatun*, "a clear sign", in the singular, meaning the station of Abraham. **[Qurṭubī]** The people of Makkah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd b. Jubayr read the singular, meaning the station of Abraham alone — they said the trace of his two feet in the station is a clear sign; and the rest read the plural. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid explained the station of Abraham as the whole *ḥaram*, holding that among its signs are Ṣafā, Marwa, the Rukn and the Maqām; and those who read the plural meant the station of Abraham, the Black Stone, the Ḥaṭīm, Zamzam and all the *mashāʿir*. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Naḥḥās said: the one who reads "clear signs" in the plural has the clearer reading, because Ṣafā and Marwa are among the signs.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7448 — Ibn ʿAbbās: "in it are clear signs" — the station of Abraham and the Mashʿar. **[Ṭabarī]** 7449 — Qatāda and Mujāhid: "in it are clear signs — the station of Abraham": the station of Abraham is one of the clear signs. **[Ṭabarī]** 7450 — al-Ḥasan, on "in it are clear signs": "the station of Abraham, and whoever enters it is secure". **[Ṭabarī]** 7451 — al-Suddī: as for "the clear signs", they are the station of Abraham. **[Ṭabarī]** 7452 — Mujāhid, on the singular reading: "his two feet in the station are a clear sign". **[Ṭabarī]** 7474 — Ibn Jurayj said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, God be pleased with him, said of "for those who can find a way to it" — the provision and the mount. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own conclusion on the disagreements about the signs and about the "way": as for the reports narrated from the Messenger of God ﷺ that the way is "the provision and the mount", they are reports in whose chains there is room for scrutiny, and it is not permissible to argue with the like of them in the religion. **[Ṭabarī]** Al-Suddī said: as for "whoever disbelieves" — whoever finds the means with which to perform ḥajj and then does not perform it is a disbeliever. **[Ibn Kathīr]** When the building was raised, Ibrāhīm stood on the Maqām so that he could raise the walls higher, while his son Ismāʿīl was handing him the stones; and the Maqām used to be situated right next to the House, until ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, during his reign, moved it farther to the east so that those who go around the House in *ṭawāf* could perform it without disturbing those who pray next to the Maqām after finishing their *ṭawāf*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-ʿAwfī said that Ibn ʿAbbās commented: "Such as the Maqām and al-Mashʿar"; and Mujāhid said: "The impression of Ibrāhīm's feet remains on the Maqām as a clear sign" — and it was reported that ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Muqātil b. Ḥayyān said similarly. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: a man would commit murder, then wear a piece of wool around his neck and enter the *ḥaram*; and even when the son of the murdered person met him, he would not make a move against him until he left the sanctuary. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of God ﷺ once gave a speech in which he said: "O people! Ḥajj has been enjoined on you, therefore perform ḥajj." A man asked, "Is it every year, O Messenger of God?" — and he remained silent until the man repeated the question three times, then said: "Had I said yes, it would have become an obligation and you would not have been able to fulfil it. Leave me alone as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed by their many questions and their disagreement." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and several others commented on "whoever disbelieves": "Whoever denies the necessity of ḥajj becomes a disbeliever, and God is far richer than to need him." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Ismāʿīlī recorded that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Whoever can afford ḥajj but did not perform it, there is no difference in his case if he dies while Jew or Christian" — and this has an authentic chain of narration leading to ʿUmar. **[Qurṭubī]** Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq said: whoever enters it with purity, as the prophets and the friends of God entered it, is secure from His punishment — and this is the meaning of his saying ﷺ: "Whoever performs ḥajj and does not commit obscenity or sin goes out from his sins as on the day his mother bore him; and the accepted ḥajj has no reward but Paradise." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan said: the accepted ḥajj, *al-ḥajj al-mabrūr*, is that one returns ascetic toward this world and desirous of the Hereafter. **[Qurṭubī]** ʿUmar, God be pleased with him, said: "I had thought to send men to the provinces, and they would look at whoever has wealth and has not performed ḥajj, and impose the *jizyah* on them" — and that is His saying "and whoever disbelieves, God is independent of the worlds". **[Qurṭubī]** Saʿīd b. Jubayr said: "If a neighbour of mine died having the means and had not performed ḥajj, I would not pray over him." **[Qurṭubī]** Ashhab said to Mālik: "Is it the provision and the mount?" He said: "No, by God — that is only according to people's capacity; one may find the provision and the mount and yet not be able to travel, while another is able to walk upon his two feet." **[Maʿārif]** Since the time the foundations of the House of Allah were laid out, Allah Almighty has, because of its enormous blessings, provided protection to the people of Makkah against enemy attacks; when Abrahah invaded Makkah with his army of elephants, Allah, in His most perfect power, destroyed them through birds. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān — Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Maʿārif]** When there is rainfall on a certain side of the House of Allah, it has been observed that the countries situated on that side are favoured with substantial rainfalls; and another unusual sign relates to the *jamarāt*, at which every pilgrim throws seven pebbles each day for three days, and yet, with millions of pilgrims coming year after year, they do not grow into a mound. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān — Isrāʾīliyyāt)*

**Rulings.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The verse establishes the obligation of ḥajj, and by texts and consensus it is obligatory once in a lifetime for the adult Muslim. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own position on ability: the soundest view is that of Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAṭāʾ, that it is according to capacity — for *al-sabīl* in the speech of the Arabs is the road, so whoever finds a road to the ḥajj with nothing to prevent him, of chronic illness, incapacity, an enemy, scarcity of water on his route, provision, or weakness in walking, upon him is the obligation of ḥajj and nothing discharges him but performing it; and whoever finds no way — that is, cannot bear the ḥajj because some of these considerations are out of his reach — is one who finds no road to it and has no ability. **[Qurṭubī]** The majority hold that ḥajj is due with latitude, not immediately — which is the madhhab of Mālik as Ibn Khuwayz Mandād reports it, and the view of al-Shāfiʿī, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan and Abū Yūsuf in one narration; some later Baghdadi Mālikīs and Dāwūd hold that it is immediate and may not be delayed when one is able. **[Qurṭubī]** The first is correct, because God said in Sūrat al-Ḥajj "and proclaim the ḥajj among the people; they will come to you on foot" (22:27), while this sūrah came down in the year of Uḥud, in year three of the Hijrah — and the Messenger of God ﷺ did not perform ḥajj until year ten. **[Qurṭubī]** Impediments to the obligation include a creditor who prevents travel until the debt is paid, and dependants whose maintenance is due — for that spending is an immediate duty while ḥajj is a deferred one, so the dependants take priority; and one sells of his goods for the ḥajj as he would for a debt. **[Qurṭubī]** Our scholars said the verse entails that whoever dies without performing ḥajj while able, the threat applies to him, and it does not suffice for another to perform ḥajj on his behalf — for if another's ḥajj dropped the obligation from him, the threat would drop from him too. **[Qurṭubī]** The *ḥaram* does not shelter a fugitive from a *ḥadd*: it is a report about the past, and Abū Ḥanīfa's position — that such a person is not to be fed, given to drink, traded with or spoken to until he leaves — is self-contradictory, since being forced out is not compatible with security.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Whoever disbelieves" is best taken as whoever denies the obligation and rejects its necessity, for God is independent of him, of his ḥajj and of all the worlds together — since "disbelief" is in origin denial, and one who denies it, if he performs ḥajj, hopes for no *birr* by it, and if he leaves it he sees no sin in it. **[Jalālayn]** The one who disbelieves in God or in what He has made obligatory of the Pilgrimage is met by God's independence of all worlds and of their devotions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Whoever denies the necessity of ḥajj becomes a disbeliever. **[Maʿārif]** The one who believes ḥajj to be an obligation and yet does not perform it despite having the means is in a way no less a denier of the Divine command: the words "and if one disbelieves" apply to him in the form of admonition and warning, since he acts like the disbelievers who do not perform ḥajj; Muslim jurists have said that this is a severe warning. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Qurṭubī]** Security from the Fire belongs to the one who enters to perform the rites, magnifying the House, knowing its right and drawing near to God — not to everyone who enters.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:125, "And take the station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer"; 29:67, "Have they not seen that We have made a sanctuary secure while people are snatched away all around them?"; 3:96 for the House. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:96 for the House; 3:98, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:96 for the House; the ḥadīth of al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī and others for the explanation of ability as provision and a ride. **[Qurṭubī]** 22:27; the ḥadīth of Ḍimām b. Thaʿlabah; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim for the ḥadīth of intercession; the ḥadīth "Whoever performs ḥajj and does not commit obscenity or sin". **[Study Quran]** 2:125 for the station of Abraham; 2:125–26, 14:35 and 28:57 for the secure sanctuary; 2:196 for the alternative view of the verse instituting ḥajj; 2:126 and the ḥadīth on the limited violence at the conquest of Makkah. **[Saʿdī]** 3:96 for the House; 3:98, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** Sūrat al-Fīl for Abrahah; Ibn Mājah and al-Ṭaḥāwī for the multiplication of prayers.

**Reflection.** Three claims are packed into one verse — signs, security, and obligation — and the commentators treat each as a separate problem **[Maʿārif]**. The signs are the easiest and the most charming: the footprints in the stone on which Abraham stood to raise the walls while Ishmael handed him the stones **[Ibn Kathīr]**, and, in the plural reading, Ṣafā, Marwa, the Black Stone, Zamzam and the fact that birds do not fly over the House **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Jalālayn]**. Security is the hardest, because the plain sense of "whoever enters it is secure" is contradicted by ordinary facts, and the tradition handles it three ways: as a report about the pre-Islamic *ḥaram*, where a murderer could walk in wearing a wool cord and walk out again **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Study Quran]**; as a legal question about whether the sanctuary shelters a fugitive from punishment, which Ibn al-ʿArabī answers by pointing out that killing happened there afterward and God's report cannot be false, so it must be about the past **[Qurṭubī]**; or as security from the Fire, which Qurṭubī immediately qualifies with the ḥadīth of intercession, noting that some who prayed, fasted and performed ḥajj are still in it **[Qurṭubī]**. Then there is the obligation, and here al-Ṭabarī is unexpectedly severe on a point of method: the famous ḥadīth defining ability as "provision and a mount" he declines to build on, saying plainly that there is room for scrutiny in its chains and that one may not argue in the religion with the like of it, preferring the view that it is a matter of capacity **[Ṭabarī]**. The warnings at the end are the sharpest in the sūrah — ʿUmar's half-serious thought of taxing those who could go and did not, Saʿīd b. Jubayr refusing to pray over such a man, and ʿUmar again: "there is no difference in his case if he dies while Jew or Christian" **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**.

## 3:98 — قُلْ يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لِمَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱللَّهُ شَهِيدٌ عَلَى مَا تَعْمَلُونَ

*"Say: 'O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God, when God is Witness of what you do?'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is He, means by this: O assembly of the Jews of the Children of Israel, and others besides them of those who profess the religion of what God has sent down of His books, of those who disbelieve in Muḥammad ﷺ and deny his prophethood — "why do you disbelieve in the signs of God?", meaning: why do you deny the proofs of God which He gave to Muḥammad in your books and elsewhere, which have been established against you as proof of his truthfulness, his prophethood and his argument? **[Ṭabarī]** "And you know" — that is: why do you deny that of his affair, when you know that he is truthful? So God, exalted is His praise, informed about them that they deliberately disbelieve in God and in His messenger, knowingly, and with knowledge of their disbelief. **[Jalālayn]** "Say: 'O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in God's verses'" — that is, the Qurʾān — "'when God is Witness of what you do?'" and will requite you for it? **[Ibn Kathīr]** In this verse God criticizes the disbelieving People of the Book for refusing the truth, rejecting God's signs and hindering those who seek to believe from His path, although they know that what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with is the truth from God. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:98–99)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** They learned this from the previous prophets and honourable messengers, may God's peace and blessings be on them all: they all brought the glad tidings and the good news of the coming of the unlettered, Arab, Hāshimī prophet from Makkah, the master of the Children of Adam, the Final Prophet and the Messenger of the Lord of the heavens and the earth. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God has warned the People of the Book against this behaviour, stating that He is Witness over what they do, indicating their defiance of the knowledge conveyed to them by the prophets; they rejected, denied and refused the very Messenger whom they were ordered to convey the glad tidings about. **[Saʿdī]** When He had established the proofs against the People of the Scripture — though before that they knew the Prophet ﷺ as they know their own sons — He rebuked the obstinate among them for their disbelief in the signs of God and their barring people from the path of God, because their common folk follow their scholars. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:98–99 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** And God, exalted is He, knows their states and will repay them for that with the fullest and most complete recompense. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** These verses relate to a particular event. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:98–100, with the story of Shammās b. Qays — cited at 3:100)* **[Maʿārif]** Here the verses begin with an admonition to the People of the Book who had engineered this, and this admonition has been done with great eloquence: before admonishing them for what they did, they were taken to task for their disbelief as well — which meant that it would have made better sense if they themselves had taken to the right path and become Muslims, rather than devoting themselves to distracting others to the wrong track. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** In 3:98–99 the Prophet is commanded to challenge the People of the Book regarding their rejection of him. *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:98–99)* **[Study Quran]** That "you are witnesses" refers to the fact that they should be conscious of the Messenger's presence among them, as in 3:101, and that the truths the Prophet teaches are not unfamiliar to them but are in fact found in their own sacred books.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "The signs of God" are glossed as the proofs God gave to Muḥammad in their books and elsewhere. **[Jalālayn]** The signs are identified here with the Qurʾān. **[Study Quran]** "Witnesses" is understood in relation to the Messenger's presence among them and to their own books.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7522 — al-Suddī: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God" — as for "the signs of God", it is Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Ṭabarī]** 7523 — al-Ḥasan, on "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God, when God is Witness of what you do": they are the Jews and the Christians. **[Ibn Kathīr]** All of the previous prophets brought the glad tidings of the coming of the unlettered, Arab, Hāshimī prophet from Makkah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God states that He is never unaware of what they do, and He will hold them responsible for their actions — "the Day whereon neither wealth nor sons will avail" (26:88).

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The question is not asked to elicit information but to record that their disbelief is deliberate and knowing. **[Ibn Kathīr]** They knew from their own prophets that the Messenger was coming, and they refused the very one they had been ordered to announce. **[Saʿdī]** The rebuke is addressed to the obstinate among them, whose common folk follow their scholars. **[Study Quran]** Their being "witnesses" means the truths he teaches are in their own books. **[Maʿārif]** The admonition is pointed: it would have made better sense for them to take the right path themselves than to busy themselves turning others off it.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 26:88, "The Day whereon neither wealth nor sons will avail"; 3:99, which continues the same rebuke; 3:100 for the event behind these verses. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:99, which follows and shares the same occasion; 3:93–95 for the preceding argument. **[Study Quran]** 3:101 for the Messenger's presence among them; 7:157 for the description of the Prophet in their books. **[Jalālayn]** 3:99 for the continuation. **[Saʿdī]** 3:99 for the continuation.

**Reflection.** After four verses about Abraham, the Torah and the House, the sūrah turns back to the People of the Scripture, and the turn is abrupt enough that Maʿārif finds it worth remarking on: these verses have a particular event behind them **[Maʿārif]**. The question asked is "why", and al-Ṭabarī is careful about what kind of question it is — it is not a request for information but a record of deliberateness, since they know he is truthful **[Ṭabarī]**. The two identifications of "the signs of God" are worth holding side by side: al-Suddī says the sign *is* Muḥammad ﷺ himself, and Jalālayn says it is the Qurʾān **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Jalālayn]** — which is to say the same thing from two ends, the messenger and the message. Ibn Kathīr's grievance is specific and personal: every previous prophet had been sent to announce this one, and they refused the very person they were commissioned to announce **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And Maʿārif notes the order of the rebuke — they are taken to task for their own disbelief before they are taken to task for diverting others, which is the rhetorical point that a person should set himself right before he spends his energy unmaking other people **[Maʿārif]**.

*Source note:* Qurṭubī's block for 3:98–99 comments only on 3:99 — its opening words are "why do you bar (*taṣuddūna*) from the path of God those who believe" — and it has nothing on 3:98; that block is cited at 3:99.

## 3:99 — قُلْ يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لِمَ تَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ مَنْ ءَامَنَ تَبْغُونَهَا عِوَجًۭا وَأَنتُمْ شُهَدَآءُ ۗ وَمَا ٱللَّهُ بِغَٰفِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ

*"Say: 'O People of the Scripture, why do you bar those who believe from the path of God, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And God is not heedless of what you do.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: O assembly of the Jews of the Children of Israel and others, of those who profess belief in the books of God — "why do you bar from the path of God", meaning: why do you lead astray from the way of God and His clear road, which He laid down for His prophets, His friends and the people of faith, "those who believe", meaning those who believe in God and His messenger and what he brought from God? **[Ṭabarī]** "Seeking to make it crooked" — seeking crookedness for it; and the *hāʾ* and *alif* in "you seek for it" refer back to "the path", which is treated as feminine because *al-sabīl* is feminine. **[Ṭabarī]** "And you are witnesses" — witnesses that what you bar them from of the path is the truth, which you know and find in your books. **[Ṭabarī]** "And God is not heedless of what you do" — God is not heedless of your deeds, of what you do of what He does not approve for His servants and otherwise, until He either hastens the punishment for you or defers it for you until you meet Him and He recompenses you for it. **[Jalālayn]** "Say: 'O People of the Scripture, why do you bar believers, causing them to turn away from God's way'" — His religion — "by denying the truth of the Prophet and concealing His graces, desiring to make it crooked": *ʿiwajan* is the verbal noun meaning *muʿawwajan*, "made crooked", inclining away from the truth — "while you yourselves are witnesses" that the religion which is upright and pleasing to God is that of Islam, as stated in your Book. **[Jalālayn]** "God is not heedless of what you do" in the way of unbelief and mendacity; rather, He gives you respite until your appointed time, and then requites you. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God criticizes the disbelieving People of the Book for refusing the truth, rejecting God's signs and hindering those who seek to believe from His path, although they know that what the Messenger ﷺ was sent with is the truth from God. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:98–99)* **[Qurṭubī]** "Why do you bar from the religion of God those who believe" — that is, *taṣrifūna*, you turn them away from the religion of God. **[Qurṭubī]** "And you are witnesses" — that is, possessors of reason; and it is said: witnesses that it is written in the Torah that the religion of God, other than which He accepts none, is Islam, since in it is the description of Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Saʿdī]** He rebuked the obstinate among them for their disbelief in the signs of God and their barring people from the path of God, because their common folk follow their scholars; and God, exalted is He, knows their states and will repay them for that with the fullest and most complete recompense. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:98–99)* **[Maʿārif]** Following the admonition of the People of the Book for what they engineered, the Muslims have been addressed and served with a word of caution, especially when they have by their side the Book and the Messenger of Allah — two powerful, never-failing sources which would help them stay firm in their belief. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:98–100, cited here and at 3:100)* **[Study Quran]** Some interpret their attempts to make the way of God crooked — compare 7:45; 11:19; 14:3 — as an act of misdirection, since, when they were asked about it, the People of the Book denied that Muhammad was foretold in their books; see 7:157. *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:98–99)* **[Study Quran]** It is understood not as a physical hindering, but as a desire on their part to misguide Muslims and turn them away from their own religion by making it crooked, that is, making it appear false, in order to create doubt in the minds of as many Muslims as possible. **[Study Quran]** That they are witnesses refers to the fact that they should be conscious of the Messenger's presence among them, and that the truths the Prophet teaches are not unfamiliar to them but are in fact found in their own sacred books.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The meaning of "you seek for it crookedness" is illustrated from the poet Suhaym, the slave of the Banū al-Ḥasḥās: "Your seeking and what you seek, until you found it — as though you had appointed it an appointment yesterday" — that is, your seeking and the thing you seek. **[Ṭabarī]** One says *ibghnī kadhā*, meaning "seek it for me"; and if they mean "help me seek it", they say *abghnī* with a *fatḥa* on the *alif* — just as one says *iḥlubnī*, "milk for me", and *aḥlibnī*, "help me milk"; and everything of this type follows the same pattern. **[Ṭabarī]** "Al-ʿiwaj" is crookedness and deviation, and what is meant by it here is misguidance from right guidance. **[Qurṭubī]** "You seek for it crookedness" — you seek for it, the *lām* being elided, as in "and when they measure to them" (83:3); one says *baghaytu lahu kadhā*, "I sought it for him", and *abghaytuhu kadhā*, "I helped him". **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ʿiwaj*, with *kasra* on the ʿayn, is deviation in religion, speech and deed, and whatever departs from the way of evenness; and with *fatḥa* it is used of a wall, a building and every standing, upright object — from Abū ʿUbayda and others. **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning of "they follow the caller; there is no *ʿiwaja* in him" (20:108) is: they cannot deviate from his call. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan read *tuṣiddūna*, with a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ* and a *kasra* on the *ṣād* — and they are two dialects, *ṣadda* and *aṣadda*, like *ṣalla al-laḥmu* and *aṣalla* when the meat stank, and *khamma* and *akhamma* when it changed.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** These two verses — from "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God" and the verses after it, up to "for those is a great punishment" — came down concerning a man of the Jews who tried to provoke discord between the two clans of the Aws and the Khazraj after Islam, so that they would revert to what they had been upon in the Jāhiliyya of enmity and mutual hatred; God censured him for that deed, made what he did repugnant to him and rebuked him for it, and He also admonished the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, forbidding them from division and difference and commanding them to come together and be harmonious. **[Ṭabarī]** 7524 — Ibn Isḥāq said, from one he trusts, from Zayd b. Aslam: Shās b. Qays — and he was an old man grown old in the Jāhiliyya, great in unbelief, violent in rancour against the Muslims and violent in envy of them — passed by a number of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ of the Aws and the Khazraj, in a gathering where they had come together to talk. What he saw of their unity, their harmony and the soundness of their relations with one another upon Islam, after the enmity that had been between them in the Jāhiliyya, enraged him, and he said: "The notables of the Banū Qayla have gathered in this land! By God, we have no standing with them if their notables gather here." So he ordered a young man of the Jews who was with him *(to recite to them the poetry of their old wars)*. **[Ṭabarī]** 7528 — al-Ḥasan, on "Say: O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the path of God": they are the Jews and the Christians; He forbade them to bar the Muslims from the path of God and to want to divert the people to misguidance. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's summary of the difference over "the path": on al-Suddī's reading the meaning is — why do you bar from Muḥammad, and prevent those who believe in him from following him, by your concealing the description of him that you find in your books? And on this reading, "Muḥammad" is "the path", and "seeking crookedness for it" means seeking destruction for Muḥammad; but the rest of the reports and sayings are along the lines of the interpretation already set out — that "the path" mentioned in this place is Islam, and what Muḥammad brought of the truth from God. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan's variant reading *tuṣiddūna* is recorded, and the parallel dialects *ṣadda* / *aṣadda* are given as *ṣalla* / *aṣalla* and *khamma* / *akhamma*.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The wrong described is not a physical blocking but a leading astray: turning people away from the way God laid down, and wanting deviation for it. **[Jalālayn]** The means spoken of are denying the truth of the Prophet and concealing His graces, and the witnesses' own Book testifies that Islam is the upright religion. **[Study Quran]** It is a desire to misguide rather than a physical hindering — to make the religion appear false and so plant doubt. **[Qurṭubī]** "Witnesses" here is taken either as people of reason or as witnesses to what is written in the Torah about Islam and about the description of Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Saʿdī]** The blame falls on the scholars in particular, because the common folk follow them. **[Ṭabarī]** God's not being heedless means either a hastened punishment or a deferred one until they meet Him.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 83:3 for the elided *lām*; 20:108 for *ʿiwaj*; 5:95 for a parallel elision. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:98, which shares the same occasion; 3:100, which continues to "a great punishment". **[Study Quran]** 7:45, 11:19 and 14:3 for making the way crooked; 7:157 for the description of the Prophet in their books; 3:101 for the Messenger's presence among them. **[Jalālayn]** 3:98 for the setting; 3:100, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:98 for the rebuke; 3:100 for the event. **[Maʿārif]** 3:100 for the event and the address to the believers.

**Reflection.** The word at the centre of the verse is "crooked", and the commentators expend real care on it **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī traces it to a line of poetry and then to a grammatical distinction that is easy to miss: *ibghnī* means "seek it for me" and *abghnī* means "help me seek it", like *iḥlubnī* and *aḥlibnī* — and that second form is the one used here, so the sense is not merely that they wanted the path crooked but that they worked to make it so, helping one another at it **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī distinguishes *ʿiwaj* with *kasra*, which is crookedness in religion, speech and deed, from *ʿawaj* with *fatḥa*, which is the lean in a wall or a standing post **[Qurṭubī]**. The charge itself is not of physical obstruction but of misdirection — making the religion look false so that doubt spreads — which both Qurṭubī and the Study Quran say outright **[Study Quran]**, **[Jalālayn]**. And there is a genuine difference recorded about what "the path" is: al-Suddī read it as Muḥammad himself, so that seeking crookedness for it means seeking his destruction, while the others take it as Islam and the truth he brought **[Ṭabarī]**. The closing clause leaves the matter open in the only way it can be left open: God is not heedless, which means either a punishment hastened or a punishment deferred until they meet Him **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Jalālayn]**.

*Source note:* The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:99 — its combined note for 3:98–99 is cited at 3:98.

## 3:100 — يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن تُطِيعُوا۟ فَرِيقًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ يَرُدُّوكُم بَعْدَ إِيمَٰنِكُمْ كَٰفِرِينَ

*"O you who believe! If you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture, they will turn you back, after your belief, as disbelievers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The people of interpretation differed over who is meant by this. **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: He means by "O you who believe" the Aws and the Khazraj, and by "those who were given the Scripture" Shās b. Qays the Jew, according to the report of Zayd b.
