Aslam already mentioned. **[Ṭabarī]** Others said the same of those meant by "those who believe", except that they said the one between whom and some men of the Anṣār words passed, until they were on the point of fighting and through whom the Jew found a point of entry against them, was Thaʿlaba b. ʿAnama al-Anṣārī. **[Ṭabarī]** The meaning of the verse: O you who have believed in God and His messenger and acknowledged what came to you from your Prophet from God — if you obey a group of those who profess the Book, of the people of the Torah and the Gospel, and accept from them what they command you, they will misguide you and turn you back, after your believing in the messenger of your Lord and after your acknowledging what he brought from your Lord, as disbelievers — meaning, deniers of what you believed and affirmed of the truth that came to you from your Lord. **[Ṭabarī]** So God, exalted is His praise, forbade them to seek their counsel, or to accept from them any opinion or advice, and taught them that they harbour malice, deceit, envy and hatred toward them. **[Jalālayn]** The following was revealed when the Jews passed by the Aws and the Khazraj and were infuriated by their comradeship, and set about reminding them of their mutual hostility in the days before Islam, so that they caused them to quarrel and the two tribes were on the verge of fighting one another. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God warns His believing servants against obeying the People of the Book, who envy the believers for the favour that God gave them by sending His Messenger ﷺ — as He said: "Many of the People of the Scripture wish that they could turn you away as disbelievers after you have believed, out of their own envy" (2:109). **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And how would you disbelieve, while unto you are recited the verses of God, and among you is His Messenger?" (3:101) — meaning: disbelief is far from touching you, since the verses of God are being sent down on His Messenger ﷺ day and night, and he recites and conveys them to you. **[Qurṭubī]** "O you who believe" means the Aws and the Khazraj; "if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture" means Shās and his companions. **[Saʿdī]** When He had established the proofs against the People of the Scripture and rebuked them for their unbelief and their obstinacy, He warned His believing servants against being deceived by them, and made clear to them that this party among them are eager to harm you and to turn you back to unbelief after faith. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:100–101 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** But, praise be to God, you, O company of believers — after God favoured you with the religion and you saw its signs, its beauties, its merits and its virtues, and the Messenger of God is among you guiding you to all your interests, and you hold fast to God and to His rope which is His religion — it is impossible that they should turn you from your religion, because a religion built on these foundations and these firm, luminous pillars draws hearts to itself, takes hold of the hearts and brings the servants to the most glorious end and the best of what is sought. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** There was a Jew, Shammās b. Qays, who harboured a chronic malice against Muslims; once, when he saw two Anṣār tribes, Aws and Khazraj, gathered together amiably at one place, his malevolence got the better of him, and he went about looking for ways to sow discord between them. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:98–100, cited here and at 3:98–99)* **[Maʿārif]** They took the warning to their hearts; they knew this was a slip caused by Satan; they embraced each other, wept and repented — and these verses were revealed in the background of this event. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** One of the Jews of Madinah happened upon a gathering of Muslims belonging to the previously warring tribes of Aws and Khazraj; he began to instigate trouble between them by reminding them of their wars and the insults they used to hurl at one another, and succeeded in heating up the gathering to the point that the Muslims almost came to blows. **[Study Quran]** When the Prophet heard this, he came out and said: "Would you return to the practices of the times of ignorance, though I am among you, and God has honoured you with Islam and reconciled your hearts?" — and they then laid down their weapons, embraced one another, and left with the Prophet.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7529 — al-Suddī: it was revealed concerning Thaʿlaba b. ʿAnama al-Anṣārī; there were words between him and some men of the Anṣār, and a Jew of Qaynuqāʿ walked between them and set some of them against others, until the two parties of the Aws and the Khazraj were on the point of taking up arms and fighting one another; so God revealed "if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture, they will turn you back after your belief, disbelievers" — meaning: if you take up arms and fight one another, you have disbelieved. **[Ṭabarī]** 7530 — Mujāhid, through Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj: the clans of the Anṣār consisted of two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, and there had been war, bloodshed and hatred between them in the Jāhiliyya, until God favoured them with Islam and with the Prophet ﷺ; God extinguished the war that had been between them and joined their hearts through Islam. **[Ṭabarī]** A man of the Aws and a man of the Khazraj were sitting talking, with a Jew sitting with them, and he kept reminding them of their days and of the enmity that had been between them, until they reviled one another and then fought; and each called his people, and they went out with weapons and drew up in ranks against one another. **[Ṭabarī]** The Messenger of God ﷺ was present in Madīna that day, and he came and kept walking between them, to these and to those, to calm them, until they went back and laid down their weapons — and God sent down the Qurʾān about it: "O you who believe, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture", up to His saying "a great punishment". **[Ṭabarī]** 7531 — Qatāda: "God has already warned you about them as you hear, has cautioned you and informed you of their misguidance; so do not entrust them with your religion, and do not seek their counsel in your affairs, for they are envying, misguided enemies. How can you trust a people who disbelieved in their own book, killed their messengers, wandered in confusion in their religion and were incapable of helping themselves? Those, by God, are the people of suspicion and enmity!" **[Ṭabarī]** 7532 — al-Rabīʿ, the like of it. **[Qurṭubī]** It was revealed concerning a Jew who wanted to renew the discord between the Aws and the Khazraj after it had ceased through the Prophet ﷺ; he sat among them and recited to them poetry that one of the two clans had composed in their war, and the other clan said: "Our poet said such-and-such on such-and-such a day" — and something of that entered them, and they said: "Come, let us restore the war fresh, as it was." **[Qurṭubī]** These called out "O people of Aws!", and those "O people of Khazraj!", and they gathered, took up weapons and drew up in ranks for battle; then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ came and stood between the two ranks and recited it, raising his voice; and when they heard his voice they fell silent and listened, and when he finished they threw down their weapons and embraced one another and wept — from ʿIkrima, Ibn Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Qurṭubī]** Jābir b. ʿAbdillāh said: "No one who came into view was more hateful to us than the Messenger of God ﷺ [that day]; then he gestured to us with his hand and we held back, and God set right what was between us; and no person became more beloved to us than the Messenger of God ﷺ — I have never seen a day uglier and more dreadful at first and better at the end than that day." **[Ibn Kathīr]** A ḥadīth states that one day the Prophet said to his Companions: "Who among the faithful believers do you consider has the most amazing faith?" They said: "The angels." He said: "Why would they not believe, since they are with their Lord?" They mentioned the prophets, and he said: "Why would they not believe, while the revelation is sent down to them?" They said: "Then, we are." He said: "Why would you not believe when I am among you?" They asked: "Who has the most amazing faith?" He said: "A people who will come after you, and who will find only books that they will believe in." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And whoever depends upon God, then he is indeed guided to the right path" (3:101) — for trusting and relying on God are the basis of achieving right guidance and staying away from the path of wickedness.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse forbids taking counsel from them or accepting their opinion, and states why: malice, deceit, envy and hatred. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Disbelief is far from touching the believers while the verses are being sent down and the Messenger is among them. **[Saʿdī]** A religion built on those foundations cannot be taken away by them, and holding fast to God is the way to safety. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse is addressed to the Aws and the Khazraj, and "a party of those who were given the Scripture" means Shās and his companions. **[Maʿārif]** The people themselves recognised the incident as an incitement from Satan and a plot from their enemy.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:109 for the envy of the People of the Book; 3:101 for "and how would you disbelieve"; 57:8, "And what is the matter with you that you believe not in God, while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord"; 3:99 for the verses that share this occasion. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:99 for the setting; the report of Zayd b. Aslam already cited; 3:101–103 for "a great punishment". **[Qurṭubī]** 3:99 for the setting; 3:101, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 3:100–106 for the passage on division among the believers. **[Saʿdī]** 3:101 for holding fast to God.

**Reflection.** This verse is one of the few in the sūrah where the occasion is not in dispute — only the name is **[Ṭabarī]**. A Jew, aged and rancorous, came upon a room of Aws and Khazraj sitting amicably together, men who had spent years killing one another before Islam, and he sent a young man in to recite the old war-poetry until the room caught fire; by the time the Prophet reached them, two armed ranks were drawn up **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. Whether the man at the centre was Thaʿlaba b. ʿAnama, as al-Suddī has it, or the Jew is Shās b. Qays, as Zayd b. Aslam's report names him, makes no difference to the point **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī's own formulation of the verse's meaning is the sharpest thing in the commentaries on it: the danger is not that they will argue you out of your religion but that you will *take their counsel*, and the reason given is not their arguments but what is in them — malice, deceit, envy, hatred **[Ṭabarī]**. Qatāda's report puts the same case in a single rhetorical question: how can you trust people who disbelieved in their own book, killed their own messengers and could not even help themselves **[Ṭabarī]**? The ending is the part worth remembering: Jābir said that on that day no one who came into view was more hateful to them than the Prophet, and by the end of it no one was more beloved — and he added that he had never seen a day uglier at first and better at the end **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:101 — وَكَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ وَأَنتُمْ تُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْكُمْ ءَايَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ وَفِيكُمْ رَسُولُهُۥ ۗ وَمَن يَعْتَصِم بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدْ هُدِىَ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍۢ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ

*"And how can you disbelieve, while the signs of God are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: "And how can you disbelieve" — O believers, after your belief in God and in His messenger, that you should turn back on your heels — "while the signs of God are recited to you", meaning the proofs of God against you which He has sent down in His Book to His prophet Muḥammad ﷺ — "and His Messenger is among you" as a further proof of God against you, alongside the signs of His Book, all of it calling you to the truth, showing you guidance and right conduct, and forbidding you error and misguidance? **[Ṭabarī]** He says to them, exalted is His remembrance: so what excuse will you have with your Lord for denying the prophethood of your prophet, and turning back on your heels, and returning to the ways of your Jāhiliyya, if you revert to it and disbelieve — when in him are these clear proofs and evident signs of the wrongness of your doing it, if you do it? **[Jalālayn]** "How can you disbelieve" — this is an interrogative of amazement and rebuke — "while you have God's verses recited to you and His Messenger is in your midst? Whoever holds fast to" — clings to — "God, he is guided to a straight path." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And how would you disbelieve, while unto you are recited the verses of God, and among you is His Messenger?" — meaning, disbelief is far from touching you, since the verses of God are being sent down on His Messenger ﷺ day and night, and he recites and conveys them to you. **[Qurṭubī]** He said this by way of astonishment — that is, "and how can you disbelieve while the signs of God", meaning the Qurʾān, "are recited to you, and His Messenger" — Muḥammad ﷺ — "is among you". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Zajjāj said: it is possible that this address is to the Companions of Muḥammad specifically, because the Messenger of God ﷺ was among them and they saw him; and it is possible that it is addressed to the whole community, because his traces, his marks, and the Qurʾān which he was given stand in our midst in the place of the Prophet ﷺ even though we did not see him. **[Saʿdī]** After God had established the proofs against the People of the Scripture and rebuked them for their unbelief and their obstinacy, He warned His believing servants against being deceived by them, and made clear to them that this party among them are eager to harm you and to turn you back to unbelief after faith. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:100–101 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** But, praise be to God, you, O company of believers — after God favoured you with the religion and you saw its signs, its beauties, its merits and its virtues, and the Messenger of God is among you guiding you to all your interests, and you hold fast to God and to His rope which is His religion — it is impossible that they should turn you from your religion. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** "And whoever holds fast to God" — that is, trusts in Him and seeks shelter in His protection — "has been guided to a straight path"; and in this is the encouragement to hold fast to Him, and that it is the way to safety and guidance. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Following this, the Muslims have been addressed and served with a word of caution, especially when they have by their side the Book and the Messenger of God — two powerful, never-failing sources, which would help them stay firm in their belief. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:98–101, whose account of Shammās b. Qays is cited at 3:98 and 3:100)* **[Maʿārif]** The expression "and whoever holds on to Allah" means one who stays firm in, and totally committed to, his faith; for *iʿtiṣām*, the act of holding on to Allah firmly, denotes that one should affirm His Being and His Attributes, be staunchly faithful to what He has ordained, and in the process be sure not to be lured into supporting the position of any adversary, whoever that may be. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** One who acts in this manner "is surely guided to the straight path" — it means that such a person is on the straight path, and being on the straight path is the key to all that is good and beneficial which the Word of God promises him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The point of this verse is that, in the face of both the revelation of the Quran and the presence of the Prophet, people have all the proof they need to keep them from disbelief. **[Study Quran]** The challenge presented by the Quran, in its eloquence and inimitability, is here coupled with mention of the Prophet himself. **[Study Quran]** The description of the Prophet's physical and spiritual presence is a major aspect of the Islamic tradition, regarding which there is an entire genre of literature; Muslims consider his physical presence and demeanour to have been signs of the truth of his message and vocation, and the Companions believed that his actual physical body carried blessings and a kind of palpable grace.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** "How" is in the accusative position; and the *fāʾ* is vowelled with *fatḥa* in the view of al-Khalīl and Sībawayhi because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, *fatḥa* being chosen for it because what precedes the *fāʾ* is a *yāʾ*, so it was felt heavy to combine a *yāʾ* with a *kasra*. **[Ṭabarī]** The root of *al-ʿaṣm* is prevention: everyone who prevents a thing is its *ʿāṣim*, and the one protected by it is *muʿtaṣim bihi*; and from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq, "I am the son of the two protectors of the Banū Tamīm, when the greatest of misfortunes befalls." **[Ṭabarī]** It is for this reason that the rope is called *ʿiṣām*, and the means by which a man reaches his need is called *ʿiṣām* — as in the saying of al-Aʿshā, "To the man Qays I lengthen the night-journey, and I take from every tribe bonds of protection," meaning the ties of *dhimma* and security. **[Qurṭubī]** One says *aʿṣama bihi* and *iʿtaṣama*, *tamassaka* and *istamsaka*, when one is protected by him from another; and *iʿtaṣamtu fulānan* means "I prepared for him that by which he might hold fast"; and everyone who holds to a thing is *muʿṣim* and *muʿtaṣim*, and everyone who prevents a thing is *ʿāṣim*. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Nābigha said: "He remains, for fear of him, with the sailor holding fast to the rudder after weariness and sweat"; and another said: "He pledged himself in it, holding fast, and cast his ropes and relied." **[Study Quran]** To "hold fast" evokes in Arabic the image of a person holding on to something to avoid falling into harm, in this case disbelief. **[Study Quran]** "Is indeed guided unto a straight path" is understood either to be identical with "holding fast" — meaning that the very act of holding fast is God's guidance for His creatures — or that in holding fast one will then become guided.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7533 — Qatāda, on "and how can you disbelieve while the signs of God are recited to you": two clear signs — the finding of the Prophet of God ﷺ and the Book of God. As for the Prophet of God, he has passed on; and as for the Book of God, God has left it among you as a mercy from God and a favour, in it His lawful and His unlawful, obedience to Him and disobedience to Him. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: there was fighting and evil between the Aws and the Khazraj in the Jāhiliyya, and they mentioned what had been between them and some of them rose against others with swords; the Prophet ﷺ was told of it and went to them — and this verse came down, "and how can you disbelieve while the signs of God are recited to you and His Messenger is among you", up to His saying "and He delivered you from it" [3:103]. **[Qurṭubī]** And everyone who did not see the Prophet ﷺ enters into this verse, because what is among them of his sunna takes the place of seeing him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7534 — Ibn Jurayj, on "whoever holds fast to God has been guided": he believes in God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** A ḥadīth states that one day the Prophet said to his Companions: "Who among the faithful believers do you consider has the most amazing faith?" They said: "The angels." He said: "Why would they not believe, since they are with their Lord?" They mentioned the prophets, and he said: "Why would they not believe, while the revelation is sent down to them?" They said: "Then, we are." He said: "Why would you not believe when I am among you?" They asked: "Who has the most amazing faith?" He said: "A people who will come after you, and who will find only books that they will believe in." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Similarly, God said: "And what is the matter with you that you believe not in God! While the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord; and He has indeed taken your covenant, if you are real believers" (57:8). **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And whoever depends upon God, then he is indeed guided to the right path" — for trusting and relying on God are the basis of achieving right guidance and staying away from the path of wickedness.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is framed as a demand for an excuse: with the Book and the Messenger both present, there is none. **[Qurṭubī]** The address may be read either as particular to the Companions, who saw him, or as general to the whole community, for whom the Qurʾān and the sunna stand in his place. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Disbelief is far from touching those to whom the verses are being sent down day and night. **[Maʿārif]** Holding fast means affirming His Being and Attributes, standing by what He has ordained, and refusing to be drawn into supporting any adversary's position. **[Study Quran]** The verse couples the Quran's inimitability with the Prophet's own presence as the two proofs. **[Saʿdī]** Holding fast to God is trust in Him and seeking His shelter, and it is the way to safety and guidance.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 57:8 for the Messenger inviting to belief in the Lord; 2:109 for the envy of the People of the Book; 3:100, which this verse answers. **[Study Quran]** 2:23, 10:38, 11:13 and 17:88 for the challenge of the Quran; 3:103 for "hold fast" again. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:100 for the Aws and Khazraj; 3:103 for the verse said to complete it. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:100 for the warning; 3:103 for the rope. **[Jalālayn]** 3:102, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:100 for the warning that precedes. **[Maʿārif]** 3:100 for the event behind these verses.

**Reflection.** The verse answers 3:100 with a question, and the question is not a request for information but a demand for an excuse **[Ṭabarī]**. Two things are named as making disbelief unintelligible — the recited signs and the living Messenger — and Qatāda's report is the one that every commentator keeps: the Prophet has gone, the Book remains, and in it are the lawful and the unlawful, obedience and disobedience **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Qurṭubī raises the obvious difficulty for later generations and answers it through al-Zajjāj: the address can be to the Companions who saw him, or to the whole community, because the Qurʾān and his traces stand in our midst in his place **[Qurṭubī]**. The ḥadīth Ibn Kathīr records makes the same point with a twist that flatters nobody present: asked who has the most amazing faith, the Companions are turned aside at every guess — angels, prophets, themselves — and told that it is a people who will come later and find only books **[Ibn Kathīr]**. And the closing clause names the mechanism of safety in a single word, which Maʿārif unpacks carefully: holding fast is not a feeling but a refusal to be pulled toward any adversary's position **[Maʿārif]**.

## 3:102 — يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ حَقَّ تُقَاتِهِۦ وَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنتُم مُّسْلِمُونَ

*"O you who believe! Fear God with the fear that is due to Him, and do not die except as Muslims."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: O assembly of those who believe in God and His messenger — "fear God", dread God and be mindful of Him, with obedience to Him and avoidance of acts of disobedience to Him; "with the fear that is due to Him" — the true fear of Him, which is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not denied, remembered and not forgotten. **[Ṭabarī]** "And do not die" — O believers in God and His messenger — "except as Muslims" to your Lord, submitting to Him in obedience, making worship and divinity sincerely His. **[Jalālayn]** "O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared" — so that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not shown ingratitude, remembered and not forgotten. **[Jalālayn]** They said: "Who, O Messenger of God, is strong enough for this task?" — but it was then abrogated by His statement "So fear God as much as you can" (64:16); "and do not die except as Muslims", professing the Oneness of God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd commented on "fear God with the fear due to Him": "That He is obeyed and not defied, remembered and not forgotten and appreciated and not unappreciated" — and this has an authentic chain of narration to ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḥākim collected this ḥadīth in his Mustadrak from Ibn Masʿūd, who related it to the Prophet ﷺ, and said it is authentic according to the criteria of the Two Shaykhs; but it appears that it is only a statement of ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, and God knows best. **[Ibn Kathīr]** It was also reported that Anas said: "The servant will not have *taqwā* of God as is its due until he keeps his tongue idle." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Bukhārī recorded from Murra, from ʿAbdullāh, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The fear due to Him is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, that He be remembered and not forgotten, and that He be thanked and not denied." **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is that He not be disobeyed for the twinkling of an eye. **[Saʿdī]** These verses urge the believing servants of God to carry out the thanks due for His great favours — that they fear Him with the fear that is truly due to Him, and that they stand in His obedience and abandon disobedience to Him, sincere to Him in that. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:102–105 as a single unit)* **[Maʿārif]** In the previous verses the Muslims were warned that the People of the Book, and others, want them to go astray from the right path, so they must remain vigilant against their moves and take steps to counter their anti-Muslim activities. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In the two verses appearing here, two important principles have been given which go to preserve them: *taqwā*, and unity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** For God to be given all due reverence is for Him to be "obeyed not defied, remembered not forgotten, thanked not denied". **[Study Quran]** "Reverence God as He should be reverenced" is similar in wording to "They did not measure God with His true measure" (6:91; 22:74; 39:67), in that both phrases use the word *ḥaqq*, which denotes a right or what something is due. **[Study Quran]** It is reported that the command in the present verse was considered too heavy a burden, one that could never be fulfilled, and caused great anxiety among the Companions; some speculated that it was therefore abrogated by 64:16, "So reverence God as much as you are able". **[Study Quran]** Indeed, some argue that to reverence God as He should be reverenced is precisely to reverence Him as much as you are able, given that God tasks no soul beyond its capacity; and it is also interpreted to mean that one should fear God's Punishment and Wrath as they should be feared.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī glosses *tuqātihi* as *ḥaqq khawfihi* — the true fear of Him — and defines that fear by three pairs: obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not denied, remembered and not forgotten. **[Study Quran]** *Ḥaqq* denotes a right or what something is due, and the same word lies behind "they did not measure God with His true measure". **[Saʿdī]** "Do not die except as Muslims" is read together with the command to stand in obedience and abandon disobedience.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7536 — from Zubayd, from Murra, from ʿAbdullāh [b. Masʿūd], on "fear God with the fear due to Him": that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, and thanked and not denied. *(al-Ḥākim recorded it in his Mustadrak from the route of Abū Nuʿaym, from Misʿar, and said: "This ḥadīth is ṣaḥīḥ according to the conditions of the Two Shaykhs, and they did not record it"; al-Dhahabī agreed. This report is isnād 7541 in Ṭabarī's numbering, without the clause "and thanked and not denied")* **[Ṭabarī]** 7537, 7538, 7539, 7540, 7541, 7542, 7543 — the same report through six further chains, all from ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd. **[Ṭabarī]** 7544 and 7545 — Abū Isḥāq, from ʿAmr b. Maymūn: the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7546 and 7547 — from Murra, from al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym: the like of it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7553 — Ibn ʿAbbās: it was not abrogated; rather, "the fear due to Him" is that you strive in God with the striving due to Him. **[Ṭabarī]** 7554 and 7555 — Ṭāwūs: "fear God with the fear due to Him" — and if you do not do it and cannot, then at least do not die except as Muslims. **[Ṭabarī]** 7556 — Qatāda: then God sent down the alleviation and the ease, and returned with His kindness and mercy towards what He knew of the weakness of His creation, and said "So fear God as much as you are able" (64:16) — and this verse came with alleviation, wellbeing and ease. **[Ṭabarī]** 7561 — Ṭāwūs, on "and do not die except as Muslims": upon Islam, and upon the sanctity of Islam. **[Qurṭubī]** The commentators mentioned that when this verse came down they said: "O Messenger of God, who is strong enough for this?" — and it was hard for them, so God sent down "So fear God as much as you are able" (64:16), and it abrogated this verse — from Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ and Ibn Zayd. **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil said: there is nothing abrogated in Āl ʿImrān except this verse. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that "So fear God as much as you are able" is a clarification of this verse, the meaning being: fear God with the fear due to Him, as much as you are able — and this is sounder, because abrogation applies only where the two cannot be reconciled, and reconciliation here is possible, so it takes precedence. **[Qurṭubī]** ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "fear God with the fear due to Him" was not abrogated, but "the fear due to Him" is that you strive in the way of God with the striving due to Him, that no blame of a blamer detain you concerning God, and that you stand for justice even against yourselves and your children. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Aḥmad recorded that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "If a drop of *zaqqūm* were to fall, it would spoil life for the people of the earth — so what of those whose food is only from *zaqqūm*?" *(recorded by al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ and al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak; al-Tirmidhī said ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ, and al-Ḥākim said it meets the conditions of the Two Ṣaḥīḥs)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Jābir said that three nights before the Messenger of God ﷺ died, he heard him say: "None of you should die except while having sincere trust in God, the Exalted and Most Honourable" — and Muslim also recorded it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Abū Hurayra said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God said: I am as My servant thinks of Me."

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** The sounder position is that 64:16 clarifies rather than abrogates this verse, because combining the two is possible and abrogation applies only where it is not. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Naḥḥās said: everything mentioned in the verse is incumbent on Muslims to act upon, and no abrogation occurs in it. *(Ṭabarī's closing note adduces the same consideration: God tasks no soul beyond its capacity)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The fear due to God is defined by three pairs — obedience without disobedience, thanks without denial, remembrance without forgetfulness. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭāwūs's reading gives the verse a floor as well as a ceiling: if you cannot reach the height, at least do not die except as Muslims. **[Study Quran]** Some argue that reverencing God as He should be reverenced just is reverencing Him as much as you are able, since God tasks no soul beyond its capacity. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Dying well is tied to one's expectation of God: none of you should die except while thinking well of Him. **[Saʿdī]** The verse calls for gratitude for God's favours expressed as obedience and sincerity.

**Cross-references.** **[Jalālayn]** 64:16, "So fear God as much as you can", as the abrogating or clarifying verse. **[Qurṭubī]** 64:16; his earlier treatment of "do not die except as Muslims" in Sūrat al-Baqarah. **[Study Quran]** 6:91, 22:74 and 39:67 for "they did not measure God with His true measure"; 2:284 and 2:286 for the parallel case of a verse said to have alarmed the community and been abrogated; 2:132 for the command to die not except in submission. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:103 for the verse that follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:103 for what follows; 6:313–317 for his earlier treatment of *tuqāh*. **[Saʿdī]** 3:103–105 for the rest of the passage. **[Maʿārif]** 3:103 for the second principle, unity.

**Reflection.** Two clauses, and the first of them caused trouble almost immediately **[Jalālayn]**. The reports say the Companions asked who could possibly bear it, and the tradition split: some said the verse was abrogated by 64:16, and Muqātil went so far as to call it the only abrogated verse in the sūrah **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī records both positions without resolving them in the body of his commentary but comes down, in the note that closes the section, on the side that keeps the verse binding — everything in it is incumbent, because God does not task a soul beyond its capacity **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī states the methodological rule explicitly and it is the useful one: abrogation applies only where two texts cannot be combined, and here they can, so reconciliation wins **[Qurṭubī]**. The definition itself is beautifully plain — obeyed not disobeyed, remembered not forgotten, thanked not denied — and it comes through something like eight chains from Ibn Masʿūd in Ṭabarī alone **[Ṭabarī]**. The second clause is where the verse stops being a demand and becomes a mercy: Ṭāwūs reads it as a floor — if you cannot do the first, at least do not die except in submission **[Ṭabarī]** — and Ibn Kathīr's closing ḥadīth gives it its emotional temperature: none of you should die except while thinking well of God **[Ibn Kathīr]**.

## 3:103 — وَٱعْتَصِمُوا۟ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعًۭا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا۟ ۚ وَٱذْكُرُوا۟ نِعْمَةَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذْ كُنتُمْ أَعْدَآءًۭ فَأَلَّفَ بَيْنَ قُلُوبِكُمْ فَأَصْبَحْتُم بِنِعْمَتِهِۦٓ إِخْوَٰنًۭا وَكُنتُمْ عَلَىٰ شَفَا حُفْرَةٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ فَأَنقَذَكُم مِّنْهَا ۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ

*"And hold fast, all of you together, to the rope of God, and do not be divided. And remember the favour of God upon you: when you were enemies and He joined your hearts, so that by His favour you became brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of fire and He delivered you from it. Thus does God make clear to you His signs, that you may be guided."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: and take hold, all of you, of the means of God — meaning: hold fast to the religion of God which He has commanded you, and to His covenant which He has covenanted with you in His Book to you, of harmony and coming together upon the word of truth, and submission to the command of God. **[Ṭabarī]** As for "the rope", it is the means by which one reaches one's object and need; and it is for that reason that a guarantee of safety is called a "rope", because it is a means by which fear is removed and one is saved from panic and dread. **[Jalālayn]** "And hold fast to" — clutch — "God's bond", namely His religion, "together, and do not scatter" after submitting to Islam; "remember God's grace" — His bestowing of favours upon you, O companies of the Aws and the Khazraj — "when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together through Islam, so that by His grace you became brothers" in religion and comradeship. **[Jalālayn]** "And you were upon the brink" — the edge — "of a pit of fire", such that to fall into it you only had to die disbelieving; "but He delivered you from it" through belief. **[Jalālayn]** "So just as He has made clear for you what has been mentioned, God makes clear to you His signs, that you might be guided." **[Ibn Kathīr]** "To the Rope of God" — it was said that it refers to God's covenant, just as He said in 3:112, "except when under a covenant from God and a covenant from men", in reference to pledges and peace treaties. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And be not divided among yourselves" orders sticking to the community of the believers and forbids division. **[Qurṭubī]** The root of *al-ʿiṣmah* is protection, and from it the escort is called *ʿiṣmah*; and "the rope", *al-ḥabl*, is a homonym, whose origin in the language is the means by which one reaches one's object and need — it is the rope of the shoulder, the long ridge of sand, the tether, the covenant, and calamity; and all of these are not intended in the verse except that which means the covenant — from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Masʿūd said: the rope of God is the Qurʾān. **[Saʿdī]** He commanded them to establish His religion and to hold fast to His rope which He has conveyed to them and made the means between them and Him — and that is His religion and His Book — and to gather upon it and not to divide. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:102–105)* **[Saʿdī]** And He reminded them of what they had been before this favour: that they had been divided enemies, and He gathered them by this religion, joined their hearts and made them brothers; and they had been on the brink of a pit of fire, and He saved them from wretchedness and opened for them the road to felicity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In the second verse the golden principle of unity has been presented with great eloquence and wisdom: the principle — being the only effective binding factor — has been identified before the command to unite was given, following which came the prohibition of disunity and chaos. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Unity is something good and desirable, a premise generally approved by all human beings, no matter what place, time, religion or life style they adhere to; a person who considers fights and disputes useful and good in themselves would be hard to find anywhere. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Yet humanity is divided apart in sects, groups and parties; there is a whole chain of sects within sects and parties within parties, reaching the limits of absurdity where even the unity of two people, in the real sense, has become a myth. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** A few people get together and agree on something under the driving force of temporary objectives; then, no sooner are interests served — or left unrealized — than unity evaporates into thin air, and instead there remains the fall-out of mutual bickering and hostility. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The rope of God is usually understood to be the community of Muslims, which would logically flow into "and be not divided"; or it refers to the Quran itself, and at the deepest level to faith in God. **[Study Quran]** In a ḥadīth the Quran is described as "a rope extended from Heaven to earth". **[Study Quran]** Others say the rope refers to a covenant or pact, reflecting the usage of "rope" in 3:112; according to some Shiites, the Imams are the rope of God; and the rope is also understood to mean devotion toward God. **[Study Quran]** "When you were enemies" is understood to be the time before the coming of Islam, when the strong would prey upon the weak; more specifically, it refers to the tribal wars among the Arabs such as those among the Aws and Khazraj in Madinah before the arrival of the Prophet. **[Study Quran]** They were on the brink of a pit of fire because of their disbelief before they were guided by Islam, and were separated from that fire only by not having died yet.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "The rope" is the means to an object, which is why a safe-conduct is called a rope; and al-Aʿshā's line — "And when the ropes of a tribe carry you past it, it takes from the next its ropes for you" — is cited, meaning guarantees of protection, since all the tribes feared Qays, so anyone making for him found safety wherever he passed. **[Ṭabarī]** And from this is His saying "except by a rope from God and a rope from men" (3:112). **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ḥabl* is a homonym: the rope of the shoulder, the long ridge of sand — as in the ḥadīth of ʿUrwa b. Muḍarris, "I have left no ridge but I stood upon it" — the tether, the covenant, and calamity; and of all these only "covenant" is meant here, according to Ibn ʿAbbās, while Ibn Masʿūd said it is the Qurʾān. **[Ṭabarī]** On "when you were enemies, then He joined your hearts": the grammarians of Basra held that the sentence breaks at "remember the favour of God upon you", and what follows explains it, reporting what they had been before the joining — as when one says "the wall held back from leaning". **[Ṭabarī]** The grammarians of Kufa held that "when you were enemies, then He joined your hearts" is a continuation of "remember the favour of God upon you".

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7562 and 7563 — al-Shaʿbī, from ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, on "hold fast to the rope of God all together": the community (*al-jamāʿah*). **[Ṭabarī]** 7564 — Qatāda: "the firm rope of God which He commanded to be held fast to — this Qurʾān". **[Ṭabarī]** 7565 — Qatāda, through another chain: by the covenant of God and His command. **[Ṭabarī]** 7566 — Shaqīq, from ʿAbdullāh: the path is beset, with devils attending it calling "O servant of God, come this way!" to turn people from the path of God — so hold fast to the rope of God, for the rope of God is the Book of God. **[Ṭabarī]** 7567 — al-Suddī: the rope of God is the Book of God. **[Ṭabarī]** 7568 — Mujāhid: by the covenant of God. **[Ṭabarī]** 7569 — ʿAṭāʾ: the covenant. **[Ṭabarī]** 7570 — al-Aʿmash, from Abū Wāʾil, from ʿAbdullāh: the rope of God is the Qurʾān. **[Ṭabarī]** 7571 — al-Ḍaḥḥāk: the Qurʾān. **[Ṭabarī]** 7575 — Qatāda, on "and do not be divided": God has disapproved division for you, and has gone before you in warning you of it, cautioning you and forbidding you from it; and He has approved for you hearing and obeying, harmony and the community — so approve for yourselves what God has approved for you if you can, and there is no power except through God. **[Ṭabarī]** 7576 — Abū al-ʿĀliya: "do not be divided" — do not be hostile to one another over it, meaning over sincerity to God; and be brothers upon it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7577 — Anas b. Mālik said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The Children of Israel split into seventy-one sects, and my community will split into seventy-two sects — all of them in the Fire except one." It was said: "O Messenger of God, which is that one?" He closed his hand and said: "The community" — and he recited "hold fast to the rope of God all together and do not be divided". *(weak: Ṭabarī's own apparatus notes that Yazīd al-Raqāshī, in the chain, is weak)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7590 — Qatāda, on "you became brothers by His favour": and it has been mentioned to us that a man said to Ibn Masʿūd, "How have you risen this morning?" and he said: "We have risen, by the favour of God, as brothers." **[Ṭabarī]** On the beginning of the enmity between the two tribes: the scholars of the Anṣār mention that the start of the enmity that inflamed the wars between the two tribes of the Aws and the Khazraj was the killing of a client of Mālik b. al-ʿAjlān al-Khazrajī, an ally of his, and the enmity continued between them until God extinguished it by His prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī on "you were on the brink of a pit of fire": you were, O assembly of believers of the Aws and the Khazraj, upon the edge of a pit of fire; and that is a parable for the unbelief they had been upon before *(Islam, from which they were delivered)*. **[Ṭabarī]** "And He delivered you from it" — He means: God delivered you from it by guiding you to Islam, and so you were saved from the fire and admitted to the Garden. *(digression: on the *shafā* / *shafan* forms of "brink" — both are attested, the word being from the defective class with a dialectal variant from the hollow)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** Muslim recorded that Abū Hurayra said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "It pleases God for you to acquire three qualities and displeases Him that you acquire three characteristics. It pleases Him that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, that you hold fast to the rope of God all together and do not divide, and that you give sincere counsel to those whom God has set in authority over you. And He displeases Him for you: gossip, excessive questioning, and squandering wealth." **[Ibn Kathīr]** In his speech to the Anṣār about the distribution of the booty, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O assembly of the Anṣār! Did I not find you misguided and God guided you by me? Were you not divided beforehand and God united you around me? Were you not poor and God enriched you because of me?" — and whenever he asked them a question they would answer: "Indeed, God and His Messenger have granted us bounty." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Tirmidhī recorded from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, or seventy-two sects, and the Christians the like of that; and my community will split into seventy-three sects" — and al-Tirmidhī said: this ḥadīth is ṣaḥīḥ. **[Qurṭubī]** He also recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "There will surely come upon my community what came upon the Children of Israel, sandal for sandal, so that if one of them were to go in to his mother openly, one of my community would do that; and the Children of Israel split into seventy-two sects, and my community will split into seventy-three — all of them in the Fire except one sect." They said: "Which is it, O Messenger of God?" He said: "That which I and my Companions are upon." *(this version goes through ʿAbdullāh b. Ziyād al-Ifrīqī, whom some declared trustworthy and others weak)* **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Dāwūd recorded it in his Sunan from Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, from the Prophet ﷺ: "The People of the Scripture before you split into seventy-two sects, and this community will split into seventy-three — seventy-two in the Fire and one in the Garden, and that is the community." *(weak: the chain of the seventy-three-sect version through ʿAbdullāh b. Ziyād al-Ifrīqī is disputed)*

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** The verse identifies the binding factor before commanding unity, which is why the prohibition of division comes after it: unity without a common attachment does not hold. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Love and consideration in the hearts of a people is purely a Divine blessing; and one can become deserving of the blessings of God only through obedience to Him — with disobedience and sin one cannot hope for this reward. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** It follows that if Muslims desire a stable organization among themselves and unity, the only alternative open to them is that they should make obedience to God their life style. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The "rope" carries both senses at once in the reports — the community and the Qurʾān — and both amount to the same thing: the covenant of God that is to be held to together. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The command is to stick to the community of the believers and to abandon division. **[Study Quran]** The rope is the community, or the Quran, or at the deepest level faith in God. **[Qurṭubī]** Of the several meanings of *ḥabl*, only "covenant" is intended, according to Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Saʿdī]** The brotherhood named here is a brotherhood produced by the religion, not by blood. **[Maʿārif]** Unity is universally praised and almost universally unrealised, because unity without a shared attachment dissolves as soon as interests shift.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:112, "except by a rope from God and a rope from men", as the parallel for *ḥabl* as covenant; 44:32, "And We chose them, by knowledge, above all the worlds", as the parallel Mujāhid cites for the conditional reading of 3:110. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:112 for the covenant usage; 3:104, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 42:13 for the same command given to Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus; 42:14 and 98:4 for the People of the Book dividing after the revelation; 8:62–63 for the joining of hearts; 15:47 and 49:10 for the believers as brothers; 9:109 for a parable about a brink; 2:84 and 3:100 for the Aws and Khazraj. **[Qurṭubī]** The ḥadīth of ʿUrwa b. Muḍarris for *ḥabl* as a ridge of sand; al-Tirmidhī, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn ʿUmar for the seventy-three sects. **[Jalālayn]** 3:102 for the verse before; 3:104, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:102 for the first principle; 3:104, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:102 for the first principle; 3:104, which follows.

**Reflection.** This is the verse the tradition returns to whenever it talks about Muslim disunity, and the first thing the commentators do is ask what the rope is. Ṭabarī's answer is philological and practical at once: a rope is whatever you hold to reach what you need, which is why a safe-conduct is called one — and then the reports split, some saying the community, some the Qurʾān, some the covenant, and several of them going back to Ibn Masʿūd **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The image that stays with me is Ibn Masʿūd's: the path is beset, with devils standing along it calling "O servant of God, come this way!" — so hold fast to the rope, for the rope is the Book **[Ṭabarī]**. The middle of the verse is the part that would have landed hardest on its first hearers, because it names the fact: you were enemies, on the lip of a pit, and you were one death away from falling in **[Jalālayn]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. Ṭabarī records the scholars of the Anṣār tracing their old feud to the killing of a single client, and an enmity that ran until God put it out by His prophet **[Ṭabarī]** — which is the same story as 3:100, told from the other end. And Maʿārif's observation about the order of the verse is the one worth carrying away: the binding factor is named first and unity commanded second, because unity without something to hold dissolves as soon as interests shift **[Maʿārif]**. The sect-ḥadīths that both Qurṭubī and Ṭabarī record say the same thing from the negative side — and Ṭabarī's own apparatus flags the weakness in his chain, which is worth keeping in view **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:104 — وَلْتَكُن مِّنكُمْ أُمَّةٌۭ يَدْعُونَ إِلَى ٱلْخَيْرِ وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ ۚ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ

*"Let there be among you a community calling to the good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong — and those are the successful."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: "let there be among you", O believers, "a community" — meaning a group — "calling" people "to the good", meaning to Islam and its laws which God has laid down for His servants; "and enjoining what is right" — meaning they command people to follow Muḥammad ﷺ and the religion he brought from God; "and forbidding what is wrong" — meaning they forbid unbelief in God and the denial of Muḥammad and of what he brought from God, striving against them with hands and limbs until they submit to you in obedience. **[Ṭabarī]** "And those are the successful" — meaning: the ones who succeed with God, abiding in His Gardens and His bliss. **[Jalālayn]** "Let there be one community of you calling to good" — to Islam — "and enjoining decency and forbidding indecency; those that call, bid and forbid are the successful", the victorious. **[Jalālayn]** The particle *min* in "of you" is partitive, since what is mentioned is a collective obligation and is not incumbent upon every individual of the community, for not every person — such as the ignorant — is up to it. **[Jalālayn]** However, it is also said that this particle is extra, and what is meant is "so that you are a community calling to good" and so on. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Let there arise out of you a group of people" that calls to righteousness, enjoins all that is good and forbids evil in the manner God commanded — "and it is they who are the successful". **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "They are a special group of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ and a special group of the transmitters" — meaning the fighters in the way of God and the scholars. **[Qurṭubī]** The *min* in "from among you" is partitive, and its meaning is that those who command must be scholars, and not all people are scholars. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that it is for specifying the genus, the meaning being: so that all of you are like that. **[Qurṭubī]** I say: the first position is sounder, for it indicates that enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is a collective obligation; and God has specified them by His saying "those who, if We establish them in the land, establish the prayer" (22:41) — and not all people are established in the land. **[Saʿdī]** He commanded them to complete this state by the strongest means by which they can establish their religion: that a party of them should stand forth, sufficient to the need, "calling to the good" — which is the religion, its fundamentals, its branches and its laws — "and enjoining what is right", which is that whose goodness is known by revelation and by reason, "and forbidding what is wrong", which is that whose ugliness is known by revelation and by reason; "and those are the successful", the attainers of every object of desire and the saved from every object of dread. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:102–105)* **[Saʿdī]** And there enter into this party the people of knowledge and teaching, those who take up public address and the admonition of people generally and particularly, and those who enforce it — who stand to oblige people to establish the prayers, to pay the zakāh and to uphold the laws of the religion, and who forbid them from wrongs. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** So everyone who calls people to good, generally or particularly, or who stands with a counsel that is general or particular, enters into this noble verse. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Muslims are not to rest at the correction of what they think and do individually; but they should, along with that, be affectionately concerned with the good of other brothers and sisters in faith — by doing so the whole community shall have the benefit of keeping its stance correct at all times, and at the same time this will guarantee closer mutual cooperation and unity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The collective well-being of Muslims depends on two things: self-correction through *taqwā* and a firm hold on the cord of God through the Qurʾān and the faith, and the correction of others through *daʿwah* and positive propagation. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The concepts of enjoining right and forbidding wrong appear again in 3:110, 3:114; 7:157; 9:71, 112; 22:41; 31:17. **[Study Quran]** In Islamic history these ideas have been invoked in discussions regarding the legitimacy of political rebellion, the right to privacy, the speaking of difficult truths to those in power, and the balance between personal and communal responsibility. **[Study Quran]** A ḥadīth often quoted in reference to this subject states: "Whosoever among you sees a wrong being done, let him change it with his hand, and if he is unable then with his tongue, and if he is unable then with his heart — and that is the feeblest of belief." **[Study Quran]** "Right" renders *maʿrūf*, which can also be translated "honorable", "decent", "good", or "fair"; it also means, literally, "what is known/recognized", and in this sense denotes what is conventional, generally acceptable, customary or familiar. **[Study Quran]** In encompassing the sense of both custom and goodness it resembles the root meaning of the English word "moral", which derives from the Latin root that means "customs". **[Study Quran]** "Wrong" renders *munkar*, which can also be translated "dishonorable", "indecent", "bad", or "foul", and literally means "that which is denied or disavowed". **[Study Quran]** Some interpret "the community" here to refer to the elect of the Companions, though others believe that "among you" does not refer to a distinct group, since the entire Muslim community is praised in 3:110 for enjoining right and forbidding wrong; as such it can be read as descriptive — "And may you be a community calling to the good". **[Study Quran]** But for others it is meant to describe a segment of the community, since many Muslims — such as many women and children and the elderly in general — would not be able to fulfil the requirements of enjoining right and forbidding wrong insofar as this requires influencing the actions of others; many believe these commands are specific to the scholars, since an ignorant person might inadvertently call one to evil or enjoin what is wrong.

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** *Min* is partitive on the reading that makes this a communal obligation. **[Qurṭubī]** The first view — partitive — is sounder because it matches the fact that not everyone is qualified or situated to do it. **[Study Quran]** *Maʿrūf* is literally "what is known/recognised", and *munkar* "what is denied or disavowed". **[Ṭabarī]** "Ummah" here is glossed as a group (*jamāʿah*), and "the good" as Islam and its laws.

**Readings.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7595 — ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar al-Qāriʾ, from Abū ʿAwn al-Thaqafī, from Ṣubayḥ: I heard ʿUthmān recite "let there be among you a community calling to the good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, **and seeking God's help in what befalls them**". **[Ṭabarī]** 7596 — Ibn ʿUyayna, from ʿAmr b. Dīnār: I heard Ibn al-Zubayr recite, and he mentioned the like of the reading of ʿUthmān we have just mentioned, exactly. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Bakr al-Anbārī said: this addition is an explanation of Ibn al-Zubayr's, words of his own in which one of the transmitters erred and attached them to the words of the Qurʾān; and what shows the correctness of what I describe is that ʿUthmān did not write it in his codex, which is the exemplar of the Muslims — he only mentioned it as an admonition, confirming what preceded it of the speech of the Lord of the worlds.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7597 — Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "let there be among you a community calling to the good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong" — they are the special ones among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they are the special ones among the transmitters. *(Ibn Kathīr adds: meaning the fighters in the way of God and the scholars)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever among you witnesses an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he is unable, then let him change it with his tongue. If he is unable, then let him change it with his heart, and this is the weakest faith" — and in another narration: "There is no faith beyond that, not even the weight of a mustard seed." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You will enjoin righteousness and forbid evil, or God shall send down a punishment from Him to you; then you will supplicate to Him, but He will not accept your supplication." *(al-Tirmidhī also collected it and said ḥasan)* **[Maʿārif]** As narrated in al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, the Holy Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hands is my life, you must bid the Fair and forbid the Unfair, lest God inflict upon you a severe punishment; you shall then pray to Him for mercy but your prayer shall not be answered." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** And: "Whoever from among you sees that an evil is being committed, then he should change it with his hands; and if he is unable to do that, then with his spoken word; and if he is unable to do even that, then with his heart — and this is the weakest degree of faith." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Into this party enter the people of knowledge and teaching, those who give public addresses and admonish people, and those who enforce the laws of the religion. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Rulings.** **[Jalālayn]** The *min* being partitive shows that this is a collective obligation (*farḍ kifāya*), not incumbent on every individual. **[Qurṭubī]** Those who command must be scholars, and not all people are scholars; and the obligation is a collective one, specified by 22:41. **[Study Quran]** Many believe these commands are specific to the scholars, since an ignorant person might enjoin what is wrong; and many see it as a communal responsibility fulfilled so long as some segment of the community is carrying it out. **[Maʿārif]** The responsibility of mutual correction has been laid on the whole community, as 3:110 shows, where the obligation is assigned to the community as such. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** "The good" is Islam and its laws, "what is right" is following Muḥammad ﷺ and his religion, and "what is wrong" is unbelief and denial — to be opposed by striving until people submit in obedience. **[Saʿdī]** What is right is known to be good by revelation *and* by reason, and what is wrong known to be ugly by both. **[Study Quran]** Some interpret right and wrong as what one's innate moral consciousness recognises as beautiful or ugly, meaning that right and wrong are determined not only through religious teaching but also by innate moral sense. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The group that does this is the successful one. **[Maʿārif]** The two pillars of collective well-being are self-correction and the correction of others.

**Cross-references.** **[Study Quran]** 3:110, 3:114, 7:157, 9:71, 9:112, 22:41 and 31:17 for enjoining right and forbidding wrong; 9:122 for the segment of the community that seeks expertise; 3:110 for the whole community being praised for it. **[Qurṭubī]** 22:41, "those who, if We establish them in the land, establish the prayer", as specifying the ones meant; his earlier treatment of commanding right and forbidding wrong at the beginning of this sūrah. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:103 for the unity that precedes; 3:105, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:105, which follows; 3:106 for the faces. **[Jalālayn]** 3:103 for the address to the Aws and Khazraj; 3:105, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:105, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:110 for the same obligation assigned to the community; 3:102–103 for the first principle.

**Reflection.** The verse turns on a single preposition, and every commentator notices it: "among you" — part of you, or all of you? **[Jalālayn]**, **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. Qurṭubī's reasoning is the practical one: those who command must know what they are commanding, and not everyone does; and the parallel in 22:41 describes people "established in the land", which not everyone is **[Qurṭubī]**. The Study Quran notes the counter-argument from 3:110, where the whole community is praised for exactly this work — and the reconciliation is that the duty is communal, discharged when enough people do it **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's identification is narrower still: a special group of the Companions and transmitters, which Ibn Kathīr glosses as the fighters and the scholars **[Ibn Kathīr]**. What everyone agrees on is the content, and al-Ṭabarī states it in the most uncompromising form: calling to Islam and its laws, commanding the following of Muḥammad ﷺ, and forbidding unbelief — by striving, if it comes to that **[Ṭabarī]**. Al-Saʿdī's list of who counts is generous and worth quoting to anyone who thinks the verse describes only a clerical office: the scholars and teachers, the preachers, and those who actually oblige people to pray and pay zakāh **[Saʿdī]**. And the ḥadīth that appears in all three of Ibn Kathīr, Maʿārif and the Study Quran supplies the gradation that has made this verse so discussable ever since — hand, tongue, heart — with the sting in its last clause: after that, not a mustard seed of faith **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Maʿārif]**, **[Study Quran]**.

## 3:105 — وَلَا تَكُونُوا۟ كَٱلَّذِينَ تَفَرَّقُوا۟ وَٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ مِنۢ بَعْدِ مَا جَآءَهُمُ ٱلْبَيِّنَٰتُ ۚ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ

*"And do not be like those who became divided and disputed after the clear proofs came to them — and those, for them is a mighty punishment."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: "and do not be", O assembly of those who believe, "like those who became divided" — of the People of the Scripture — "and disputed" concerning the religion of God and His command and His prohibition, "after the clear proofs came to them" from the proofs of God concerning what they disputed over, and they knew the truth in it and deliberately opposed it, and opposed the command of God and broke His covenant and His compact, in audacity towards God. **[Ṭabarī]** "And those, for them" — meaning: for these who became divided and disputed of the People of the Scripture after the clear proofs came to them — "is a punishment" from God, "mighty". **[Ṭabarī]** He says, exalted is His praise: so do not divide, O assembly of believers, in your religion as these divided in their religion, and do not do their deeds and follow their way in your religion, lest there be for you of the punishment of God the like of what is theirs. **[Jalālayn]** "Be not as those who scattered in their religion and disputed over it after the clear proofs came to them" — and these are the Jews and the Christians — "those, there awaits a mighty chastisement." **[Qurṭubī]** It means the Jews and the Christians, in the view of the majority of the commentators; and some said they are the innovators of this community. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Umāma said: they are the Ḥarūriyya, and he recited the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** Jābir b. ʿAbdillāh said, on "like those who became divided and disputed after the clear proofs came to them": the Jews and the Christians. **[Ibn Kathīr]** In this verse God forbids this *ummah* from imitating the division and discord of the nations that came before them; these nations also abandoned enjoining righteousness and forbidding evil, although they had proof of its necessity. **[Saʿdī]** Then He forbade them the way of those who divided, those to whom the religion and the clear proofs came — which required them to uphold it and gather upon it — yet they divided and disputed and became sects. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:102–105)* **[Saʿdī]** And that did not proceed from ignorance and misguidance; rather it proceeded from knowledge, and an evil purpose, and the oppression of some of them against others — and for that reason He said "and those, for them is a mighty punishment". *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** It means that Muslims should not be like Jews and Christians who, even after the clear injunctions of God had reached them, became divided in the implementation of the basic code of faith simply because they preferred to follow the dictates of their desires. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Thus, thrown into violent mutual disputations, vocal and physical, they brought Divine punishment upon themselves; and this verse is in fact a complement of "hold fast to the cord of God, all of you" (3:103), where Muslims were asked to seek unity and strength by attaching themselves to God's commands, individually and collectively. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** This verse refers to the People of the Book.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** On "there came to them", *jāʾahum* is masculine for the plural, and *jāʾathum* would be for the group. **[Ṭabarī]** "The clear proofs" are the proofs of God concerning the very thing they disputed, which they knew and then deliberately opposed. **[Jalālayn]** "Scattered" and "disputed" are read together as dividing in religion after the proofs.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7598 — al-Rabīʿ, on "and do not be like those who became divided and disputed after the clear proofs came to them": they are the People of the Scripture; God forbade the people of Islam to divide and dispute as the People of the Scripture divided and disputed. **[Ṭabarī]** 7599 — ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa, from Ibn ʿAbbās, on "and do not be like those who became divided and disputed": and the like of this in the Qurʾān — God commanded the believers to stay with the community, forbade them disagreement and division, and informed them that those before them were destroyed only by argumentation and disputation concerning the religion of God. **[Ṭabarī]** 7600 — al-Ḥasan: they are the Jews and the Christians. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Umāma said: they are the Ḥarūriyya, and he recited the verse; and Jābir b. ʿAbdillāh said: the Jews and the Christians. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū ʿĀmir ʿAbdullāh b. Luḥayy said: "We performed ḥajj with Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān; when we arrived at Makkah he stood up after praying ẓuhr and said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ said, "The People of the Two Scriptures divided into seventy-two sects, and this *ummah* will divide into seventy-three sects — all in the Fire except one, and that is the community. And there will emerge among my *ummah* peoples whose desires race through them as rabies races through its victim; no vein or joint will be saved from these desires."'" **[Ibn Kathīr]** Muʿāwiya added: "By God, O Arabs! If you do not adhere to what came to you from your Prophet ﷺ, then other people are even more prone not to adhere to it." *(Abū Dāwūd recorded something similar)*

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** The divisiveness censured in this verse is division that arises from arrogant and egotistic self-assertiveness, whether in the fundamentals of religion or in its subsidiaries — and the phrase "after the clear signs had come to them" is an obvious pointer to that reading. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** All the fundamentals of religion are clear, and even some subsidiaries are so clear that they allow no margin of disagreement unless there is a selfish motive behind it. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** But there are subsidiary issues that are not so definite: they may have no clear support from the texts of the Qurʾān and the Sunnah and be deduced by scholars on the basis of analogy, or the text they rest on may be open to more than one interpretation — and the resulting difference of opinion in understanding these subsidiaries is not included in the sense of this verse. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The well-known authentic ḥadīth narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ is more than enough to permit it: the Prophet ﷺ said that one who performs *ijtihād* and arrives at a correct ruling gets a twofold reward, and if he errs in his *ijtihād* he gets one reward. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The wrong in the verse is not error but deliberate opposition to a known truth and the breaking of a covenant. **[Saʿdī]** What is censured is division that proceeds from knowledge and from an evil purpose and from some oppressing others — not from ignorance. **[Maʿārif]** The verse complements 3:103: unity comes from attachment to God's command, and division comes from preferring desire. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The nations before were destroyed not by ignorance but by abandoning enjoining right and forbidding wrong despite having proof that it was necessary. **[Qurṭubī]** The majority say the People of the Scripture are meant; some say the innovators of this community, and Abū Umāma named the Ḥarūriyya.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:103 for the unity commanded just before; 3:104 for the obligation those before abandoned; 3:106, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:104 for the abandonment of enjoining right and forbidding wrong; 3:106, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:213 and 3:19 for the People of the Book dividing; 3:103 for the command to unity. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:103 for the command; 3:106 for when the punishment falls. **[Jalālayn]** 3:104 for the community; 3:106, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:104 for the callers; 3:106 for the timing of the punishment. **[Maʿārif]** 3:103 for the complement; the ḥadīth of ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ from al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

**Reflection.** The prohibition is not "do not divide" but "do not be *like those who* divided" — and the likeness is specified with a detail that makes all the difference: after the proofs had come **[Ṭabarī]**. Division before the evidence arrives is one thing; division after it is another, because then it is not a mistake but a choice, and al-Saʿdī says plainly that it proceeded from knowledge and from an evil purpose and from some oppressing others **[Saʿdī]**. The identification is contested in an interesting way: the majority say the Jews and Christians, but some — and Abū Umāma by name — say the innovators of this community, the Ḥarūriyya **[Qurṭubī]**, which is a warning aimed inward rather than outward. Maʿārif draws the distinction that keeps the verse from being used to flatten legitimate disagreement: the censured division is the self-assertive kind, in fundamentals or in subsidiaries that are clear; where the texts genuinely admit more than one reading, difference is not what this verse is about, and the ḥadīth of the double reward for the mujtahid settles it **[Maʿārif]**. That is a careful and useful line to draw. And Ibn Kathīr's report ends on the note the whole passage has been building toward — the sect-ḥadīth, with Muʿāwiya's addition that if the Arabs will not hold to what their Prophet brought, others certainly will not **[Ibn Kathīr]**.

## 3:106 — يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌۭ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌۭ ۚ فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ أَكَفَرْتُم بَعْدَ إِيمَٰنِكُمْ فَذُوقُوا۟ ٱلْعَذَابَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ

*"On the Day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened — as for those whose faces are blackened: 'Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve!'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: those — for them is a mighty punishment on the day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened. **[Ṭabarī]** As for His saying "as for those whose faces are blackened — did you disbelieve after your belief?", its meaning is: as for those whose faces are blackened, it will be said to them: did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve. And "as for" (*ammā*) must have its answer with a *fāʾ*; and when the answer was dropped, the *fāʾ* was dropped with it, and it is permissible to leave out the mention of "it will be said" because what is said indicates it. **[Jalālayn]** "The day when some faces are blackened and some faces whitened" — that is the Day of Resurrection. As for those whose faces are blackened, these being the disbelievers, who are thrown into the Fire and to whom it is said in rebuke: "Did you disbelieve after you had believed, on the day the covenant was made? Then taste the chastisement for what you disbelieved!" **[Qurṭubī]** It means the Day of Resurrection, when they are raised from their graves: the faces of the believers will be whitened and the faces of the disbelievers blackened. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that this is at the reading of the book: when the believer reads his book and sees his good deeds in it, he rejoices and his face is whitened; and when the disbeliever and the hypocrite reads his book and sees his evil deeds in it, his face is blackened. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that it is at the balance: if his good deeds outweigh, his face is whitened, and if his evil deeds outweigh, his face is blackened. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that it is at His saying "And be separated this day, O you guilty" (36:59). **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: when the Day of Resurrection comes, every party is commanded to gather to what it worshipped; and when they come to it they grieve and their faces are blackened, and the believers, the People of the Scripture and the hypocrites remain — and God says to the believers: "Who is your Lord?" and they say "Our Lord is God", and He says "Will you know Him when you see Him?" and they say "Glory be to Him! If He describes Himself by an attribute that truly belongs to Him, we will know Him" — and they see Him as God wills, and the believers fall prostrate before God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "On the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black" — on the Day of Resurrection; this is when the faces of the followers of the Sunnah and the community will radiate with whiteness, and the faces of the followers of innovation and division will be darkened, as has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Then taste the torment (in Hell) for rejecting faith" — and this description befits every disbeliever. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:104–109)* **[Saʿdī]** God, exalted is He, informs of the differing of creation on the Day of Resurrection in felicity and wretchedness: the faces of the people of felicity — those who believed in God, affirmed His messengers, complied with His command and avoided His prohibition — are whitened, and God admits them to the Gardens and lavishes upon them all kinds of generosity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:106–107 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** And the faces of the people of wretchedness, who denied His messengers, disobeyed His command and split their religion into sects, are blackened — and they are rebuked, and it is said: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" — so how did you choose disbelief over belief? — "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** According to the majority of commentators, "brightness" signifies the brightness of the light of faith — the faces of believers shall be resplendent with the light of faith, fresh and smiling due to happiness at the rewards bestowed upon them by Allah; and "darkness" signifies the darkness of disbelief, the faces of the disbelievers covered with the gloomy anguish of disbelief and the added soot of sin. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Ḥaḍrat ʿAṭāʾ says that the faces of the Muhājirīn and Anṣār shall be bright and the faces of the Banū Qurayẓah and Banū al-Naḍīr shall be dark. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Imām al-Tirmidhī narrates a ḥadīth from Sayyidnā Abū Umāmah which identifies these as relating to the Khawārij, the oldest sect of rebels: the dark faces shall belong to the Khawārij and the bright faces to those whom they shall kill. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** When Sayyidnā Abū Umāmah was asked if he had heard the ḥadīth from the Holy Prophet ﷺ, he replied, while counting on his fingers, that he would not have narrated it had he not heard it from the Holy Prophet ﷺ seven times. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Sayyidnā ʿIkrimah says that the dark faces shall belong to those from among the People of the Book who did confirm the coming of the Holy Prophet ﷺ before he was ordained, but when he was given prophethood they did not accept and support him; on the contrary, they started falsifying him. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** "On the Day" is either directly connected with the previous verse or stands alone with an implied word, so that it would mean "Remember the Day when…"; and the implied phrase "it will be said to them" is understood to come after "as for those whose faces blacken". *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:106–107)* **[Study Quran]** Faces blackening is an Arabic idiom describing a state of distress, shame or grief, as in 43:17, when a man's face blackens upon hearing news of an infant girl;
