a similar meaning is invoked in 10:26, where neither darkness nor abasement will come over the faces of the virtuous. **[Study Quran]** Conversely, when faces whiten denotes joy and relief, and spiritually refers to the light of faith. **[Study Quran]** Some interpret 3:106 to refer to Muslims who renounce their faith before they die; others interpret it as the renunciation or disavowal of the primordial pretemporal covenant when human beings bore witness that God was their Lord (see 7:172), or as a reference to hypocrites generally, insofar as they attest to faith and then knowingly commit actions that contradict it. **[Study Quran]** Those who disbelieve after having believed are variously identified as all disbelievers in general, or as the various sects that appeared in later Islamic history after the death of the Prophet, including the Khawārij.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "As for" (*ammā*) requires its answer to be introduced by a *fāʾ*; here the answer is omitted and the *fāʾ* goes with it, and the unstated "it will be said" is understood from the sense. **[Qurṭubī]** The grammarians of Arabic are agreed that the *fāʾ* in the answer to *ammā* is indispensable, because the meaning of "as for Zayd, he is going" is "whatever may be, Zayd is going". **[Study Quran]** Blackening of the face is an Arabic idiom for distress, shame or grief; whitening denotes joy and relief.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7601 — Qatāda, on "the day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened": people have certainly disbelieved after their belief, as you hear; and it has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of God ﷺ used to say: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad, there will be brought to me at the Basin men who kept my company, until, when they are raised to me and I see them, they are snatched away from me — and I shall say: 'My Lord! My Companions! My Companions!' And it will be said: 'You do not know what they introduced after you.'" *(al-Bukhārī recorded it in his Ṣaḥīḥ with other wording)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7604 — Abū al-ʿĀliya, from Ubayy b. Kaʿb, on "the day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened": they became two parties on the Day of Resurrection, and He said to those whose faces were blackened, and reproached them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve" — and that is the belief that was before the disagreement, in the time of Adam, when He took their covenant and their compact from them and they all acknowledged servitude, and He created them upon Islam, so they were one community, Muslims: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" — meaning, after that which was in the time of Adam. **[Ṭabarī]** And of the others he said: those who stood firm upon that belief of theirs and made religion and deed sincerely His, God whitened their faces and admitted them into His good pleasure and His Garden. **[Ṭabarī]** 7605 — al-Ḥasan: they are the hypocrites; they gave the word of faith with their tongues and denied it in their hearts and their deeds. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own conclusion: the soundest of the views mentioned is the one related from Ubayy b. Kaʿb — that all the disbelievers are meant by it, and that the "belief" they are reproached for abandoning is the acknowledgement of God's oneness and of His covenant and compact which He took from them, that they should associate nothing with Him and make worship sincerely His. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: the faces of the people of the Sunnah are whitened and the faces of the people of innovation are blackened; and Qurṭubī said: this saying of Ibn ʿAbbās was transmitted by Mālik b. Sulaymān al-Harawī from Mālik b. Anas from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar as a saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ — and al-Khaṭīb said of it: *munkar* as a ḥadīth of Mālik. *(weak)* **[Qurṭubī]** ʿAṭāʾ said: the faces of the Emigrants and the Anṣār are whitened, and the faces of the Banū Qurayẓa and al-Naḍīr blackened. **[Qurṭubī]** Ubayy b. Kaʿb said: those whose faces are blackened are the disbelievers, and it is said to them "did you disbelieve after your belief" because of their acknowledgement when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam like atoms — and this is al-Ṭabarī's choice. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan: the verse is about the hypocrites. Qatāda: it is about the apostates. ʿIkrima: they are a people of the People of the Scripture who affirmed their prophets and affirmed Muḥammad ﷺ before he was sent, and when he was sent they disbelieved in him — and that is His saying "did you disbelieve after your belief", and it is al-Zajjāj's choice. Mālik b. Anas: it is about the people of caprice. Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī, from the Prophet ﷺ: it is about the Ḥarūriyya. And in another report he ﷺ said: it is about the Qadariyya. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: "They are the hypocrites." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī recorded that Abū Ghālib said: "Abū Umāma saw heads of the Khawārij sect hanging on the streets of Damascus, and he commented: 'The dogs of the Fire, and the worst dead people under the cover of the sky; the best dead men are those whom these have killed' — and he then recited 'on the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black'." **(the Study Quran notes that commentators adduce various aḥādīth in which the Prophet describes visions of the Hereafter where, to his dismay, some Companions were driven away from his presence, and he was told that he did not know what they would do after him)**

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** His own choice: all the disbelievers are meant, and the "belief" they are reproached for abandoning is the acknowledgement of God's oneness and of the covenant taken from them, that they should associate nothing with Him. **[Qurṭubī]** The interpretations recorded range widely — the people of the Sunnah against the people of innovation, the Emigrants and Anṣār against the Banū Qurayẓa and al-Naḍīr, all disbelievers, the hypocrites, the apostates, the People of the Book who recognised the Prophet and then rejected him, the people of caprice, the Ḥarūriyya, the Qadariyya. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The description befits every disbeliever, and the specific application to the people of the Sunnah and the people of innovation comes from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Saʿdī]** The people of felicity are those who believed, affirmed the messengers, complied and avoided; the people of wretchedness are those who denied, disobeyed and split their religion into sects. **[Maʿārif]** There are other explanations besides those cited, but they all lead to the same conclusion and are not contradictory. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** The context would suggest that the phrase refers to the disbelievers mentioned in 3:90 and 3:100–101.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 36:59, "And be separated this day, O you guilty"; 3:105, to which the "Day" is attached; 3:107, which follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:105 for the punishment; 7:172 for the covenant in the time of Adam; 3:107, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:105 for the division; 3:107, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 43:17 for the face blackening at news of an infant girl; 10:26 for the faces of the virtuous; 39:60 for blackened faces; 7:172 for the primordial covenant; 10:26–27, 14:50, 17:97, 18:29, 23:104, 75:22–24 and 80:38–41 for other verses using faces to describe the state in the Hereafter; 3:90 and 3:100–101 for the disbelievers in view. **[Maʿārif]** 39:60, "you shall see those who lied against God with their faces blackened"; 80:38–41; 75:22. **[Jalālayn]** 3:105 for the punishment; 3:107, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:107, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is an image before it is an argument — two crowds, one lit and one dark — and then a single sentence spoken to the dark one: did you disbelieve after your belief **[Ṭabarī]**? The commentators immediately ask who is being addressed, and the list Qurṭubī assembles is the most striking thing in the passage: all disbelievers, the hypocrites, the apostates, the People of the Book who recognised the Prophet before his coming and then rejected him, the people of caprice, the Ḥarūriyya, the Qadariyya, and — in a report he records and then flags as *munkar* in its marfūʿ form — the people of the Sunnah against the people of innovation **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī chooses the broadest reading and grounds it in the covenant taken in the loins of Adam, so that the "belief" being abandoned is the acknowledgement every human being made of God's oneness **[Ṭabarī]**; the Study Quran records the same interpretation and gives it its proper name, the pretemporal covenant of 7:172 **[Study Quran]**. The reports of when the whitening and blackening happen are worth collecting too — at the reading of the book, at the balance, at the separation of the guilty, at the gathering of each party to what it worshipped — and they are all attempts to locate the moment in the sequence of the Day **[Qurṭubī]**. And the ḥadīth of the Basin, which Qatāda attaches to this verse, is the one that has always made it personal: men who kept the Prophet's company, snatched away from him at the last, and he told that he does not know what they introduced after him **[Ṭabarī]**.

## 3:107 — وَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ٱبْيَضَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ فَفِى رَحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ هُمْ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ

*"But as for those whose faces are whitened — they shall be in the mercy of God; therein they abide."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** "But as for those whose faces are whitened" — and these are the believers — "they shall be in God's mercy", that is to say, in Paradise, "abiding therein". **[Ṭabarī]** "But as for those whose faces are whitened", of those who stood firm upon the covenant of God and His compact, who did not change their religion nor turn back on their heels after acknowledging the oneness and bearing witness to their Lord's divinity, and that there is no god other than Him — "they are in the mercy of God", meaning: they are in the mercy of God, that is, in His Garden and its bliss and what God has prepared for its people in it; "therein they abide", meaning: remaining in it forever, without end and without limit. *(Ṭabarī's block covers 3:106–107 as a single unit)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And for those whose faces will become white, they will be in God's mercy (Paradise), therein they shall dwell forever" — in Paradise, where they will reside for eternity and shall never desire to be removed. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:104–109)* **[Qurṭubī]** "Then, in the mercy of God, they shall abide therein" — that is, in His Garden and the abode of His generosity, abiding, remaining. *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:106–107 as a single unit; he closes it with a supplication that God make us of them and keep us far from the paths of innovation and misguidance)* **[Qurṭubī]** These are the people of obedience to God and of faithfulness to His covenant. *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:106–107)* **[Saʿdī]** The faces of the people of felicity — those who believed in God, affirmed His messengers, complied with His command and avoided His prohibition — are whitened, and God admits them to the Gardens and lavishes upon them all kinds of generosity, and they abide therein. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:106–107)* **[Maʿārif]** The sentence "they rest in Allah's mercy" is immediately qualified by "they are there forever", which means that the mercy in which the believers shall rest will not be temporary — it would be forever and eternal, and this blessing will never be taken away or reduced in their case. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In contrast to this are those whose faces shall turn dark; for them it has not been expressly mentioned whether they shall be in that state forever. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās says that "mercy" in the verse means *Jannah*, Paradise; and the wisdom behind giving the name "mercy" to Paradise is, quite obviously, that man, no matter how worshipful and pious he may be, shall not enter Paradise unless it be through the sole mercy of Allah. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The reason is that being devoted in acts of worship is no feat of human excellence as such: on the contrary, the very ability to do so is in itself a gift of Allah — so worship does not, in itself, create an inherent right to enter Paradise; it is Allah's mercy alone through which one can enjoy the bliss of Paradise. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** "Mercy" is glossed as Paradise. **[Maʿārif]** "Therein they abide" qualifies "mercy" immediately, so that the eternity is stated for the believers and left unstated for the dark-faced. **[Ṭabarī]** "Abiding" is defined as remaining in it forever, without end and without limit.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7601 — Qatāda: "and as for those whose faces are whitened, they are in the mercy of God" — those are the people of obedience to God and of faithfulness to the covenant of God; God said "in the mercy of God they abide therein". *(the report is cited in full at 3:106)* **[Qurṭubī]** The grammarians of Arabic are agreed that the *fāʾ* in the answer to *ammā* is indispensable — as in "as for Zayd, he is going", whose meaning is "whatever may be, Zayd is going". *(cited at 3:106)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** The description of the whitened faces as the followers of the Sunnah and the community, and of the blackened as the followers of innovation and division, has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. *(cited at 3:106)*

**Belief.** **[Maʿārif]** Eternity is stated explicitly for the people of mercy and left unstated for the others — and the commentators note the asymmetry. **[Maʿārif]** Paradise is named "mercy" because no amount of worship earns it: even the ability to worship is itself a gift, so entrance is by mercy alone. **[Jalālayn]** The whitened faces are the believers, and the mercy is Paradise. **[Qurṭubī]** They are the people of obedience and of faithfulness to the covenant. **[Ṭabarī]** They are those who stood firm on the covenant and did not turn back after acknowledging the oneness. **[Ibn Kathīr]** They reside in Paradise for eternity and shall never desire to be removed.

**Cross-references.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:106 for the faces; 3:108, which follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:106 for the setting; 3:108, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:106 for the setting; 3:108, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:106 for the blackened faces; 3:108, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:106 for the setting; 3:108, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:106 for the punishment; 3:108 for "God desires no wrong for the worlds".

**Reflection.** A single clause answers the whole of 3:106 — and for those who are saved it says only that they are *in mercy* **[Jalālayn]**. The choice of that word is the point, and Maʿārif draws out why: Paradise is called mercy because nothing earns it, since even the ability to worship was given **[Maʿārif]**. That is a deliberately deflationary note at the end of a passage about division and punishment. The second thing Maʿārif notices is an asymmetry in the grammar that is easy to miss: eternity is stated for the people of mercy, and it is *not* stated for the people of the blackened faces — and the commentators leave it there rather than filling it in **[Maʿārif]**. The identification of who is meant runs exactly parallel to 3:106, and al-Ṭabarī's formulation is the tightest: those who stood firm on the covenant, who did not change their religion nor turn back on their heels after acknowledging the oneness **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī ends his discussion of the two verses with a prayer rather than an argument — that God make us of them and keep us from the paths of innovation — which is perhaps the only honest way to end a passage like this **[Qurṭubī]**.

*Source note:* The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:107 — its combined note for 3:106–107 is cited at 3:106.

## 3:108 — تِلْكَ ءَايَٰتُ ٱللَّهِ نَتْلُوهَا عَلَيْكَ بِٱلْحَقِّ ۗ وَمَا ٱللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ظُلْمًۭا لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ

*"These are the signs of God which We recite to you in truth — and God desires no wrong for the worlds."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by His saying "these are the signs of God": these are the signs of God. **[Ṭabarī]** And "the signs of God" means His admonitions, His lessons and His proofs; "We recite them to you" — We read them to you and relate them; "in truth" — meaning in truthfulness and certainty. **[Ṭabarī]** And He means by "these are the signs of God": these verses in which He has mentioned the affair of the believers among the helpers of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the affair of the Jews of the Children of Israel and the People of the Scripture, and what He will do with the people of faithfulness to His covenant and with those who change His religion and break His covenant after acknowledging it. **[Ṭabarī]** Then He informed His prophet Muḥammad ﷺ that He recites that to him in truth, and let him know that whomever He punishes of His creation with what He has said He will punish him with — of blackening his face and making him abide in His painful punishment and mighty penalty — and whomever He rewards of them with what He has rewarded him with — of whitening his face, honouring him and ennobling his station with Him, by making him abide in His lasting bliss — it is not by any wrong from Him to either party; rather it is by a right they have earned, and by deeds of theirs that have gone before, for which He recompenses them. **[Ṭabarī]** So He said, exalted is His remembrance: "and God desires no wrong for the worlds" — meaning by that: God is not, O Muḥammad, by blackening the faces of these and making them taste the mighty punishment, and whitening the faces of those and giving them bliss in His Garden, seeking to place anything of what He has done in other than its place — informing His servants thereby that nothing will be sound in His wisdom for His creation other than what He has promised the people of His obedience and faith in Him, and other than what He has threatened the people of His disobedience and unbelief in Him; and as a warning from Him to those and a glad tidings from Him to these. **[Jalālayn]** "Those" — that is to say, these verses — "are the verses of God which We recite to you, O Muḥammad, in truth; and God desires not any injustice for the worlds" — punishing them for no crime. **[Qurṭubī]** "Those are the signs of God" — subject and predicate, meaning the Qurʾān. **[Qurṭubī]** "We recite them to you" — meaning: We send Gabriel down to you and he reads them to you; "in truth" — meaning in truthfulness. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Zajjāj said: "those are the signs of God" — the proofs of God and His evidences that have been mentioned. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that "those" has the sense of "these", but since they have drawn to a close they became as though distant, so "those" was used; and it is possible that "the signs of God" is a substitution for "those" and not an adjective, because the ambiguous is not qualified by the genitively annexed. **[Qurṭubī]** "And God desires no wrong for the worlds" — meaning that He does not punish them without a sin. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And God wills no injustice for the worlds" — for He never treats them with injustice; rather, He is the Just Ruler Who is able to do everything and has knowledge of everything. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:104–109)* **[Saʿdī]** God, exalted is He, commends what He has recounted to His prophet of His signs, by which the distinction is made between truth and falsehood and between the friends of God and His enemies, and what He has prepared for the one party of reward and for the others of punishment. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And that is what His bounty, His justice and His wisdom require: He has not wronged His servants, has not diminished anything of their deeds, does not punish anyone without a sin, nor lay upon him the burden of another. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The punishment on that Day is not from Allah but is a consequence of what man has earned while living his mortal life, for the truth is that the blessings of Paradise and the hardships of Hell are simply a changed form of our very deeds. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:107–109)* **[Maʿārif]** So, later on in verse 108 it was said "and God wants no injustice for anyone in the worlds", which means that God has no intention of being unjust to His creation; whatever reward or punishment there is, is nothing but justice and the very perfect expression of the divine wisdom and mercy. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** One reading of 3:108 says that God does not desire that human beings do wrong. *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:108–109)* **[Study Quran]** Another reading connects this verse with 3:109 and says that God has no need to wrong or to be unjust to anything or anyone, since He has power over all things and all things belong to Him, or it simply means that God does not in fact wrong anyone. **[Study Quran]** These verses raise the question of God's relationship to good or evil — namely, what does it mean to say that God desires no wrong for the worlds? **[Study Quran]** One perspective, typified in Ashʿarite theology, states that God does no wrong because wrong is definable as trespassing upon what belongs to another, and since everything belongs to God, nothing He does could amount to a wrong. **[Study Quran]** Another prominent perspective, typified by the Muʿtazilite school, states that God is always just, and what is just or unjust are objective features of the world recognizable by human beings. **[Study Quran]** Some philosophers and Sufis make a distinction between God's "prescriptive command" and the "engendering command": the former refers to what God asks of human free will and the latter to God's Power to create; being free, human beings can choose what God does not want, but cannot oppose what God wills to be.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Those" is used where "these" would be expected, and Ṭabarī says he has already explained how the Arabs put "that" and "those" in the place of "this" and "these". **[Qurṭubī]** The same point is made, with the reason: since the verses have drawn to a close they became as though distant; and "the signs of God" may be a substitution rather than an adjective, because the ambiguous is not qualified by the genitively annexed. **[Ṭabarī]** "The signs of God" are His admonitions, lessons and proofs; "recite" is to read and relate; "in truth" is in truthfulness and certainty. **[Study Quran]** "Wrong" renders *ẓulm*.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is the passage's own defence of the justice of what it has just described: the blackening and the whitening are by a right earned and by deeds already done, not by any misplacement. **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning is that He does not punish without a sin. **[Ibn Kathīr]** He never treats them with injustice; He is the Just Ruler, able to do everything and knowing everything. **[Saʿdī]** What the verse describes is what His bounty, justice and wisdom require — no diminution of deeds, no punishment without sin, no bearing of another's burden. **[Maʿārif]** Reward and punishment are a changed form of our own deeds. **[Study Quran]** The Ashʿarite reading defines wrong as trespass on another's property, and since everything belongs to God nothing He does can be a wrong; the Muʿtazilite reading holds justice and injustice to be objective features recognisable by human beings; and some distinguish the prescriptive from the engendering command.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:106–107 for the blackening and whitening just described; 3:109, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:109 for the connection al-Mahdawī draws; 3:106–107 for the setting. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:109, which follows and grounds the claim in God's ownership of everything. **[Study Quran]** 3:109 for the connection; the essay "The Quran and Schools of Islamic Theology and Philosophy". **[Jalālayn]** 3:106–107 for the signs just recited; 3:109, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:106–107 for the reward and punishment; 3:109 for God's command and decree. **[Maʿārif]** 3:106 for "taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve".

**Reflection.** After the white faces and the black ones, the sūrah pauses to say that none of it is arbitrary — and it says so in a single line that has generated a great deal of theology **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī's reading is the most careful: God is not placing anything other than where it belongs, and what each party receives is by a right earned and by deeds already done **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī puts it negatively — He does not punish without a sin — and Ibn Kathīr turns it into a statement about God's nature: He is the Just Ruler, able to do everything and knowing everything, and therefore has no need to be unjust **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The Study Quran lays out the two classical positions and then a third distinction between what God asks of the will and what He creates, which is the one that keeps human choice from being swallowed **[Study Quran]**. Al-Saʿdī's formulation is the most pastorally useful of them: no diminishing of deeds, no punishment without sin, no bearing of another's burden **[Saʿdī]**. And Maʿārif's image is the strangest and perhaps the truest to the passage: the blessings of Paradise and the hardships of Hell are a changed form of our own deeds **[Maʿārif]**.

## 3:109 — وَلِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ ٱلْأُمُورُ

*"And to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth — and to God all matters are returned."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: He punishes those who disbelieve after their belief with what He has mentioned that He punishes them with, of the mighty punishment and the blackening of faces; and He rewards the people of faith in Him, who stood firm upon affirmation and faithfulness to the covenants they had covenanted, with what He has described that He rewards them with, of abiding in His Gardens — without any wrong from Him to either of the two parties in what He has done, because He has no need of wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** That is because the wrongdoer only wrongs another to add glory to his glory by wronging him, or power to his power, or dominion to his dominion, or to complete some deficiency in his means, making up by wronging another for what was lacking in his means. **[Ṭabarī]** As for Him to whom belongs all that is between the furthest reaches of the Easts and the Wests, and all that is in this world and the Hereafter, there is no sense in His wronging anyone, nor can He wrong anything — because none of His means is deficient such that it needs completing, that He should complete it by wronging another; exalted is God, greatly exalted. **[Ṭabarī]** And it is for that reason that He said, exalted is His remembrance, following His saying "and God desires no wrong for the worlds": "and to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and to God all matters are returned". **[Ṭabarī]** As for "and to God all matters are returned", He means, exalted is His remembrance: to God is the destination of the affair of all His creation — the righteous of them and the corrupt, the doer of good and the doer of evil — and He will recompense each according to what he deserves from Him, without wronging any of them. **[Jalālayn]** "To God belongs all that is in the heavens and in the earth" — as possessions, creatures and servants — "and to Him all matters are returned." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mahdawī said: the aspect of this connecting with what precedes it is that, when He mentioned the states of the believers and the disbelievers and that He desires no wrong for the worlds, He joined it to the mention of the vastness of His power and His freedom from need of wrong, since whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth is in His grasp. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that it is the beginning of a new statement, making clear to His servants that all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, so that they should ask Him and worship Him and worship none other than Him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And to God belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth" — they are all His servants and His property. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:104–109)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And all matters go back to God" — for His is the decision concerning the affairs of this life and the Hereafter, and His is the Supreme Authority in this life and in the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** When He mentioned that His are the command and the revealed law, He mentioned that His is the complete dominion, disposal and authority, and said: "and to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and to God all matters are returned" — and He will recompense the doers of good for their good and the doers of evil for their disobedience. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** And God oftentimes mentions His three judgements together, making clear to His servants that He is the absolute ruler: His is the decreed judgement, the revealed judgement and the recompensing judgement — so He is the judge between His servants in this world and the next, and everything other than Him among created things is judged over, having nothing of the command. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** This is connected by some with 3:108: God has no need to wrong or to be unjust to anything or anyone, since He has power over all things and all things belong to Him. *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:108–109)*

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The Arabs' use of the explicit noun where a pronoun would do — some of the grammarians of Basra compared it to "as for Zayd, Zayd went" and to the poet's line "I do not see death: nothing outstrips death"; the grammarians of Kufa replied that in the verse the two clauses are independent statements, each complete in itself and needing nothing from the other. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own verdict: the second view is sounder, because the meanings of the Book of God and the clarification in it are not to be directed to the irregular and outlandish in speech and meaning, while it has a sound and present face in the eloquent of expression and the apparent of meaning. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mahdawī takes the two clauses as connected; others take the second as the beginning of a new statement.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** Some of the grammarians of Basra cited the verse of ʿAdī b. Zayd — "I do not see death: nothing outstrips death; death has embittered the rich and the poor" — as the parallel for repeating the explicit noun. *(the line is cited in the Ḥamāsa of al-Buḥturī, Sībawayhi, the Khizāna and the Amālī of Ibn al-Shajarī)* **[Ṭabarī]** The grammarians of Kufa replied that the position of the second "death" in the line is the position of a pronoun, since it is one word; whereas in the verse, "to God belongs what is in the heavens and the earth" is a predication that has nothing to do with "and to God all matters are returned", since each of the two statements has a meaning separate from the other, self-sufficient and in no need of the other. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī preferred the Kufan view, on the ground that the Qurʾān is not to be interpreted by the irregular. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mahdawī's connection of the two clauses is given, and the alternative that it opens a new statement. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The whole address closes with "This is because they disbelieved in the signs of God and killed the Prophets without right" and "This is because they disobeyed and used to transgress" — the commentary running on into 3:112. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:104–109, and his commentary continues into 3:110–112)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The argument of the verse is an argument from independence: wrong is done by someone who lacks something, and God lacks nothing — so He cannot wrong anyone. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Mahdawī takes the clause as grounding God's freedom from any need to wrong in His ownership of everything. **[Ibn Kathīr]** All things are His servants and His property, and the decision in this life and the next is His. **[Saʿdī]** The verse completes a triad that recurs in the Qurʾān: the decreed judgement, the revealed judgement and the recompensing judgement. **[Jalālayn]** Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him as possessions, creatures and servants. **[Study Quran]** The connection some draw with 3:108 is that God has no need to be unjust since all things belong to Him.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 3:108 for the connection; 3:110, which follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:108 for the verse it grounds; Sībawayhi and the Ḥamāsa for the poetic parallel; 3:110, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:108 for the justice of God; 3:112 for the continuation of the passage. **[Saʿdī]** 3:108 for the command and the law; 3:110, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:108 for the signs; 3:110, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 3:108 for the connection.

**Reflection.** Read on its own, the verse looks like a formula — and it is one of the most repeated sentences in the Qurʾān. What makes it interesting here is that it is doing a job: it is the reason for the claim just made in 3:108 **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Study Quran]**. Al-Ṭabarī spells the reason out with an unusual piece of moral psychology. A person wrongs another, he says, in order to gain — more glory, more power, more dominion, or to patch some deficiency in his own means. But the one who owns everything between the furthest Easts and Wests cannot gain and lacks nothing, so wronging is not merely beneath Him but unintelligible in His case **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Kathīr says the same thing in three words — they are all His servants and His property **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Then there is the small grammatical quarrel that Ṭabarī records about why the Name is repeated: the Basrans compare it to a line of poetry where a poet says "death" twice, the Kufans answer that in the verse the two clauses are simply independent statements, and Ṭabarī sides with the Kufans on a principle worth noting — the Qurʾān is not to be interpreted by the outlandish in speech when it has a sound face in the eloquent **[Ṭabarī]**. And al-Saʿdī's observation about the three judgements is the one that gives the verse its full scope: decree, revealed law and recompense, all His **[Saʿdī]**.

*Source note:* The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:109 — its combined note for 3:108–109 is cited at 3:108; and Maʿārif's block for 3:107–109 is a single unit whose discussion belongs to 3:106–108, with nothing separate for 3:109.

## 3:110 — كُنتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ أُخْرِجَتْ لِلنَّاسِ تَأْمُرُونَ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَتَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ ۗ وَلَوْ ءَامَنَ أَهْلُ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَكَانَ خَيْرًۭا لَّهُم ۚ مِّنْهُمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ وَأَكْثَرُهُمُ ٱلْفَٰسِقُونَ

*"You were the best community brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and you believe in God. Had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are iniquitous."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The people of interpretation differed over the interpretation of "you were the best community brought forth for mankind". **[Ṭabarī]** Some said: they are those who emigrated with the Messenger of God ﷺ from Makkah to al-Madīnah in particular, from among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: the meaning is — you were the best community brought forth for mankind if you are upon these conditions with which He has described them; so the interpretation on their view is: you were the best community, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong and believing in God, brought forth for mankind in your time. **[Ṭabarī]** On "and had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them" — God means: had they believed in Muḥammad ﷺ and in what he brought them from God, that would have been better for them. **[Ṭabarī]** "Among them are believers, but most of them are the iniquitous" — meaning: those who go out of their religion; and that is because it is of the religion of the Jews to follow what is in the Torah and to affirm Muḥammad ﷺ, and it is of the religion of the Christians to follow what is in the Gospel, and to affirm him and what is in the Torah; and in both Books is the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, his attributes and his sending, and that he is the prophet of God — and both parties, the Jews and the Christians, deny that, so that is their iniquity and their going out of the religion they claim to profess. **[Jalālayn]** "You", O community of Muḥammad, "are the best community brought forth" — manifested — "to men", according to God's knowledge, "enjoining decency and forbidding indecency and believing in God. Had the People of the Scripture believed, their belief would have been better for them; some of them are believers", such as ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions; "but most of them", the disbelievers, "are wicked". **[Ibn Kathīr]** God states that the community of Muḥammad ﷺ is the best nation ever: "You are the best of peoples ever raised up for mankind". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Tirmidhī recorded from Bahz b. Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say about "you were the best community brought forth for mankind": "You complete seventy communities; you are the best of them and the most honourable of them with God" — and he said: this ḥadīth is ḥasan. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Hurayra said: "We are the best of people for the people; we drive them in chains to Islam." **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are those who emigrated from Makkah to al-Madīnah and witnessed Badr and al-Ḥudaybiyya; and ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb said: whoever does their deed is like them. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: they are the community of Muḥammad ﷺ — meaning the righteous among them and the people of merit; and they are the witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection. **[Qurṭubī]** Mujāhid said: "you were the best community brought forth for mankind" — upon the conditions mentioned in the verse. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: its meaning is "you were, in the Preserved Tablet"; and it is said: you were, from the time you believed, the best community; and it is said: this came because of the preceding glad tidings of the Prophet ﷺ and his community, the meaning being: you were, with those before you of the People of the Books, the best community. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Akhfash said: He means the people of a community — that is, the best people of a religion. **[Saʿdī]** This is a preferment from God for this community by these causes, by which they are distinguished and by which they surpass all other communities: that they are the best of people for the people, in sincerity, love of good, calling, teaching, guidance, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and combining the perfecting of character and striving after people's benefits as far as possible, with the perfecting of the self by faith in God and standing by the rights of faith. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:110–111 as a single unit)* **[Saʿdī]** And if the People of the Scripture had believed in the like of what you have believed in, they would have been guided, and it would have been better for them — but none of them believed except a few; as for the many, they are iniquitous, outside the obedience of God and the obedience of His messenger, warring against the believers and striving to harm them with all they can. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** These are the very reasons why God has conferred upon the community of Muḥammad ﷺ the status of "the best of communities", dignified and elevated, when it does what it has been charged to do. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The most important reason for declaring this community the best appeared in Sūrat al-Baqarah: "And in the same way We made you a moderate community" (2:143) — and the moderation is its great characteristic, visible in all departments of its collective life. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In this verse another reason has been given: this community has been raised for the sole purpose of dispensing good to all beings created by God, and has actually been charged with the function of remaining concerned with their spiritual and moral reformation. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Seen in the perspective of past communities, it was this community which contributed most in the mission of bidding the Fair and forbidding the Unfair, even though this was already enjoined upon past communities; but several past communities did not have *jihād* as a religious obligation, in which case the mission could only be carried out by heart and tongue, whereas the followers of Muḥammad ﷺ have a third option, the power of the hand, which also includes all sorts of *jihād*. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Toward the end of the verse, it has been said about the People of the Book that there are some Muslims among them — and this refers to those who confirmed the prophethood of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, such as ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and others. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** Some understand this verse to mean that Muslims are destined to be the best religious community as already "written" in the Preserved Tablet, and that it is implied that Muslims should live up to this destiny — a reading that is possible because the verb can be read as either present or past tense. **[Study Quran]** Another understanding, also based on a past-tense reading, understands these words as being spoken to the Muslims in Paradise to describe their life in the world; and the verb can also signify that they "become" the best community by virtue of enjoining right and forbidding wrong. **[Study Quran]** This community is interpreted variously to mean the Emigrants who left Makkah for Madinah with the Prophet, the elect of the Companions, or the Prophet's Companions as a whole; it can also refer to the Islamic community as a whole when compared with other religious communities. **[Study Quran]** "Best community" may also refer to those who are the best people toward other people, which is the domain of enjoining right and forbidding wrong and explains why action is placed before faith in this verse. **[Study Quran]** In its plain sense, "were the People of the Book to believe, that would be better for them" could be interpreted as saying that if they all believed it would be better for them, and indeed some of them are believers — a view seemingly adopted by al-Zamakhsharī, who makes a distinction between belief in God in general and belief in Muhammad as His Prophet. **[Study Quran]** Moreover, since belief is contrasted with being iniquitous rather than with being a disbeliever, the sense of being false to their own religions seems to be highlighted here; al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī both interpret "iniquitous" as referring to Jews' and Christians' failure to observe their own faiths — al-Rāzī as an act of being false to what is already false, al-Ṭabarī as being false to the true teachings of the Torah and the Gospel, which, most Muslims maintain, demand acceptance of the Prophet Muhammad. **[Study Quran]** Many understand "among them are believers" as a reference to prominent Jews and Christians who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and the Abyssinian Negus — although according to this later interpretation the Negus became a Muslim himself, which is problematic and contradicts other accounts.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Naḥḥās said: on Abū Hurayra's reading the estimate is "you were, for mankind, the best community"; and on Mujāhid's reading, "you were the best community when you were enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Akhfash said: He means the people of a community, that is, the best people of a religion. **[Study Quran]** The verb can be read as either present or past tense, which is what opens up the several interpretations. **[Ṭabarī]** "The iniquitous" are those who go out of their religion.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7606 — Saʿīd b. Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, on "you were the best community brought forth for mankind": they are those who went out with him from Makkah. **[Ṭabarī]** 7607 — ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās: they are those who emigrated from Makkah to al-Madīnah. **[Ṭabarī]** 7608 — al-Suddī: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Had God willed He would have said 'you are' — and then we would all be it; but He said 'you were', concerning a particular group of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ; and whoever does the like of their deed was the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." **[Ṭabarī]** 7609 — Ibn Jurayj said, ʿIkrima said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Masʿūd, Sālim the client of Abū Ḥudhayfa, Ubayy b. Kaʿb and Muʿādh b. Jabal. **[Ṭabarī]** 7610 — al-Suddī, from one who told him, that ʿUmar said, on "you were the best community brought forth for mankind": "It belongs to our first ones and does not belong to our last ones." **[Ṭabarī]** 7612 — Qatāda: it has been mentioned to us that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, in a ḥajj he performed, saw from the people a deplorable appearance, and recited this: "you were the best community brought forth for mankind", the verse; then he said: "O people, whoever is pleased to be of that community, let him fulfil the condition God has required of it." **[Ṭabarī]** 7613 — al-Ḍaḥḥāk: they are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ in particular — meaning, they were the transmitters and the callers whom God commanded the Muslims to obey. **[Ṭabarī]** 7614 and 7615 — Mujāhid: "you were the best community brought forth for mankind" — on this condition: that you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong and believe in God; meaning, for those among whom you are, like His saying "And We chose them, by knowledge, above all the worlds" (44:32). **[Ṭabarī]** 7625 — Qatāda, on "among them are believers, but most of them are the iniquitous": God blamed most people. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Al-Bukhārī recorded that Abū Hurayra commented on this verse: "(You, Muslims, are) the best nation of people for the people; you bring them tied in chains on their necks and they later embrace Islam." **[Ibn Kathīr]** At-Tirmidhī recorded from Bahz b. Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said about this verse: "You are the final of seventy nations; you are the best and most honoured among them to Allah" — and he said it is ḥasan, and it is also narrated from Muʿādh b. Jabal and Abū Saʿīd. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I was given what no other Prophet before me was given." They said: "O Messenger of God, what is it?" He said: "I was given victory by fear, I was given the keys of the earth, I was called Aḥmad, the earth was made a clean place for me, and my community was made the best community." *(the chain of narration for this ḥadīth is ḥasan)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** The Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded that Abū Hurayra said: "A group of seventy thousand from my community will enter Paradise, while their faces are radiating, just like the moon when it is full" — and ʿUkkāsha b. Miḥṣan stood and asked to be made one of them, and the Prophet ﷺ said "O God, make him one of them"; then a man of the Anṣār stood and asked the same, and he said: "ʿUkkāsha has preceded you in it." *(the report continues in Ibn Kathīr)* **[Qurṭubī]** Sufyān, from Maysara al-Ashjaʿī, from Abū Ḥāzim, from Abū Hurayra, on "you were the best community brought forth for mankind": "You drag the people in chains to Islam." **[Qurṭubī]** The imams recorded from ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The best of people is my generation, then those who come after them, then those who come after them" — and this indicates that the first of this community are better than those after them, which is the view of most scholars. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said: the community of Muḥammad ﷺ became the best community because the Muslims among them are more numerous, and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is more widespread among them; and it is said that this is for the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, as he ﷺ said: "The best of people is my generation" — meaning those among whom I was sent. **[Maʿārif]** The Messenger of God ﷺ made this prophecy: "In this community there shall be, right through to the Day of Doom, a group of people who will remain firm and stick to the task of bidding the Fair and forbidding the Unfair." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** "You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong" is praise of this community so long as they uphold it and are described by it; but if they abandon changing wrong and connive at it, the name of praise departs from them and the name of blame attaches to them, and that becomes a cause of their destruction. **[Qurṭubī]** Since it is established by the text of the revelation that this community is the best of communities, and the ḥadīth of ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn shows that its first generations are better than those after them. **[Maʿārif]** The praise is conditional on doing what has been charged; and the third option of the hand, including every kind of *jihād*, is what distinguishes this community's discharge of the duty. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The iniquity of the People of the Scripture consists precisely in this: both the Torah and the Gospel contain the description of Muḥammad ﷺ and that he is the prophet of God, and both parties deny him — so they go out of the religion each claims to follow. **[Study Quran]** Since belief is contrasted with iniquity rather than with disbelief, what is highlighted is their being false to their own religions; al-Ṭabarī reads it as being false to the true teachings of the Torah and the Gospel. **[Jalālayn]** The believers among them include ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions. **[Maʿārif]** The second distinguishing feature of this community is that they "believe in God" — and while belief is common to all communities, the degrees of perfection in belief differ, and the degree given to the community of Muḥammad ﷺ is in a class of its own. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** The preferment is by these causes: sincerity, love of good, calling, teaching, enjoining and forbidding, perfecting character and striving after people's benefit, together with perfecting the self through faith. **(the Study Quran notes that "among them are believers" is often skipped in the commentaries of al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Māturīdī)**

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 44:32, "And We chose them, by knowledge, above all the worlds", as the parallel Mujāhid cites for the conditional reading; 1:249–250, 3:561 and 1:221, 3:74, 100, 128, 141, 275–277 for the meaning of *ummah*; 3:104 for the same obligation; 3:111, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 2:143 for the moderate community; 22:41; his earlier treatment of enjoining right and forbidding wrong at the beginning of the sūrah; the ḥadīth of ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn; 3:111, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 5:48 for the Quran as a protector over other scriptures; 3:111–112, which follow. **[Study Quran]** 85:22 for the Preserved Tablet; 6:163 and 3:96 for "first" as "foremost"; 2:143 for the moderate community; 5:48 for the Quran as *muhaymin*; 3:113 for "among the People of the Book is an upright community"; 5:82–83 for the Negus; 3:85 for the scope of *muslim*; 3:104 for the same obligation. **[Maʿārif]** 2:143 for the moderation of the community; Sūrat al-Baqarah for the witnesses over the people. **[Jalālayn]** 2:143; 3:111, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:111, which follows.

**Reflection.** "You were the best community" — and the first question every commentator asks is whether that is a description, a promise, or a condition **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The reports divide accordingly: Ibn ʿAbbās, through two chains, says it means those who emigrated; ʿIkrima names four men — Ibn Masʿūd, Sālim, Ubayy and Muʿādh; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the Companions in particular, the transmitters and callers; and ʿUmar's remark is the sharpest of all — had God willed He would have said "you are", and then we would all be it, but He said "you were", of a particular group, and whoever does their deed joins them **[Ṭabarī]**. Mujāhid's reading makes it explicitly conditional, on the terms stated in the verse itself, and ʿUmar's sermon at the ḥajj draws the practical consequence: whoever wants to be of that community, let him fulfil its condition **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī closes with the same point in a harsher form — the praise holds only while they uphold it; if they abandon correcting wrong and connive at it, the praise departs and becomes a cause of destruction **[Qurṭubī]**. The second half of the verse is a small masterpiece of restraint: some of them believe, most are iniquitous — and al-Ṭabarī's definition of that iniquity is exact, because it is not that they disbelieve but that both their Books contain the description of Muḥammad ﷺ and both parties deny him, so they are false to the religion each claims to hold **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. And the reason given for the community's precedence is worth keeping in front of us, because it is so unflattering: it is best not by descent or by numbers but by what it does for other people — which is why, as the Study Quran notices, action is named before faith in this verse **[Study Quran]**, **[Maʿārif]**, **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:111 — لَن يَضُرُّوكُمْ إِلَّا أَذًى ۖ وَإِن يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ يُوَلُّوكُمُ ٱلْأَدْبَارَ ثُمَّ لَا يُنصَرُونَ

*"They will not harm you except a hurt; and if they fight you they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: they will not harm you, O people of faith in God and His messenger — these iniquitous ones among the People of the Book, by their disbelief and their belying your prophet Muḥammad ﷺ — at all; "except a hurt", meaning by that: but they hurt you by their associating partners, by making you hear their unbelief, by what they say about Jesus and his mother and ʿUzayr, and by their calling you to misguidance — and they will not harm you by that. **[Ṭabarī]** This is of the disconnected exception (*al-istithnāʾ al-munqaṭiʿ*) which differs in meaning from what precedes it, as when it is said "he complained of nothing but good" (*mā ishtakā shayʾan illā khayran*) — and this is a phrase reported from the Arabs by hearing. **[Ṭabarī]** As for "and if they fight you they will turn you their backs", He means: if the People of the Book fight you, the Jews and the Christians, they will be routed from you and turn their backs to you in flight. **[Ṭabarī]** "They turn you their backs" is a metonymy for their rout, because the one routed turns his back toward the direction of the pursuer, fleeing to a refuge and shelter to escape from him, in fear for himself, while the pursuer is on his track — so the back of the pursued is then opposite the face of the routing pursuer. **[Ṭabarī]** "Then they will not be helped" means: then God will not help them, O believers, against you, because of their disbelief in God and His messenger and your faith in what He has given you — because God, mighty and majestic, has cast terror into their hearts, and so has aided you, O believers, with help against them. **[Ṭabarī]** This is a promise from God to His prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and the people of faith, of help over the disbelievers among the People of the Book. **[Jalālayn]** "They", the Jews, "will not hurt you" O company of Muslims, "except with a trifling hurt", such as slander and threats; "and if they fight against you they will turn their backs to you" in retreat, "then they will not be helped" against you, but you will be helped against them. **[Qurṭubī]** "They will not harm you except a hurt" — meaning their lying, their distortion and their slander, not that they will have the upper hand, from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda. So the exception is connected, and the meaning is "they will not harm you except a slight harm", so "hurt" stands in the place of the verbal noun. **[Qurṭubī]** Thus the verse is a promise from God to His messenger ﷺ and to the believers that the People of the Book will not overcome them and that they will be helped over them, and that no uprooting will reach them from them — only hurt by slander and distortion; as for the outcome, it belongs to the believers. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that it is disconnected, the meaning being "they will not harm you at all, but they hurt you by what they make you hear." **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil said: the heads of the Jews — Kaʿb, ʿAdī, al-Nuʿmān, Abū Rāfiʿ, Abū Yāsir, Kināna and Ibn Ṣūriyā — went to those of their own who had believed, ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions, and hurt them for having become Muslims; so God revealed "they will not harm you except a hurt", meaning with the tongue. Then "and if they fight you they will turn you their backs", meaning routed; and "then they will not be helped" is a fresh sentence, which is why the *nūn* is retained in it. **[Qurṭubī]** And in this verse is a miracle for the Prophet, peace be upon him, because everyone among the Jews who fought him turned his back. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Delivering the good news to His believing servants that victory and dominance will be theirs over the disbelieving People of the Scriptures, God then said: "They will do you no harm, barring a trifling annoyance; and if they fight against you, they will show you their backs, and they will not be helped." *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:110–112)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is what occurred, for at the battle of Khaybar God brought humiliation and disgrace to the Jews; and before that the Jews in al-Madīnah — the tribes of Qaynuqāʿ, al-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah — were also humiliated by God. Such was the case with the Christians in the region of Syria later on, when the Companions defeated them in many battles and took over its leadership forever. There shall always be a group of Muslims in Syria until ʿĪsā son of Maryam descends while they are like this — apparent and victorious; ʿĪsā will at that time rule according to the law of Muḥammad ﷺ, break the cross, kill the swine, abolish the *jizyah* and accept nothing but Islam from the people. **[Saʿdī]** For all that, they will not harm the believers except a hurt of the tongue; and if they fight them they will turn their backs, and then they will not be helped. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:110–111)* **[Saʿdī]** And what God informed of has indeed occurred: when they fought the Muslims they turned their backs, and God helped the Muslims against them. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** In previous verses (98–101) it was shown how hostile to Muslims the People of the Book were and how they planned to bring religious harm to them; mentioned in the present verse are their plans to harm Muslims materially, and the last sentence carries the prophecy that they shall not succeed. **[Maʿārif]** This prophecy of the Holy Qurʾān was proved true when, during the entire period of prophethood, the People of the Book were unable to overcome the noble Companions, who are the primary addressees here — and this applies particularly to the Jewish tribes who had tried to sow seeds of discord among the Companions. The outcome was that these people were disgraced: some paid *jizyah*, some were killed, and others were exiled. **[Maʿārif]** The next verse (112) makes the description complete. **[Study Quran]** The hurt (*adhā*) refers to an insult or a taunt, or to blasphemous claims about God (R, Ṭ, Th). That the People of the Book would, when challenged with physical danger, turn their backs is also mentioned in 59:12, where it also says that they will not be helped. Not being helped, or not having helpers, is a fate often associated with perdition in the Hereafter and in this world (e.g., 2:270, 3:22, 56; 4:52; 9:74; 16:37).

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The exception is *munqaṭiʿ* — disconnected, its meaning differing from what precedes, like the Arabic saying "he complained of nothing but good". **[Ṭabarī]** "They turn you their backs" is *kināya* for rout: the routed man turns his back to his pursuer. **[Ṭabarī]** On the grammar of "then they will not be helped": it is in the indicative although "they turn you their backs" is jussive, because it is a fresh sentence (*istiʾnāf*) — the verse-endings before it end in *nūn*, so this was made to follow them, just as He said "and they will not be given leave to offer excuses" (77:36) in the indicative, while in another place He said "they will not be judged so as to die" (35:36), since that is not a verse-ending. *(al-Farrāʾ, Maʿānī al-Qurʾān 1:229)* **[Qurṭubī]** On the connected reading, "hurt" stands in the place of the *maṣdar*; on the disconnected reading the sentence ends at "harm you". "Then they will not be helped" is a fresh sentence, hence the retained *nūn*.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7626 — Qatāda, on "they will not harm you except a hurt": "They will not harm you except a hurt you hear from them." **[Ṭabarī]** 7627 — al-Rabīʿ b. Anas: "A hurt you hear from them." **[Ṭabarī]** 7628 — Ibn Jurayj: "Their associating partners with God in ʿUzayr, and Jesus, and the cross." **[Ṭabarī]** 7629 — al-Ḥasan: "You hear from them a lie against God; they call you to misguidance." **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil's account of the heads of the Jews and their hurting ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions for their Islam, as the occasion of the verse. *(cited above)* **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda: the harm is their lying, distortion and slander, not that they will have the upper hand. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The fulfilment at Khaybar and in al-Madīnah, and the promise that a group will remain in Syria until the descent of Jesus. *(cited above)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is a promise of help to the Prophet and the believers over the disbelievers among the People of the Book, and the harm that remains is a harm of the tongue and of what they make the believers hear. **[Maʿārif]** The verse predicts that the material harm planned by the People of the Book will not succeed, and Maʿārif treats this as a prophecy fulfilled within the lifetime of the Prophet. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The promise extends beyond the Jews of al-Madīnah to the Christians of Syria, and reaches its term with the descent of Jesus. **[Study Quran]** The hurt is an insult, a taunt, or blasphemous claims about God. **[Qurṭubī]** In the verse is a miracle for the Prophet: everyone among the Jews who fought him turned his back.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:110 for "most of them are iniquitous", to which this verse is attached; **77:36** and **35:36** for the grammatical point about the verse-ending; 3:112, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 59:12 for the same promise about the People of the Book turning their backs; 2:270, 3:22, 3:56, 4:52, 9:74 and 16:37 for the fate of having no helpers. **[Maʿārif]** 3:98–101 for the religious harm described before this verse; 3:112, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:110 for the people in question; 3:112, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:110 for the setting; 3:112, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:110 for the praise of the ummah; 3:112, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:110 for the setting; 3:112, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is a promise, and the commentators are noticeably eager to say that it was kept **[Maʿārif]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Ṭabarī's framing is the most careful: the harm is real but it is limited to what the believers *hear* — their associating partners, their statements about Jesus and his mother and ʿUzayr, their calling to misguidance — and it is not harm in the sense of overcoming **[Ṭabarī]**. The grammar carries part of the argument, which is why Ṭabarī pauses over the disconnected exception and over why "then they will not be helped" is in the indicative: because it is a new sentence, and because the verse-ending is in *nūn* **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī names the men — Kaʿb, ʿAdī, al-Nuʿmān, Abū Rāfiʿ, Abū Yāsir, Kināna, Ibn Ṣūriyā — who set upon ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions, and he reads the verse as a *muʿjiza*: every Jew who fought the Prophet turned his back **[Qurṭubī]**. Maʿārif's distinction is useful for reading the whole run of verses: 3:98–101 described harm to the religion, and this verse describes harm to the person and the property, with the last clause foretelling that it will fail **[Maʿārif]**. Ibn Kathīr extends the promise past Khaybar and the three Madinan tribes to the Christians of Syria, and past that to the descent of Jesus **[Ibn Kathīr]** — which is a long arc to hang on a short sentence, but it is what the commentators heard in "they will not be helped".

## 3:112 — ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلذِّلَّةُ أَيْنَ مَا ثُقِفُوٓا۟ إِلَّا بِحَبْلٍۢ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَحَبْلٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍۢ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْمَسْكَنَةُ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا۟ يَكْفُرُونَ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَيَقْتُلُونَ ٱلْأَنۢبِيَآءَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّۢ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِمَا عَصَوا۟ وَّكَانُوا۟ يَعْتَدُونَ

*"Abasement is stamped upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from God and a rope from the people; and they have incurred anger from God, and destitution is stamped upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right; that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Abasement is stamped upon them" means: they have been made to cling to abasement; and "abasement" is the *faʿla* from *dhull*. "Wherever they are found" means: wherever they are met. He says, exalted is His praise: the Jews who belie Muḥammad ﷺ have been made to cling to abasement wherever they are of the earth and in whatever region of its regions, in the lands of the Muslims and of the idolaters — "except by a rope from God and a rope from the people". **[Ṭabarī]** As for the "rope" God has mentioned in this place, it is the means by which they are secure for their lives, their property and their offspring, from a covenant and a guarantee of safety contracted for them before they are found in the lands of Islam. **[Ṭabarī]** The grammarians of Kufa differed over what brings the *bāʾ* in "except by a rope from God": some of them said it is an elided verb whose mention has been left out, the meaning being "except that they hold fast by a rope of God and a rope from the people". **[Ṭabarī]** Then God informs why He did that to them: "that is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right; that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress" — and He closes by making it a reminder to His servants of what He did to those people of the People of the Book, of bringing down abasement and disgrace upon them in the near life, alongside what He has stored up for them in the term to come of punishment and exemplary chastisement and painful suffering, since they transgressed the limits of God and made lawful what He had made unlawful — as a reminder from Him to them and an alert to the place of the affliction from which it came upon them, that they might turn back and take heed; and as an admonition from Him to our community, that they should not imitate their way nor ride their path, lest He lead them by their paths and bring down upon them of His vengeance and exemplary punishments what He brought down upon them. **[Jalālayn]** "Abasement shall be cast upon them wherever they are found", so that they have no strength and no protection, "save if they be clinging to a rope of God and a rope of the believing people" — this being the latter's covenant of security for them on the condition that they pay the *jizyah*; in other words, they have no protection other than this. "They have incurred" — they have ended up with — "anger from God, and poverty shall be cast upon them; that", repeated for emphasis, "is because they disbelieved in God's signs and slew the prophets without right; that is because they disobeyed" God's command "and used to transgress", passing from what is lawful into what is unlawful. **[Qurṭubī]** It means the Jews. "Wherever they are found" — wherever they are found and encountered — and the sentence ends. **[Qurṭubī]** "Except by a rope from God" is a disconnected exception, not from the first: rather, they hold fast by a rope from God. "And a rope from the people" means the *dhimmah* they have; and "the people" are Muḥammad and the believers, who pay them the *kharāj* and so make them secure. There is an ellipsis in the wording, the meaning being "except that they hold fast by a rope from God", the verb being suppressed — as al-Farrāʾ said. **[Qurṭubī]** "And they have incurred anger from God" — that is, they have returned with it; and it is said, they have borne it; and its root in the language is that it clung to them. **[Qurṭubī]** Then He informed why He did that to them: "that is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right; that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress." **[Ibn Kathīr]** God has placed humiliation and disgrace on them wherever they may be, and they will never be safe "except when under a covenant from Allah" — under the *dhimmah* from God that requires them to pay the *jizyah* and makes them subservient to Islamic law — "and a covenant from men", meaning covenants such as pledges of protection and safety offered to them by Muslim men and women, and even a slave, according to one of the sayings of the scholars. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:110–112)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "They have drawn on themselves the wrath of Allah" means they earned God's anger, which they deserved; "and destitution is put over them" means they deserve it by decree and legislatively. **[Ibn Kathīr]** What drove them to this was their arrogance, transgression and envy, earning them humiliation, degradation and disgrace throughout this life and the Hereafter; and what lured them to disbelieve in God's signs and kill His messengers is the fact that they often disobeyed His commands, committed His prohibitions and transgressed His set limits — we seek refuge from this behaviour. **[Saʿdī]** This is a report from God, exalted is He, that the Jews have had abasement struck upon them: they are afraid wherever they are found, and nothing makes them safe except a treaty and a means by which they are secure, submitting to the rulings of Islam and acknowledging the *jizyah*. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** "Or by a rope of the people" — that is, if they are under the authority and oversight of others, as has been observed of their condition formerly and latterly; for in recent times they were unable to establish even a temporary state in Palestine except through the victory of the great powers and their smoothing of every means for them. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** "And they have incurred anger from God" — God was angry with them and punished them with abasement and misery. And the cause of that is their disbelief in the signs of God and their killing the prophets "without right" — meaning, not out of ignorance, but out of insolence and obstinacy. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Those varied punishments upon them are "because they disobeyed and used to transgress"; for God, exalted is He, did not wrong them or punish them without sin — rather, what He brought upon them was because of their insolence, their enmity, their disbelief, their belying of the messengers and their hideous crimes. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** A detailed discussion on this subject has already appeared under the commentary on verse 61 of Sūrat al-Baqarah, where the text mentions no exception; that discussion also covers the exception given in the present verse. **[Maʿārif]** Briefly, the verse means that the Jews shall remain stamped with disgrace and misery except under two situations: first, through a Covenant of Allah — for example, a minor child or a woman shall not be killed, and this exception is meant by the words "through a source from Allah"; and second, through a treaty obligation, that is, "through a source from men". Such patronage may cause their disgrace and misery not to become manifest, and the specific words used in the Qurʾān — "a source from men" — cover all men, believers and disbelievers. **[Study Quran]** Similar themes, including abasement, wrath and indigence, are addressed in 2:61. They are understood by some to refer to the status of the People of the Book during times of war when they are belligerents, whose property could be legitimately seized as spoils and children taken as prisoners, among other things (R). **[Study Quran]** Others say the abasement refers to the *jizyah*, the indemnity levied on non-Muslims, and to *dhimmah*, the state of living as a non-Muslim treaty people under Muslim rule (Q; see 9:29). Some, however, dispute that this abasement refers to the *jizyah*, because the *jizyah* does not disappear with the "rope from God and rope from mankind", interpreted to mean a covenant with God and a covenant with the believers (Ṭ). **[Study Quran]** Others point to the historical situation of Jews as exiles who are historically poor and powerless, since the verb could be understood as referring to the past or the future (R).

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Wherever they are found" (*ayna mā thuqifū*) is glossed as "wherever they are met"; the *bāʾ* in "except by a rope" is explained by the Kufans through an elided verb. **[Qurṭubī]** The exception is disconnected, and the meaning is "but they hold fast by a rope from God"; there is an ellipsis of the verb, as al-Farrāʾ said. **[Qurṭubī]** *Bāʾū* is glossed as "they returned" or "they bore", its root sense being that it clung to them. **[Jalālayn]** The repetition of "that" (*dhālika*) is for emphasis. **[Study Quran]** The verb could be understood as past or future, which is what opens up the historical and the eschatological readings.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7630 — al-Ḥasan, on the whole verse: "This community has overtaken them — and the Magians take the *jizyah* from them." **[Ṭabarī]** 7631 — al-Ḥasan: "God abased them, so they have no protection, and God put them under the feet of the Muslims." **[Ṭabarī]** 7632 — Mujāhid: "except by a rope from God" — by a covenant; "and a rope from the people" — by their covenant. **[Ṭabarī]** 7633 — Qatāda: "except by a covenant from God and a covenant from the people"; and 7634 — Maʿmar, from Qatāda, the same. **[Ṭabarī]** 7635 — ʿIkrima: "by a covenant from God and a covenant from the people"; 7636 — al-Suddī, the same; 7637 — al-Rabīʿ, the same. **[Ṭabarī]** 7638 — Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is a covenant from God and a covenant from the people, just as a man says, 'the protection of God and the protection of His messenger ﷺ' — and that is the compact." **[Ṭabarī]** 7639 — Ibn Jurayj: Mujāhid said "by a covenant from God and a covenant from the people for them"; and Ibn Jurayj said, ʿAṭāʾ said: "the covenant is the rope of God." **[Ṭabarī]** 7640 — Ibn Zayd: "except by a covenant" — and they are the Jews. He said: the rope is the covenant; and that is the saying of Abū al-Haytham b. al-Tayyihān to the Messenger of God ﷺ when the Anṣār came to him at al-ʿAqabah: "O man, we are cutting ropes between us and the people" — meaning covenants. And the Jews are not secure in any land. **[Ṭabarī]** 7641 and 7642 — al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "by a covenant from God and a covenant from the people." **[Ṭabarī]** 7643 — Qatāda, on "that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress": "Avoid disobedience and transgression, for by those two those destroyed before you were destroyed." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn ʿAbbās said that "except by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from men" refers to a covenant of protection from God and a pledge of safety from people; and the like was said by Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and al-Rabīʿ b. Anas.

**Rulings.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** The "rope from God" is the *dhimmah* that requires the *jizyah* and makes them subservient to Islamic law; the "rope from men" is a pledge of safety from Muslims, and according to one saying of the scholars even from a slave. **[Qurṭubī]** "The people" are Muḥammad and the believers, who pay them the *kharāj* and thereby render them secure. **[Saʿdī]** The rope of the people covers being under the authority and oversight of others, whether Muslims or not. **[Maʿārif]** The two exceptions are a covenant of God — under which, for instance, a child or a woman is not killed — and a treaty obligation, under which the patronage of any people, believers or disbelievers, may keep their abasement from becoming visible. **[Study Quran]** The interpretations divide between the jizyah-and-dhimmah reading (Q) and the covenant reading (Ṭ), with some reading the abasement as a description of the wartime status of belligerents (R).

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The abasement is tied to a stated cause — disbelief in the signs of God and killing the prophets without right — and is presented as a warning to this community not to follow their path. **[Saʿdī]** The justice of it rests on the fact that their denial was not ignorance but insolence, and that God punished them only for their insolence, enmity and belying of the messengers. **[Ibn Kathīr]** What drove them was arrogance, transgression and envy, and they deserve their destitution by decree and legislatively. **[Maʿārif]** The disgrace is not absolute: God's covenant and a treaty obligation both suspend its manifestation. **[Study Quran]** The debate turns on whether the abasement is a legal status under Muslim rule or a historical condition, and the verb's tense allows both.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 2:61 for "abased and humiliated"; 3:103 for the rope of God; 3:111 for the promise that precedes; 3:113, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** His earlier treatment of "abased and humiliated" in al-Baqarah; 3:103 for the rope; 3:113, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:110 for the ummah praised; 3:111 for the promise of victory; 3:113, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:61 for the parallel themes; 9:29 for the *jizyah* and the state of *dhimmah*; 3:103 for the "rope". **[Maʿārif]** 2:61 for the detailed discussion; 3:113, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:111 for the promise; 3:113, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:111 for the setting; 3:113, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse is uncomfortable and the commentators do not soften it, but they do disagree about what it describes **[Study Quran]**. Is the abasement a legal status — the *jizyah* and the *dhimmah* — or is it a description of a people at war, whose property is spoil and whose children are captives, or is it simply the observed historical condition of a people who were exiled and poor **[Study Quran]**? Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr take the legal reading: the rope from God is the *dhimmah* that requires the *jizyah* and makes them subservient to the law, and the rope from the people is a pledge of safety from any Muslim, even a slave **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Ṭabarī's isnāds keep repeating the single word *ʿahd* — covenant, covenant, covenant, from Mujāhid, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk — and Ibn Zayd adds the wonderful detail from al-ʿAqabah, where Abū al-Haytham told the Prophet "we are cutting ropes between us and the people", meaning covenants, which shows how the metaphor worked in living Arabic **[Ṭabarī]**.
