The two reports from al-Ḥasan are the hardest-edged thing in the passage: "this community has overtaken them, and the Magians take the *jizyah* from them", and "God put them under the feet of the Muslims" **[Ṭabarī]**. And then Ṭabarī does something worth noticing: he turns the verse into an admonition to *this* community, warning them not to imitate the way of those they are reading about, lest the same thing be brought down on them **[Ṭabarī]**. Al-Saʿdī, writing in the twentieth century, does the same from the other direction — he reads the contemporary condition of the Jews through the verse, and his remarks about Palestine and the great powers are unmistakably those of his own time **[Saʿdī]**. Maʿārif, likewise, applies the exception to the modern state of Israel **[Maʿārif]**. What survives all three applications is the moral structure Ṭabarī and Saʿdī both insist on: the punishment is not arbitrary, because their denial was not ignorance but insolence **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:113 — لَيْسُوا۟ سَوَآءًۭ ۗ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ أُمَّةٌۭ قَآئِمَةٌۭ يَتْلُونَ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ءَانَآءَ ٱلَّيْلِ وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ

*"They are not all alike. Among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God means by "they are not all alike": the two parties of the People of the Book — the people of faith among them and the people of unbelief — are not alike; they are not equal, but differ in righteousness and corruption, in good and evil. **[Ṭabarī]** It was said "they are not all alike" because it contains the mention of the two parties of the People of the Book whom God mentioned in "had the People of the Scripture believed, it would have been better for them; among them are believers, but most of them are iniquitous" — then He informed of the state of the two parties with Him, the believing and the disbelieving, and said "they are not all alike"; then He began the report, exalted is His praise, of the description of the believing party among the People of the Book, praising them and commending them, after He had described the iniquitous party by what He described them with of panic, faintness of heart, alliance with abasement and contempt, clinging to want and destitution, and bearing the shame of this world and the exposure of the next; and He said "among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate", the three verses, up to "and God knows the God-fearing". **[Ṭabarī]** Others said: the meaning is, the People of the Book and the community of Muḥammad ﷺ that stands by God's right are not equal with God. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own conclusion: the sounder of the two views is the view of those who say that the narrative is complete at "they are not all alike" — God having already reported the affair of the believers among the People of the Book and the unbelievers among them — and that "among the People of the Scripture is an upright community" is a fresh sentence praising the believers among them and describing them by their attribute, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and Ibn Jurayj said. **[Ṭabarī]** "An upright community" means a group firm upon the truth; and the commentators differed over "upright": some said it means just, others that it is a community standing upon the Book of God and upon what He has commanded in it, others that it is obedient. Ṭabarī preferred the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda, and then gave the parable of the ship: the one who stands by the limits of God and the one who falls into them are like people who boarded a ship. **[Ṭabarī]** The interpretation of the sentence is therefore: among the People of the Book is a community holding fast to the Book of God, cleaving to it, firm in acting according to it and according to what His messenger prescribed for them. **[Jalālayn]** "Yet they", the People of the Scripture, "are not all alike", equal; "some of the People of the Scripture are a community upright", with integrity, adhering to the truth — such as ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions — "who recite God's verses in the watches of the night", that is, during its hours, "prostrating themselves", performing prayer; *wa-hum yasjudūn*, "prostrating themselves", is a circumstantial qualifier. **[Qurṭubī]** "They are not all alike" — the meaning is that the People of the Book and the community of Muḥammad ﷺ are not alike, from Ibn Masʿūd; and it is said the meaning is that the believers and the disbelievers among the People of the Book are not alike. *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:112–115)* **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn ʿAbbās said: "among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate" — those who believed with the Prophet ﷺ. **[Qurṭubī]** Ibn Isḥāq, from Ibn ʿAbbās: when ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, Thaʿlaba b. Saʿya, Usayd b. Saʿya, Asad b. ʿUbayd, and those of the Jews who became Muslims with them, believed and affirmed and desired Islam and were firmly rooted in it, the rabbis of the Jews and the unbelievers among them said: "None has believed in Muḥammad and followed him but the worst of us; had they been of the best of us they would not have left the religion of their fathers and gone to another" — so God, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning that saying of theirs: "they are not all alike; among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God", up to "and those are among the righteous". **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is "among the People of the Scripture are the people of a community", that is, the people of a good way; and he cited a line of poetry. **[Qurṭubī]** And it is said that there is an ellipsis, the estimate being "an upright community and another not upright", the second being dropped as sufficiently indicated by the first, as in the line of Abū Dhuʾayb. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Farrāʾ said: "community" is in the nominative by "alike". Al-Naḥḥās said: this is wrong from several angles — one is that it makes "community" nominative by "alike", so that nothing returns to the noun of *laysa*; it makes it nominative by something that is not predicated of the verb; and it suppresses what there is no need to suppress, since the mention of the disbeliever has already preceded, so there is no point in suppressing this. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū ʿUbayda said: this is like their saying "the fleas ate me" (*akalūnī al-barāghīth*). Al-Naḥḥās said: this too is an error, because their mention has already preceded, whereas in "the fleas ate me" there is no preceding mention. **[Qurṭubī]** "The watches of the night" (*ānāʾ al-layl*) are its hours, singular *inan*, *anan* and *uny*, and it is in the accusative as an adverb of time. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Muḥammad b. Isḥāq and others, including al-ʿAwfī who reported it from Ibn ʿAbbās, said: these verses were revealed about the clergy of the People of the Scriptures who embraced the faith — for instance ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, Asad b. ʿUbayd, Thaʿlaba b. Saʿya, Usayd b. Saʿya and so forth. This verse means that those among the People of the Book whom God rebuked earlier are not at all the same as those among them who embraced Islam. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** These two types of people are not equal, and there are believers and also criminals among the People of the Book. As for "an upright community", they implement the Book of God, adhere to His law and follow His Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, and so this type is on the straight path; and "they recite the verses of God during the hours of the night, prostrating themselves in prayer" means they often stand in prayer at night for *tahajjud* and recite the Qurʾān in their prayer. **[Ibn Kathīr]** This is the same type of people mentioned at the end of the sūrah: "And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture those who believe in God and in that which has been revealed to you, and in that which has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before God" (3:199). **[Saʿdī]** When God mentioned the deviant among the People of the Book, He clarified the state of the upright among them: that among them is a community who establish the fundamentals of the religion and its branches. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:113–114)* **[Maʿārif]** In verse 110 it was said that among the People of the Book there are those who believe, yet most of them are disbelievers; details appear in the present verse, which gives a complementary profile of those who believed from among the People of the Book, and who, by becoming Muslims, adopted the distinguishing hallmarks of the faith that go to make believers the best of communities. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Study Quran]** Although this verse is usually interpreted as setting up a distinction among different kinds of People of the Book, some understand "they are not all alike" to refer to Muslims and the People of the Book together, meaning that Muslims are not like the Jews and Christians (Q, Ṭ). The word "upright" renders *qāʾimah*, which connotes justice (Ṭ) as well as evoking the literal "standing up" of worshippers in prayer. Some think the upright community refers to a group of Jews who became good Muslims (Ṭ); see 3:110c. **[Study Quran]** Several somewhat enigmatic occasions of revelation are provided for this verse. Some mention an incident in which the Muslims were waiting for the Prophet to lead the night prayer in the mosque and the Prophet said to them, "No people from among any of the religions are remembering God at this hour other than you" — and vv. 113–15 were then revealed. Another version states that this upright community refers specifically to forty people of Najrān, thirty-two people from Abyssinia, and three from Byzantium who followed the religion of Jesus and affirmed the truth of Muhammad. Another account says that it refers to a people who prayed between sunset and the end of twilight (R). **[Study Quran]** One interpretation of this verse identifies Muslims as People of the Book, since they do indeed follow a Book from God, and thus sees this as a comparison between Muslims, the upright community, on the one hand, and Jews and Christians on the other (R), while others say "People of the Book" can mean a people following a "good way". Some state, without exposition, that there are believers among the People of the Book (M). To be upright is interpreted as meaning being just (Ṭ) and maintaining the limits set by God, obeying Him and not distorting the Books (M, Th).

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Upright" (*qāʾimah*) is variously "just" (Mujāhid), "standing upon the Book of God, His obligations and His limits" (Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ), "rightly guided, standing upon the command of God" (Ibn ʿAbbās) and "obedient" (*qānitah*, al-Suddī); Ṭabarī prefers the first two. **[Ṭabarī]** "The watches of the night" is glossed as "the hours of the night"; Ṭabarī adds that the differing views are close in meaning and that the soundest is the ʿishāʾ prayer, because it is a prayer that none of the People of the Book performs. **[Ṭabarī]** On "and they prostrate": some Arab philologists held that "prostration" here means the prayer rather than prostration proper, since recitation does not take place in prostration or in bowing — that is the view of al-Farrāʾ; Ṭabarī rejects it, holding that they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night *in their prayer*, and that with that they also prostrate in it, so that "prostration" is prostration as it is known in the prayer. **[Qurṭubī]** "The watches of the night" is an adverb of time; al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj took "they prostrate" to mean "they pray", since recitation is not in bowing or prostration; al-Thawrī took it as the prayer between the two ʿishāʾs, and others as the night vigil. **[Jalālayn]** "Prostrating themselves" is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). **[Study Quran]** *Qāʾimah* connotes justice and evokes the standing of worshippers in prayer.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7644 — Ibn ʿAbbās, through Muḥammad b. Isḥāq: when ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, Thaʿlaba b. Saʿya, Usayd b. Saʿya, Asad b. ʿUbayd and those Jews who became Muslims with them believed and affirmed and desired Islam and were firmly rooted in it, the rabbis of the Jews and the unbelievers among them said: "None has believed in Muḥammad nor followed him but the worst of us; had they been of the best of us they would not have left the religion of their fathers and gone to another" — so God revealed concerning that saying of theirs "they are not all alike; among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God", up to "and those are among the righteous". **[Ṭabarī]** 7645 — the same, through Yūnus b. Bukayr from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, from Saʿīd b. Jubayr or ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Ṭabarī]** 7646 — Qatāda: "Not every one of the people has perished; God has kept a remnant among them." **[Ṭabarī]** 7647 — Ibn Jurayj: "'an upright community' — ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, and Thaʿlaba his brother, and Saʿya, and Mubashshir, and Usayd and Asad the two sons of Kaʿb." **[Ṭabarī]** 7648 — Ibn Masʿūd, through al-Ḥasan b. Yazīd al-ʿIjlī: "The People of the Book and the community of Muḥammad ﷺ are not equal." **[Ṭabarī]** 7649 — al-Suddī: "These Jews are not like this community which is standing." **[Ṭabarī]** 7650 — Mujāhid: "'an upright community' — just." **[Ṭabarī]** 7651 — Qatāda: "standing upon the Book of God, His obligations and His limits"; and 7652 — al-Rabīʿ, the same. **[Ṭabarī]** 7653 — Ibn ʿAbbās: "a rightly guided community, standing upon the command of God, not stripping itself of it and abandoning it as the others abandoned it and let it go." **[Ṭabarī]** 7654 — al-Suddī: "these Jews are not like this community which is *qānitah* to God" — and *qānitah* is the obedient one. **[Ṭabarī]** 7655 — the parable of the one who stands by the limits of God and the one who falls into them, like people who boarded a ship. **[Ṭabarī]** 7656 — Qatāda: "they recite the signs of God in the watches of the night" — the hours of the night; 7657 — al-Rabīʿ, the same; 7658 — Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAbdullāh b. Kathīr: "We heard the Arabs say 'the watches of the night' meaning its hours." **[Ṭabarī]** 7659 — al-Suddī: "the watches of the night" — the middle of the night. **[Ṭabarī]** 7660 — Ibn Masʿūd, through al-Ḥasan b. Yazīd al-ʿIjlī: "the ʿatama prayer — they perform it, and those other than them among the People of the Book do not perform it." **[Ṭabarī]** 7661 — Ibn Masʿūd, through Zirr b. Ḥubaysh: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was detained from us one night — he was with one of his family and his wives — and he did not come to us for the ʿishāʾ prayer until part of the night had gone; then he came, and some of us were praying and some lying down, and he gave us good tidings and said: 'None of the People of the Book prays this prayer!' — and God revealed..." **[Ṭabarī]** 7662 — the same, through ʿĀṣim from Zirr b. Ḥubaysh: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came out to us while we were waiting for the ʿishāʾ — meaning the ʿatama — and said to us: 'There is no one upon the earth among the people of the religions who waits for this prayer at this hour other than you!' He said: and then 'they are not all alike; among the People of the Scripture is an upright community who recite the signs of God...' was revealed." **[Ṭabarī]** 7663 — al-Thawrī, from Manṣūr: "It has reached me that it was revealed concerning what is between the maghrib and the ʿishāʾ." **[Qurṭubī]** Abū Khaythama Zuhayr b. Ḥarb — Hāshim b. al-Qāsim — Shaybān — ʿĀṣim — Zirr — Ibn Masʿūd: "The Messenger of God ﷺ delayed the ʿishāʾ prayer one night, then came out to the mosque, and there were the people waiting for the prayer; and he said: 'There is none among the people of the religions who remembers God, exalted is He, at this hour other than you.' He said: and this verse was revealed, 'they are not all alike; among the People of the Scripture is an upright community', up to 'and God knows the God-fearing'." And Ibn Wahb narrated the same. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The names given by Ibn Isḥāq and others: ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, Asad b. ʿUbayd, Thaʿlaba b. Saʿya, Usayd b. Saʿya. *(weak isnāds are not flagged by the sources here)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse rests on a distinction within the People of the Book, not between them and the Muslims — that is Ṭabarī's own conclusion, against the reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī. **[Ibn Kathīr]** There are believers and also criminals among the People of the Book, and the upright community implements the Book of God, adheres to His law and follows His Prophet. **[Jalālayn]** The upright community includes ʿAbdullāh b. Salām and his companions. **[Study Quran]** The plain sense suggests that Muslims are being told how to judge the belief and actions of the People of the Book, and that God does not reject their good deeds when they are truly good. **[Qurṭubī]** The occasion of revelation is the taunt of the Jewish rabbis that only the worst of them followed Muḥammad. **[Maʿārif]** The verse gives the complementary profile of those among the People of the Book who believed and so adopted the hallmarks of the faith.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:110 for the two parties mentioned before; 3:114–115 for the rest of the description; 3:199 for the parallel praise at the end of the sūrah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:110 for the rebuke that precedes; 3:114–115, which follow; 3:199 for the same type of people. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:110 for "among them are believers"; 25:60 and 53:62 for "prostrate" meaning pray; 3:114, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 3:110c for the identification of the upright community; 2:62 and 5:69 for the parallel questions; 3:199 for the same type. **[Saʿdī]** 7:159, "and of the people of Moses is a community guiding by the truth and thereby doing justice"; 3:114, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:110 for "among them are believers"; 3:114, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:110 for the setting; 3:114, which follows.

**Reflection.** "They are not all alike" — three words that undo a great deal of what the passage before it has been saying, and the commentators are careful about exactly what is being distinguished **[Study Quran]**. The majority reading, and Ṭabarī's own, is that the division runs *inside* the People of the Book: the believing party and the iniquitous party named in 3:110 are not the same, and the verses that follow are praise of the first **[Ṭabarī]**. But there is a second reading, from Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī, that reads it as a comparison between the People of the Book and the community of Muḥammad — and the Study Quran notes that "Muslims" and "People of the Book" are treated as overlapping categories only in the commentaries trying to make sense of exactly these verses **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Study Quran]**. The occasion of revelation is the sharper thing: the rabbis said that only the worst of them had followed Muḥammad, and the verse answers them **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Jurayj names the men — ʿAbdullāh b. Salām, his brother Thaʿlaba, Saʿya, Mubashshir, Usayd and Asad the sons of Kaʿb **[Ṭabarī]**. And then the phrase "in the watches of the night" produces a small, beautiful dispute: Qatāda says the hours of the night, al-Suddī says its middle, al-Thawrī says between the two ʿishāʿs, and Ibn Masʿūd — through two chains — says specifically the ʿishāʾ prayer, because the Prophet came out late one night, found some of them standing and some lying down, and told them: "None of the People of the Book prays this prayer" **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**. Ṭabarī adopts that reading, on the neat ground that it is a prayer no other religious community performs; and he quietly overrules al-Farrāʾ, who wanted "they prostrate" to mean simply "they pray", insisting that the prostration is real prostration within the prayer **[Ṭabarī]**. Maʿārif's summary of the whole movement is the best one-line reading of the verse: after the rebuke of 3:110, this is the complementary profile of those among them who believed, and who by becoming Muslims took on the hallmarks of the faith **[Maʿārif]**.

## 3:114 — يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْءَاخِرِ وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَيُسَٰرِعُونَ فِى ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ

*"They believe in God and the Last Day, and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds — and those are among the righteous."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** "They believe in God and the Last Day" means: they affirm God and the raising after death, and know that God will recompense them for their deeds — and they are not like the idolaters, who deny the oneness of God and worship other than Him with Him, who deny the raising after death and deny the recompense for deeds, and the reward and the punishment. **[Ṭabarī]** "And they enjoin what is right": He says, they command people to faith in God and His messenger, and to affirm Muḥammad ﷺ and what he has brought them. "And forbid what is wrong": He says, and they forbid people from disbelief in God and from belying Muḥammad and what he has brought them from God — meaning by that that they are not like the Jews and the Christians, who command people to disbelief and to belying Muḥammad in what he has brought them, and forbid them from the right of deeds, which is affirming Muḥammad in what he has brought them from God. **[Ṭabarī]** "And hasten to good deeds": He says, they press forward to do good deeds, fearing that it should escape them before their deaths overtake them. **[Ṭabarī]** Then God, exalted is His praise, informs that those whose attribute this is, from among the People of the Book, are of the number of the righteous — because whoever among them was iniquitous has incurred anger from God for his disbelief in God and His signs, and their killing the prophets without right, and his disobeying his Lord and transgressing His limits. **[Jalālayn]** "They believe in God and in the Last Day, enjoining decency and forbidding indecency, vying with one another in good works; those", described in the way God has mentioned, "are of the righteous" — and some of them are not like this and are not righteous. **[Qurṭubī]** "They believe in God" — meaning they affirm God and believe Muḥammad ﷺ. *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:112–115)* **[Qurṭubī]** "And enjoin what is right" — it is said that it is general; and it is said that what is meant by it is commanding the following of the Prophet ﷺ. **[Qurṭubī]** "And forbid what is wrong" — and forbidding what is wrong is forbidding opposition to him. **[Qurṭubī]** "And hasten to good deeds" — which they do, pressing forward, not dragging behind, because of their knowledge of the worth of their reward; and it is said: they press forward with the deed before it is missed. **[Qurṭubī]** "And those are among the righteous" — meaning, with the righteous; and they are the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ in Paradise. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "They believe in Allah and the Last Day; they enjoin *al-maʿrūf* and forbid *al-munkar*; and they hasten in all good works; and they are among the righteous" — the same type of people mentioned at the end of the sūrah: "And there are, certainly, among the People of the Scripture those who believe in Allah and in that which has been revealed to you, and in that which has been revealed to them, humbling themselves before Allah" (3:199). *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Saʿdī]** They believe in God and the Last Day and enjoin what is right — which is all good — and forbid what is wrong, which is all evil, as God, exalted is He, said: "and of the people of Moses is a community guiding by the truth and thereby doing justice". *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:113–114, cited at 3:113)* **[Saʿdī]** "And they hasten to good deeds" — and hastening to good deeds is something over and above merely doing them, so it describes them as doing good deeds, initiating them, and completing them with everything that perfects them of obligations and recommended acts. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; cited at 3:113)* **[Study Quran]** Whether these verses refer to the Muslims or to the People of the Book depends on how the upright community is identified in 3:113 and how "among them are believers" is interpreted in 3:110. *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:114–115)* **[Study Quran]** These verses are similar in content to 2:62 and 5:69 and address similar issues of identifying what it means to believe in God and the Last Day and to be righteous.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** Belief in "the Last Day" is unpacked as affirming the raising after death and knowing that God recompenses deeds — set against the idolaters, who deny the oneness, the resurrection and the recompense. **[Ṭabarī]** "Enjoining what is right" is glossed specifically as commanding faith in God and His messenger; "forbidding what is wrong" as forbidding disbelief and belying the Prophet. **[Ṭabarī]** "Hasten" is glossed as pressing forward for fear the deed escape them before death. **[Qurṭubī]** The command to what is right is either general or specifically the following of the Prophet; "among the righteous" may mean "with the righteous". **[Saʿdī]** "Hastening" adds to mere doing: it is doing, initiating and completing.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The five attributes are set against their opposites, and the point of the verse is that these believers among the People of the Book are not like those of their number who command disbelief. **[Qurṭubī]** The "right" they command may be general or may be specifically following the Prophet. **[Ibn Kathīr]** These are the same type as those praised at 3:199. **[Jalālayn]** Some of the People of the Scripture are like this and some are not. **[Study Quran]** The identification of who is meant tracks the reading given to 3:113 and 3:110. **[Saʿdī]** The three attributes — belief, enjoining right and forbidding wrong, and hastening to good — are what distinguish the upright among them.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:113 for the community described; 3:115, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:110 for the connection with "you enjoin what is right"; 3:115, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:199 for the parallel at the end of the sūrah; 3:113 for the identification; 3:115, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:62 and 5:69 for the parallel content; 3:110 and 3:113 for the identification. **[Saʿdī]** 7:159, "and of the people of Moses is a community guiding by the truth and thereby doing justice"; 3:115, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:113 for the setting; 3:115, which follows.

**Reflection.** The five attributes are almost a formula, and the interest is in how each commentator tightens them. Al-Ṭabarī's handling of the first pair is characteristic: belief in God and the Last Day is not mere assent but affirming the resurrection and knowing that deeds are recompensed, and it is defined negatively too, against the idolaters who deny oneness, resurrection and recompense all at once **[Ṭabarī]**. Then he does something sharper with the second pair: enjoining right and forbidding wrong are not general moral exhortations here but specifically commanding faith in the Messenger and forbidding the belying of him — which is precisely what the Jews and Christians are said to do the opposite of **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī records both possibilities, the general and the specific, and then adds a small psychological gloss on "hasten": they do good without dragging behind, because they know the worth of the reward, or because they press forward before the deed is missed **[Qurṭubī]**. Al-Saʿdī's refinement is the nicest of them: hastening is *more* than doing, because it adds initiating and completing, with everything obligatory and recommended that perfects the act **[Saʿdī]**. And hanging over the whole verse is the question the Study Quran keeps returning to — whether these five attributes describe Muslims or the believers among the People of the Book — and its own answer is worth keeping: the plain sense is that the verse is addressed to Muslims unsure how to judge the People of the Book, telling them that God does not reject good deeds that are truly good **[Study Quran]**.

*Source note:* Saʿdī and Maʿārif each treat 3:113–114 (Maʿārif 3:113–117) as a single unit; their material on the two verses is cited at 3:113, and neither has anything separate for 3:114.

## 3:115 — وَمَا يَفْعَلُوا۟ مِنْ خَيْرٍۢ فَلَن يُكْفَرُوهُ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌۢ بِٱلْمُتَّقِينَ

*"And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it — and God knows the God-fearing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** The meaning of the verse is: they are not denied it; rather they are thanked for what they have done of that and generously rewarded for it. **[Ṭabarī]** As for "and God knows the God-fearing", He says, exalted is His remembrance: God has knowledge of whoever fears Him, by obeying Him and avoiding what He has forbidden, and He preserves their righteous deeds until He rewards them for them and recompenses them by them — as glad tidings from Him to them in the near life, and as an urging to them to hold fast to what they are upon of the sound traits of character He has approved for them. **[Jalālayn]** "And whatever good you do", O community — *tafʿalū*, "you do"; or if this is read *yafʿalū*, "they do", then it refers to them, the upright community — "you shall not be denied it"; read in both ways, *fa-lan tukfarūhu*, "you shall not be denied it", or *fa-lan yukfarūhu*, "they shall not be denied it" — you shall not be deprived of its reward, but you will be rewarded for it; "and God knows the God-fearing". **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning of the verse is: whatever good you do, you will not be denied its reward; rather you will be thanked for it and recompensed for it. *(Qurṭubī's block covers 3:112–115)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And whatever good they do, nothing will be rejected of them" — meaning, their good deeds will not be lost with God; rather, He will award them the best rewards. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "For Allah knows well the *muttaqīn*" — for no deed performed by any person ever escapes His knowledge, nor is any reward for those who do good deeds ever lost with Him. **[Saʿdī]** Then God, exalted is He, clarified that whatever good they do, little or much, God will accept it, where it proceeds from faith and sincerity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** "So they will not be denied it" — meaning, what they have done will not be disowned and will not be let go to waste; "and God knows the God-fearing" — and they are the ones who perform the good deeds and abandon the prohibitions, intending the pleasure of God and seeking His reward. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** Some understand "they will not be denied it" as a way of reassuring the former Jews who were grieved by the assertions of their former coreligionists, who said that their actions were futile now that they had abandoned Judaism and embraced Islam (IK, R). *(the Study Quran's note covers 3:114–115)* **[Study Quran]** Some read the verb here in the second person, giving the translation "you will not be denied it" (Q, Ṭ).

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verb is read *yafʿalū* (third person, about the upright community) or *tafʿalū* (second person, addressing the believers), and likewise *yukfarūhu* or *tukfarūhu*. **[Jalālayn]** Both readings of each verb are given, with the referent shifting accordingly. **[Qurṭubī]** The two readings are distributed among the readers, as set out below.

**Readings.** **[Ṭabarī]** The readers differed over the reading of this. The generality of the readers of Kufa read "and whatever good they do, they will not be denied it" (*wa-mā yafʿalū min khayrin fa-lan yukfarūhu*), with *yāʾ* in both, referring back to the description of the people whom He, exalted is His praise, described as enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** The generality of the readers of Madīnah and the Ḥijāz, and some of the readers of Kufa, read both with *tāʾ*: "and whatever good you do, you will not be denied it" (*wa-mā tafʿalū min khayrin fa-lan tukfarūhu*) — meaning, whatever good you do, O believers, your Lord will not deny you it. **[Ṭabarī]** And some readers of Baṣra considered both readings permissible in it, with *yāʾ* and with *tāʾ*, in both words. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own choice: the correct reading in our view is "and whatever good they do, they will not be denied it", with *yāʾ* in both words, meaning thereby the report about the upright community who recite the signs of God. **[Ṭabarī]** We have chosen that because the verses before this one are a report about them; so joining this verse to the meanings of the verses before it — since there is in it no indication pointing to a turning away from their description — is sounder than diverting it from the meanings of what precedes it. And Ibn ʿAbbās used to read it according to the reading we have chosen. **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Aʿmash, Ibn Waththāb, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ and Khalaf read both with *yāʾ*, as a report about the upright community — and it is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and the choice of Abū ʿUbayd. **[Qurṭubī]** The rest read both with *tāʾ*, as address, because of His saying "you were the best community brought forth for mankind" (3:110) — and it is the choice of Abū Ḥātim; and Abū ʿAmr used to consider both readings, *yāʾ* and *tāʾ*, permissible.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7664 — Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ said: "It has reached me that Ibn ʿAbbās used to read them both with *yāʾ*." **[Ṭabarī]** 7665 — Qatāda, on "and whatever good you do, you will not be denied it": "It will not be lost from you"; and 7666 — al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, the same. **[Qurṭubī]** The reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and adopted by Abū ʿUbayd, against the choice of Abū Ḥātim. *(cited above)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** The reassurance to the former Jews grieved by the taunts of their former coreligionists. *(the Study Quran attributes this reading to IK)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is a promise that the good of the upright community is thanked and generously rewarded, and that God's knowledge preserves the deeds of the God-fearing until He recompenses them. **[Saʿdī]** Acceptance is conditional on the deed proceeding from faith and sincerity. **[Ibn Kathīr]** No deed escapes God's knowledge and no reward for good is ever lost with Him. **[Study Quran]** The reassurance is read by some as directed at those who had left Judaism for Islam and were told their earlier good was futile. **[Jalālayn]** On either reading, the reward is not withheld.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:113–114 for the people described; 3:116, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:110 for the argument from "you were the best community"; 3:116, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:113–114 for the upright community; 3:116, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:113–114 for the deeds in question; 3:116, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:113–114 for the setting; 3:116, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 3:110 and 3:113 for the identification of who is addressed; 2:62 and 5:69 for the parallel content.

**Reflection.** A great deal turns on one letter. Read *yafʿalū*, the verse continues the description of the upright community of 3:113 — "whatever good *they* do"; read *tafʿalū*, it turns to address the Muslim community directly — "whatever good *you* do" **[Ṭabarī]**. Ṭabarī's argument for the first is a principle of interpretation rather than a point of grammar: the verses before are a report about them, and there is no indication of a shift, so the verse should be joined to what precedes **[Ṭabarī]**. Qurṭubī distributes the readings among the readers and notes that Abū Ḥātim preferred the *tāʾ* precisely because of 3:110's "you were the best community" — the same word, the same addressee — while Abū ʿAmr simply allowed both **[Qurṭubī]**. What the dispute exposes is a substantive question that the Study Quran puts plainly: are these verses about Muslims, or about the People of the Book who believed **[Study Quran]**? And the answer matters pastorally, because one of the oldest readings of the verse — which the Study Quran attributes to Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī — is that it was sent down to reassure former Jews who had been told by their old community that everything they had done before was now worthless **[Study Quran]**. Al-Saʿdī's condition is the one that settles it in practice: God accepts whatever good is done, little or much, *where it proceeds from faith and sincerity* **[Saʿdī]**.

*Source note:* The Study Quran has no separate block for 3:115 — its combined note for 3:114–115 is cited at 3:114; and Maʿārif treats 3:113–117 as a single unit whose discussion is cited at 3:113, with nothing separate for 3:115.

## 3:116 — إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ لَن تُغْنِىَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَٰلُهُمْ وَلَآ أَوْلَٰدُهُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ شَيْـًۭٔا ۖ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ أَصْحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِ ۖ هُمْ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ

*"Truly those who disbelieve — neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against God; and those are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** This is a threat from God, mighty and majestic, to the other, iniquitous party among the People of the Book — those of whom He has informed that they are iniquitous and that they have incurred anger from Him — and to whoever is their like among the people of disbelief in God and His messenger and in what Muḥammad ﷺ brought from God. **[Ṭabarī]** He says, exalted is His remembrance: "truly those who disbelieve" — meaning those who deny the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ and belie him and what he has brought them from God — "their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against God", meaning: the wealth he amassed in this world and the children he raised in it will not push back anything of God's punishment on the Day of Resurrection, if He defers it for them to that Day, nor in this world if He hastens it for them there. **[Ṭabarī]** He singled out his children and his wealth because a man's children are the nearest of his kinsfolk to him, and he has more power over his own wealth than over the wealth of another. **[Ṭabarī]** Then He informed, exalted is His praise, that they are the people of the Fire by His saying "and those are the inhabitants of the Fire" — and He made them its *companions* because they are its people, who do not leave it and do not part from it, like a man's companion who does not part from him and his intimate who does not leave him. Then He confirmed that by His informing that they are "abiding therein" — that their companionship of it is a companionship with no breaking off, since there are among things those that part from their companion in some states and leave him at some times, whereas the companionship of those who disbelieved with the Fire which they are made to broil in is not like that: it is a lasting companionship with no end and no severance. We seek refuge in God from it and from whatever of word or deed draws near to it. **[Jalālayn]** "As for the disbelievers", from among them, "their riches shall not avail", protect, "them neither their children against God", that is, against His chastisement — these two are singled out for mention because a person usually avails himself either by paying a ransom or by resorting to the help of his children; "those are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein". **[Qurṭubī]** "Truly those who disbelieve" is the noun of *inna*, and the predicate is "their wealth and their children will not avail them anything against God". **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil said: when He mentioned the believers among the People of the Book, He mentioned their disbelievers, and that is His saying "truly those who disbelieve". And al-Kalbī said: He made this a fresh opening, and said: truly those who disbelieve, their abundance of wealth and their abundance of children will not avail them anything of the punishment of God; and He singled out children because they are the nearest of their kinsfolk to them. **[Qurṭubī]** "And those are the inhabitants of the Fire" — subject and predicate; and likewise "they abide therein". And all of this has already been dealt with. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Surely, those who disbelieve, neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them against Allah" — meaning, nothing can avert Allah's torment and punishment from striking them; "They are the dwellers of the Fire, therein they will abide." *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Saʿdī]** God, exalted is He, clarified that for the disbelievers who disbelieve in the signs of God and belied His messengers, no rescuer will rescue them from the punishment of God, nothing beneficial will benefit them, and no intercessor will intercede for them with God. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:116–117)* **[Saʿdī]** And that their wealth and their children, which they used to prepare for hardships and calamities, will not avail them anything. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Soon after praising those who had embraced Islam from among the People of the Book, the text censures those of them who did not embrace Islam and insisted on retaining their stance of disbelief, not realizing that their wealth and their children will be unable to save them from the punishment of Allah, and that Hell shall be their eternal abode. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Study Quran]** Some note that wealth and children are thought to be the most dependable and beneficial goods in life, but they will nevertheless be of no use to anyone in the Hereafter (R). Elsewhere the Quran states that wealth and children will not avail save for him who comes to God with a sound heart (26:89). Possessing wealth and children deludes the disbeliever into a sense of security and superiority simply because he possesses wealth and children (68:14), a theme also developed in 34:35–37, where the positive dimension of wealth and children is mentioned. See also 9:85; 17:64; 18:46; 19:77; 23:55; 71:21.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** "Inhabitants" (*aṣḥāb*) is not incidental: Ṭabarī explains it as companionship that never breaks off, and notes that other things do part from their companion at times. **[Jalālayn]** The two things named — wealth and children — are named because these are the two means by which a person normally saves himself: ransom, or the help of his children. **[Qurṭubī]** Grammatically, "truly" takes "their wealth will not avail them" as its predicate; "and those are the inhabitants of the Fire" is a fresh subject and predicate. **[Ṭabarī]** The reason wealth and children are singled out: a man's children are his nearest kin, and his wealth is what he most commands.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse is addressed first to the iniquitous party among the People of the Book and then, by extension, to everyone like them in disbelief. **[Qurṭubī]** Muqātil reads it as the counterpart to the praise of the believers among them; al-Kalbī reads it as a fresh opening about disbelievers generally. **[Maʿārif]** The censure is of those among the People of the Book who refused to embrace Islam and did not realize that wealth and children cannot save them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Nothing can avert God's torment from striking them, and their abiding in the Fire is unending. **[Study Quran]** Wealth and children are the goods in which people place their trust, and the Qurʾān insists they are of no avail in the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]** No rescuer, no benefit and no intercessor remains to them.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:112 for the iniquitous party; 3:113 for the believers among them; 3:117, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:113 for the praise that precedes; 3:117, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:113–115 for the upright community; 3:117, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 26:89 for "save him who comes to God with a sound heart"; 68:14 for the delusion of security; 34:35–37 for the positive dimension of wealth and children; 9:85, 17:64, 18:46, 19:77, 23:55 and 71:21 for the same theme. **[Maʿārif]** 3:113 for the praise; 3:117, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:117, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:113 for "some of them"; 3:117, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse turns the page back from the upright community of 3:113–115 to the other party, and al-Ṭabarī makes the structure explicit: this is a threat to "the other, iniquitous party among the People of the Book", and then to everyone like them **[Ṭabarī]**. The two things named are chosen with precision — wealth and children — and the reason given is worth sitting with: they are the two means by which a person normally saves himself, either by paying a ransom out of his property or by calling on his children **[Jalālayn]**, **[Ṭabarī]**. That is why their failure is the point. Then there is the word *aṣḥāb*, "inhabitants" or "companions", which Ṭabarī dwells on at some length: a companion is someone who does not part from you, and most things do part from their companion at some time, but not the Fire and those who are made to broil in it **[Ṭabarī]**. It is a grim little piece of lexicography, and it is doing the work that "abiding" does in the next clause. The Study Quran's framing is broader and useful: wealth and children are simply the goods in which human beings place their trust, and the Qurʾān keeps insisting — here and at 26:89, 68:14, 34:35–37 and a dozen other places — that they are not available currency in the Hereafter **[Study Quran]**. Muqātil and al-Kalbī differ over whether the sentence continues the preceding passage or opens a new one, and the difference is not trivial: on Muqātil's reading the disbelievers in view are specifically the unbelievers among the People of the Book, on al-Kalbī's they are disbelievers generally **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:117 — مَثَلُ مَا يُنفِقُونَ فِى هَٰذِهِ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا كَمَثَلِ رِيحٍۢ فِيهَا صِرٌّ أَصَابَتْ حَرْثَ قَوْمٍۢ ظَلَمُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُمْ فَأَهْلَكَتْهُ ۚ وَمَا ظَلَمَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَلَٰكِنْ أَنفُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ

*"The likeness of what they spend in the life of this world is as the likeness of a wind wherein is a biting cold that smote the tillage of a people who wronged themselves, and destroyed it. God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His praise, means by this: the likeness of what the disbelievers spend — that is, the likeness of what the disbeliever gives in charity of his wealth, giving it to whomever he gives it by way of seeking nearness to his Lord, while he is a denier of the oneness of God and a belier of Muḥammad ﷺ — in that it does not benefit him given his disbelief, and perishes at the moment of his need for it, gone after the benefit he had hoped would return to him from it — is as the likeness of a wind in which is intense cold, which struck "the tillage of a people", meaning the crop of a people who had hoped to reach it and hoped for its yield and the benefit returning from it, "who wronged themselves", meaning the owners of the crop, who disobeyed God and transgressed His limits, "and destroyed it", meaning the wind in which is the *ṣirr* destroyed that crop of theirs, after the hope they had in it and their expectation of benefit from it. **[Ṭabarī]** He says, exalted is His remembrance: so did God do with these disbelievers — He nullified the reward of their deeds and voided their wages, not as a wrong from Him to them, but the disbeliever is the one who wrongs himself, by earning for it, through his disobedience of God and his opposing His command, that which brings him into the fire of Jahannam and makes him broil in the blaze of Saqar. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī's own description of the *ṣirr*: it is the intensity of cold, that being with a gusting of the north wind in a whirl of dew and moisture, on a dark morning following a clear night. **[Jalālayn]** "The likeness", the description, "of what they", the disbelievers, "expend in the life of this world" in the way of enmity towards the Prophet, or in the way of voluntary almsgiving or the like, "is as the likeness of a wind wherein is a blast", of extreme heat or cold, "that smote the tillage", the crops, "of a people who have wronged themselves" through unbelief and disobedience, "and destroyed it", so that they could not profit from it; so it is with what they expend — it perishes and they profit nothing from it. "God did not wrong them" when they lost what they expended, "but they wronged themselves" through unbelief, which necessitated this loss. **[Qurṭubī]** "Like the likeness of a wind" — that is, like the blowing of a wind. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the *ṣirr* is intense cold. It is said that its root is from *ṣarīr*, which is sound — the sound of the violent wind. Al-Zajjāj said: it is the sound of the flame of the fire that was in that wind. **[Qurṭubī]** And in the ḥadīth: he forbade the locusts killed by the *ṣirr* — the *ṣirr* in that ḥadīth being the cold. **[Qurṭubī]** The meaning of the verse: the likeness of the expenditure of the disbelievers, in its nullity, its perishing and the absence of any benefit in it, is like a crop struck by a cold wind or a fire, which burned it and destroyed it, so that its owners derived no benefit at all after they had hoped for its benefit and use. **[Qurṭubī]** "God did not wrong them by that — but they wrong themselves" — by disbelief, disobedience and withholding the right of God, exalted is He. And it is said: they wronged themselves by sowing at other than the time of sowing, or in other than its place, so God disciplined them for putting the thing in other than its place — reported by al-Mahdawī. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allah gave a parable for what the disbelievers spend in this life, as Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "A wind of *ṣirr*" — a frigid wind, as Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ bin Anas and others have said. ʿAṭāʾ said that *ṣirr* means cold and snow. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid are also reported to have said that *ṣirr* means fire. This latter meaning does not contradict the meanings mentioned above, because extreme cold weather, especially when accompanied by snow, burns plants and produce, and has the same effect fire has on such growth. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "It struck the harvest of a people who did wrong against themselves and destroyed it" — by burning. This verse mentions a calamity that strikes produce that is ready to harvest, destroying it by burning and depriving its owner of it when he needs it the most. Such is the case with the disbelievers, for Allah destroys the rewards for their good deeds in this life, just as He destroyed the produce of the sinner because of his sins. Both types did not build their work on firm foundations. **[Saʿdī]** Their expenditures which they spent in the world to support their falsehood will vanish; "and the likeness of it is like" a crop which "a severe wind" struck, "in which is *ṣirr*" — that is, intense cold or a burning fire — "and it destroyed that crop, and that by their wrongdoing; so God did not wrong them and punish them without sin, but they wronged themselves." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:116–117)* **[Saʿdī]** And this is like His saying, exalted is He: "Those who disbelieve spend their wealth to bar from the way of God; they will spend it, then it will become a regret for them, then they will be overcome." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Verse 117 declares through a similitude that disbelievers simply waste what they spend in this worldly life, for belief in Islam is a pre-condition in order that such spendings be acceptable with Allah, of whatever sort they may be. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Maʿārif's block covers 3:113–117)* **[Maʿārif]** The similitude stresses the fact that disbelievers inflict this injustice upon themselves when their spendings go to waste in this world and remain rewardless in the Hereafter. If they were not to wrong themselves — if they were to embrace Islam — they would have been like other Muslims who, on suffering a worldly loss, are compensated by Allah through reward and forgiveness of sins, as reported in aḥādīth. **(Bayān al-Qurʾān)** **[Study Quran]** Other verses invoke the wind's destructive power in order to describe how unrooted and sterile the actions of disbelievers are in this life. In this verse the wind is cold, while in 2:266 it burns, and in 14:18 the deeds of disbelievers are already ashes waiting to be blown away. Verses involving the nourishing dimension of wind include 7:57; 25:48; 30:46; 35:9. The wronging of oneself is mentioned numerous times in the Quran (3:135; 4:97; 9:70; 16:33; 29:40; 30:9; 34:19; 35:32; 37:113).

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** "What" (*mā*) may be a *maṣdar*, or a relative pronoun with the resumptive pronoun elided — "the likeness of what they spend it". "Like the likeness of a wind" is elliptical for "like the blowing of a wind". **[Ṭabarī]** *Ṣirr* is described as intense cold with a gusting of the north wind in a whirl of dew and moisture, on a dark morning after a clear night. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The two reported meanings of *ṣirr* — intense cold, and fire — are reconciled by the fact that extreme cold burns plants as fire does. **[Qurṭubī]** The root is said to be *ṣarīr*, sound — the sound of the violent wind, or, per al-Zajjāj, of the flame within it. **[Jalālayn]** The blast may be of extreme heat or extreme cold.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7667 — Mujāhid, on "the likeness of what they spend in the life of this world": "the disbeliever's expenditure in this world". **[Ṭabarī]** 7668 — al-Suddī: rather it is what he says with his tongue that his heart does not affirm — "the likeness of what he says, which is not accepted from him, is like this crop when the wrongdoing people sowed it and a wind with a *ṣirr* struck it and destroyed it; likewise they spent, and their idolatry destroyed them." Ṭabarī notes that he has already explained which of the two readings is sounder. **[Ṭabarī]** 7669 — ʿIkrima: "a wind wherein is a *ṣirr*" — intense cold. **[Ṭabarī]** 7670 — Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "intense cold and *zamharīr*"; 7671 — Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī: "cold"; 7672 — Ibn ʿAbbās, through Hārūn b. ʿAntara from his father: "cold". **[Ṭabarī]** 7673 — Qatāda: "intense cold"; 7674 — al-Rabīʿ, the same; 7675 — al-Suddī: "intense cold"; 7676 — Ibn ʿAbbās: "a wind wherein is cold". **[Ṭabarī]** 7677 — Ibn Zayd: "cold, which destroyed their crop" — and he said: the Arabs call it *al-ḍarīb*; the wind comes cold and in the morning it is *ḍarīb*, having burned the crop, and they say "it was struck tonight". **[Ṭabarī]** 7678 — al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "a wind wherein is cold". **[Qurṭubī]** In the ḥadīth: he forbade the locusts killed by the *ṣirr* — the *ṣirr* in that ḥadīth being the cold. **[Ibn Kathīr]** ʿAṭāʾ said that *ṣirr* means cold and snow; and Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid are also reported to have said that it means fire.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The nullification of the disbelievers' deeds is not a wrong from God but a self-wronging: the disbeliever earns through disobedience what brings him into the Fire. **[Maʿārif]** Belief in Islam is the pre-condition for any spending to be acceptable, whatever sort it is; and had they embraced Islam, even a worldly loss would have been compensated by reward and forgiveness. **[Qurṭubī]** On one report the wronging consisted in sowing at the wrong time or in the wrong place, and God disciplined them for putting a thing where it does not belong. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Both the disbelievers and the owners of the ruined crop failed to build their work on firm foundations. **[Saʿdī]** The point is that God did not punish them without sin. **[Study Quran]** The parable belongs to a family of wind-parables describing the sterility of the disbelievers' actions.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:116 for "those who disbelieve"; 3:118, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:116 for those whose spending is meant; 2:266 for the burning wind; 3:118, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 2:266 for the burning wind; 3:116 for the disbelievers; 3:118, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:266 for the burning wind; 14:18 for the deeds as ashes; 7:57, 25:48, 30:46 and 35:9 for the nourishing wind; 3:135, 4:97, 9:70, 16:33, 29:40, 30:9, 34:19, 35:32 and 37:113 for the wronging of oneself. **[Saʿdī]** 8:36, "those who disbelieve spend their wealth to bar from the way of God"; 3:118, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:116 for the spenders; 3:118, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:116 for the disbelievers; 3:118, which follows.

**Reflection.** The image is agricultural and specific: a crop that is *ready*, struck the morning after a clear night, destroyed at the very moment its owners were counting on it **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The commentators are careful about the word *ṣirr*. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ all say it is intense cold; ʿAṭāʾ says cold and snow; and Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid are also reported to have said it means fire **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The reconciliation is neat — extreme cold burns plants exactly as fire does — and it is worth noting that Ṭabarī describes the phenomenon from observation: a gusting of the north wind, a whirl of dew, a dark morning after a clear night **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Zayd adds the dialect word, *al-ḍarīb*, and the saying "it was struck tonight" **[Ṭabarī]**. Then there is a small disagreement about what is being spent: Mujāhid says it is the disbeliever's actual expenditure, and al-Suddī says it is rather what he says with his tongue and does not affirm in his heart, which is not accepted from him **[Ṭabarī]**. Al-Mahdawī's reported reading, through Qurṭubī, is the most interesting variant: the crop was ruined because they sowed at the wrong time or in the wrong place, and God disciplined them for putting a thing where it did not belong **[Qurṭubī]**. Maʿārif's conclusion is the one that gives the parable its edge — belief is the pre-condition for any spending to be acceptable, and had they embraced Islam even a worldly loss would have been turned into reward and forgiveness **[Maʿārif]**. And the closing clause is doing quiet theological work again: God did not wrong them; they wronged themselves, which is the same claim the sūrah made at 3:108 and will make again about Ṣabr and Taqwā at 3:120 **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Saʿdī]**.

## 3:118 — يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَتَّخِذُوا۟ بِطَانَةًۭ مِّن دُونِكُمْ لَا يَأْلُونَكُمْ خَبَالًۭا وَدُّوا۟ مَا عَنِتُّمْ قَدْ بَدَتِ ٱلْبَغْضَآءُ مِنْ أَفْوَٰهِهِمْ وَمَا تُخْفِى صُدُورُهُمْ أَكْبَرُ ۚ قَدْ بَيَّنَّا لَكُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ ۖ إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ

*"O you who believe, do not take as intimates any apart from yourselves; they spare nothing to ruin you. They wish you to suffer. Hatred has appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater. We have made clear to you the signs, if you understand."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His remembrance, means by this: O you who have affirmed God and His messenger and acknowledged what their prophet brought them from their Lord, "do not take as intimates any apart from yourselves" — He says: do not take for yourselves patrons and friends "apart from yourselves", meaning apart from the people of your religion and your community, that is, other than the believers. **[Ṭabarī]** He only made "the intimate" (*al-biṭānah*) a simile for a man's close friend, likening him to the garment that is next to his belly, because of his occupying — in his access to his secrets and to what he hides from strangers and from many of his relatives — the place of the garment that is next to his body. **[Ṭabarī]** So God forbade the believers in Him to take friends and confidants from the disbelievers in Him; then He made them know what they harbour for them of deceit and betrayal, and their seeking harm for them, and warned them thereby against them and against close friendship with them. **[Ṭabarī]** On "they spare nothing to ruin you" (*lā yaʾlūnakum khabālan*): some said its meaning is "they wish that you go astray from your religion" (al-Suddī), and others "in your religion — meaning they wish that you suffer hardship in your religion" (Ibn Jurayj). **[Ṭabarī]** And Ṭabarī raises the grammatical question: how is it that He said "they wish what you suffer" (*waddū mā ʿanittum*), bringing the report about the intimates in the past tense in the position of a circumstantial clause, after the report was complete — when circumstantial clauses take only the form of nouns and of future verbs? **[Ṭabarī]** On "hatred has appeared from their mouths": Ṭabarī records the report of Qatāda that it means "hatred has appeared from the mouths of the hypocrites to their brothers among the disbelievers, from their deceit toward Islam and its people and their hatred of them" — and then rejects it: this saying has no meaning, for God only forbade the believers to take as intimates those whom they already knew to be deceitful toward Islam and its people and full of hatred, whether by clear indications pointing to that being their attribute or by their manifesting it. **[Ṭabarī]** "And what their breasts conceal is greater" — greater than what they have disclosed with their tongues (Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ). **[Ṭabarī]** "We have made clear to you the signs" — "the signs" meaning the lessons (*al-ʿibar*). **[Jalālayn]** "O you who believe, do not take as intimates", as sincere friends, revealing to them your secret thoughts, "anyone apart from yourselves", from among the Jews, Christians and hypocrites; "such men spare nothing to ruin you" — *khabālan* is in the accusative because the preposition that usually precedes it, i.e. *fī'l-khabāl*, has been omitted — that is to say, they would not be remiss about corrupting you; "they would love", they wish for, "you to suffer" — *al-ʿanat* means extreme hardship. "Hatred", enmity towards you, "is revealed", is manifested, "by their mouths", by sowing discord among you and informing the idolaters of your secret plans; "and what their breasts conceal" of enmity "is yet greater. Now We have made clear to you the signs" of their enmity; "if you understand" this, then do not befriend them. **[Qurṭubī]** First: God, exalted is He, confirmed the rebuke against inclining to the disbelievers, and it is connected to what preceded in His saying "if you obey a party of those who have been given the Scripture, they will turn you back, after your faith, disbelievers" (3:100). *(Qurṭubī's block on 3:118 treats six questions)* **[Qurṭubī]** The *biṭānah* is a *maṣdar* by which one and many are named; a man's *biṭānah* are his special people who are privy to his affair; and its root is from the belly (*al-baṭn*) which is the opposite of the back (*al-ẓahr*). One says *baṭana fulānun bi-fulānin*, when he is special to him. And the poet said: "Those are my sincere ones, yes, and my intimate ones, and they are my repository of secrets above every kinsman." **[Qurṭubī]** Second: by this verse God forbade the believers to take from the disbelievers, the Jews and the people of caprice, "incomers" and "insiders" — discussing opinions with them and entrusting their affairs to them. And it is said: everyone who is opposed to your way and your religion, you should not converse with him. The poet said: "Ask not about the man — ask about his companion, for every companion follows the one he accompanies." **[Qurṭubī]** And in the *Sunan* of Abū Dāwūd, from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ: "A man is upon the religion of his close friend, so let one of you look to whom he befriends." And it is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: "Judge people by their brothers." **[Qurṭubī]** Then He clarified the meaning for which He forbade close association, and said "they spare nothing to ruin you" — meaning corruption; that is, they do not spare effort in your corruption — meaning that even if they do not fight you outwardly, they do not spare effort in scheming and deception. **[Qurṭubī]** Third: "apart from yourselves" means other than you. Al-Farrāʾ said: "and they do deeds other than that" means besides that; and it is said that "apart from yourselves" means in conduct and in the goodness of one's way. And the meaning of "they spare nothing to ruin you" is: they do not fall short in what brings corruption upon you, and it stands in the position of an adjective qualifying "an intimate other than yourselves". One says *lā ālū juhdan* — I do not fall short. And Imruʾ al-Qays said: "And a man, so long as the last breath of his soul remains, will not attain the ends of affairs, nor fall short." **[Qurṭubī]** And *al-khabāl* is *al-khabl*, and *al-khabl* is corruption — and that may be in deeds, in bodies and in minds. And in the ḥadīth: "whoever is afflicted with blood or *khabl*" — meaning a wound that ruins the limb. *Al-khabl* is the corruption of the limbs; a man is *khabl* and *mukhtabal*; and "love corrupted him" (*khabalahu al-ḥubbu*) means it ruined him. Aws said: "Sons of Lubaynā, you are not a hand — except a hand whose upper arm is corrupt", meaning ruined. And al-Farrāʾ recited: "Ibn Saʿd looked a look and rose with it — there was for your companions and the mounts corruption." And *khabālan* is in the accusative as the second object, because *alā* takes two objects; or, if you wish, as a *maṣdar*, i.e. "they corrupt you with corruption"; or, if you wish, by the removal of the preposition, i.e. "with corruption", as when they say "I hurt him with a beating". And *mā* in "they wish what you suffer" is a *maṣdar* — i.e., they wish your suffering, meaning what is hard upon you; and *al-ʿanat* is hardship. **[Qurṭubī]** Fourth: "hatred has appeared from their mouths" — meaning enmity and your being belied has appeared from their mouths. *Al-baghḍāʾ* is *al-bughḍ*, the opposite of love, and it is a feminine *maṣdar*. And He singled out mouths for mention rather than tongues to point to their gaping and chattering in these sayings of theirs, for they are worse than the one who conceals it whose hatred shows in his eyes. And from this meaning is his prohibition, peace be upon him, that a man should open his mouth wide against his brother's honour. **[Qurṭubī]** And no argument by implication is to be understood from this ḥadīth permitting one to take someone's honour in a whisper, for that is forbidden by the agreement of the scholars; and in the revelation "and do not backbite one another" (49:12), and he ﷺ said: "Your blood, your property and your honour are sacred to you." The mention of gaping is only a pointer to garrulity and effusiveness, so know that. **[Qurṭubī]** Fifth: in this verse is evidence that the testimony of an enemy against his enemy is not permissible — and with that said the people of Madīnah and the people of the Ḥijāz, while permission for that is narrated from Abū Ḥanīfa. And Ibn Baṭṭāl related from Ibn Shaʿbān that he said: the scholars are agreed that the testimony of an enemy against his enemy is not permissible in anything, even if he is upright — and enmity removes uprightness, so how much more the enmity of a disbeliever. **[Qurṭubī]** Sixth: "and what their breasts conceal is greater" — a report and information that they harbour more hatred than they disclose with their mouths. And ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd recited "hatred has *appeared*" with the verb in the masculine, since *al-baghḍāʾ* has the sense of *al-bughḍ*. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God forbids His believing servants from taking the hypocrites as allies, so that the hypocrites do not have the opportunity to expose the secrets of the believers and their plans against their enemies. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:118–120)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** The hypocrites try their very best to confuse, oppose and harm the believers any way they can, and by using any wicked, evil means at their disposal; they wish the very worst and most difficult conditions for the believers. "Take not as your *biṭānah* those other than your own" refers to taking followers of other religions as consultants and allies, for advisors of a certain person have access to his most secret affairs. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, but what their breasts conceal is far worse" — meaning, enmity appears on their faces and in what they sometimes utter, as well as the enmity they have against Islam and its people in their hearts. Since this fact is apparent to every person who has sound comprehension, therefore "Indeed We have made plain to you the signs, if you understand". **[Saʿdī]** This is a warning from God to His servants against the friendship of the disbelievers and taking them as *biṭānah*, as confidants and friends, to whom they confide and disclose the secrets of the believers. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:118–119)* **[Saʿdī]** So He clarified to His believing servants the things that make it necessary to disown taking them as intimates: that they "spare no effort to ruin you" — that is, they are eager and unstinting in bringing harm to you; and hatred has appeared from their speech and the slips of their tongues; and what their breasts conceal of hatred and enmity is "greater" than what has appeared to you of their words and deeds. So if you have understandings and minds, God has made their affair clear to you. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** There were Jewish settlements around Madīnah with old friendly ties to the tribes of Aws and Khazraj; individuals from these tribes were also on friendly terms with individuals from the Jewish settlements, and in their tribal capacity Aws and Khazraj were their neighbours and allies. When these two tribes embraced Islam they continued to maintain their old ties with them. But the Jews were so hostile to the Holy Prophet ﷺ and to the religion he brought that they were unwilling to be sincere and loving to anyone who had said yes to the prophetic call; so outwardly they went along with the old relationships, but inwardly they had turned into their enemies, and the apparent friendship they allowed to remain became their cover for fomenting trouble among the Muslims and for finding out their organizational secrets and passing them on to the enemies. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The word *biṭānah* used here means a friend, a confidant, one with whom secrets are shared. The lining or inside part of a dress which stays close to the body is also known as *biṭānah*; derived from *baṭn* (inside), it is used for everything opposed to *ẓahr* (outside) — that which is outside is *ẓahr* and that which is inside is *baṭn*. In garments, the outer part is *zihārah* and the inner part touching the body, such as a lining, is called *biṭānah* — and there is an expression in English, "hand in glove", which comes close to this sense. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The well-known and quite reliable lexicon of Arabic, *Lisān al-ʿArab*, explains *biṭānah* as meaning that a person's *biṭānah* is one who knows his secrets and has access to his affairs in which he seeks his advice; and al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī in his *Mufradāt* and al-Qurṭubī in his *Tafsīr* have given the same meaning. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** So it has been enjoined upon Muslims through this verse that they should not take persons other than those from their own community as confidants and advisers, in a way that leads one into spilling the sensitive secrets of one's own government, community or state. No doubt, under the shade of its universal mercy, Islam has given unusual instructions to Muslims in order that they treat non-Muslims with compassion, goodwill, beneficence, kindliness and tolerance — and not leaving it at that, the Holy Prophet ﷺ put these into actual practice in all affairs concerning non-Muslims. But, at the same time and in perfect wisdom, binding instructions were given so as to make sure that the organized body of Muslims and its particular hallmarks stay protected. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Study Quran]** "Intimates" renders *biṭānah*, meaning confidants or trusted friends, denoting both the singular and the plural; it also literally means the inner lining of a garment, evoking a sense of direct closeness and intimacy. They are those to whom one tells one's secrets (Ṭ). **[Study Quran]** "They will not stint you in corruption" means that when it comes to the act of corruption, they will not be miserly in providing that corruption. This is interpreted by some commentators to mean that in certain important matters pertaining to the affairs of Muslims, such as writing contracts or sending significant messages, one should not rely on non-Muslims (IK, Q); in this vein al-Qurṭubī bemoans the fact that in his day Muslims were relying on Jews and Christians as scribes and secretaries, although this is a reflection of the society of his day. **[Study Quran]** Others seem to interpret this as a statement on human nature in general, mentioning a ḥadīth that states, "God has sent no prophet, nor appointed any vicegerent, save that he had two groups of intimates. One group enjoins and encourages what is right while the other enjoins and encourages what is evil. He is protected who is protected by God," which is interpreted to mean that God will protect whom He will from the evil promptings of those who are close to them.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** The *biṭānah* is a simile drawn from the garment closest to the body, because the confidant occupies, with respect to secrets, the place that the inner garment occupies with respect to the skin. **[Qurṭubī]** It is a *maṣdar* used of one and many, derived from *baṭn* as opposed to *ẓahr*. **[Maʿārif]** The metaphor runs from the inner lining of a garment, and *Lisān al-ʿArab*, al-Rāghib and al-Qurṭubī all give "one who knows a man's secrets" as the sense. **[Qurṭubī]** *Khabālan* is in the accusative either as the second object of *alā*, or as a *maṣdar*, or by removal of the preposition. **[Ṭabarī]** Ṭabarī raises the grammatical difficulty in "they wish what you suffer" — a past-tense verb standing where a circumstantial clause would normally be a noun or a future verb. **[Jalālayn]** *Khabālan* is accusative through the suppression of the preposition. **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-baghḍāʾ* is a feminine *maṣdar*, and mouths are mentioned rather than tongues to indicate gaping and chattering.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7679 — the ḥadīth "whoever is afflicted with blood or *khabl* (injury)", related by Aḥmad in his *Musnad* (4:31) and al-Bayhaqī in the *Sunan* (8:53), from Abū Shurayḥ al-Khuzāʿī: "Whoever is afflicted with blood or *khabl* — *al-khabl* being wounds — has the choice of one of three: either he retaliates, or he takes the blood-money, or he pardons; and if he wants a fourth, then restrain his hand; and if he does any of that and then transgresses afterwards and kills, then the Fire is his, abiding therein forever." *Blood* here means the killing of a person, and *khabl* or *jirāḥ* the cutting off of a limb. **[Ṭabarī]** 7680 — Ibn ʿAbbās, through Muḥammad b. Isḥāq: "There were men among the Muslims who kept up relations with men among the Jews, because of the neighbourliness and alliance that had been between them in the Jāhiliyyah; so God, exalted is He, revealed concerning them, forbidding them from taking them as intimates, for fear of trial upon them from them: 'O you who believe, do not take as intimates any apart from yourselves', up to His saying 'and you believe in the Book entire'." *(Sīrat Ibn Hishām 2:207)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7681 — Mujāhid: it is about the hypocrites of Madīnah; God forbade the believers to take them as allies. **[Ṭabarī]** 7682 — Qatāda: God forbade the believers to take the hypocrites as intimates, or to befriend them, or to take them as allies instead of the believers. **[Ṭabarī]** 7683 — Ibn ʿAbbās: "they are the hypocrites"; 7684 — al-Rabīʿ, the same as Qatāda; 7686 — al-Suddī: the *biṭānah* are the hypocrites; 7687 — Ibn Jurayj: a believer must not take a hypocrite as an intimate in place of his brother; 7688 — Ibn Zayd: these are the hypocrites, and he recited "hatred has appeared from their mouths". **[Ṭabarī]** 7685 — Anas b. Mālik said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not seek light by the fire of the idolaters, and do not engrave on your signets in Arabic." He said: we did not know what that meant until they went to al-Ḥasan and asked him, and he said: yes — as for his saying "do not engrave on your signets in Arabic", he is saying: do not engrave "Muḥammad" on your signets; and as for his saying "do not seek light by the fire of the idolaters", he means the idolaters, saying: do not consult them in anything of your affairs. Al-Ḥasan said: and the confirmation of that is in the Book of God, then he recited this verse. **[Ṭabarī]** 7689 — al-Suddī, on "they wish what you suffer": "they wish that you go astray"; 7690 — Ibn Jurayj: "in your religion — meaning they wish that you suffer hardship in your religion". **[Ṭabarī]** 7691 — Qatāda, on "hatred has appeared from their mouths": "hatred has appeared from the mouths of the hypocrites to their brothers among the disbelievers, from their deceit toward Islam and its people and their hatred of them" — a reading Ṭabarī rejects, as set out above; 7692 — al-Rabīʿ: "from the mouths of the hypocrites". **[Ṭabarī]** 7693 — Qatāda, on "and what their breasts conceal is greater": "greater than what they have disclosed with their tongues"; 7694 — al-Rabīʿ: "greater than what they have disclosed with their tongues". **[Qurṭubī]** In the *Sunan* of Abū Dāwūd, from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ: "A man is upon the religion of his close friend, so let one of you look to whom he befriends"; and from Ibn Masʿūd: "Judge people by their brothers." **[Qurṭubī]** It is narrated from Abū Umāma, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, concerning "O you who believe, do not take as intimates any apart from yourselves; they spare nothing to ruin you": "They are the Khawārij." **[Qurṭubī]** It is related that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī employed a *dhimmī* as a scribe, and ʿUmar wrote to him rebuking him and recited this verse to him. And Abū Mūsā came to ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, with an account which he raised to ʿUmar and which pleased him; then a letter came to ʿUmar and he said to Abū Mūsā: where is your scribe, to read this letter to the people? He said: he does not enter the mosque. He said: why — is he in a state of major impurity? He said: he is a Christian. So he rebuked him and said: do not bring them near when God has put them far; do not honour them when God has humiliated them; do not trust them when God has declared them treacherous. **[Qurṭubī]** And ʿUmar said: do not employ the People of the Book, for they consider bribery lawful *(in one manuscript: usury)*; and seek help in your affairs and over your subjects from those who fear God, exalted is He. **[Qurṭubī]** And it was said to ʿUmar: there is here a man from the Christians of al-Ḥīrah — no one writes better than he and no one is more skilled with the pen; shall he not write for you? He said: "Then I would be taking an intimate from other than the believers."
