So it is not permissible to employ the People of the Book as scribes, nor any of their other dispositions in buying and selling, nor to delegate to them. **[Qurṭubī]** Qurṭubī adds: "I say — things have so changed in these times that the People of the Book have been taken as scribes and keepers of secrets, and they have thereby gained mastery over the ignorant, foolish governors and commanders." **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Bukhārī related from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, from the Prophet ﷺ: "God has not sent any prophet, nor appointed any successor, but that he had two intimacies: one commanding him to what is right and urging him to it, and one commanding him to evil and urging him to it — and the one protected is he whom God protects." **[Qurṭubī]** Anas b. Mālik said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not seek light by the fire of the idolaters, and do not engrave on your signets anything foreign." Al-Ḥasan b. Abī al-Ḥasan explained it: he meant, peace be upon him, "do not consult the idolaters in anything of your affairs, and do not engrave 'Muḥammad' on your signets". And al-Ḥasan said: and the confirmation of that is in the Book of God, exalted and majestic — "O you who believe, do not take as intimates any apart from yourselves", the verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** al-Bukhārī and al-Nasāʾī recorded that Abū Saʿīd said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Allah has not sent any Prophet nor was there any *khalīfah* but they have two types of allies, one that commands him with righteousness and advises it, and another that commands him with evil and advises him with it. Only those whom Allah gives immunity are immune." **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported that Ibn Abī al-Dahqānah said: "ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb was told, 'There is a young man here from the people of al-Ḥīrah who is a proficient scribe; why do you not appoint him as a scribe?' ʿUmar said, 'I would then be taking advisors from among the disbelievers.'" **[Ibn Kathīr]** This verse and the story about ʿUmar testify to the fact that Muslims are not allowed to use *Ahl al-Dhimmah* to be scribes in matters that affect the affairs of Muslims and expose their secrets, for they might convey these secrets to combatant disbelievers. **[Maʿārif]** Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrates that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was asked to appoint a young non-Muslim as the chief manager and scribe in his office since he was very good at that, and he replied: "If I were to take him in, in that case I will be taking an insider from among non-Muslims, which is against the Qurʾānic authority." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** Imām al-Qurṭubī says, with marked pensive longing, that contravention of this teaching of the Qurʾān has produced evil results for Muslims: "Things have so changed these days that Jews and Christians were trusted with secrets and considered trustworthy, through which they were able to prevail over the ignorant rich, the rulers and the chiefs." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** About non-Muslims resident in Islamic states or tied to Muslims through a treaty: the Holy Prophet ﷺ has said, "Whoever harms a *dhimmī*, I shall be his opponent on the Day of Judgment, and I always defeat the one whom I oppose" (reported by Ibn Masʿūd); "My Lord has prohibited me to wrong the one protected by a treaty, or anyone other than him" (narrated by ʿAlī); and "Beware — whoever wrongs a non-Muslim protected by treaty, or usurps his right, or obligates him to do what is beyond his power, or takes from him something without his genuine consent, then I shall be the advocate for him on the Day of Judgment." *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** And the sentence "they want you to be in trouble" is a perfect mirror of the mentality of disbelievers; the in-depth teaching here is that no non-Muslim can ever be the real friend and well-wisher of Muslims. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** It is not permissible to employ the People of the Book as scribes, nor to delegate to them in buying and selling or in any other disposition, when that exposes the affairs of the Muslims and their secrets. **[Qurṭubī]** In this verse is evidence that the testimony of an enemy against his enemy is not permissible — the view of the people of Madīnah and the people of the Ḥijāz, while permission is narrated from Abū Ḥanīfa; and Ibn Shaʿbān reports agreement that enmity removes *ʿadāla*. **[Qurṭubī]** The mention of gaping mouths in the ḥadīth is not to be taken as implying that backbiting in a whisper is permitted: that is forbidden by agreement, on the basis of 49:12 and the ḥadīth of blood, property and honour. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Muslims are not allowed to use *Ahl al-Dhimmah* as scribes in matters affecting Muslim affairs. **[Maʿārif]** The prohibition is against taking them as confidants and advisers where that would spill the sensitive secrets of the community; it does not touch the obligation to treat non-Muslims with compassion, beneficence and protection. **[Study Quran]** Some commentators read the prohibition as applying to specific matters such as writing contracts or sending significant messages.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse turns on knowledge: the believers are told what these people harbour, and warned on that basis. **[Saʿdī]** The grounds for disowning them are stated one by one — their eagerness to harm, the hatred on their tongues, and the greater hatred concealed. **[Maʿārif]** The rule protects the organised body of the Muslims and its hallmarks; it does not license harshness towards non-Muslims living under Muslim rule or bound by treaty. **[Study Quran]** Some read the verse as a statement about human nature generally, on the basis of the ḥadīth of the two intimacies. **[Qurṭubī]** The application is not limited to one group: Abū Umāma is reported to have applied it to the Khawārij, and the verse names the disbelievers, the Jews and the people of caprice.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 3:100 for the verse to which this is joined; 49:12 for backbiting; 3:119, which follows. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:100 for the setting; 3:119, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:119–120, which follow; the story of Uḥud, to which the passage now turns. **[Study Quran]** 3:120 for "they wish for you to suffer"; 2:14 and 2:76 and 5:41 for the parallel of saying "we believe" and then the opposite. **[Maʿārif]** 3:119, which follows; 3:125, 12:90 and 3:200 for *ṣabr* and *taqwā*. **[Saʿdī]** 3:119, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:119, which follows.

**Reflection.** The word *biṭānah* is the whole verse in miniature — the lining of a garment, the thing nearest the skin, and therefore the person who knows what nobody else knows **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Maʿārif]**, **[Study Quran]**. The occasion of revelation is strikingly mundane: men of Aws and Khazraj had kept up their old pre-Islamic ties with Jewish neighbours, and nothing about that seemed wrong to them until this came down **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Maʿārif]**. The commentators divide over who is meant — Mujāhid, Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ and Ibn Zayd say the hypocrites, while the sīra report says the Jews of Madīnah — and Ṭabarī records both without forcing them **[Ṭabarī]**. What follows is where the passage gets difficult for a modern reader, and it is worth being precise about what each source actually says. Qurṭubī derives a ruling about scribes and secretaries, and his evidence is ʿUmar: ʿUmar refusing the skilled Christian secretary from al-Ḥīrah, ʿUmar rebuking Abū Mūsā for employing one, and — in a report he records without grading — ʿUmar's words to Abū Mūsā about a man who would not enter the mosque **[Qurṭubī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Qurṭubī then adds his own complaint about the practice of his own day **[Qurṭubī]**. Maʿārif quotes the same complaint and, importantly, sets it beside the ḥadīths protecting *dhimmīs* — "whoever harms a dhimmī, I am his opponent on the Day of Judgement" — so that the two are read together rather than one against the other **[Maʿārif]**. The Study Quran notices that Qurṭubī's complaint is a reflection of the society of his day, and sets beside it the ḥadīth of the two intimacies, which reads the verse as a statement about human nature rather than about a religious out-group **[Study Quran]**. And Ṭabarī, characteristically, does two things the others do not: he raises the grammatical difficulty of "they wish what you suffer", and he *rejects* Qatāda's reading that the hatred came "from the mouths of the hypocrites to their brothers among the disbelievers" — on the ground that the verse is forbidding intimacy with people whose enmity is already known, so reporting that they disclosed it to each other would be pointless **[Ṭabarī]**. That is a small but real piece of reasoning, and it is why Ṭabarī is worth reading even where his conclusions are not adopted.

## 3:119 — هَٰٓأَنتُمْ أُو۟لَآءِ تُحِبُّونَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِبُّونَكُمْ وَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْكِتَٰبِ كُلِّهِۦ وَإِذَا لَقُوكُمْ قَالُوٓا۟ ءَامَنَّا وَإِذَا خَلَوْا۟ عَضُّوا۟ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْأَنَامِلَ مِنَ ٱلْغَيْظِ ۚ قُلْ مُوتُوا۟ بِغَيْظِكُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ

*"Lo, you are the ones who love them, and they do not love you, though you believe in the Book entire. And when they meet you they say, 'We believe'; but when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage. Say: 'Die in your rage! Truly God knows what is in the breasts.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His remembrance, means by this: these whom God has forbidden the believers to take as intimates in place of themselves, and whom He has described by their attribute — when they meet the believers among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, they give them with their tongues, out of caution and fear for themselves from them, "we have believed and affirmed what Muḥammad ﷺ has brought"; and when they are alone, in a place where the believers do not see them, they bite — at what they see of the harmony of the believers, the unity of their word and the soundness of their relations with one another — their fingertips, in rage at the resentment they harbour against them, and in grief at the lack of a backing to which they could lean in order to wage open enmity against them and fight them outright. **[Ṭabarī]** On "Say: die in your rage": this utterance comes out in the form of a command, but it is a supplication which God, exalted is His remembrance, made His prophet Muḥammad ﷺ make against them — that God destroy them from chagrin at the rage they feel towards the believers, before they see in them what they wish for them of hardship in their religion and misguidance after their guidance. So He said to His prophet: say, O Muḥammad, perish in your rage. **[Ṭabarī]** "Truly God knows what is in the breasts" — God, exalted is His remembrance, means: God has knowledge of what is in the breasts of those who, when they meet the believers, say "we believe", and of the rancour and grief they harbour against them and the enmity and hatred they hold towards them; and of what is in the breasts of all His creation — preserving for all of them what each harbours of good and evil, until He recompenses them all for what they have sent ahead of good and evil, and for what they have believed of faith or disbelief, and what they have harboured towards His messenger and the believers, of sincere counsel, or of rancour and grudge. **[Ṭabarī]** And Ṭabarī notes the wording: He said "lo, you are those" (*hā antum ulāʾi*) and did not say "these are you" (*hāʾulāʾi antum*), separating *hā* from *ulāʾi*. **[Jalālayn]** "Lo", *hā* is for calling attention to something, "there you are", O believers, "you love them", on account of their kinship and their pretence of friendship towards you, "but they love you not", since they oppose you in religion; "you believe in the Book", all of it — that is to say, in the Books, all of them — "but they do not believe in your Book; and when they meet you they say 'We believe', but when they are alone they bite at you their fingertips in rage", in extreme fury at what they see of your mutual affection — the biting of the fingertips is used figuratively to express the severity of rage even if there be no biting involved. "Say: 'Perish in your rage'", that is, be this way until the end of your lives, for you shall not see what will please you; "God knows what is in the breasts", what is in the hearts, including that which these conceal. **[Qurṭubī]** "Lo, you are the ones who love them and they do not love you" — meaning the hypocrites, the proof of it being His saying "and when they meet you they say 'we believe'"; said by Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil. *(Qurṭubī's block on 3:119 covers 3:119 only)* **[Qurṭubī]** And love here has the sense of sincere friendliness — that is, you, O Muslims, are sincerely friendly to them and they are not sincerely friendly to you, because of their hypocrisy. And it is said: the meaning is, you want Islam for them while they want disbelief for you. And it is said: what is meant is the Jews — said by the majority. **[Qurṭubī]** "The Book" is a generic noun; Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the Books. And the Jews believe in part of it, as God, exalted is He, said: "And when it is said to them, believe in what God has sent down, they say: we believe in what was sent down to us, and they disbelieve in what is beyond it" (2:91). **[Qurṭubī]** "And when they meet you they say 'we believe'" — in Muḥammad ﷺ, and that he is the Messenger of God ﷺ. "And when they are alone" among themselves, "they bite at you the fingertips" — meaning the tips of the fingers — "in rage" and spite against you, and some of them say to others: "Do you not see these people — they have appeared and become numerous?" **[Qurṭubī]** And biting is an expression of intense rage together with the inability to carry it out; and from it is the saying of Abū Ṭālib: "They bite in rage behind us with the fingertips." And another said: "When they see me — may God prolong their rage — they bite, from rage, the tips of the thumbs." **[Qurṭubī]** One says *ʿaḍḍa yaʿaḍḍu ʿaḍḍan wa-ʿaḍīḍan*. And *al-ʿuḍḍ*, with *ḍamma* of the ʿayn, is the fodder of the beasts of the people of the cities, like oil-cake and crushed date-stones — one says *aʿaḍḍa al-qawm* when their camels ate the *ʿuḍḍ*; and a camel is *ʿuḍāḍiyy*, that is, fat, as if attributed to it. And *al-ʿiḍḍ*, with *kasra*, is the cunning man and the eloquent schemer. **[Qurṭubī]** And the biting of the fingertips is the act of the enraged one who has missed what he has no power over, or upon whom has descended what he has no power to change; and this biting is with the teeth, like biting the hand over something missed that was near to being missed, and like the striking of the tooth of the regretful one, and so on — like counting pebbles and drawing lines upon the ground for the anxious. And this biting is written with the dropped *ḍād*, whereas "time bit him" is with the raised *ẓāʾ*, as the poet — al-Farazdaq — said: "And the biting of time, O son of Marwān, has left of the wealth nothing but what is swept away or scraped." **[Qurṭubī]** And the singular of *anāmil* is *unmula*, with *ḍamma* of the *mīm* — and it is said with *fatḥa*, the *ḍamma* being the more famous. **[Qurṭubī]** And Abū al-Jawzāʾ, when he recited this verse, used to say: "They are the Ibāḍiyya." And Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this description may apply to many of the people of innovation until the Day of Resurrection. *(Qurṭubī's editor notes that the Ibāḍiyya are innocent of that charge, and that the exegesis of God's word is to be kept free of such statements.)* **[Qurṭubī]** On "Say: die in your rage" — if it is said: how is it that they did not die, when God, exalted is He, says to a thing "be" and it is? The answer is twofold. First — al-Ṭabarī and many of the commentators said: it is a supplication against them, that is, say, O Muḥammad, may God perpetuate your rage until you die. On this view it is fitting to supplicate against them with this, face to face and otherwise, unlike cursing. Second: the meaning is, inform them that they will not attain what they hope for, for death stands between them and it. On this meaning the sense of supplication lapses and the sense of rebuke and provocation remains. This meaning runs with the saying of Musāfir b. Abī ʿAmr: "And he wishes, in our root... and we gouge the eye of the one who envied." And to this meaning looks the saying of God, exalted is He: "Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope to the heaven, then let him cut" (22:15). **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Lo! You are the ones who love them but they love you not" — meaning, O believers, you like the hypocrites because you think they are believers, for they pretend to be so, but they do not like you publicly or secretly. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:118–120)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** "And you believe in all the Scriptures" — meaning, you have no doubt in any part of Allah's Book, while the hypocrites have deep doubts, confusion and reservations about it. Muḥammad bin Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said that it means: you believe in your Book, their Book and the previous Books, while the hypocrites disbelieve in your Book — and this is why they deserve that you dislike them instead of them disliking you. Ibn Jarīr collected this statement. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "The *Anāmil*" means the tips of the fingers, as Qatādah stated. This is the behaviour of the hypocrites, who pretend to be believers and kind when they are with the believers, all the while concealing the opposite in their hearts in every respect. This is the exact situation that Allah describes — and rage is extreme anger and fury. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "Say: Perish in your rage" — for no matter how much you envy the believers and feel rage towards them, know that Allah shall perfect His favour on His believing servants, complete His religion, raise high His Word and give dominance to His religion. Therefore, O hypocrites, die in rage. **[Ibn Kathīr]** And "Allah knows what is in the breasts" — for He has perfect knowledge of what you conceal in your hearts and chests, and of the rage, envy and hatred you have against the believers. He will punish you for all this in this life, and they will have the good that you dislike for them; and in the Hereafter you will suffer severe torment in the Fire, where you will remain for eternity. **[Ṭabarī]** 7695 — Ibn ʿAbbās, through Ibn Isḥāq: "'you believe in the Book entire' — that is, in your Book, and their Book, and the Books that came before that, while they disbelieve in your Book; so you have more right to hatred of them than they have to hatred of you." **[Saʿdī]** And also — what calls you to love them and take them as allies and intimates, when you know from them the great deviation in religion and in return for your good treatment? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān; Saʿdī's block covers 3:118–119)* **[Saʿdī]** For you are upright upon the religions of the messengers, believing in every messenger God sent and every book God sent down, while they disbelieve in the most magnificent of books and the noblest of messengers; and you expend for them of compassion and love that with which they do not repay you the least of the little. So how do you love them when they do not love you, and they flatter you and dissemble to you? *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** Thus "when they meet you they say 'we believe'; but when they are alone" with their own kind, "they bite their fingertips at you" from the intensity of rage and hatred for you and for your religion. God, exalted is He, said: "Say: die in your rage" — that is, you will see of the might of Islam and the abasement of disbelief what grieves you, and you will die in your rage, and you will not attain relief for that by what you intend. "God knows what is in the breasts" — so He clarified to His believing servants what the breasts of the enemies of the religion conceal, of the disbelievers and the hypocrites. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** After that, in this verse, Muslims have been told that it is certainly strange that you go about loving them as friends, yet they are no friends of yours; indeed, they are your worst enemies. Still more unusual is the situation because you believe in all Scriptures without any reservations as to the people they address, the time when they were sent down and the prophet they were revealed to. Contrary to this, they do not accept your Book and your Prophet ﷺ; their belief in their own Books is not correct either. Given this state of affairs it would have been expected that they should have been affectionate towards you, and that you should have been the ones to give them a cold shoulder. But what is happening here is just the reverse of what it should have been. **[Study Quran]** Depending on whether these enemies are hypocrites or People of the Book, this love can refer to various matters. "You are the ones who love them, while they love you not" can mean that, although you love them in Islam as religious brothers and sisters, they in truth do not love you; or it can mean that you wish for them to become Muslim — an act of love — while they wish for you to remain or become disbelievers; or it can mean that you do not wish for them to fall into distress, while they wish that you be afflicted by trouble (R). **[Study Quran]** "Though you believe in the Book entire" refers to Muslims' affirmation not only of the Quran, but also of what was revealed before it (IK, Ṭ). Making the claim that "we believe", but saying something different when one is alone with one's true allies, is also described in 2:14, 76; 5:41. "Die in your rage!" is interpreted to be a call to increase the cause of their rage, namely the success and flourishing of Islam, rather than a direct call for death (R, Z).

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** *Al-ʿanāmil* is the plural of *unmula*, the tip of the finger, with *ḍamma* of the *mīm* as the more famous of two readings. **[Qurṭubī]** The biting is distinguished by its letter from *ʿaẓẓa al-zamān*, "time bit him", which is written with *ẓāʾ*; and it is grouped with other physical expressions of helpless rage — biting the hand, striking the tooth, counting pebbles, drawing lines on the ground. **[Ṭabarī]** The wording is "lo, you are those" (*hā antum ulāʾi*) rather than "these are you", and Ṭabarī remarks on the separation of *hā* from *ulāʾi*. **[Jalālayn]** *Hā* is for calling attention; the biting of the fingertips is figurative, and may involve no actual biting. **[Qurṭubī]** "The Book" is a generic noun, and Ibn ʿAbbās took it as "the Books". **[Qurṭubī]** On the two answers to the objection that the imprecation was not fulfilled: supplication, or information that they will not attain their hope.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7699 — Qatāda, on "and when they meet you they say 'we believe', and when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage": "When they meet the believers they say 'we believe', though there is nothing in them but fear for their blood and their property, so they ingratiate themselves with that; and when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage — from the rage and hatred they find in their hearts for what you are upon. If they found any power, they would be upon the believers; so they are as God, exalted is He, has described them." *(the phrase "rīḥ" in the report means power and upper hand)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7700 — al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, the same, except that he said "from rage at their hatred of what you are upon" and did not say "if they found any power" and what follows it. **[Ṭabarī]** 7701 — Yaḥyā b. ʿAmr b. Mālik al-Nukarī, from his father: "Abū al-Jawzāʾ, when he recited this verse — 'and when they meet you they say "we believe", and when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage' — used to say: they are the Ibāḍiyya." *(Ṭabarī's editor notes in the chain: Yaḥyā b. ʿAmr b. Mālik al-Nukarī is munkar al-ḥadīth; his father ʿAmr b. Mālik is trustworthy but was criticised by al-Bukhārī and declared weak)* *(weak)* **[Ṭabarī]** 7702 — Qatāda: "the fingertips — the tips of the fingers"; 7702m — al-Rabīʿ, the same; 7703 — al-Suddī: "the fingers". **[Ṭabarī]** 7704 — ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, through Wakīʿ — Isrāʾīl — Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, on "they bite their fingertips at you in rage": "they bit upon their fingers". **[Qurṭubī]** Abū al-ʿĀliya and Muqātil said that those meant are the hypocrites, the proof being "when they meet you they say 'we believe'"; and the majority said that the Jews are meant. **[Qurṭubī]** Abū al-Jawzāʾ used to identify them with the Ibāḍiyya, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya generalised the description to many of the people of innovation until the Day of Resurrection. *(Qurṭubī's editor distances the Ibāḍiyya from the charge)* **[Qurṭubī]** The lines of Abū Ṭālib and of another poet on biting the fingertips and the thumbs in rage, and the line of al-Farazdaq on the biting of time. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Ibn ʿAbbās, through Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, on "you believe in the Book entire": "you believe in your Book, their Book and the previous Books, while the hypocrites disbelieve in your Book — and this is why they deserve that you dislike them instead of them disliking you." Ibn Jarīr collected this statement.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The verse exposes the gap between what is said on the tongue and what is held in the breast, and closes by grounding the whole in God's knowledge of what breasts contain. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Whatever rage the hypocrites feel, God will perfect His favour on His believing servants, complete His religion and raise high His Word — and it is that, not their death, which the imprecation is about. **[Qurṭubī]** The imprecation "die in your rage" is either a supplication or, more probably on the second reading, information that they will not attain what they hope for; and the second reading is supported by 22:15. **[Saʿdī]** The asymmetry is the point: you extend compassion they do not repay in the least. **[Maʿārif]** What is strange is that the situation is the reverse of what it ought to be. **[Study Quran]** "Die in your rage" is best read as a call to increase the cause of their rage — the success of Islam — rather than a direct call for death.

**Cross-references.** **[Qurṭubī]** 2:91 for "they believe in what was sent down to us and disbelieve in what is beyond it"; 22:15 for the parallel to "die in your rage"; 3:120, which follows. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:118 for the prohibition of intimates; 3:120, which follows. **[Study Quran]** 2:14, 2:76 and 5:41 for saying "we believe" and then its opposite; 3:118 for the identification of the enemies. **[Ṭabarī]** 3:118 for those forbidden as intimates; 3:120, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:118 for the setting; 3:120, which follows. **[Saʿdī]** 3:118 for the warning; 3:120, which follows. **[Maʿārif]** 3:118 for the background; 3:120, which follows.

**Reflection.** "Lo, you are the ones who love them" — and the commentators each supply the sense in which the love is misplaced: you take them as friends, or you want Islam for them, or you do not wish distress upon them, while in each case the reverse is true of them **[Study Quran]**. Qurṭubī gives two identifications — the hypocrites, on the evidence of "when they meet you they say 'we believe'", and the Jews, which he says is the view of the majority — and he adds the nice detail that "the Book" is a generic noun, so that the claim is that *you* believe in all of it while *they* believe only in part, as 2:91 says of them **[Qurṭubī]**. The centre of the verse is the gesture, and the commentators treat it as a piece of physiology before it is a piece of rhetoric: biting the fingertips is what the enraged do when they have missed what they cannot attain or cannot change, and Qurṭubī sets it beside biting the hand, striking the tooth, counting pebbles and drawing lines in the dust **[Qurṭubī]**. Abū Ṭālib's line and al-Farazdaq's are adduced for it, and Qurṭubī is careful about the letter — *ʿaḍḍa* with *ḍād*, *ʿaẓẓa al-zamān* with *ẓāʾ* **[Qurṭubī]**. Then there is the difficulty: the Prophet was told to say "die in your rage", and they did not die **[Qurṭubī]**. Qurṭubī's two answers are both worth having — that it is a supplication for the perpetuation of their rage until death, or that it is not a supplication at all but information that they will not attain what they hope for, death standing between them and it, in which case the sense is rebuke **[Qurṭubī]**. The Study Quran takes the same line: a call to increase the cause of their rage, which is the success of Islam **[Study Quran]**. And Qatāda's report supplies the thing that makes the whole verse cohere — there is nothing in them, when they say "we believe", but fear for their blood and their property; if they found any power they would be upon the believers **[Ṭabarī]**. It is worth recording, too, that the report identifying these people with the Ibāḍiyya is flagged by Ṭabarī's own editor as resting on a *munkar* transmitter, and that Qurṭubī's editor adds a note distancing them from the charge **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]**.

## 3:120 — إِن تَمْسَسْكُمْ حَسَنَةٌۭ تَسُؤْهُمْ وَإِن تُصِبْكُمْ سَيِّئَةٌۭ يَفْرَحُوا۟ بِهَا ۖ وَإِن تَصْبِرُوا۟ وَتَتَّقُوا۟ لَا يَضُرُّكُمْ كَيْدُهُمْ شَيْـًٔا ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا يَعْمَلُونَ مُحِيطٌۭ

*"If good fortune befalls you it vexes them, and if evil befalls you they rejoice in it. But if you are patient and fear God, their guile will not harm you at all; truly God encompasses what they do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** God, exalted is His remembrance, means by His saying "if a good touches you it grieves them": if you attain, O believers, joy at your appearing over your enemy, and at people entering your religion in succession, and at their affirming your prophet and helping you against your enemies, it grieves them; "and if an evil befalls you they rejoice in it" — if distress befalls you through the failure of an expedition of yours, or through an enemy of yours inflicting upon you, or through disagreement arising among your community, they rejoice at it. **[Ṭabarī]** "And if you are patient and fear God, their guile will not harm you at all" — and if you are patient, O believers, in obeying God and following His command in what He has commanded you, and in avoiding what He has forbidden you — from taking intimates for yourselves from these Jews whose attribute God has described, in place of the believers, and the rest of what He has forbidden you — "and fear your Lord", so that you fear to put yourselves forward before Him in what He has made binding upon you and obligatory for you of His right and the right of His messenger — "their guile will not harm you at all", that is, the guile of those whose attribute He has described. **[Ṭabarī]** And by "their guile" He means the harms they seek for the Muslims, and their scheming against them to turn them away from the guidance and the path of the truth. **[Ṭabarī]** "Truly God encompasses what they do" — He says, exalted is His remembrance: God encompasses all that these disbelievers do in His servants and His lands, of corruption and of barring from His path and of enmity to the people of His religion, and other disobedience of God besides; He preserves it all, nothing of it escapes Him, until He pays them in full their recompense for all of it and makes them taste His punishment for it. **[Jalālayn]** "If good fortune", a favour such as victory or booty, "befalls you, it is evil for them", it grieves them; "but if evil", such as defeat or drought, "befalls you, they rejoice thereat" — the conditional statement here is semantically connected to the previous conditional, and what comes in between is a parenthetical statement, the meaning being that their enmity towards you is endless, so why do you befriend them? Avoid them! "Yet if you endure" their harm "and fear God", by not befriending them and so on, "their guile will not hurt you" — read either *lā yadirkum* or *lā yadurrukum* — "at all; God encompasses what they do" — *yaʿmalūn*, or it may be read *taʿmalūn*, "what you do" — He has knowledge of it and will requite them for it. **[Qurṭubī]** "If good fortune befalls you it vexes them" — al-Sulamī read it with *yāʾ*, and the rest with *tāʾ*. And the wording is general with respect to everything that is good and evil; and what the commentators have mentioned — of fertility and drought, of the unity of the believers and the entry of division among them, and other such sayings — are examples, not a genuine disagreement. *(Qurṭubī's block on 3:120 covers the verse in full)* **[Qurṭubī]** And the meaning of the verse is that whoever has this attribute, of intense enmity and rancour and rejoicing at the descent of hardships upon the believers, is not fit to be taken as an intimate — least of all in this grave matter of *jihād*, which is the mainstay of this world and the next. And the poet said well in his saying: "All enmity may be hoped to recover, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy." **[Qurṭubī]** "And if you are patient" — over their hurt, and over obedience and allegiance to the believers — "and fear God, their guile will not harm you at all." One says *ḍārra yaḍūruhu wa-yaḍīruhu ḍayran wa-ḍawran*; so God made the negation of their harm conditional upon patience and the fear of God, and that was a consolation to the believers and a strengthening of their souls. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "If a good befalls you, it grieves them, but if some evil overtakes you, they rejoice at it" — this only emphasizes the severity of the enmity that the hypocrites feel against the believers. *(Ibn Kathīr's block covers 3:118–120)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** If the believers enjoy fertile years, victories, support, and their numbers and following increase, the hypocrites become displeased. When the Muslims suffer a drought or their enemies gain the upper hand against them, by Allah's decree — just as occurred during the battle of Uḥud — the hypocrites become pleased. **[Ibn Kathīr]** "But if you remain patient and have *taqwā*, not the least harm will their cunning do to you" — Allah directs the believers to safety from the wickedness of evil people and the plots of the sinners, by recommending them to revert to patience and by having fear of Allah and trusting Him. Allah encompasses the enemies of the believers, all the while the believers have no power or strength except from Him. Whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will, does not occur. Nothing happens in His Kingdom except with His decision and according to His decrees. Verily, whoever relies on Allah, Allah shall suffice for him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** Allah then mentions the story of Uḥud — the defeat that He tested the believers with, His distinguishing the believers from the hypocrites, and their patience. **[Saʿdī]** "If a good touches you" — might, victory, well-being and good — "it grieves them; and if an evil befalls you", from the turn of the enemy or the occurrence of some worldly misfortunes, "they rejoice at it"; and this is the description of the enemy of intense enmity. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Saʿdī]** When God, exalted is He, clarified the intensity of their enmity and expounded the evil attributes they have, He commanded His believing servants to patience and to keeping to *taqwā* — and that if they uphold that, the guile of their enemies will not harm them at all. For God encompasses them and their works and the plots they plot against you, and He has promised you, upon your keeping to *taqwā*, that they will not harm you at all — so do not doubt that it will come about. *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)* **[Maʿārif]** The mentality of disbelievers has been further clarified by "if something good happens to you, it annoys them, and if something evil befalls you, they are delighted with it". How can Muslims remain protected against the aftermath of the sinister moves of the hypocrites and the deadly hostility of opponents? For this, a simple and effective prescription was suggested: "And if you keep patience and fear Allah, their cunning shall not harm you at all. Surely, Allah is All-Encompassing of what they do." **[Maʿārif]** *Ṣabr* and *taqwā* are the panacea for Muslims. The Holy Qurʾān has prescribed them as an effective measure against all hardships, and this elemental teaching has been conveyed not only here but at many other places: in the section that follows immediately, "Why not? If you stay patient and fear Allah and they come upon you in this heat of theirs, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand of the angels having distinct marks" (3:125) — where the promise of divine help has been made conditional upon *ṣabr* and *taqwā*; in Sūrat Yūsuf, "Whoever fears Allah and keeps patience" (12:90) — where prosperity and success have been tied to them; and towards the end of this very sūrah, "O those who believe, be patient, be more patient than others, and guard your frontiers, and fear Allah so that you may be successful" (3:200). **[Maʿārif]** The two words, though looking like a short title, are nevertheless very comprehensive; they contain within themselves a successful rule for all aspects of individual and collective life, as well as public, governmental and military affairs. **[Study Quran]** This verse reflects the statement in 3:118 that "they wish for you to suffer". The same sentiment appears in a supplication of Moses in 7:150: "Let not the enemies rejoice in my misfortune." To be patient carries the sense of being steadfast and constant. That "their plot will not harm you at all" echoes the message of 3:111, where it is said that they cannot harm except through insults and taunts. Moreover, beyond simple self-interest, their joy at another's suffering shows just how severe their enmity is (IK).

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** The wording is general as to every good and evil, and the specific instances given by the commentators — fertility and drought, unity and division — are examples rather than disagreement. **[Qurṭubī]** *Ḍārra yaḍūruhu wa-yaḍīruhu*, "he harmed him", gives *ḍayr* and *ḍawr*. **[Jalālayn]** The conditional clause is joined semantically to the one before it, with the intervening material parenthetical. **[Jalālayn]** The final verb is read *yaʿmalūn*, "what they do", or *taʿmalūn*, "what you do". **[Ṭabarī]** "Their guile" is unpacked as the harms they seek and their scheming to turn the believers from the path. **[Study Quran]** "To be patient" carries the sense of being steadfast and constant.

**Readings.** **[Qurṭubī]** Al-Sulamī read "if good fortune befalls you" with *yāʾ*, and the rest with *tāʾ*. **[Qurṭubī]** On "it will not harm you": the two Ḥaramīs and Abū ʿAmr read *lā yaḍirkum*, from *ḍārra yuḍīru* — and from it is the phrase *lā ḍayra* — with the *yāʾ* elided for the meeting of two quiescents: when the *ḍamma* is dropped from the *rāʾ*, the *rāʾ* and the *yāʾ* are both quiescent, so the *yāʾ* is elided, being more entitled to elision since what precedes it indicates it. Al-Kisāʾī related that he heard *ḍārra yaḍūruhu*, and permitted *lā yaḍurkum*; and he claimed that in the reading of Ubayy b. Kaʿb it is *lā yaḍrirkum*. The Kūfans read *lā yaḍurrukum* with *ḍamma* and *shadda* of the *rāʾ*, from *ḍarra yaḍurru*. **[Qurṭubī]** It may be nominative with an implicit *fāʾ* — the meaning being "so it will not harm you" — and of that is the poet's saying, Ḥassān b. Thābit: "Whoever does good deeds, God thanks them" — and this is the view of al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ. Or it may be nominative on the intention of fronting, as Sībawayhi cited: "Indeed, if your brother is thrown down, you are thrown down" — meaning, your patience and your fear of God will not harm you. Or it may be jussive, with the *rāʾ* given *ḍamma* for the meeting of two quiescents in following the *ḍamma*; and likewise the reading of those who give the *rāʾ* *fatḥa*, on the basis that the verb is jussive and the *fatḥa* is given for the meeting of two quiescents because of the lightness of *fatḥa* — narrated by Abū Zayd from al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim, related by al-Mahdawī. And al-Naḥḥās related that al-Mufaḍḍal al-Ḍabbī reported from ʿĀṣim *lā yaḍurrikum* with *kasra* of the *rāʾ* for the meeting of two quiescents. **[Jalālayn]** Read either *lā yadirkum* or *lā yadurrukum*.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ṭabarī]** 7705 — Qatāda, on "if a good touches you it grieves them, and if an evil befalls you they rejoice in it": "When they see from the people of Islam harmony, unity and appearing over their enemy, that enrages them and grieves them; and when they see from the people of Islam division and disagreement, or a part of the Muslims is afflicted, that pleases them, and they are delighted by it and rejoice at it. So whenever a generation of them goes forth, God belies its tale, lays low its station, nullifies its argument and exposes its shame — and that is God's decree concerning those of them who have passed and those who remain until the Day of Resurrection." **[Ṭabarī]** 7706 — al-Rabīʿ b. Anas: "they are the hypocrites; when they see from the people of Islam unity and appearing over their enemy, that enrages them with a mighty rage and grieves them; and when they see from the people of Islam division and disagreement, or a part of the Muslims is afflicted, that pleases them and they are delighted by it." Then he cites "and if you are patient and fear God, their guile will not harm you at all; truly God encompasses what they do". **[Ṭabarī]** 7707 — Ibn Jurayj: "'if a good touches you it grieves them' — when they see from the believers unity and harmony, that grieves them; and when they see from them division and disagreement, they rejoice." **[Qurṭubī]** The line of poetry: "All enmity may be hoped to recover, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy." **[Qurṭubī]** The readings of Ubayy b. Kaʿb, ʿĀṣim and the Kūfans, as set out above. **[Ibn Kathīr]** The rejoicing of the hypocrites at the setback of Uḥud, as an instance of the verse. **[Maʿārif]** The ḥadīth of Abū Dharr: "I know a verse which, if people were to take to it, would suffice them" — and that is "And whoever fears Allah, for him He shall make a way out" (65:2). *(narrated by Aḥmad)* *(Bayān al-Qurʾān)*

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** The promise is conditional in a specific way: patience is defined as perseverance in obedience and in avoiding what God has forbidden — explicitly including taking intimates from those described — and *taqwā* as fearing to put oneself before God in His right and the right of His messenger. **[Ibn Kathīr]** God directs the believers to safety through patience, fear of God and trust; nothing happens in His Kingdom except by His decision and decree, and whoever relies on God, He suffices him. **[Saʿdī]** The promise is a promise: God has promised, on the condition of *taqwā*, that they will not harm you at all, so do not doubt it. **[Maʿārif]** *Ṣabr* and *taqwā* together constitute a comprehensive rule for individual, collective, public, governmental and military life. **[Study Quran]** Being patient carries the sense of steadfastness and constancy. **[Qurṭubī]** The verse closes the argument of 3:118: a person of this degree of enmity is not fit to be taken as an intimate.

**Cross-references.** **[Ṭabarī]** 3:118 for the intimates and the patience commanded; 3:111 for the limitation of the harm they can do; the story of Uḥud, which follows. **[Qurṭubī]** 3:118 for the argument to which this returns; 3:121 ff., the story of Uḥud. **[Ibn Kathīr]** 3:118 for "they wish you to suffer"; the story of Uḥud, to which the sūrah now turns. **[Study Quran]** 3:118 for "they wish for you to suffer"; 7:150 for Moses' supplication "let not the enemies rejoice in my misfortune"; 3:111 for the limitation of their harm. **[Maʿārif]** 3:125 for the five thousand angels, conditioned on *ṣabr* and *taqwā*; 12:90 for "whoever fears Allah and keeps patience"; 3:200 for the closing command of the sūrah; 65:2 for the verse that would suffice people. **[Saʿdī]** 3:118–119 for the enmity described; the story of Uḥud, which follows. **[Jalālayn]** 3:118–119 for the setting; the story of Uḥud, which follows.

**Reflection.** The verse names a feeling most people recognise instantly — the person who is pained by your good news and cheered by your bad — and then does something unexpected with it: it makes the observation the premise of a promise **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Ibn Kathīr]**. The promise is conditional, and Ṭabarī is precise about the conditions: patience means persevering in obedience and in avoiding what has been forbidden, explicitly including the taking of intimates from those just described, and *taqwā* means fearing to put oneself forward before God in what is due to Him and to His messenger **[Ṭabarī]**. Qatāda's report is the one that gives the verse its long view: whenever a generation of them goes forth, God belies its talk, lays low its station, nullifies its argument and exposes its shame — and that, he says, is God's settled decree for all of them until the Resurrection **[Ṭabarī]**. Ibn Kathīr supplies the instance everyone would have thought of first: Uḥud, where the enemies gained the upper hand and the hypocrites were pleased **[Ibn Kathīr]**. Maʿārif does the thing the other commentaries do not and traces the pair *ṣabr* and *taqwā* through the sūrah — 3:125, with its five thousand angels, 12:90, and the closing verse of the sūrah at 3:200 — and his claim that two short words contain a rule for public, governmental and military affairs is the reason this verse has been quoted so often in practice **[Maʿārif]**. And Qurṭubī's closing point ties the verse back to where the passage began: someone with this degree of enmity is simply not fit to be taken as an intimate, least of all in a matter as grave as *jihād* **[Qurṭubī]**. The line he quotes is worth keeping: all enmity may be hoped to recover, except the enmity of one who opposes you out of envy **[Qurṭubī]**.
